title: ‘I spent a week crying. I’ve never had an injury in my life!’ Why do so many fitness fans end up needing surgery? | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: From the 47-year-old runner who needs a double hip replacement to the 27-year-old CrossFitter with a ruptured ACL, those who push their bodies too hard often regret it. What are the lessons for the rest of us?
Author: Anna Moore
Headline: From the 47-year-old runner who needs a double hip replacement to the 27-year-old CrossFitter with a ruptured ACL, those who push their bodies too hard often regret it. What are the lessons for the rest of us?
Content: Composite: Guardian Design; Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design; Getty ImagesHealth & wellbeing‘I spent a week crying. I’ve never had an injury in my life!’ Why do so many fitness fans end up needing surgery?From the 47-year-old runner who needs a double hip replacement to the 27-year-old CrossFitter with a ruptured ACL, those who push their bodies too hard often regret it. What are the lessons for the rest of us?Anna MooreMon 3 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJonathan Price has always been active and exercise-focused. Growing up in south Wales, rugby was his first love. Through school, university and beyond, he also surfed, rowed, played squash and ran competitively – on track, in 10k races and cross-country. Career and family demands meant that much of this fell away in later years, but the running stuck. He found time for marathons, half marathons – “I’d run a half marathon every weekend just for fun,” he says – and, through the working week, regular 30- or 40-minute runs to manage stress and clear his head. “I travel a lot for work,” says Price, now 50, a company CEO. “With running, all you need is a pair of running shoes and you can do it anywhere.”By his mid-40s, though, Price’s body was beginning to object. He wasn’t recovering so well. “I could run just fine but I’d be in pain for two or three days afterwards,” he says. On top of this, every six months or so, his lower back seemed to seize up completely. A physiotherapist thought it was “tight hip flexors” and pointed Price towards “hip opening” exercises, designed to reduce stiffness and increase range of motion. Someone else prescribed him muscle relaxants, but the pain only deepened, and his range of movement continued to dip. Finally, in the summer of 2023, a chance encounter with a hip surgeon led to the diagnosis of osteoarthritis and, at the end of that year, Price, then 47, had a double hip replacement.Was Price unlucky, or did decades of exercise accelerate his joint damage? After so many years, so many miles, and so many cycles of use, had he simply, as his surgeon, Giles Stafford, puts it, “hit his number”?View image in fullscreenOrthopaedic surgeons recommend swimming or cycling to soften the impact on our joints.Photograph: microgen/Getty ImagesAs a consultant orthopaedic hip surgeon specialising in sports-related hip disorders, Stafford often sees patients who are experiencing joint problems earlier than most. “They are usually active people who have done a lot of sport and knackered their joints through that,” he says. Stafford likens our joints to bearings in a car. “There’s clearly a genetic aspect, but also a big mechanical aspect too,” he says. “We all have a certain number of cycles in us before the damage sets in, and someone who is going to the gym, running marathons, taking on high-impact, high-intensity, repetitive exercise programmes might hit their number younger and faster.”Osteoarthritis (OA) is the painful result of the breakdown of cartilage, the smooth, slippery tissue that cushions the ends of our bones so that we can move our joints freely without friction. OA is on the rise. Each year,more than a quarter of a million people in the UKhave joint replacement surgery, and by 2060demand is expectedto have risen by 40%. While there is evidence ofrising cases in younger people, by the age of 70 one in two UK adults will have OA. For some, that might just mean some stiffness while walking up the stairs. For others, it could mean needing help to wash and dress. In old age, OA will often determine whether someone can live independently and if their final years are spent navigating pain.When it comes to causes, though, the picture is confusing. The way we are made is key. Our genes help determine our build, our gait, how we load our joints and where the pressure falls when we move. Genetics are also believed to play a role in the quality of our cartilage and the inflammatory responses that can damage it and drive OA forward. Price now knows that he was born with a subtle shape abnormality that is not uncommon. The ball of his hip joint’s ball-and-socket wasn’t quite spherical, so it didn’t rotate smoothly without friction, which quietly, over time, accelerated damage with each cycle of use. Beyond genetics, though, is asking too much of our bodies, or asking too little raising our OA risk? Should we worry about over-exercise, not enough exercise or the wrong kind of exercise? The answer, unfortunately, seems to be all three.View image in fullscreen‘A lot of people don’t understand how important recovery is.’Photograph: Nick David/Getty ImagesA sedentary lifestyle is a major driver. This is partly due to OA’s link with obesity, which increases the weight on our joints, and raises inflammation, but exercise matters beyond this. Cartilage relies on synovial fluid – joint fluid – for its nourishment, and we need to move around in order for that fluid to circulate. “Sitting for long periods of the day also seems to cause metabolic changes that are pro-inflammatory,” says Dr Benjamin Ellis, consultant rheumatologist at Imperial College Healthcare in London. Building strength and muscle also acts to absorb impact and stabilise our joints. “Our joints, our bones, our bodies strengthen under challenge and that is done by tiny micro-injuries,” says Ellis. “The body goes in to heal them and that healing builds bone and muscle.”On the other hand, if we overload the body’s capacity to heal, or sustain too great an injury, we’re back in the OA danger zone, though it may take decades for the effects to be felt. An anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury – a tear or sprain in the centre of the knee – is one example. Professional footballers, who are prone to ACL injuries, have two or three times the average risk of OA in later life.Research also points toa raised OA risk among competitive runners – while recreational running seems to be protective. (Unhelpfully, the definition of “recreational” and “competitive” varies between studies.) Many orthopaedic surgeons – Stafford included – recommend cycling, swimming or anelliptical trainerover running, or running on grass or a treadmill rather than tarmac to soften the impact on our joints.According to David Vaux, an osteopath,consultant for Arthritis Actionand author of Stronger, exercise in midlife should be viewed a bit like a dosage of medicine. “If you do too much or too little, you’re going to be in trouble,” he says. “The main thing I see in clinic are people who are injured, and people who are burnt out – and those two things are kryptonite in midlife.” Both can lead someone to stop exercising altogether, or to keep going too hard before they have recovered. Either can result in OA.For most midlifers, says Vaux, a healthy exercise programme is steady and consistent, with plenty of built-in recovery time. He says: “It can look quite boring, but boring is good.”View image in fullscreen‘I usually prescribe starting with an isometric-only strength programme – such as wall sits and planks.’Photograph: Ramon Ivan Moreno Prieto/Getty Images/iStockphotoSaket Tibrewal, a consultant orthopaedic surgeon at Cromwell hospital in London who specialises in the knee, makes a similar point. “As we get older, our capacity to heal takes longer,” he says. “I do see a lot of runners who have taken it up in the last few years, and are starting to get knee pain and knock-on effects. They might be going for a run, then doing it again the next day, or maybe just having one day off. A lot of people don’t understand how important recovery is.”Several orthopaedic surgeons have expressed reservations about high-intensity, high-impact exercise programmes. “Anything that involves a lot of deep-weighted squats, and repeatedly taking your body to end range under load, can damage your joints,” says Stafford.Gareth Jones, a specialist knee surgeon at Imperial College, has seen patients in theirmid-20s and early 30s who have already lost a lot of cartilage from under their kneecaps through following such programmes. One of Tibrewal’s patients is Naomi Pannell, 27, who recently tore her ACL competing in a CrossFit event.View image in fullscreen‘The runner’s mindset is it’ll be all right. It’ll repair itself’ ... Chris Dunn competing in an Ironman event in July.Photograph: Courtesy of Chris Dunn“I was in the semi-finals in Madrid, my biggest competition yet,” says Pannell. “It happened on day three, the last day, in 36C heat.” Pannell and her partner had completed the chest-to-bar pull-ups and the double-unders (like skipping except the rope passes under your feet twice in one jump) and next came four rounds of “sandbags” (lifting a heavy sandbag from the floor and resting it on the shoulder). “When I went to lift the sandbag for my second round, my knee popped out and popped in again,” says Pannell. “I didn’t fall to the floor. I went to lift it again and it did the same thing.” She completed some of the remaining circuit – including a handstand walk – and by the end her knee was badly swollen. “When I found out it was a full ACL rupture, I spent a week crying,” says Pannell. “I’ve never had an injury in my life.” Tibrewal, who will be operating on Pannell, blames fatigue. “These programmes are very good for cardiovascular fitness and strength, but they involve high repetition and high loading, and fatigue is a badge of honour,” he says. “After multiple rounds, if you’re pushed to the point where your muscles are really tired, then you can lose neuromuscular control of the joint. You lose proprioception – your body’s internal awareness of where it is in time and space – and that’s when something simple that you’ve done many times before can go wrong.”According to Vaux, a healthy midlife exercise regime that’s protective against OA involves “steps and reps”. “A walk, a jog, a bike ride a couple of times a week and you need strength training, too. I usually prescribe following anisometric-only strength programme– such as wall sits and planks, which you can do anywhere – for at least two months before you do anything more dynamic [in terms of strength training]. If someone is doing that, I’ll take that person’s chances on healthy joints in 20 years’ time over anyone doing anything extreme and get-fit-quick.”The most important thing is listening to your body. “Pain alone isn’t always a reliable guide because some discomfort can be a normal part of adaptation,” says Vaux, “but persistent joint pain, night pain or pain on certain movements, swelling and stiffness should not be ignored. It’s your body telling you there is an issue.” It’s also important to understand your level of fatigue. “Is your performance stable, improving or decreasing? Decreasing performance indicates you are not recovering properly. How are you sleeping? Is your heart rate significantly elevated first thing the day after exercise? The solution to any of these might be to get something checked out, or to modify your exercise and rest.”View image in fullscreen‘I’d be in pain for two or three days after running’ ... Jonathan Price (left) takes part in the world’s deepest marathon in Sweden.Photograph: Samuel McElwee Studios/BecomingX/World’s Deepest MarathonChris Dunn, 49, a dedicated runner, waited until he had grade-four bone-on-bone OA in his knee before he stopped running and had it looked at. “I can probably track it back to 2015, when a bad tackle in football twisted my ACL,” he says. Despite the injury, that same year he completed an Ironman triathlon and a marathon. In the years since, he had continued to compete in many more marathons, as well as regular triathlons. “My leg was probably weakened and I weakened it more, my alignment shifted to compensate, and that overloaded different parts of the knee joint,” he says. “Silly really – I left it too long – but once you’re in the runner’s mindset, you think: ‘It’ll be all right. It’ll repair itself.’ When you push yourself to the limits, it’s uncomfortable anyway! You tell yourself it’s just a twinge. By 2023, it had got to the point where I was only able to do 5 or 6km of running and afterwards it was so painful I could only hobble.”In May 2024, Dunn underwent five hours of surgery to straighten his leg and try to offload the damaged area. It was very successful. “I was home the next day with a knee brace,” he says. “I stayed on crutches until August. The following April, I did the London Marathon and in July I did an Ironman. At the moment, running feels comfortable. There’s a chance that years down the line I might need a knee replacement, but we’ll play it by ear. I want to enjoy it while I can.”Price also got back to running after his double hip replacement. Last year, he completed the world’s deepest marathon, which took place in a zinc mine in Sweden. “It took a while to get past that strange sensation where everything feels different, but once I started running, it got easier and easier,” he says. Pannell, meanwhile, is hoping to compete in the CrossFit Open in February.“There’s no universal threshold beyond which exercise becomes harmful,” says Vaux. “It’s shaped by so many factors – such as age, genetics, previous injuries – and it isn’t fixed: it can expand as tissues adapt. That’s one of the remarkable things about the human body. But we need to give it time to get there, and to listen to what it’s telling us on the way.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Does Andy Burnham really hate London? He wouldn’t be the only one | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Both left and right have it in for Britain’s capital. But is London a stabby wasteland, a den of faceless bureaucrats, or just a mess of overprivileged wokerati, asks Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Both left and right have it in for Britain’s capital. But is London a stabby wasteland, a den of faceless bureaucrats, or just a mess of overprivileged wokerati, asks Zoe Williams
Content: ‘Faceless’ and ‘out of touch’? London’s Regent Street during the queen’s platinum jubilee in 2022.Photograph: Chunyip Wong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Faceless’ and ‘out of touch’? London’s Regent Street during the queen’s platinum jubilee in 2022.Photograph: Chunyip Wong/Getty ImagesOpinionLondonDoes Andy Burnham really hate London? He wouldn’t be the only oneZoe WilliamsBoth left and right have it in for Britain’s capital. But is London a stabby wasteland, a den of faceless bureaucrats, or just a mess of overprivileged wokerati?Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 13.09 EDTShare‘I’ve seen no evidence of Andy being anti-London,” the capital’smayor, Sadiq Khan, told the Evening Standardlast week, which is quaint and adorable: evidence isso2009. This is all about feels. Some feel that the prime minister disfavours the capital because he frequently mentions that neoliberalism hasn’t delivered a fair deal for the north of England; tacitly, then, someone’s deal has been unfair in the other direction, and that would be the south, which must be London. Where else would Burnham mean – Hastings? The institution of No 10 North gestures audibly towards there being some problem with the OG Downing Street, and the use of the words “Whitehall” and “Westminster” as anything but geographical denominations – connoting “faceless” or “out of touch” or “rigid” or “having contempt for the ordinary person” – gives strong anti-London vibes, since Whitehall and Westminster are, indisputably, in London.double quotation markExpressing any attitude that might distinguish you from Enoch Powell places you in the ‘metropolitan liberal elite’You could group all that as leftwing shorthand. For those moments when you want to describe a shallow, mammon-worshipping society, lurching blindly from one shiny, meaningless prize to the next, empty of proper feeling for others or for nature, “London” pretty well covers it.That vibe – which only ever described a sliver of the capital, basically the bit of Notting Hill where Boris Johnson might once have lived and Canary Wharf – was repurposed by the (British) right wing a decade ago to become the “metropolitan elite”. In 2016, this version of the typical Londoner had all the same characteristics as before – they’re in a bubble, they’re rolling in gold, they neither understand nor care about the conditions of the common man – but with the appended trait of liberalism, or wokeratiness (if you prefer).By a process so transparently syllogistic and stupid that for a while it was hard to even discuss it without howling like a wolf, the expression of any attitude that might distinguish you from Enoch Powell placed you squarely in the “metropolitan liberal elite” and therefore rendered you dispensable, inauthentic. There were a ton of other markers of privilege – coffee shops, public transport infrastructure, tofu, the Guardian! – so you were checkmated everywhere you went. This wasn’t really about living in London, or even any big city: you could get your passport to the metropole from drinking matcha, believing in universal human rights or knowing how to board public transport, rather than dithering near the door like an idiot. But obviously all of this was so much morerifein the capital.When it comes to predicting the future, why are TV writers better than politicians? | Zoe WilliamsRead moreThis is quite distinct from what the global right wing hates about Londoners, which is, briefly, that we’re savages who won’t stop killing each other. As I’ve written before, the former Guardian stafferGary Youngecame back from the US in 2016, where he had been reporting on the Maga right, with a fascinating account of a dinner with some Republicans who had asked him how he could possibly feel safe living in London, now that the Muslims had elected “their” mayor and the rest of us weren’t even allowed guns.It seemed so extraordinary then, and now is an absolute commonplace, to hear the capital described as a “stabby wasteland” where grinding poverty interlaces with intractable race wars to create a brutal place, the global nidus of civilisational decay. There’s some overlap with the British right, insofar as London is where multiculturalism is supposed to have failed, and taken society down with it. But there are no liberal elitists in the global right’s concept of “Londonistan”; it would be way too rough and dangerous for our luxury-softened paws. No data or firsthand testimonials can dispel this myth of the capital. It works better if it isn’t true; it makes insisting on reality that little bit more exhausting.None of this answers, definitively, the question of whether the prime minister hates London, since there are signals in the other direction. His plan to give regional mayors a slice of their tax take would work better for Khan than almost anyone, what with London’s feverish mammon-love.I will meet some of these detractors halfway and accept that Londoners definitely lack something in the areas of gentleness and humility. To everyone else, I’d channel Millwall: no one likes us, we don’t care. Multiculturalism in action, in a single London heart.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘The obsession with endless growth can only end in tears’: your questions on extreme weather this summer answered  | Environment | The Guardian
description: From Europe’s deadly heat to floods in Asia, it’s been a terrifying summer. Environment writers Jonathan Watts and Ajit Niranjan answered Reddit users’ questions about their work – and their sources of hope
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: From Europe’s deadly heat to floods in Asia, it’s been a terrifying summer. Environment writers Jonathan Watts and Ajit Niranjan answered Reddit users’ questions about their work – and their sources of hope
Content: Guardian environment writers Jonathan Watts (left) and Ajit NiranjanIllustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenGuardian environment writers Jonathan Watts (left) and Ajit NiranjanIllustration: Guardian DesignConversationsEnvironment‘The obsession with endless growth can only end in tears’: your questions on extreme weather this summer answeredFrom Europe’s deadly heat to floods in Asia, it’s been a terrifying summer. Environment writers Jonathan Watts and Ajit Niranjan answered Reddit users’ questions about their work – and their sources of hopeJonathan WattsandAjit NiranjanMon 3 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExtreme weather supercharged by the climate crisis is fuelling an explosive wildfire season inEuropeand extreme rainfall across Asia this summer.Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather stoking wildfiresat least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France. EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year for the area of land burned.Meanwhile,unprecedented rains continue across Asia. As South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, in Japan and Vietnam torrential rain has led to landslides. Extreme rainfall across the world is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown.The Guardian’s Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan has been covering the extreme heat and wildfires across Europe this summer, while global environment writer Jonathan Watts reported on the floods in Asia.Ajit and Jonathan answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.View image in fullscreenHaze and smoke from the 2023 the Canadian wildfires shrouds the Manhattan skyline in June 2023.Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/ReutersDesenrasco asked: How scared should I be about wildfires?To consider it in the bluntest of terms, wildfires kill surprisingly few people: perhaps hundreds around the world each year, compared to thousands from floods and hundreds of thousands from heatwaves. That is, of course, of little comfort to the people across Spain and France returning to burned-out homes, or to the families of firefighters, locals and tourists who have died in the past few weeks. But what scares me far more is the smoke. Recent studies peg the global death toll from wildfire smoke at 1.5 million people per year. The wildfire season in Canada three years ago was so bad, one study found, that more than 80,000 people died from smoke inhalation – and 20,000 of them were in Europe, as winds carried the pollution over the Atlantic.Sg_plumberasked: How come pretty much everybody (at least on TV) always forgets to mention thatyes, the climate crisis is fuelling these extreme weather events?Jonathan Watts:I agree. This is not just exasperating, it is frightening. The climate and nature crises are the greatest threats humanity has faced, yet many media organisations downplay or ignore it. Social media is even worse, propagating misinformation and distracting people from the root cause of the problem (petrochemical companies, big agriculture and every rising emissions of greenhouse gases). The Guardian is able to devote much of its resources to covering these topics because it does not have an owner and because our readers make very clear that they want a big share of theircontributionsto go to this topic.Economy-Fee5830asked: You’ve written about oil majors profiting as the world heats. But European wildfire deaths and flood deaths are overwhelmingly determined by local building codes, evacuation planning and firefighting budgets. Does the Big Oil accountability framing crowd out the more boring domestic policy failures that actually determine the body count?Ajit:I broadly agree with your question but slightly disagree with the premise.Rapid analysis studiesin recent years have attributed 40-70% of the death toll from big European heatwaves to the increase in temperatures from carbon pollution.With wildfires and floods it’s much harder for scientists to say how much climate breakdown contributed to the death toll. I’ve coveredEuropean floodswhere they’ve shown the rainfall that triggered the floods to have been made stronger or more likely by up to 20% but, as one scientist put it to me after floods in central Europe last year, it’s a binary problem: the dam will either fail or not. In cases like the floods in Germany’s Ahrtal in 2021, or in Valencia, Spain, in 2024, we saw both jaw-dropping evacuation failures and climate-exacerbated rain.Cutting fossil fuel pollution is indeed a fundamental solution, and it must be accompanied by a never-ending list of other adaptation measures. I would argue our coverage is pretty good at including both bits. Every article I’ve written on wildfires this summer has included rising temperatures and land abandonment. Our flood coverage had the failures of authorities at the forefront.View image in fullscreenFloods in Valencia in 2024 killed 229 people following evacuation failures and climate-exacerbated rain.Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The GuardianOwl1917 asked: With climate anxiety on the rise, particularly amongst younger generations, what advice would you give to those who see the future as hopeless?Ajit:More than anything else, I would challenge anyone who feels hopeless to be specific about what’s troubling them. This is obviously easier said than done, but if you take a couple of hours to write down what it is that scares you about climate breakdown, what makes you angry, and what leaves you feeling hopeless, the fears become (hopefully) easier to confront.In my case, reporting on the climate has made me way less worried about some problems and way more worried about others. In terms of hope, I am, perhaps unpopularly, a firm believer in the idea that we have far more agency than anyone around me seems to realise (with the exception of a handful of scientists). Too many people my age claim a powerlessness that is not backed up by data. Sure, your ability to replace a coal plant with a wind turbine may be limited (it’s still not nothing, if you live in a democracy) but you have power over what you eat, how you get around, how much you buy. Consider diets: our collective choice to eat meat and dairy is responsible for 12-20% of planet-heating emissions, and doctors recommend people in rich countries eat far less of it for their own health, let alone the climate. Does this sound like our actions are pointless?Gold-Loan3142 asked: How do we challenge the mainstream ‘“perpetual growth” economics that infuses almost all discussion of the economy?Jonathan:You have touched on one of the core issues. Theobsession with endless GDPgrowth on a finite planet can only end in tears. The only question is when. There have been numerous academic challenges to this and alternatives, such asKate Raworth’s Doughnut EconomicsandBill McKibben’sEconomics as if the World Mattered. There are also some very interesting studies and books on degrowth by the likes ofJason Hickelland many others.If I can stray outside my journalist role, I have long believed that what the world needs is not just economic degrowth but ecological regrowth. We need a system of trade, currency, taxation, incentives that rewards countries and companies for restoring the world’s battered ecosystems.SurinamPam asked: A lot of carbon is emitted for road transportation, building heating/cooling, and electricity generation. And, the world is quickly switching to EVs, heat pumps, and building out solar, wind, and batteries. If all those carbon sources go to zero, how much of an effect will it have on future climate change?Jonathan:That is a fascinating point. I haven’t done or seen the calculations on this. But, speaking far more broadly, the energy transition is one of four great causes for hope that I have right now. Wind, solar and electric vehicles have taken off far more quickly than almost anyone expected even a decade go. This has the potential to change the global balance of power and, I believe, may also be behindrising US aggressionin terms of military conflict, tariffs and attacks on democracy.View image in fullscreenNissan Leaf EVs being made in Sunderland. The rapid switch to electric cars is a cause for hope.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianDistracted-Nomad asked:In terms of advocacy, what are the most powerful things you can say to convince individuals that their efforts (ie lifestyle change) are important? Most people I know say whatever they do won’t make a difference and governments and corporations need to change before we do.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJonathan:This is one of the most common and important questions that climate journalists get. I agree the priority must be political action because the required changes – higher taxes on fossil fuels, a wealth tax on billionaires, more investment in renewables, more incentives for plant-based diets, etc – need to come at a national and international level. That said, I disagree that individual action is meaningless. It can set an example to others. And it can show that change can be beneficial to health and wallet. Imagine, for example, how much money electric car owners have saved during the recent oil price spikes. The key is to do this whilenever letting the petro-companies off the hook. They have tried in the past to convince people that the responsibility for the climate crisis lies with individual consumers. That was why they pushed the idea of carbon calculators. But the real blame lies with them. Most of the big oil companies are expanding production and makingrecord profits.Karenadona asked: How much longer do we have until we run out of time to save the planet?Ajit:In one sense, it is never too late, and in another sense, it already is too late. The planet will survive, and even apocalyptic scenarios do not really consider an end to life on Earth as a result of climate breakdown. But while there is technically no time limit to action – climate scientists stress that each extra ton of carbon dioxide heats the planet a bit more – the likelihood of triggering catastrophic tipping points rises the hotter it gets. The 1.5C global heating target, which world leaders agreed to in Paris in 2015, looks extremely likely to be missed. (I am not saying definitely, as it is physically still possible, even if emissions have risen to a level where it is perhaps societally implausible.) Keeping below 2C of warming is, however, very much still possible. Current projections put us on track for somewhere between 2C and 3C by the end of the century.Szabolcs85 asked: Is there anything to be hopeful about? The future looks very bleak.Jonathan:I am also pessimistic, but there are still many things to fight for. Every fraction of a degree of warming that we can prevent will help millions of people and billions of other forms of life. UN-led action have already helped in this way, but not enough. But international cooperation is worthwhile.My four other causes for hope:Theenergy transition, particularly in China.The rise of therights for nature movement, which - although imperfect – is confronting the core of our problems, which is a broken relationship with the non-human part of the planet.Alternative ways of thinking and being found in the global south, particularly amongindigenous communities.The prospect of theglobal population peaking before 2050, which should reduce pressure on the environment.Set against this, unfortunately, are the huge military and financial forces of petrostates, such as the US, Russia and Saudi Arabia, often aligned with big corporations.View image in fullscreenBrazilian Indigenous Peoples minister Sonia Guajajara speaks to members at Cop30. Indigenous communities are offering alternative ways of thinking about how we protect the planet.Photograph: André Penner/APFraggin601 asked: How do you think our economic systems must change to cope with climate change?Jonathan:Great subject. The first step should be a realistic appraisal of the economic risks posed by the climate and nature crises. Currently, most economists are absurdly complacent. The Nobel prize winner William Nordhaus assumes a very low hit to GDP but he omits – as the commentatorGenevieve Guenthernotes – the full costs of labour productivity, buildings, infrastructure, transportation, non-coastal real estate, insurance, communication, government services and other sectors. Most worrying to me is that most economic model assume smooth linear warming, even though many climate scientists warn of tipping points that are likely to bring jolts, acceleration and catastrophe. It is as though a doctor treats everything as a chronic, manageable ailment while ignoring the very real risks of acute, life-threatening diseases.Nature also needs to be much more highly valued – and not just in economic terms. Then there is the question of inequality – between nations, communities and species. There is no GDP without a healthy environment. And there is no greater theft from the poor than the loss of clean air, fresh water, fertile soil and a stable climate. On a positive note, I have been very impressed by the recent work done by theWorld Inequality Labto try to incorporate more planetary boundaries into their projections of what a cleaner and fairer world could look like.Lightning7Boltasked: What can a 17-year-old like me do to fight for change?Jonathan Watts:Find out all you can from news articles, books and films. Then spread the word. The great climate science communicatorKatherine Hayhoesays the most important thing you can do to fight climate change is to talk about it. Age can be to your advantage. Your generation is the future. Older people are threatening that.Greta Thunbergwas 15 when she started fighting for change, sitting outside the Swedish parliament with a sign saying “School Strike for Climate”. By the time she was 17, the movement had gone global. Millions took to the streets and the head of Opec, the world’s biggest oil cartel, declared theyouth protest“perhaps the greatest threat to our industry.”View image in fullscreenGreta Thunberg was 15 when she started campaigning.Photograph: Michael Campanella/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentConversationsExtreme heatWildfiresEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content
