title: From wine coolers to the ultimate walking sandals: 11 things you loved most in July | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Whether it’s budget barbecues or clever travel pillows, here are the favourites defining your summer
Author: Lily Smith
Headline: Whether it’s budget barbecues or clever travel pillows, here are the favourites defining your summer
Content: View image in fullscreenThe FilterLife and styleFrom wine coolers to the ultimate walking sandals: 11 things you loved most in JulyWhether it’s budget barbecues or clever travel pillows, here are the favourites defining your summerDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereLily SmithMon 3 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.July’s hitlist paints a picture of a month well spent. A barbecue and nifty wine cooler sleeve suggest alfresco evenings, while a bargain tent and cool box point to camping trips. Sensible but stylish walking shoes and a trusty water bottle also suggest time spent in the great outdoors.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.All in all – despite the climate crisis-chargedheatwavesandhosepipe bans– it sounds like you’re making the most of the summer. From a cooling mattress topper to a cheap-and-cheerful mascara, here are your favourite things from last month.The cooling mattress topperView image in fullscreenPanda bamboo topper, double£125.96 at PandaRavi Meah’s guide tosleeping in a heatwaveis full of helpful tips and recommendations, including this cooling bamboo mattress topper. It is “breathable and moisture-wicking, helping sweat evaporate more easily and reducing the chance of overheating on hot nights,” he says.Jane Hoskynalso gave the toppera five-star review.Supportive walking sandalsView image in fullscreenTeva Hurricane XLT3From £65.50 at Amazon“My trusty Hurricanes have been worn at a whole host of places, from the hills in the Himalayas to home in the Cotswolds, so I know they’re built to last,” saysSian Lewisin her test of thebest walking sandals. A comfortable and affordable shoe for “relaxed summer walking and exploring”.The perfect picnic wine coolerView image in fullscreenLe Creuset wine cooler sleeve£29 at John LewisRated as best for picnics inMina Holland’s test of thebest wine coolers, this jazzy Le Creuset sleeve is perfect for keeping wine chilled on the go. “A natty little number to keep in your freezer for the times you need to rapidly chill a room-temp bottle,” saysMina.The bargain tubing mascaraView image in fullscreenMaybelline Lash Sensational Sky Tubes tubing mascara, 7ml£11.80 at AmazonWhen it comes to beauty, what’s worth splurging on, and where should you save your pennies?Anita Bhagwandashas the answers in herspend or save beauty guide. “There are plenty of brilliant, affordablemascarason the high street,” she says, including this tubing mascara from Maybelline. “Expect length, volume, lift and impressive hold.”The budget cool boxView image in fullscreenCampingaz Icetimecool box£34.58 at AmazonThis cool box is “sturdier than it looks and would make a solid companion for overnight camping trips or festivals”, saysLinda Geddesin her roundup of thebest cool boxes. Its robust design and respectable results during testing earned it the title of best budget.An ingenious travel pillowView image in fullscreenTrtl travel pillow£42.49 at TrtlClearly plenty of you have a long journey coming up, landing the Trtl travel pillow on last month’s hitlist.Pete Wiserated it the best for side sleepers in his test of thebest travel pillows. “The whole thing packs down very neatly into its carry case,” making it ideal for your next trip.The easy breezy barbecueView image in fullscreenWeber kettle charcoal barbecue£105 at ArgosNothing says summer like alfresco dining, so it’s no surprise many of you snapped up this affordable barbecue. “It’s effortless to light and use, it makes great food, and it’s easy to store,” saysAlex David, who rated it the best overall in his guide to thebest BBQs.Handy on-the-go storageView image in fullscreenSquare flexi-tub£10.95 at Tooled Up“Camping with kids is no picnic,” saysMatt Collins, whose handy guide is filled with helpful advice onsurviving family camping. This flexi-tub is ideal for keeping things organised in your tent.Comfy and reliable period pantsView image in fullscreenWuka midi brief period pants£16.99 at WukaWinner of Zoë Phillimore’s test of thebest period pants, the Wuka midi briefs are “substantial enough to give you peace of mind without looking like something Bridget Jones would wear”.A sustainable water bottleView image in fullscreenOcean Bottle Go£38 at Ocean BottleThe Go bottle’s compact size, insulation and leak-proof design impressedZoë Phillimoreduring her test of thebest water bottles. “Ocean Bottle goes above and beyond in terms of sustainability. It’s a certified B Corp, and makes impressive pledges with every bottle you buy,” she says, making it a useful and feelgood buy.A spacious and straightforward tentView image in fullscreenColeman Darwin 3 plus tent£89.99 at Halfords“Coleman’s Darwin Plus delivers impressive performance for less than £100,” saysSian Lewisin her guide tothe best tents. It’s “spacious, practical and straightforward to pitch”, making itSian’s best budget pick – perfect for rookies or casual campers.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe FilterSleepInteriorsWomen's shoesWineBeautySkincarenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: The body snatchers: how a young Nigerian man was lured to London in an organ-trafficking plot | Human trafficking | The Guardian
description: The long read: Daniel was working at a market in Lagos when he was given the chance to start anew in the UK. He had no idea what was expected of him in return
Author: Alexis Okeowo
Headline: The long read: Daniel was working at a market in Lagos when he was given the chance to start anew in the UK. He had no idea what was expected of him in return
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Image Source/Reuters/AFP/APView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Image Source/Reuters/AFP/APThe long readHuman traffickingThe body snatchers: how a young Nigerian man was lured to London in an organ-trafficking plotDaniel was working at a market in Lagos when he was given the chance to start anew in the UK. He had no idea what was expected of him in returnThe summer issue of the Long Read magazine is out now.Click hereto orderAlexis OkeowoMon 3 Aug 2026 13.10 EDTFirst published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 00.00 EDTShareDaniel arrived in Lagos for the first time in 2016. He had come from a village in Ebonyi, a state in south-easternNigeria. He was 15 years old, the eldest of nine siblings, and his parents were farmers. When he was a boy, his father became sick and Daniel started working to assist his family, helping to cut trees and clear land. A few years later, he decided to seek his fortune in Lagos.In Nigeria’s commercial capital, Daniel spent his days in the open-air Ikotun Market, where thousands of people shop every day for everything from tomatoes and fabric to suitcases and electronics. He sold cellphone accessories out of a wheelbarrow under a wide umbrella, making less than £10 a day. After living with a relative, he moved into a room with friends, including a young man named Chukwudi, who also worked in the market. Daniel had grown up in the same village as Chukwudi. A photo from their early childhood shows the boys together, Daniel in a red sportswear shirt.Daniel was short and slight, with an unassuming face and sleepy eyes. He was playful and liked to joke around, Chukwudi recalled, “not a troublemaker”. They often hung out with another friend from the market, Ben, who was older and carried himself like he was destined for better things. “Ben was living big boy life,” Chukwudi told me. “He was balling out, flexing; he can go and eat anything he like.”One day in 2021, Ben disappeared from the market. He wouldn’t be in touch again until later that year, when he called Daniel and told him the good news: he had got a job in the UK. “Wow, God has done for you then?” Daniel said. Ben asked if Daniel was interested in working abroad. Ben sent his friends videos of himself dancing in London, living the good life. He had accomplished the dream: he had escaped the dim economic prospects offered by his home country and got out. (There is a Yoruba slang term for it: “japa”, or as one Lagosian put it to me, “It’s like running for your life.”) Daniel was interested in doing the same.Soon after, Daniel received a call from a man named Obinna Obeta, who had got his number from Ben. Obeta said that he could help Daniel get to the UK, where he would provide him with accommodation and work. But first, he said, Daniel would need to go to Abuja, Nigeria’s capital, to undergo some medical tests. Daniel wasn’t sure what to make of this, until he received the money for his trip to Abuja. “That is the day that I knew he was serious,” Daniel later told a court in London. He assumed the medical tests were part of the process for getting a visa.In February 2022, Daniel said goodbye to Chukwudi at a bus station in Lagos and began his journey to Britain. He had never met Obeta in person. When later asked in court why he thought Obeta was helping him, he responded simply: “Because I think it’s from God.”Obinna Obeta, the man who contacted Daniel, was a Nigerian radiologist who had moved to London to seek treatment for kidney failure. Nigeria suffers from high rates of kidney disease, but few have health insurance or can afford dialysis and medications. “Kidney disease treatment in Nigeria: people are just moving from here to the morgue. It’s traumatising honestly,” Obeta would later say. It was not until 2025 that Nigeria introduced comprehensive standards and guidelines for organ transplants, and only 2,000 or so kidney transplants have taken place there. Many Nigerians who have undergone organ transplants have done so abroad.Even in countries with advanced healthcare systems, the wait time for a kidney can be long: two to three years, on average, in the UK, and up to five years or more in the US. According to the World Health Organization, organ transplant tourism – where patients travel abroad to purchase organs – accounts forat least 5% to 10%of transplants worldwide. Organ trafficking is believed to take place in about 50 countries, and it is one of the most under-reported forms of human trafficking. The UK considers moving people across international borders for the purpose of harvesting their organs a form of slavery, treating human beings as commodities to be bought and sold.In July 2021, seven months before Daniel left for the UK, Obeta had undergone a successful kidney transplant at the Royal Free hospital in north London. It cost him £70,000. He used the services of a medical tourism company, run by a Nigerian doctor who was then anNHSconsultant. The kidney donor was Daniel’s friend Ben, whom Obeta had falsely claimed was his cousin.On the flight to London, Daniel knew none of this. Accompanied by a man and woman he had not met before, he had only a few possessions: some clothes, lotion and soap. No shoes besides the ones on his feet. It was his first time on a plane, and he slept for much of the flight. After landing, the man took Daniel to a house off the Old Kent Road in south London, where he met Obeta for the first time. Daniel was told he would sleep in the living room.As Daniel would later testify, Obeta treated him like a “houseboy”. “Every day I wash plates, I wash toilet, I wash, I sweep,” he recalled. Daniel did not have any money and was reliant on Obeta for his meals. Even his passport was taken. There seemed to be no escape.Across London, in Willesden Green, Sonia Ekweremadu was getting sicker. Less than two months before Daniel arrived in the UK, she had posted an end-of-year recap reel on her Instagram page. It showed her, a light-skinned 24-year-old woman, dancing, going out with friends, and lying in a hospital bed with a pink teddy bear. Her family home was in Abuja but she lived in London, having attended various private schools in England. With several family properties in Nigeria, as well as in the US and UAE, she had the privileged upbringing that is typical of a Nigerian politician’s children.Sonia’s father was Ike Ekweremadu, one of the most prominent and powerful figures in Nigeria. Ike Ekweremadu had been elected to the Nigerian senate for a fifth consecutive term in 2019, and served as deputy president of the senate. His reputation extended beyond national borders, after his stint as speaker of the parliament of the Economic Community of West African States in the 2010s.It was while Sonia was studying for her master’s degree in film at Newcastle University, in 2019, that she became sick. As she grew weaker, she had to drop out. A family friend eventually referred her to the Royal Free in Hampstead, which specialises in treating kidney disease. Sonia was diagnosed with FSGS nephrotic syndrome, a rare disease where kidney scarring leaks protein into the urine and causes bodily swelling. In August 2021, Sonia met with Peter Dupont, a consultant nephrologist at the Royal Free, who noted that she would require dialysis or a renal transplant. She received dialysis in a private patients’ unit on the top floor.In September 2021, the court later heard, Sonia’s uncle, Isaac “Diwe” Ekweremadu, who is a doctor, called an old medical school classmate to talk about the transplant that he had at the Royal Free that year. Diwe wanted to know whether his niece might be able to have a similar operation. His former classmate was Obinna Obeta.At the time, Obeta was in desperate need of money. As a non-UK resident, he still owed £27,000 to the Royal Free as part of the £70,000 he was paying for his kidney transplant. He also had to spend £1,600 every month on immunosuppressants, so his body wouldn’t reject the kidney, and other medications and tests. “It just kept increasing. Just kept increasing,” he later said of his debt. For an initial sum of just under £2,000, Obeta agreed to help find a kidney donor for Sonia. He referred the Ekweremadus to the medical concierge service he had used for his own transplant. Soon after, Obeta got in touch with the young man who had provided him with his kidney, Ben, to ask for help finding a donor. Through him, he found Daniel.By November 2021, Ike Ekweremadu had a solution for his daughter. He forwarded a message to his wife: Diwe had found a donor who “matched very well”. The next step was to get the donor a passport and then a visa to the UK. Daniel had no idea that the following statement was written on his visa application:“I wish to state on conclusion of this application that I would be donating an organ to my closest cousin (Sonia Chinonso Ekweremadu) in appreciation for her sacrifices towards me, my family, and our community. I’m willing to put my life on the line for her to live and continue her good service to humanity. Finally, I wish to state that I’ll be travelling in company with my uncle, Obinna. He has been a father‑figure since I lost my biological father.”None of this was true: Sonia was not a relative of Daniel’s, nor was Obinna Obeta. He had never met them. His biological father was still alive. He had never discussed the prospect of organ donation with anyone.View image in fullscreenIkotun Market in Lagos where Daniel and Chukwudi worked, 9 July 2021.Photograph: NurPhoto SRL/AlamyDaniel arrived in London in February 2022. Before his arrival, Sonia’s doctor at the Royal Free had written a letter to the Nigerian doctor who ran the concierge service, stating that she was not responding well to treatments and agreeing that a transplant would be the “best way forward for her”. The family had informed the Royal Free that they had a candidate, telling them that Daniel was 19 and a distant cousin of Sonia’s. The doctor added in his letter that this prospective donor was younger than he would consider ideal and, because he was not a close relative, there could be difficulties gaining approval from the hospital and the UK Human Tissue Authority.In the UK, kidney transplants are highly regulated. If the donor is alive, they have to go through extensive physical and psychological evaluations to make sure they are medically suitable and willing to donate. Once the surgical team approves the donation, the Human Tissue Authority must interview both the donor and the recipient to determine whether the donor has given consent and to ensure that no payment or coercion is involved.According to the court transcript, Diwe told her parents that they should now say that Daniel was a first cousin of Sonia, not a distant one. He also later told them that there was a medical secretary at the hospital who would act as Daniel’s interpreter. For a fee of £1,500, she had agreed to coach Daniel on what to say during the interview he’d need to do for his kidney donation to be approved. She recommended that Daniel be at the hospital during Sonia’s dialysis treatments to show his firm commitment to his cousin’s health.The week of Daniel’s arrival in London, Obeta took him to a west African restaurant on the Old Kent Road to have lunch with a young woman and an older woman. Daniel had no idea who they were, and testified that the women didn’t ask him any questions about himself. They seemed afraid of something, he said. At the end of the lunch, the group took a photo. The two women were Sonia and her mother, Beatrice Ekweremadu.Later that week, Obeta took Daniel to the Royal Free, where he saw Sonia and Beatrice outside. Before Obeta began talking with them, he told Daniel to stand away so he could not hear. “Obinna would just tell me where to stay and he would go with them and they would start discussing. Like they was controlling me,” Daniel testified. He was confused to learn that he would be meeting with a doctor. “They said if the doctor ask me the school that I go, I should tell the doctor that I go to higher institution,” Daniel told the court. “If the doctor ask me who is Sonia, I should say that Sonia is my cousin. They give me many things to answer the doctor. I should tell the doctor that they not pay me.”On 24 February 2022, Daniel went in for a meeting with Peter Dupont, the consultant nephrologist at the Royal Free, while Obeta waited outside. “He told me that I want to do a kidney transplant,” Daniel later recalled. “I was shocked because that is the first day that I hear about this kidney transplant.” Dupont asked him about his relationship to Sonia and what had motivated him to be a donor; about whether he was working or studying; and about what his parents did for a living.Daniel gave the answers he had been coached to provide. In court, Dupont recalled that Daniel had been subdued: “We spoke for perhaps 15 or 20 minutes. His answers were very brief: single sentences, single words. He didn’t really appear to have any understanding of what it was that he was signing up for.” Dupont explained that there were dangers associated with the procedure, such as excess bleeding, infections and blood clots, and “a small risk of death”, as he wrote in his notes. Even if the operation went well, Daniel would have an increased risk of chronic kidney disease and end‑stage renal disease. He would require regular follow-ups for the rest of his life to monitor his kidney function, blood pressure and urine protein levels.Noticing Daniel’s uneasiness, Dupont asked if he was scared to tell the Ekweremadus that he did not want to go ahead. Daniel said he did not want to donate his kidney. It was only when Dupont made clear that the operation would not happen that Daniel finally made eye contact, the doctor testified. “He was nervous that I would say or imply that the decision not to proceed was his fault. I assured him that confidentiality was paramount and the intended recipient would be told he was unsuitable.” He recalled Daniel saying about Obeta: “He had not told me anything about this. I would never have agreed to any of this. My body was not for sale.”Afterward, Daniel told Obeta that he answered what questions he could, but there were some he could not. Obeta was angry. “He say that if I don’t do this – he used Igbo language to say this – if I don’t do this … I will find it difficult,” Daniel testified. (Obeta insisted to the court that he had discussed the kidney transplant with Daniel before the meeting.) Obeta also told Daniel that he had 1.2m naira, or about £2,000 then, for him if he went through with the operation.At the end of March, the decision was taken out of their hands. The Royal Free formally ruled out the possibility of allowing Daniel’s transplant operation to go ahead.Daniel was relieved, but he was still living in limbo. He was not allowed to leave the house, and spent much of his time with Obeta’s kids when he was not doing chores. A few weeks after the Royal Free declined to proceed with the operation, two people came to Obeta’s house to examine Daniel. They asked him to remove his clothes and applied pressure to his stomach. They still wanted to do the transplant, Daniel said, and Obeta told Daniel he had booked him a flight back to Nigeria. Daniel was unsure what they had planned for him. “That is when I start to become afraid because I don’t know what I am going to do. Because all the plans, everything they are doing is behind my back,” Daniel testified.As Daniel later told Chukwudi, his childhood friend, he had been in a state of panic. “He was even crying, he don’t know what to do,” Chukwudi recalled. “Even me, when he was telling me everything, I was crying. I didn’t know what to do. Because if he comes back, he has nothing to do again. He has already sold his market [stock], he used the money to buy some clothes for his trip.”View image in fullscreenIke Ekweremadu (left) when he was deputy president of the Nigerian senate in March 2012.Photograph: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP/Getty ImagesIn court, Daniel and Obeta’s accounts of what happened next differed in a few small ways. But the likeliest story is that on 2 or 3 May 2022, a friend of Obeta’s took Daniel to Heathrow airport for a flight back to Abuja. But Daniel decided he could not go back to Nigeria, where he feared he would be coerced into donating his kidney. Despite carrying little more than a used Samsung phone, AirPods, chargers and £27.90 in cash, he fled. He ended up walking around for three days, sleeping outside. He then ran into a stranger on Kingston Road in Staines, who gave him food and let him take a shower in his flat.On 5 May, Daniel went to nearby Staines police station, where he told officers a story that was mostly fictional. He said he had been begging for money on the streets of Lagos before coming to London, and that he was an orphan with no family in Nigeria. He told officers that the man he had travelled with had promised him money, but that he couldn’t say what the money was for. He said he was only 15. (Daniel would later testify that he was trying to give the impression of being a vulnerable youth with nowhere to live in Lagos, so he wouldn’t be deported.)According to Chukwudi, who spoke to Daniel not long after he went to the station, a Nigerian woman hosted Daniel at her home when the police released him into protective care. On the call, Daniel still sounded afraid about the attempted kidney transplant, but he said the Nigerian woman was taking him to church. He thought he might even get the chance to go to school.With Daniel now gone, the Ekweremadus needed a new plan. After consulting with friends and colleagues, they decided on a new transplant location: Turkey. While the Ekweremadus maintain that Sonia had no knowledge of the plan to illegally get a kidney donor, she responded to her father’s WhatsApp messages that had photos of new potential donors. To one photo of two young Black men, Sonia wrote: “OK, that’s fine. Thank you. Are they still more to test?”Her father told her: “Yes, but by the end of the week, I will decide who to proceed with. We will get it right this time.”Sonia wrote back: “I trust you, daddy, thank you ❤️”. Then she added: “The dark one looks better, the light one looks like he’ll run away 😂😂😂”.In June 2022, on Father’s Day, Sonia wrote to her father on the family group chat: “Happy Father’s Day, daddy, you mean the world to us … You are the best father in the world. I know lots of people say that about their fathers, but mine is really the best … I pray for long life and prosperity, to be able to see your grandchildren and great-grandchildren in Jesus’ name. Amen. I want to especially thank you for everything you’ve done and are doing regarding this transplant process. You and mummy have gone above and beyond for me, and it never goes unnoticed and unappreciated … I hope that one day I’ll be able to take care of you, and mummy, the way that you’ve taken care of us all these years (don’t worry, I haven’t forgotten your Range Rover gift).”Ike replied: “I know you didn’t forget, sweetheart … I will spare nothing to ensure your good health and comfort. I have the support of mummy on this objective 100%. By the grace of God, you will be out of this challenge before the end of August. It’s a promise. Just be strong for all of us.”Two days later, Ike and Beatrice Ekweremadu were arrested at Heathrow as they travelled back from Turkey. They were charged with conspiracy to commit human trafficking for the purpose of exploitation, specifically organ harvesting. The couple had at least £30,000 in cash on them. Sonia was arrested the same day at her home in London. Obeta was arrested the next month. Sonia’s uncle Diwe remained in Nigeria and was not extradited to the UK. (I was unable to reach Diwe for comment.)It is extremely rare for a Nigerian politician of Ekweremadu’s status to face criminal charges. In the UK, the story was widely covered in the media, but in Nigeria, the case attracted a different level of interest, dominating the front pages of newspapers and sparking discussions on primetime TV news, as well as endless social media posts and WhatsApp messages across both Nigeria and the diaspora. One of Daniel’s uncles, Linus, who had given him a place to stay when he first came to Lagos, discovered his nephew’s story on social media like everyone else. “If I had known, I wouldn’t have allowed him to go,” Linus told me.On 6 February 2023, the trial of Obinna Obeta and Ike, Beatrice and Sonia Ekweremadu began at the Old Bailey in London. All pleaded not guilty. Ike claimed that he thought Daniel was donating a kidney to his daughter out of kindness, and that he never agreed to pay him. He accused Obeta of scamming him out of money, and he argued that Daniel had lied to the police so that he could get asylum in the UK. “D was never exploited, D accepted and agreed, volunteered to help my daughter with this kidney and we believed him,” Ike told the court. “But looking back now it was obvious that he was scamming everybody, he just wanted to come to England and take refuge.”Ike downplayed Daniel’s vulnerability. “Lagos is a place where you get wiser by the day for you to survive. So, even a young person in Lagos cannot be intimidated,” he said in court. “Because they are just streetwise.” When asked if he knew Daniel was selling phone accessories out of a wheelbarrow, he responded: “I didn’t know in particular but that’s also a big business, he’d make millions with that.”Ike did admit to fabricating the familial relationship to Daniel. “That is what Dr Obeta advised us,” he said. “My daughter was sick, and somebody had told us what we would need to do, and we didn’t see any corruption in this; we didn’t corrupt anybody.” (Contacted before publication of this article, the Royal Free declined to comment. After publication, it sent the following statement: “We would like to pay tribute to the victim for his bravery in coming forward and sharing his experience. National guidance for the clinical assessment of living donor transplantation, which applies to both our NHS and private patients, was followed in this case and a decision taken not to go ahead with the procedure.”)Both Ike and Beatrice kept saying during the trial that their lies to the Royal Free about Daniel’s identity were “not who we are” – they were just desperate to save their daughter’s life. “She was born premature, so we struggled to save her life from day one,” the former senator said. He refused to admit any guilt. When asked if he was the victim in all this, Ekweremadu said: “Yes.”View image in fullscreenIke Ekweremadu (left), Dr Obinna Obeta (top right) and Beatrice Ekweremadu on 23 March 2023 after their arrests.Photograph: APThe trial shed more light on Obeta, who had obtained a UK medical visa for his own transplant and then stayed to work in the country illegally, getting a job as a cleaner during the pandemic. “It was amazing … I’ve never seen this kind of, you know, surgery skill,” Obeta told the court of his transplant experience. “I want to use this opportunity to thank the people of the UK for saving my life.”On 23 March 2023, at the end of the six-week trial, Ike and Beatrice Ekweremadu werefound guilty of organ trafficking. Ike was later sentenced to nine years and eight months; Beatrice to four and a half years. Sonia, who had also been charged with conspiracy to arrange organ harvesting, was acquitted. Obeta was convicted of organ trafficking and sentenced to 10 years. The Ekweremadu case was the first successful organ-trafficking conviction in the UK under the Modern Slavery Act.After he testified in court via a video link in February 2023, Daniel vanished. The police had placed him in protective custody, and none of his family or friends in Nigeria knew where he was. He had told the court: “I have no one here [in the UK], no family or friends. I’m having to start my life again. I am wary of new people that come into my life now. My plan now is to work and to get an education and to play football.”In Lagos, in 2024, I met a childhood friend of Daniel’s, Jeremiah Nwamkpuma. In a beige, shabby office upstairs from the stalls in Ikotun Market, we chatted over the noise of hawkers and shoppers. Nwamkpuma told me that he’d recently visited Daniel’s dad in the family village. “[He] asked me about Daniel. I’m telling him that I’m not hearing from him. He’s crying. Since Daniel left, he’s not heard from him,” Nwamkpuma said. “Tension is high in the family.”The family was confused and hurt that Daniel had disappeared from their lives, even though they understood that he, too, was likely afraid. His parents were angry, Nwamkpuma said. They farmed cassava, plantain, yam and other crops, but had little money. When Daniel was selling cellphones, he would send money back home to help them. “We’re happy he’s saved, but there’s no proper communication,” Jeremiah Mbah, who is the pastor of a church Daniel occasionally attended, told me. “It’s as if he’s lost.”For more than two years no one heard from Daniel, but then last year, he called from the UK. He reached Chukwudi, who was surprised and relieved. “He wanted to hear from me, and know how his parents are doing. I explained to him that his daddy is very sick, and that they needed him present. But he said there was no way for him to come. He was feeling bad,” Chukwudi told me. In court, Daniel had said that he was concerned about his safety if he returned home. Ekweremadu “has a lot of people that know him. In Nigeria, those people can do anything.” He asked Chukwudi to help with the cost of Daniel’s father’s care. “He told me that he was going to school. He sounded very good,” Chukwudi said.Daniel’s father died last August. Nwamkpuma called him to let him know of the death. Daniel cried, Nwamkpuma recalled, but said that he still couldn’t come because of his studies; Nwamkpuma told him to stay.Chukwudi, Nwamkpuma and Daniel’s family have tried to reach him since then, with no success.After her parents were convicted, Sonia gavea short interviewto the BBC. She looked poised, wearing understated gold jewellery, with her hair in braids. “It’s sad. It’s been really hard to really wrap my head around it,” she said. “I understand the conviction, personally I disagree with it. However, that’s from a very biased perspective as their daughter. I would obviously always, always back my parents. However, the law has taken its course, and we just have to now move forward as a family.” She admitted she was aware “to an extent” of her parents’ plan, but that she “didn’t really know anything leading up to it”. She added that she didn’t “feel anything” towards Daniel, but wished him “all the best”.‘For me, there was no other choice’: inside the global illegal organ tradeRead moreShe was now in a precarious medical situation. “Either I stay on dialysis for the rest of my life, or I get a transplant; these are my two options,” she said. She had visited her parents in jail, and said they seemed calm. “I feel guilty,” she said, her voice breaking. “Because I feel like all this has happened because of me.” (Sonia declined to comment for this article, but on her Instagram, she often posts stories with bible verses and prayers, as well as photos with friends.)The Ekweremadu case is still the only successful conviction for organ trafficking under the Modern Slavery Act in the UK. There is a simple reason that such convictions are rare, particularly in Nigeria, says Frank Tietie, a human rights lawyer: “Those who are involved are usually very powerful people, and they’re able to influence our justice system.” While Ike Ekweremadu remains in prison, Beatrice was released in January, after serving the custodial portion of her sentence. Upon her return to Nigeria, local media reported that she was greeted with celebrations in her home town of Mpu.Late last year, in a sign of Ike’s continued status in his home country, Nigeria’s foreign minister met with officials at the UK Ministry of Justice to request that he be returned to Nigeria to serve out the rest of his sentence there. The UK rejected the request. Nigeria has arrested and charged several other people with organ trafficking, but the trials have lagged. As Tietie said: “So it’s still going on, largely unreported, largely unchecked.”This article, first published on 30 July 2026, was re-edited to protect the anonymity of some individualsView image in fullscreenThe Long Read magazine summer editionAI in the classroom, vending machines in the canteen, homeless people in the library, no one in the pub. Surprising stories from our strange new world in the new edition of the Long Read magazine.Buy your copy here.Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.

title: Rapists, child abusers and groomers will not leave prison early, says PM | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until October
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Andy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until October
Content: About 6,000 offenders had been due for early release in September amid official predictions that prisons will be full in November.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenAbout 6,000 offenders had been due for early release in September amid official predictions that prisons will be full in November.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyPrisons and probationRapists, child abusers and groomers will not leave prison early, says PMAndy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until OctoberRajeev SyalandAlexandra ToppingMon 3 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will be excluded fromearly release plansto ease critical prison overcrowding in a major intervention by Andy Burnham.The prime minister said on Tuesday that he would delay the planned early release of thousands of prisoners acrossEnglandand Wales by a month until October.But he will still allow domestic abusers and killers to go free, including two men jailed for their role inthe death of PC Andrew Harper.The decision will put the lives of women and girls “at risk” and has “let down” serving police officers, a watchdog and a pressure group have warned.It follows the suspension of Keir Starmer’s plans to release up to 6,000 offenders from prison early in September amid official predictions that prisons will be full in November.Burnham suspended the schemein his second week as PM after coming under intense pressure from MPs, victims, campaigners and frontline prison officers to halt the early release of serious sexual and violent offenders.In a statement, Burnham said: “I asked for an urgent review of the prisoner release scheme. I fully understand the anger, anxiety and distress that’s been caused. I’ve heard that loud and clear. That’s why we’re making significant changes: offenders who have been sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and other grooming offences will be excluded from the changes.”The Ministry of Justice has declined to release the numbers of prisoners who will no longer be freed as a result of Burnham’s intervention.It has also declined to say when its own internal modelling predicts that prisons will be full again, and if there are already plans for further early release schemes.The domestic abuse commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, said the decision to exclude those who have abused their partners was “wrong” and “puts victims’ lives at risk”.“As I told the lord chancellor just last week, the danger perpetrators pose to their victim should not be underestimated. These are individuals who are fixated on their victim and will stop at nothing to control and cause harm.“Measures that will keep domestic abuse victims safe still appear to be an afterthought.”Andrea Simon, the London victim’s commissioner, said the failure was concerning, given a shortage of probation officers with experience of handling complex offenders.“This will alarm many survivors of abuse that are desperately concerned about their safety, particularly when there are real challenges in delivering tougher community supervision,” she said.An early release scheme in 2024 included specific protections for victims of domestic abuse.Victims’ groups had objected to the proposal for 6,000 people to be freed early from September under the newSentencingAct. Debbie Adlam, the mother of the police officer Andrew Harper, said last month that the proposed inclusion of two of her son’s killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – was “another letdown” for their family.Prisoners serving longer sentences of four years or more would be eligible for release at the halfway point of their term, rather than at two-thirds as had previously been the case.The changes were due to be phased in, beginning with prisoners serving sentences of less than 575 days, going up to prisoners jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release in June next year.The government has said that, after listening to victims’ concerns, rapists and child sexual offenders will not be eligible for the sentencing changes.Prisoners serving time for some sexual or violent offences where the automatic release stage is set at two-thirds will become eligible for release at the halfway point, provided they have not committed serious breaches of prison rules.This applies to Bowers and Cole, two of Harper’s killers, who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter. Henry Long, the main perpetrator, will not be subject to early release.Tiff Lynch, national chair of the Police Federation, said: “Allowing those who take an officer’s life to be released earlier to save the prison system from collapsing gravely risks undermining not only public safety but public confidence, causing real distress to bereaved families and sending entirely the wrong message about the value we place on those who protect us. The government must urgently rethink this decision.”The chief constable of Thames Valley police, Jason Hogg, said: “I am beyond disappointed the government is continuing to allow PC Andrew Harper’s killers to be released early from prison despite the overwhelming recent public outcry.“It is simple: if Andrew’s killers were convicted today, they would receive life sentences due to the law that was created in his name. They would not be eligible for early release.“We will continue to lobby the government to make the right decision.”The Ministry of Justice also announced a £10m package for victim support and said the new justice secretary, Alex Norris, would look at reviewing “outdated”Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences.Other community measures will be put in place to protect victims of crime including tougher periods of supervision and restriction zones for offenders, Burnham said.“I wanted to go even further as I know there will still be concerns about other offenders having their sentence shortened. But it’s not possible without the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing, which would put public safety at much greater risk,” Burnham said.The announcement follows days of wrangling inside the Ministry of Justice and No 10 over how to calm public anger while still ensuring that the criminal justice system does not seize up.Prisons have become a major point of political contention, with Labour blaming the Conservatives for creating the overcrowding crisis by increasing sentences while failing to build enough jails.Responding to Burnham’s announcement, the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said: “Labour whipped their MPs to vote to let rapists, paedophiles and grooming gang perpetrators out of prison early. Now they admit the Conservative campaign to stop this was right – this is a victory for victims.“But their U-turn doesn’t go far enough. Some child sex offenders and killers, like those responsible for the death of PC Harper, will still be released early. And the trauma of victims being told their abusers may be released can’t be undone.“One of Andy Burnham’s first acts as prime minister will be to let thousands of criminals – including killers and paedophiles – out early.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesSentencingCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage admission over timing of Reform leadership talks raises fresh doubts over £5m gift | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Nigel Farage admits he discussed returning as Reform leader months before election, appearing to undermine previous claims
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Nigel Farage admits he discussed returning as Reform leader months before election, appearing to undermine previous claims
Content: Nigel Farage told a press conference on Monday that he discussed returning to lead the party in spring 2024.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage told a press conference on Monday that he discussed returning to lead the party in spring 2024.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPANigel FarageFarage admission over timing of Reform leadership talks raises fresh doubts over £5m giftNigel Farage admits he discussed returning as Reform leader months before election, appearing to undermine previous claimsBen QuinnandJessica ElgotMon 3 Aug 2026 13.28 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage has made his clearest admission that he was in talks to return to lead Reform UK months before the 2024 general election, casting fresh doubt on previous claims that he was not involved in politics when he received a £5m gift.The admission will reopen questions about the nature of the gift – Farage has repeatedly insisted it was not linked to his political career since the Guardian first revealed it in April.On Monday, Farage admitted he had struck a deal with the party’s then leader, Richard Tice, and the convicted fraudster George Cottrell to return to frontline politics. Labour said the claim “has blown a gaping hole in his excuse” about why he did not declare the gift.Farage has previously said he did not need to declare the £5m from Christopher Harborne or benefits in kind from Cottrell because he was not in politics at the time they were received. He has said he had no intention of returning to politics until June 2024, just before the election.Sources have previously told the Guardianthat Farage told senior figures in Reform UK he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.The tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UKRead moreThe news comes with Farage facing a reopened investigation into his conduct by the Commons standards commissioner should he, as expected, win the byelection in Clacton.It caps a testing period for the Reform leader, who has seen his party’s average poll rating decline to its lowest level in 15 months – and his own rating with the public slip to its lowest since he returned to the role.Meanwhile on Monday:Senior naval figures and the French authorities dismissed Reform’s plans touse military vessels to stop small boats crossing the Channel, saying the proposals “lacked substance” and amounted to a “violation of maritime law and international law”.Farage continued to face a challenge from Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party, with Lowe accusing him of lying over an exchange of messages between the pair about an offer to work together.Parliament’s standards watchdog opened an investigation into Tice, now Reform’s deputy leader, which Tice said was over “whether I should have referenced my register of interests at the start of a debate on UK democracy and Israeli influence”.Farage, who last summer dominated much of the media cycle with a stream of interventions on immigration, attempted to reset the narrative on Monday morning with a news conference on the party’s proposals to use the Royal Navy in the Channel. But once again he was forced to answer multiple questions about the party’s finances.He said: “I had no intention about returning to politics, or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if … I was to come back to that position.”The Sunday Timesreportedthat Farage had negotiated the deal in March and April 2024, which was said to have involved Reform agreeing to repay or write off more than £1m in loans to Tice’s company.“You would be a bit of a mug if you were to walk into a job and not find out what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial,” Farage said.“That was useful for me to know but it wasn’t a deal. It wasn’t an agreement. It was subject to if I came back. And if you want clarification on this, that came some time after the gift, which perhaps is the important point.”After the comments admitting he had discussed a return as party leader, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Nigel Farage has blown a gaping hole in his excuse for why his secret £5m ‘gift’ from a crypto billionaire did not need to be declared.“Farage has desperately tried to distract from his catalogue of scandals. But the embattled Reform leader has run out of road and must come clean with the public. If he had done nothing wrong, he surely would have explained himself by now.“With grubby pacts, police probes and support from a convicted fraudster, Reform are up to their neck in sleaze and they clearly think the rules don’t apply to them.”Pressed later at the same Reform event about when he had started to think about returning in 2024 to frontline politics, Farage said he had been “bullied and bullied for months by lots of different people”.He claimed he had been “60/40” in favour of going to America, where an exciting period potentially beckoned for him in his role as a GB News host covering US politics.Get in touchContact Ben Quinn about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Ben using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. When asked to choose a recipient please switch to the Journalists list and select Ben Quinn.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailben.quinn@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreThe press conference was further overshadowed as news broke shortly before Farage’s appearance that Tice wasunder investigation by parliament’s standards watchdogover a possible failure to declare an interest.Farage has held far fewer press conference since coming under scrutiny over his finances. In a departure from its usual routine,Reform UKlimited the number of questions from media outlets. Farage would previously make a show of taking questions from everyone.The Reform UK leader is widely expected to win the byelection in Clacton next week after all the mainstream parties declined to stand candidates. A poll from Survation on Monday put Farage on 75% of the vote with his nearest challenger – Count Binface – on 20%. Turnout is expected to be low.However, victory in the Essex constituency would trigger the restarting of two investigations by the parliamentary commissioner for standards, one into the £5m given to Farage by Harborne and the other into undisclosed benefits from Cottrell. Other parties have indicated they intend to stand in Clacton later this year in the event of another byelection, which could be triggered by any findings against Farage.Farage has given varying explanations for the £5m gift since it wasfirst revealed by the Guardian in April. In May, he said it was a “reward” for campaigning for Brexit, whereas previously he had said the gift was given for security purposes, to keep him “safe and secure” for the rest of his life.The money underlined the pivotal role Harborne has played in British politics, bankrolling Farage personally and the parties he has led over the past seven years. Last year, he donated £9m to Reform UK – the largest ever single donation by a living person to a British political party.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKParty fundingClacton byelection August 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing | Spain | The Guardian
description: Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity
Content: People sit in the shade of a tree on a beach in Ceuta on Monday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople sit in the shade of a tree on a beach in Ceuta on Monday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersSpainCeuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossingJuan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarityExplainer: why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint?Ashifa Kassamin Madrid,Okba Mohammadin Ceuta andLisa O’Carrollin LondonMon 3 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA growing chorus of voices has accusedMoroccoof helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”.Spanish officials ⁠said on Monday that an estimated 69,500 people who had arrived late last week in Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in northAfrica, had returned to Morocco in recent days. About 2,500 people who had made the crossing were believed to still be in Ceuta.The extraordinary influx hadoverwhelmedthe city of 84,000 people and set offa political crisisacross the EU as some member states laid blame on Spain.In Ceuta, leaders pointed to the broader picture of what had transpired. “It’s an atrocity,” said Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of the territory. “There are 88 bodies in the morgue, and there are more on the other side of the border.”How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The LatestRead moreHe said local people watched the events play out with a mix of sadness, worry and anguish. “People see this not as a migration crisis; it was fundamentally an attack, a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” Vivas told El País newspaper. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco.”He drew a parallel with May 2021, when Rabat loosened border controls,allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceutaover the course of two days, during a diplomatic standoff over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.This time around, analysts have suggested that Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s arch-enemy Algeria could have triggered a response from Morocco.View image in fullscreenPeople who crossed from Morocco sit on a street in Ceuta on Monday.Photograph: Reduan/EPASpeaking on Monday, Spain’s defence minister, Margarita Robles, also seemingly signalled Rabat’s involvement. “Neither Spain nor Morocco can look the other way when it comes to this tragedy,” she told reporters. “I ask the Moroccan government to fully investigate what happened.”The insinuation appeared to be backed by the preliminary assessment of Spanish intelligence services, who cited suspicions that the influx had not been planned by Moroccan authorities but concluded that Morocco had failed to stem the tide of people rushing towards the border and in some cases had even facilitated their passage.Intelligence sources told El País that the roots of the influx probably lay in a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported. As the hoax gained steam online, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum until it was completely lifted late last week, allowing tens of thousands of people to stream through.In Ceuta on Monday, hundreds of people continued to sleep rough on the beach or near Ceuta’s mosques. One local official told reporters that those who remained in the city included 862 unaccompanied minors.Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streetsRead moreAshraf, 28, said he had defied his mother’s warnings against crossing into Spain after spotting posts on social media that said the border had been opened. While he had made it to Ceuta, what had followed was a days-long ordeal as he scrambled to find food and shelter while fending off the memories of what he had lived through.“You might see me smile a little but inside I’m shattered,” the Moroccan national said as he recalled swimming past bodies to reach Ceuta. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you. The Moroccan police were pushing us toward the water and telling us ‘swim, swim’.”Others were desperately seeking loved ones who were missing. One mother said she had been roaming the streets of Ceuta for days, frantically searching for any sign of her children, aged 13 and 16.She had left Morocco alone, finding out later that her two children had followed her by plunging into the sea to make their way around the border.“I need help,” she said as she held up a photo of a smiling young boy flashing a thumbs-up sign. “Some migrants told me they had seen them in Ceuta, but I can’t find them.”10:29How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The LatestAcross the EU, the crisis in Ceuta had seemingly ushered in a moment of reckoning after a handful of EU countries responded to the crisis by calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Italy said it had suspended passport-free Schengen travel arrangements with Spain for one month, despite the fact that Ceuta is not part of Schengen.Before an emergency video meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday to address the crisis, Spain’s foreign minister said the country would demand solidarity from EU members after several had, in his view, “fallen short” of what was expected.“There was a synchronised reactionary international effort that very quickly amplified what was happening, spreading lies and fake news about the integrity of the Schengen area and about Spain’s actions,” José Manuel Albares told the broadcaster TVE. “Unfortunately, these falsehoods have even been amplified by some European governments.”What had transpired in Ceuta was “very unusual”, he said. “Spain currently has the lowest number of irregular entries on the Mediterranean route,” he added, while Italy “was the country with the highest number of irregular entries in Europe”.He said he had been in contact with Moroccan authorities throughout the crisis. “They showed a willingness from the very beginning to mobilise police forces to help stem the flow of migrants.”View image in fullscreenPeople wait outside Ceuta’s temporary migrant centre, which is at full capacity.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersUrsula von der Leyen, theEuropean Commission president, said in a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, that the Tuesday meeting would be a chance to draw lessons from what happened in Ceuta, and she commended Madrid for its swift handling of the crisis. “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points,” she said.At a meeting of member states on Saturday, the Guardian was told that while Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, had criticised Spain for what had happened, there was a strong suspicion that the crisis was not an accident but had been coordinated.There was widespread recognition that Spain could not simply pin the blame on Morocco, given the close cooperation needed to return those who had crossed and, in the longer term, for migration control and security, a source said.EU states also spoke about the threat of Russian disinformation and how it could exploit the crisis to heighten tensions across the bloc, the source added.The concerns came into public view late last week when Ukraine’s acting foreign minister said more than 1,500 publications regarding Ceuta had been identified in pro-Russian networks.“We have detected an intensive Russian propaganda campaign across Europe using pictures from Ceuta to sow destabilisation,” Andrii Sybiha wrote on social media. “This is not about the situation itself but about the way Russia tries to exploit any topic that can benefit its agenda.”Explore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoEuropean UnionEuropeAfricaMigrationMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Former neo-Nazi activist selected as Tory candidate for Somerset council election | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Joshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Joshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP
Content: Joshua Bonehill-Paine has previously described himself as a ‘nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights’.Photograph: Channel 4 News/YoutubeView image in fullscreenJoshua Bonehill-Paine has previously described himself as a ‘nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights’.Photograph: Channel 4 News/YoutubeConservativesFormer neo-Nazi activist selected as Tory candidate for Somerset council electionJoshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MPBen QuinnPolitical correspondentMon 3 Aug 2026 14.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former neo-Nazi activist with convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP has been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election inSomerset.Joshua Bonehill-Paine, thecreator of the viral Crewkerne Gazette series of AI clips, is due to stand for election to Somerset council next year in a new Crewkerne South district. He told the Guardian he was an executive member of the Tories’ Yeovil branch, working as an events organiser.“The branch and indeed party are fully aware of my past. Our chairman has been a vocal advocate and has supported me since I became a member of the party. I am very grateful for the support,” he said.Bonehill-Paine, who previously described himself as a “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights”, re-emerged in recent years as the creator of the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical online account that has gained a cult following.While notably critical of Labour and Reform UK, its skits have cast the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, in a favourable light.Rebecca Harris, the Conservative chief whip, wascriticised earlier this yearfor reposting one video in which Badenoch and the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, were depicted as characters in the gangster film Scarface. This was after Bonehill-Paine had been revealed as the person behind the account.Bonehill-Paine has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station, and was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester.Hewas jailed in 2015for more than three years after posting “vile” antisemitic material online ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally.In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at the then Labour MP Luciana Berger, who is Jewish, which included posting messages to his blog calling Berger a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”. He was also thefounder and leader of the National British Resistance, a far-right group.He told the Guardian on Monday that his criminal convictions had been spent and that he held various Home Office counter-extremism certifications. He said he had spoken alongside MPs where he talked about his past and highlighted antisemitism faced by Britain’s Jewish community.However, the Conservative party’s opponents on the right were quick to accuse the Tory leader of hypocrisy and being weak on claims to oppose antisemitism.A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Kemi claims the Tories have changed and they will have a new generation of candidates – it’s now clear what calibre of candidates they will be. Kemi claims to support the fight against antisemitism yet selects a convicted antisemite Nazi as a candidate. The hypocrisy is breathtaking.”The selection of Bonehill-Paine comes as Badenoch is accused of freezing out centrist Tories. Last month it emerged that all prospective Tory MPs must align with her pledge to scrap the 2050 net zero target and leave the European convention on human rights.At the weekend, a young Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network. Cody Butler claimed in a public letter that he no longer believed there was a home for one nation conservatism in the party.Badenoch told the BBC last week that she led “a brand new party full of new people” after it emerged that the former cabinet minister Grant Shapps had been rejected as a Tory parliamentary candidate.The Conservative party has been approached for comment.Get in touchContact Ben Quinn about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Ben using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories.
