title: NHS radiographers report rise in overt racist abuse by patients | NHS | The Guardian
description: Survey reveals medics were called ‘monkeys’ and ‘dirty foreigners’, and patients refused to be seen by black or Asian staff
Author: Tobi Thomas
Headline: Survey reveals medics were called ‘monkeys’ and ‘dirty foreigners’, and patients refused to be seen by black or Asian staff
Content: The head of the NHS Race and Health Observatory said: ‘There must be a clear, consistently enforced zero-tolerance approach’ to racism across the NHS.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe head of the NHS Race and Health Observatory said: ‘There must be a clear, consistently enforced zero-tolerance approach’ to racism across the NHS.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianNHSNHS radiographers report rise in overt racist abuse by patientsSurvey reveals medics were called ‘monkeys’ and ‘dirty foreigners’, and patients refused to be seen by black or Asian staffTobi ThomasHealth and inequalities correspondentMon 3 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNHS radiographers are experiencing racist abuse by patients, who have called them “monkeys” and refused to be seen by black and Asian staff, according to a report.A survey of 381 members of the Society of Radiographers revealed a “noticeable” rise in instances of overt racism experienced and witnessed by radiographers across the health service over the past 18 months.Examples included staff being called “dirty foreigners”, patients complaining about the skin colour of those attending to them, and patients making comments in front of staff about “people coming over here and taking our jobs”.One patient made jokes about a radiographer’s headscarf and complained they couldn’t understand her; she speaks with a mild Yorkshire accent. Another patient waiting to be X-rayed refused to accept a black radiographer and said: “Black people frighten me.”The chief executive of the NHS Race andHealthObservatory, Prof Habib Naqvi, said such cases were a “sobering reminder of the racism, prejudice and hatred that persist in our society, and of the profound impact they have on healthcare staff and the communities they serve”.“They create real fear, trauma and anxiety among our diverse workforce, who continue to provide diligent, compassionate care to patients at some of the most vulnerable moments in their lives,” he said.“The NHS could not function without the skill, dedication and compassion of healthcare workers from across the world. We strongly condemn these reported racist incidents, and there must be a clear, consistently enforced zero-tolerance approach across the NHS, including in cases where patients display racist or otherwise unacceptable conduct.”Paul Awah, 39, a radiographer based in Bedfordshire who moved to the UK from Nigeria five years ago, has frequently experienced patients claiming they are unable to understand what he’s saying even though English is his first language.View image in fullscreenPaul Awah“Sometimes no matter how clear you’re speaking to a particular patient, a white patient, independent of whether the patient is sick or not, they just pretend not to understand,” he said.“They seem to understand people speaking with an Irish or a Scottish accent, but they claim to not understand me even though I am speaking clearly. Some patients also assume that we are not qualified.”For Awah, the current political climate and rhetoric about immigration from the far right has a part to play in the increase in racism experienced by NHS staff. “What used to be something people wouldn’t say, now the rhetoric has changed,” he said.“Immigrants are blamed for the cost of living, energy bills, the worsening situation in the country, and people feel it’s OK to say it.”Previous surveys have revealed the extent of racism directed at staff throughout the NHS. The Royal College of Nursing revealed in October that the number of racistincidents experienced by its members had risen 55%over a three-year period, while the latest NHS staff survey found thatone in five black and minority-ethnic staff had reported abuse, bullying or harassmentfrom patients or the public, compared with just one in 20 white staff.The chief human resources and organisational development officer at NHS England, Thomas Simonssaid: “Racist abuse towards NHS staff is completely unacceptable and has no place in our health service.“Our new national staff standards are clear that NHS organisations must take meaningful action to prevent and respond to racism, support affected staff and ensure there are clear consequences for patients who racially abuse or discriminate against NHS staff – including the option to refuse care in non-emergency situations.”Explore more on these topicsNHSRaceHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Athens suitcase death: suspect admits hiding body but denies murder | Greece | The Guardian
description: Police are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killing
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Police are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killing
Content: Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body was found inside a suitcase in Athens.Photograph: FacebookElisabeth-Jane Ross’s body was found inside a suitcase in Athens.Photograph: FacebookGreeceAthens suitcase death: suspect admits hiding body but denies murderPolice are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killingHelena Smithin AthensMon 3 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek authorities are investigating what may have motivated a 26-year-old Afghan man to kill aScottish charity workerfound dead in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens last month.Inquiries have focused increasingly on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s last few hours alive and police believe they hold the key to revealing why the 38-year-old was targeted.On Sunday the suspect, identified as Sharif Ahmadzai, was accused of intentional homicide after three days of questioning. He will appear before an investigating magistrate to be formally charged on Wednesday.George Kalliakmanis, the honorary president of the police officers’ association in Athens, told the Guardian the homicide division was now intent on discovering the motive behind “the murder” because the Afghan was continuing to deny any role in it, although he had confessed to hiding Ross in a suitcase.“He has admitted to carrying her body to the site. Police have CCTV footage of him doing this on the night of 16 July. He has also confessed to withdrawing €10,000 from ATMs using credit cards that belonged to her. But he has denied murder which police do not believe,” Kalliakmanis said.The Afghan, a professional boxer in the lightweight division, is believed to have arrived in Greece via the island of Lesbos as a child refugee at the height of Europe’s migration crisis 10 years ago.View image in fullscreenSharif Ahmadzai  and his wife, US citizen Alaina Hall. She is said to have played a ‘significant role’ in the investigation.Photograph: Twitter/XHe has been quoted as telling police he discovered Ross’s lifeless body in the first floor flat of an apartment block he helped manage in Exarchia, a bohemian district in downtown Athens popular among leftists, foreigners and NGOs.Ahmadzai, who married a US citizen and devout Christian, Alaina Hall, in 2023, had keys to the flat where their own refugee solidarity group, Love Every Nation, regularly met.Investigators have confirmed that Ross, a friend of Hall’s with similar volunteering experience and religious views, had moved to the apartment on 10 July after staying with Greek friends when she arrived in the Athens from Edinburgh on 26 June.Her last telephone call was made from her mobile phone on the night of 15 July – three days before her body was discovered by a homeless man in an abandoned building in Kypseli, about two miles away.Two possible scenarios in the run up to Ross’s death were being studied, police said. “We believe there was a confrontation,” said one source. “But was that spurred by Ross discovering the Afghan rummaging through her things and stealing her credit cards, or was it a case of sexual assault or the Briton spurning his advances?”View image in fullscreenSharif Ahmadzai arrived in Greece via the island of Lesbos as a child refugee. He has been accused of intentional homicide.Photograph: Twitter/XForensic scientists believe Ross was “likely asphyxiated” after an initial on-site postmortem, which showed there were no evident signs of injuries on her body. However, the autopsy was also deemed inconclusive because of advanced decay.Further toxicological tests and analysis of vital organs are expected to determine the exact cause of death in the coming days.Hall, who met Ahmadzai on Lesbos, is widely described as having played a “significant role” in the investigation.After allegedly becoming suspicious of Ahmadzai’s movements – and newfound wealth, the result of making cash withdrawals with Ross’s credit cards – she reportedly contacted the police, handed over cash he had given her and moved into a hotel.Adding to the mystery that has engulfed the inquiry, Ross’s phone was used for several days after her death, with text messages sent to family and friends. The messages were described as “deliberately misleading” by police, who believe they were sent in a bid to delay Ross being declared missing. One spoke of her “need to be alone”.“The Afghan’s partner was very helpful,” said Kalliakmanis. “From the day the victim was identified the investigation faced several challenges but thanks to the homicide division being so thorough they cracked it.”Police, who collaborated with the UK’s National Crime Agency and the Scottish service, combed through CCTV footage from cameras in the area where the suitcase was found and from banks where cash withdrawals were made before identifying the suspect.Explore more on these topicsGreeceEuropeScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump says | Iran | The Guardian
description: US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington
Content: Donald Trump said on Monday he expected negotiations with Iran on reopening the strait of Hormuz to begin imminently.Photograph: Allison Robbert/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump said on Monday he expected negotiations with Iran on reopening the strait of Hormuz to begin imminently.Photograph: Allison Robbert/EPAIranFresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump saysUS president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with WashingtonPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 3 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” forIranto forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday.Trump said he expected negotiations to begin in the next day or two to reopen the strait of Hormuz and create a pathway for Iran to address the US’s concerns about its nuclear programme.“The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearisation,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “And that will take a little while.”Trump reiterated that he was running out of patience with Iran. “This is the last chance for them to sign a good document.”Iran has been in discussions withOmanabout the creation of a temporary route through the strait that would allow commercial shipping to resume, but is not yet reviving talks with the US, Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said earlier on Monday.Esmail Baghaei denied claims by Trump that talks between the two sides covering all the major disputes between them could restart as early as Monday. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” he said.Trump claimed he had held off from launching the biggest strike on any country “since world war two” over the weekend after Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, rang him to urge diplomacy. Trump said the cancellation was conditional on Iran reaching a deal quickly.Trump says Iran talks set for Monday as Tehran and Oman discuss strait of Hormuz dealRead moreIt is thought to be the 12th time in the war between the US and Iran that Trump has called off threatened strikes.On Monday, the US president called the Iranian leadership “unbelievably duplicitous” in a post on social media.“They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg’, talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’. They then go on to give their usual blather in saying, theStrait of Hormuzwill be operated powerfully by them, when it is already completely controlled by the United States Navy and our ‘Blockade’.”A middle route through the strait would represent progress. Iran is claiming full sovereignty over the strait and has been making demands over its routes and future management, including the possibility of charging fees in return for providing ships with maritime services.One proposal is to create a joint Omani-Iranian company that would provide all the services that insurance companies used to provide at high costs, but at lower prices, and with preferential tariffs for some countries.View image in fullscreenIran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said it was discussing with Oman the possibility of an intermediate route through the strait of Hormuz to be used temporarily.Photograph: ReutersUnlocking a mutually acceptable route through the strait is the precondition to unlocking all the other agreements laid out in the memorandum of understanding, the ceasefire document both sides signed on 18 June. Disagreements about the memorandum’s obligations has led to a resumption of the war, which has spread to the Red Sea and to Iraq.Last week, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said Tehran was demanding that ships entering the strait take a route to the north close to Iran, but that some ships could take a southern route. Iran rejected the traffic being divided evenly between the two routes, and also that a third country could start de-mining the routes.Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran: “We are now talking about a corridor that will have a round trip route, not two or three separate routes. This intermediate route is to be used temporarily until a decision is made on a fixed route.”He framed the route as an alternative to the transport separation scheme, the longstanding prewar route overseen by the UN’s International Maritime Office. He said maps had been exchanged by the two sides.Baghaedi said an agreement on a route would not solve all the problems, pointing to the continuing US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, and that unless the US approach changed, there would be no significant improvement in the situation in the strait.Recently there had been gloom in Omani circles about reaching an agreement with Iran on routes, leading to a revival of preparations for Oman’s European allies to start to clear the southern route of mines, a step that might have provoked direct conflict between Iran and European powers.In a sign of the pressure Tehran diplomats face, a statement from the Assembly of Experts, the body of clerics that elects the supreme leader, warned against investing any trust in the US, saying: “Hope for understanding and agreement with this bullying regime will lead nowhere.”However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he believed the “memorandum of understanding would prove to be the centre of gravity of our foreign relations in the future”.The Saudis’ intervention came in a week in which Riyadh attacked Iranian-backed forces inside Iraq and raised the temperature in its dispute with the Iranian-backed Houthis in northern Yemen, underlining the extent to which Saudi Arabia fears the consequence of an all-out US war against Iran spiralling out of control across the Middle East.Additional reporting by Associated PressExplore more on these topicsIranStrait of HormuzUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaOmannewsShareReuse this content

title: More European countries’ FAs withdraw support for Infantino as pressure intensifies | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: The English FA and Serbia’s have followed Wales’s and Finland’s in dropping support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid as Fifa president
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The English FA and Serbia’s have followed Wales’s and Finland’s in dropping support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid as Fifa president
Content: Gianni Infantino’s decade-long reign at the head of Fifa remains under intense scrutiny.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s decade-long reign at the head of Fifa remains under intense scrutiny.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APGianni InfantinoMore European countries’ FAs withdraw support for Infantino as pressure intensifiesFA no longer endorses Fifa president for re-electionWales and Serbia join Finland in withdrawing backingNick AmesandMatt HughesMon 3 Aug 2026 15.24 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 03.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean countries began turning their backs onGianni Infantinoas moves intensified across the globe to end his crisis-hit tenure as Fifa president.The Football Association was the highest-profile of severalUefamember associations to drop its support for Infantino’s proposed re-election next year. It will write to Fifa confirming it no longer endorses Infantino for a fourth term in charge after the intense controversy surrounding his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors.Wales and Serbia publicly confirmed that they had withdrawn their backing, following a lead taken by Finland last week. Along with the FA, those federations had all previously written letters in favour of Infantino prolonging his tenure but patience has run out across the continent. The Swedish Football Association, which was one of five European FAs not to write letters of support, issued a statement confirming it would oppose his candidature in the election in March.Football Daily | Scrapped proposals, statement wars and the ongoing Infantino furoreRead moreThe FA had previously fallen into line behind Infantino, who will helm an extraordinary Fifa congress confirming the United Kingdom’s hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup in November if he is still in position. But it has been consistent in condemning his doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, publicly and in private representations. On Saturday it called for a “full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance”, and its latest move is a further escalation.It is joined by the Football Association of Wales, which said in a statement: “The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino for re-election asFifapresident for the 2027-2031 term.“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”View image in fullscreenSeveral Uefa nations are mobilising against the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Pierre Albouy/ReutersStriking a similar tone, the Football Association of Serbia explained recent events had “seriously damaged the reputation and credibility of bothFifaand its president”, saying a withdrawal was “the only logical and rational step”.In a sign that consensus may not be easy to achieve, the Swiss Football Association stopped short of abandoning its countryman. Instead it asked for “another personal exchange of views with the Fifa president” and said it would “continue to review the developments surrounding Fifa” before the leadership election.More countries are, however, expected to withdraw their support for Infantino in what amounts to a vote of no confidence. The intended effect is for the embattled president to resign although some insiders are braced for a drawn-out process. While the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which runs the sport in North and Central America, have both strongly criticised Infantino there has been no move by any of their individual federations to call back letters in favour of his re-election.Ensuring they do so may be critical to the ongoing efforts to remove Infantino quickly. There is acknowledgement in some parts of Europe that other continents should be seen taking the lead if enough of a groundswell for his departure is to be reached. Only 15 countries have publicly supported Infantino since he shelved the FFE project on Saturday but there is an appetite to form a broad coalition against his re-election quickly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is a contender to take over if Infantino is deposed. Montagliani is understood to be in consensus with the Uefa and AFC hierarchies that new leadership is needed at Fifa.View image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani consoles Lionel Messi after the World Cup final.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAIn another blow to Infantino, lawyers acting for Uefa have ordered him and other staff to identify, locate and preserve all documents related to the FFE scheme. Their letter includes Arsène Wenger, the Fifa chief of global football development, among those obliged to comply with its order. It says Uefa is “actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints ... arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan”.Thrive Eternal, the investment firm that had been expected to lead a group taking a 20% stake in FFE, is believed to have been sent a similar letter. JP Morgan, which was enlisted for an advisory role in the scheme, is also understood to have received an order related to FFE.On Monday afternoon the US State Department denied reports that Infantino had been scheduled to meet Marco Rubio, the United States secretary of state, in a bid to stoke up support for his continued reign as president.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoThe FAFifaFootball politicsUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Clacton voters need a serious person’: the independent candidates taking on Nigel Farage – and Count Binface | Clacton byelection August 2026 | The Guardian
description: Attieh Fard and Andy Erlam make their byelection pitch to voters, but Reform UK’s leader is conspicuously absent
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Attieh Fard and Andy Erlam make their byelection pitch to voters, but Reform UK’s leader is conspicuously absent
Content: Attieh Fard, an independent candidate in the Clacton byelection says it is ‘a shame’ Nigel Farage and Count Binface have failed to attend street hustings.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenAttieh Fard, an independent candidate in the Clacton byelection says it is ‘a shame’ Nigel Farage and Count Binface have failed to attend street hustings.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAClacton byelection August 2026‘Clacton voters need a serious person’: the independent candidates taking on Nigel Farage – and Count BinfaceAttieh Fard and Andy Erlam make their byelection pitch to voters, but Reform UK’s leader is conspicuously absentHelena HortonMon 3 Aug 2026 10.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the town square in Clacton, in the blazing midday sunshine, some of the candidates for the upcoming byelection made their pitch to a scattering of potential voters, passing Deliveroo drivers and a giant gull.But as the independent candidate Attieh Fard shouted into a megaphone that she would be a voice for Clacton, a passing youth shouted: “Where’s Binface?”At one of the hustings being held before polling day on 13 August, the two main contenders in the election, Nigel Farage andCount Binface, were conspicuous by their absence.Fard, a former Tory; and a fellow independent candidate, Andy Erlam, will be holding hustings at midday in the town centre of the Essex town every day until voting day. But Farage and the Count have failed to respond to the invitation.View image in fullscreenThe independent candidate Andy Erlam says the people of Clacton should not have a comedian representing them in Westminster.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAThe byelection has been regarded as somewhat of a joke by the main political parties, the media, and the novelty bin candidate, afterFarage triggered itamid mounting pressure over his finances. Rather than wanting the parliamentary authorities to adjudicate whether he should have declared a £5m gift from a crypto billionaire prior to being elected, Farage resigned his seat in parliament and asked the people of Clacton to decide.‘The lead singer is unavailable’: is Nigel Farage spending his summer in hiding?Read moreAll the large political parties thus decided not to stand, hoping the public would see the ridiculousness of Farage spending the summer, as Rachel Reeves put it, having an argument with a bin.New polling by Survation for Mandate Research suggests Farage would win 73% of the vote on a low turnout, but that 20% would vote for Jonathan Harvey, the comedian who pretends to be a space lord named Count Binface and who wears a bin as a helmet.But Fard, a smartly dressed lawyer, said: “Clacton voters need a serious person to vote for.”View image in fullscreenFard and Erlam take part in a street hustings.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA“Our democratic system should not be made into a joke or used in this way, this election should be about the people of Clacton,” she added.She said she was disappointed there had been no hustings arranged by the council or other local groups.“There has been nothing arranged; it’s been up to the candidates to organise hustings,” she said, “Farage should have shown up. I’m less surprised by Count Binface, whose campaign has been very much virtual and he said he wouldn’t show up in Clacton in person. But if either of them showed up we would probably have had a bigger audience for our hustings, so it is a shame.”One 62-year-old spectator, Roy Andrews, seemed convinced by Fard’s campaign. “I didn’t vote last time but she’s got my vote. She seems like a very nice lady. I’m not about to vote for a bin,” he told the Guardian.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage promotes his proposal to mobilise the navy to stop people crossing the Channel from France.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAFarage had a clash in his schedule: he was busy in Londonannouncing a policy to use warshipsto send people attempting to cross the Channel back to France.Fard said: “Our hustings tomorrow is the immigration themed one. So if he wants to tell the people of Clacton his views on this, he should attend.”Erlam, who was formerly an adviser to a Labour cabinet minister, told the small crowd that the anti-Farage vote should not be given to a bin. “Westminster is a jungle, and you don’t want a comedian to represent you.”On the Reform UK leader’s failure to attend, he said: “Nigel Farage and his team have not responded, it remains to be seen whether he will appear alongside the rest of the candidates as an equal.”View image in fullscreenFard and Erlam have committed to daily street hustings despite the hot weather and a lack of participation from fellow candidates and the public.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAFarage has kept somewhat of a low profile since he fired the starting gun on the campaign. Monday was his first national press conference since May, and he has not appeared keen to debate with Binface or the other 32 candidates.Erlam was less impressed to be asked about Binface. “He is completely irrelevant,” he said. “The joke has run out. Only six candidates have bothered to put a leaflet in the post, they are who need to come to the hustings.”Despite the lack of presence from the two frontrunners, and the seeming apathy gripping most of the residents of Clacton, the hustings will continue to be held every day. “We will be here to answer questions from the people of Clacton every day. It is up to Nigel Farage if he decides to find the courtesy to respond to our invitation,” said Erlam.But on a sunny August day, the people of Clacton seemed more interested in the sandy beach, the amusement arcade and the rides on the pier than listening to what their would-be MPs had to say.View image in fullscreenCount Binface was also one of the candidates in June’s Makerfield byelection, which the now prime minister, Andy Burnham, won.Photograph: Jon Super/APCount Binface told the Guardian that the invitation had been lost in his inbox.He said: “I’m very sorry to have disappointed the candidates who took part, and I’m even sorrier to have disappointed any constituents who came to listen. If I’d known about the event, and if I couldn’t have made it, I would have at least sent through a written statement as I have done at previous elections.“I did visit the constituency last week and really enjoyed meeting local residents in Clacton and Frinton, and I’m hoping to be able to do more in the days ahead. I can certainly say already that the people and the area are fantastic, and whoever wins the byelection, they deserve a devoted MP.”Reform UK was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026Nigel FarageCount BinfacefeaturesShareReuse this content
