title: ‘They are such neat, busy little folk’: the unexpected superpowers of the common woodlouse | Insects | The Guardian
description: This detritivore – known by a range of colourful names – tidies up our world and can withstand toxic pollution
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: This detritivore – known by a range of colourful names – tidies up our world and can withstand toxic pollution
Content: The woodlouse hasn’t needed to make many design refinements over the years because it found such a useful niche from the start.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe woodlouse hasn’t needed to make many design refinements over the years because it found such a useful niche from the start.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Insects‘They are such neat, busy little folk’: the unexpected superpowers of the common woodlouseThis detritivore – known by a range of colourful names – tidies up our world and can withstand toxic pollutionRevealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the yearPatrick BarkhamMon 3 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChucky pig. Slater. Monkey pea. Roly-poly. Boat-builder. Butchy boy. Cheeselog. Hobbling Andrew. Wood pig. If there were a prize for the range and joyfulness of a creature’s English-language names, the humble woodlouse would undoubtedly triumph over its million-plus invertebrate rivals.Over centuries of easy cohabitation with humans, it has acquiredmore than 300 regional namesin Britain alone, and many more in other languages (such as Gwrach y Coed, “witch of the wood”, in Welsh).There are lovely words for woodlouse actions too: an animal rolling its body into a neat ball is known as conglobation, or volvation in zoology.Their nicknames reflect our fondness for this most accessible of isopoda, an order of crustaceans, which is found in houses and gardens across Europe and the US.View image in fullscreenA common shiny woodlouse (Oniscus asellus).Photograph: Henk Wallays/AlamyThe common rough woodlouse,Porcellio scaber, is more widespread and found in South America and Australia too but it does not curl up in a ball. Hopefully, woodlouse voters in all continents can set aside their love for their local representative and consider the common woodlouse to stand for the entire 5,000-species-strong suborder.The woodlouse was a trendsetter, its ancient ancestors moving on to land about 500m years ago, long before most animals. The woodlouse hasn’t needed to make many design refinements over the years because it found such a useful niche from the start. As a detritivore, it feeds on rotting plant matter and breaks down wood.Sally Roe, one of many Guardian readers to nominate the woodlouse, has a good story. When she installed biodegradable bamboo kitchen countertops, she used an offcut in the garden to weigh down the cardboard suppressing weeds in her pumpkin patch. After a (successful) harvest, she moved the solid slab of bamboo and found a large colony of woodlice underneath. “The formerly very solid, very heavy slab of bamboo worktop was now a paper-light wood honeycomb,” she says. “Woodlice demonstrated to me extremely clearly that something being ‘biodegradable’ relies heavily on invertebrates.”As well as tidying up our world, another of the woodlouse’s superpowers is its ability to withstand toxic pollution and even store heavy metals within special compartments in its body. Studies have shown it canhelp stabilise heavy metals in compost.View image in fullscreenA common pill woodlouse (Armadillidium vulgare), another of the many types of woodlouse – this one commonly found in Europe and familiar to many of us.Photograph: Natural History Museum/AlamyMany readers have expressed their love for what one calls “detrivore royalty”. Another wants to get a woodlouse tattoo (great idea!). Chris Pickard is consoled by their longevity. “They will undoubtedly be here long after humans have followed dinosaurs and dodos into the extinct category,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd if you aren’t smiling at all their great names, you can invent your own. Peter Gregory calls them the “bumbling mumbling ombudsmen”.So if you’re looking to celebrate an invertebrate that’s just brilliant company, vote woodlouse!It’sinvertebrate of theyear again! From August 3-12, every day we’ll be profiling one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated, and then, when you’ve got to hear about all of them, we’ll open the voting soyou can choose your favourites. Don’t hesitate to get in touch with thoughts and ideas: email us at environment.desk@theguardian.com with Invertebrate in the subject line.Explore more on these topicsInsectsInvertebrate of the year 2026WildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Celebrity Hunted review – if this lot can outwit our national security, we’re all in trouble | Television | The Guardian
description: This near-hour of frothing wildness, in aid of Stand Up to Cancer, is utter chaos – interspersed with awareness-raising videos full of dignity and grace
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This near-hour of frothing wildness, in aid of Stand Up to Cancer, is utter chaos – interspersed with awareness-raising videos full of dignity and grace
Content: Targets … Lucy and Brian Conley on Celebrity Hunted.Photograph: Colin Hutton/Channel 4/Shine TVView image in fullscreenTargets … Lucy and Brian Conley on Celebrity Hunted.Photograph: Colin Hutton/Channel 4/Shine TVTV reviewTelevisionReviewCelebrity Hunted review – if this lot can outwit our national security, we’re all in troubleThis near-hour of frothing wildness, in aid of Stand Up to Cancer, is utter chaos – interspersed with awareness-raising videos full of dignity and graceLucy ManganMon 3 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf it’s early August, it must be Celebrity Hunted’s annual series in aid of the charity Stand Up to Cancer. The dozen famouses must evade capture for two weeks, which is a shorter time than civilians are required to manage it. Is it because celebrity schedules are fuller or their brains emptier? By the end of the first couple of episodes, I know which way I’m leaning.The contestants, working in six pairs, include Britain’s last vaudevillian Brian Conley (“I’m like a coiled sponge!”) and his daughter Lucy (“Dad! Stop beingfunny”), TV property presenter siblings – a sort of hyphenate from hell – Scarlette and Stuart Douglas, plus comedians Jen Brister and Laura Smyth. In a game where predictability is the greatest – well, predictor – of failure, they may have the best plan. “I’m just not going to take my HRT for a week and let’s see what happens,” says Jen.At Hunter HQ, Ray Howard (whose every feature still suggests thrillingly that only this gainful and well-publicised employment is keeping him from laying waste to everyone within a 50-mile radius, and I for one am going into hiding the minute he is forced to retire) has gathered his team about him. As ever, it comprises ex-police and military types, counter-terrorist dooberries, cyberwhatsits, analysts and profilers. The last two are vital because no one else is qualified to say things such as: “They will be using the networks they have,” “They could be hiding in plain sight,” or, if operating at peak performance levels, “They may have gone out the back way.” These all-seeing gods direct the “ground hunters” as to where best they might cut the fugitives off at the pass, and they do it expertly badly.No matter how dim a prey may be – and God love the brace of children from Love Island, Chris and Toby, who dutifully tap in and out at the end of their Transport for London journeys and show HQ exactly where they are – the predator can be counted on to be dimmer, for at least as long as the producer needs them to be.The Douglases go on a live morning news programme to promote their new show but – oh, they are whisked away in a taxi just in time to avoid capture!Jen appears at a well-advertised gig in Brighton (“Jen is appearing at a well-advertised gig in Brighton!” announces one analyst, pretty much) but happens to have 400 Jen masks ready-printed (though not ready-strung with the necessary elastic) for the audience, to confuse any pursuers.Brian calls his friend and member of “the Prat Pack” Joe Pasquale on a phone he knows is tapped and gives him the time and address at which to collect him and Lucy. “Sometimes it’s gruelling and analytical work,” grins Howard’s right-hand man Dr Steve Hersee. “And sometimes they just tell you exactly where they are.” The Conleys still escape, though. This is where you find yourself hoping fervently that it is all exactly as staged as it looks. Because if the people in charge of our national safety and security can be outwitted by Joe Pasquale, we are all in much worse shape than we ever suspected.There are occasional outbreaks of competence, such as when one of the hunter team triangulates a phone belonging to the driver of the cab taken by ex-soldier and presenter JJ Chalmers and disability advocate Sophie Morgan and a phone it called during the journey. This gives them the name of the person who provided the fugitives with a switch in transport and thus the identity of the new vehicle. This is briefly reassuring, until you get to thinking about how widely and deeply we are all surveilled on the regular and how much information any bad actor at any time could get on us all … So it’s a good thing that Strictly Come Dancing stars Amy Dowden and Carlos Gu are on hand to distract us by attending Craig Revel Horwood’s gold-spangled 60th birthday bash on the grounds that Amy really, really wants to go and the hunters “can’t dictate what we do for the next two weeks! I’ve given up so much already!” But don’t worry – it’s still too early in the series for them to get caught and they are soon wading across a stream to freedom.At the end of each near-hour of frothing wildness, however, you are dropped into an ice bath of reality. Each episode ends with a story told by someone with cancer – or, in some cases, by those who have survived them. Unlike what has gone before, these are told simply and stripped of any kind of manipulation. They speak of unbounded love and unfathomable loss and they break your heart. They are there to raise awareness and money, and do so with dignity and grace. The rest? Utter chaos, in the service of good.Celebrity Hunted is on Channel 4Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewReality TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t understand what Gaz was singing. It’s about needing a hug’: how Reef made Place Your Hands | Music | The Guardian
description: ‘We were swept up in the moment and full of testosterone. The 90s wasn’t a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive’
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: ‘We were swept up in the moment and full of testosterone. The 90s wasn’t a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive’
Content: Gary Stringer and Jack Bessant of Reef play Glastonbury in 1995.Photograph: Brian Rasic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGary Stringer and Jack Bessant of Reef play Glastonbury in 1995.Photograph: Brian Rasic/Getty ImagesHow we madeMusic‘I didn’t understand what Gaz was singing. It’s about needing a hug’: how Reef made Place Your Hands‘We were swept up in the moment and full of testosterone. The 90s wasn’t a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive’Interviews byRich PelleyMon 3 Aug 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Bessant, bassWe were hanging out with the lovely producer George Drakoulias at Abbey Road. He said, “We’re going to bring in some instruments for you guys” – and replaced the fairly low-budget ones we’d been playing. I was given this beautiful 1960s Fender Jazz bass.Sometimes you pick up an instrument you’ve never touched before and immediately start playing stuff you wouldn’t normally play. It made me want to come up with something cool, James Jamerson-style, with that Motown feel. I found the riff that became the bassline to Place Your Hands, showed it to Gaz, and he came up with this chilled melody about going down by the water. When Kenwyn House, our guitarist, added that classic opening guitar riff, it changed from something mellow into something much more action-packed.It was just a lovely time to be alive. We were young and everyone in the band was talented, even though we didn’t really know what we were doing. We were rockers at heart, but we were very open-minded. We listened to everything from Motown and Bob Marley to Van Morrison’sCommon One– Summertime in England can still make me cry. I eventually bought an old Telecaster bass – you can definitely hear the reggae influence in the bass during the bridge to Place Your Hands.I’ve always thought the emotion Gaz brought to it was incredible, but I didn’t fully understand what he was singing about until quite recently. He explained that “put your hands on” was a metaphor for wanting a hug, to help him through the grief of losing his grandfather. I hadn’t realised at the time because we were young rockers, swept up in the moment and full of testosterone, with no time to think about anything. The 90s wasn’t really a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive – there were all the lads’ mags, and we were playing that game to an extent. We certainly didn’t discuss our feelings in the way we would now. Looking back, I think the lyrics are beautiful.I don’t think we’ll ever get bored of playing it because it’s so funky and full of rhythm and spirit. We’ve had quite a few lineup changes, and Place Your Hands is the song that has always pulled us together. It gets people dancing and putting their hands up – even though the lyric is actually “Put your hands on”.Gary Stringer, vocalsWe were signed to S2 in 1993, under the legendary figures Lincoln Elias and Muff Winwood. Our first album reached the Top 10, we had three Top 40 singles and played Glastonbury, so we were really happy. We were touring the west coast of the US with stoner-rock band Kyuss when Lincoln suggested we meet George Drakoulias, who had worked with Rick Rubin at Def Jam and helped discover the Beastie Boys. George turned up wearing flowing white robes, which made quite an impression, and we decided to go with him for the second album.We recorded three or four songs at Abbey Road. George hired a 1960s Fender bass. Jack was fiddling around with it and started playing what would become the bassline to Place Your Hands. Kenwyn dropped his guitar’s E string down to D and came up with the riff that sits over Jack’s bassline. At first, I sang it quite gently, but then thought: “That’s too airy-fairy.” We went to Los Angeles to finish the album with George, taking the bassline and guitar riff with us.The lyrics are about the death of my grandfather, Kenneth. I was on the tour bus when I got a call saying he had died. I went to the morgue and my auntie said: “Do you want to see Ken?” I’d seen a dead body beside the road while on a surfing trip in Morocco when I was 18, but this had a different impact. The lyrics are essentially asking for comfort – for a cuddle. That’s why it’s “Put your hands on”. I’m sure if it was “Put your hands up” the song would have been even bigger.Chris Evans was a huge supporter of the band and played the single to death on Radio 1. When you went on TFI Friday, it didn’t matter if you were Dave Grohl or Oasis – you had to do the It’s Your Letters segment and sing those words to the melody of the song you were on the show promoting. For some reason, our version of It’s Your Letters stuck. “Put your hands on” and “It’s your letters” have the same number of syllables, so they used it every week ever after.The video cost about £250,000. We were turning head over heels on wires that had to be threaded through holes cut into our trousers. Place Your Hands accounts for a lot of my income. If we had 10 songs like that, I’d be a multimillionaire.Reef perform atLakefest festivalin Eastnor, Herefordshire, on 8 AugustExplore more on these topicsMusicHow we madePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A rug helps anchor all the pieces’: how to start decorating your home | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Designers share tips on creating a space you love, from mixing eras and colors to not getting in your head
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: Designers share tips on creating a space you love, from mixing eras and colors to not getting in your head
Content: Illustration: Carmen Casado/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Carmen Casado/The GuardianHow to startWell actually‘A rug helps anchor all the pieces’: how to start decorating your homeDesigners share tips on creating a space you love, from mixing eras and colors to not getting in your headMadeleine AggelerMon 3 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 18.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHome is where you sleep. It’s also where you eat, work, cry, laugh, socialize and celebrate. It is a spatial extension of the self – which can make home decorating daunting to some.“People get in their heads about decorating their space,” says Drew Michael Scott, interior designer and founder of the lifestyle and decor brand Lone Fox. It can be hard to know where to start, what you can afford or accomplish, or if you’re getting it wrong.“Decorating your home is not that serious, and it’s nothing to lose sleep over,” Scott says. “Your house is probably never going to look like it belongs in a magazine, and that’s OK. The goal should be to create a space you love, and that will look different for each person.”Whether you’re moving into a new place, refreshing an old one, renting or buying, here are some tips from experts on how to start decorating your space.Why does decorating your home matter?If you’vedated straight menwho are in their 20s, you’ll know that some people don’t see the point in decorating.But research has shown that the physical spaces we inhabit can have a profound impact on our mental wellbeing and productivity – one small study showed thatcurved rooms, for example, increased creative thinking, and research showscluttercan increase levels of stress and anxiety.“Home is where you’re supposed to feel safe, happy and completely free,” says Imani Keal, content creator and interior decorator. “Loving your home is an extension of loving yourself.”And if you feel safe, happy and completely free in an undecorated apartment, that’s fine too.“If you don’t mind a blank space, don’t enjoy decorating and can’t afford to hire someone to do it for you, then live in your blank space,” says Scott.How do you start decorating your home?Identify how you need your space to function.“It won’t matter how nice [a space] is if it’s not functional,” says Tara Pallay, interior designer and YouTuber.Consider your day-to-day needs. Will your space need a lot of storage, comfortable seating or a workspace? Do you need to take other people’s needs into account, or a pet? Once you have the answers to the relevant questions, you can make a plan.Be honest with yourself about how you live. “If you watch TV regularly, hiding a TV for the sake of aesthetics is stupid,” says Keal.Think of how you want the space to feel.Once you’ve identified the function of a room, imagine how you want to feel in it, says Dani Klarić, interior designer and co-founder of the Euphoria Collective design group.“Do you want your bedroom to feel romantic and calming? Do you want your living room to feel playful and energetic? Once you identify an emotion, the design decisions become much easier,” she says.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Start with the big stuff.The items and elements that take up the most space visually – a rug, sofa, paint color – play a major role in the look and feel of a room, so experts agree it’s good to start with them and go from there.Scott recommends starting with a rug, because “a rug helps anchor all the pieces and helps determine the color scheme”.Make it personal.Mood boards and inspiration pics are great, but if you hew to them too closely, “you can end up with a technically beautiful home that looks like a storefront with no soul”, says Keal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKeal made a list of seven essential items you should include in a space when decorating: something you’ve made, something thrifted, something stolen (!), something gifted, something you saved for, something you’ve inherited and something you’ve earned.Even if you don’t have all seven, choosing items you have a connection to will make it feel more personal and alive.“If someone walks into your home and says: ‘This feels so you,’ then you’ve done it right,” says Klarić.Which rug is best for your room? 21 expert picks, plus tips on choosing pile, size and materialRead moreLet the space evolve.Too often, experts say, people feel pressure to finish a space quickly. But “the most beautiful homes are layered over time”, says Klarić. Buying everything all at once can make a space feel more like a showroom than a home.And if you make a design decision and decide you hate it? “Change it,” says Keal. “It’s not a big deal. Paint over it, sell it on Facebook Marketplace and buy something else. We’re decorating, not doing brain surgery.”More from How to start:How to start meditatingHow to start weightliftingHow to start budgetingHow to start runningHow to start finding your personal styleWhat are the biggest decorating mistakes to avoid?Not sizing properly.“People struggle a lot with scale,” says Scott. “Rugs are often too small, curtains too short and couches too oversized.”Other designers also bemoan undersized rugs. “The rug is almost always too small,” says Keal. “A 5’x7’ has no place in a living room.”Focusing too much on trends.“The decorating process should be about cultivating personal style rather than trying to copy what’s popular,” says Pallay.Following trends can also quickly leave a space feeling dated. “I always encourage people to mix eras, mix colors, and incorporate pieces that carry meaning,” says Klarić.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyHow to startDesignfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: On the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all time | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts at the Czech’s chip
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts at the Czech’s chip
Content: Antonin Panenka left Sepp Maier flailing in the 1976 Euros final, but not every attempt to emulate him has gone as well.Photograph: Colorsport/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAntonin Panenka left Sepp Maier flailing in the 1976 Euros final, but not every attempt to emulate him has gone as well.Photograph: Colorsport/ShutterstockSoccerOn the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all timeThe 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts at the Czech’s chipGuardian sportMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.30 EDTShareIt is 50 years since Antonin Panenka won the European Championship for Czechoslovakia with the most audacious penalty ever taken. His signature chip wasn’t instantly eponymous. A search of the British newspaper archives shows that it was barely mentioned until Francesco Tottidusted it offfor the internet generation at Euro 2000.It was at least another decade before Panenka was commonly used as a noun, and it did not have its own Wikipedia page until 2014, but in 2026 every football fan has an idea of what it means.The 50th anniversaryis the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts.A Panenka is in the eye of the beholder.Ben Lyttleton, doyen of penalties and author of the superb Twelve Yards,asked the man himselfwhat constituted a true Panenka. Their criteria is strict, based on the line of the ball, its trajectory and where it hits the net. But that disqualifies, among others, Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 World Cup final (“This penalty is the obvious misuse of the Panenka classification!”), so we’ve used a looser definition. If the ball was kissed rather than kicked, the penalty is eligible.Rob SmythView image in fullscreenThe man himself, pictured earlier this year.Photograph: Björn Steinz/The GuardianAntonin Panenka, 1976Czechoslovakia 2-2 West Germany (5-3 pens)This oneneeds no introduction.RSAntonin Panenka, 1979Czechoslovakia 2-0 FranceThe next high-profile Panenka came almost three years after Belgrade, when he fooled the France keeper Dominique Dropsywith a sensual chipin a vital European Championship qualifier. Czechoslovakia ultimately pipped an emerging France – Michel Platini et al – and finished third at Euro 80.RSDiego Maradona, 1984Napoli trainingMost of Diego Maradona’s penalties were high-wire acts, Panenkas in spirit, with the ball pointedly passed nowhere near the corner toensure maximum vaccination. We can’t find any examples of him taking an actual Panenka in a professional game, so we’re including one he took in training at Napoli. Two reasons: one, it’s Maradona; and two, the arc of his penalty shouldn’t be possible. But then we’d alreadyseen him do it in open play.RSEric Cantona, 1989Bordeaux 1-1 Beauvais (3-4 pens)In February 1989, Eric Cantona was famed more for attitude than ability, having served bans for a tackleof comic-book violence, insulting the France coach, and greeting a friendly substitution by blootering the ball into crowdand tossing his shirt. So Marseille loaned him to Bordeaux and, when a cup game against lower-division Beauvais went to penalties, he went last. Juggling his way to the spot,he tried a Panenka, but the effort held up in the wind before landing in a puddle, allowing the keeper, who’d gone the wrong way, to wander over and pick it up, confirming the upset.Daniel HarrisGianluca Vialli, 1990Monaco 2-2 SampdoriaIn the 20th century, certainly in England, a Panenka was generally referred to as a “cheeky chip”. It was also a favourite of a cheeky chap. Gianluca Vialli scored several for Sampdoria, often under extreme pressure:against Genoain the Scudetto-winning season of 1990-91, and twice during Samp’s Cup Winners’ Cup triumph of 1989-90.The firstwas against Borussia Dortmund in the last 16,the secondin the first leg of the semi-final against Arsène Wenger’s Monaco. Vialli scored two goals in four minutes that night, then two in three when Sampdoria beat Anderlecht 2-0in the final.RSMichal Bilek, 1990Czechoslovakia 5-1 USAIt’s neat that another Czech player was the first to try a Panenka at a World Cup, even if the circumstances were completely different. Czechoslovakia were 4-1 up in a group game against the USA when Michal Bilek, who had already scored one orthodox penalty, tried to pay tribute to 1976.He fluffed it. After making a simple save, the USA keeper Tony Meola barked: “Get that shit outta here!”RSGary Lineker, 1992Nottingham Forest 1-1 TottenhamNobody ever talks about the Panenkas that Gary Lineker scored. There were at least three for Tottenham, and we’re pretty sure he’s the first serial Panenka-er in English football. The first completed a hat-trick on live TV – a big deal back in 1990 – and led toa brief post-match discussionin which only one of Elton Welsby and Glenn Hoddle knew about the Euro 76 final. Lineker also scored “a nifty little Panenka”, as he put it, in a Rumbelows Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest.This one was particularly sweet– the keeper was Mark Crossley, a penalty-saving expert who had denied Lineker from the spot in the previous season’s FA Cup final.RSGary Lineker, 1992England 1-1 BrazilA kick remembered for comedic reasons, largely through Micah Richards and Alan Shearerchuckling about it every few months on their podcast. But at the time this was a moment of pathos and heartbreak,as Lineker passed up his best, if not his last, chance to equal Bobby Charlton’s all-time England goal record.Jonathan LiewView image in fullscreenWith a share of England’s goalscoring record for the taking, Gary Lineker dinks tamely into the arms of the Brazil goalkeeper Carlos.Illustration: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty ImagesEric Cantona, 1994Manchester United 1-1 Newcastle United (5-6 pens)In May 1994, Eric Cantona was untouchable, having inspired Manchester United to a league title then a double. In the FA Cup final,he’d gently rolled two penaltiesinto the same corner of the net, Chelsea’s Dmitri Kharine diving the wrong way as if compelled by the shamanic power of Gallic flair. But in a shootout against Newcastle at that summer’s illustrious Ibrox International Challenge Trophy, the success of his previous Panenka in 1989 persuaded him to try another. Pavel Srnicek obligingly dived out of the wayonly for the kick to sail over the baras United lost 6-5.DHDjalminha, 1995Guarani 2-1 InternacionalBrazil’s Djalminha, the maverick’s maverick, is best remembered for hissignature rainbow flick, so it’s no surprise he was partial to a rainbow kick from the penalty spot.The first of manywas scored against Sergio Goycoechea,whose elastic penalty saveshad taken Argentina to the final of Italia 90. “I noticed that he always jumped early and committed to a corner,” said Djalminha, “so I thought that was the moment to try the chip.” It quickly became tried and trusted.RSDwight Yorke, 1996Sheffield United 0-1 Aston VillaDwight Yorke was so sick of Mark Bosnich saving his penalties in training, he tried something completely different. It worked, so he promised to do it for real the next time Aston Villa were given a spot-kick. That was met with ridicule,but Yorke was true to his wordand settled an FA Cup tie at Bramall Lane with a goal that changed his life. “Suddenly,” said Yorke in Born to Score, “the football world was very aware of this cheeky young buck who had dared to execute such an outrageous spot-kick. I definitely detected an increased interest in me after that match.”RSGianluca Vialli, 1996Chelsea 2-4 WimbledonThere’s no Internet Panenka Database (IPDb), which makes it impossible to say categorically who did what when. ButVialli’s consolation Panenka, at the end of a game in which Chelsea were thrashed by a rampant Wimbledon, may be the first of the Premier League era. Neil Sullivan, who had been beaten from the halfway line bya very different kind of chipearlier in the season, came tantalisingly close to saving it.RSDwight Yorke, 1998Aston Villa 1-0 Arsenal“If the penalty taker has the bottle to do that, good luck to him,” said David Seaman,who was Panenka-edon the last day of the 1997-98 season. “There isn’t much a goalie can do except look pretty stupid when it goes in.” Or hold their position, which Seaman did when Yorke took another penalty against him nine months later in an epic league match between Manchester United and Arsenal. His bluff called,Yorke sidefooted wide.RSJohn Eyre, 1999Torquay 0-1 Hull CityIf only there was a transcript of the great Neville Southall’s internal monologue asthis piece of effronteryfloated gently past him.RSFrancesco Totti, 2000Netherlands 0-0 Italy (1-3 pens)In their Euro 2000 semi-final with the co-hosts, Italy put on a defensive masterclass while down to 10 men. In the inevitable shootout, Frank de Boer was denied by Francesco Toldo and Jaap Stam blasted his kick into orbit. Stam was immediately followed by Francesco Totti,whose falling leaf penaltyfoxed Edwin van der Sar and had the Dutch lurching towards despair. It also introduced the Panenka to a new generation.John BrewinView image in fullscreenFrancesco Totti brings the Panenka into the 21st century.Illustration: Henri Szwarc/Bongarts/Getty ImagesMixu Paatelainen, 2001Hibernian 0-0 HeartsA last-minute penalty to win an Edinburgh derby is the stuff of dreams – and nightmares.Mixu Paatelainen only took itbecause Hibs’ usual taker, Russell Latapy, had gone awol two days earlier. After scoring a hat-trick against Hearts earlier in the season, Paatelainen probably thought he could do anything. As his chipped effort sailed over the bar, he was disabused of the notion.RSThierry Henry, 2003Arsenal 3-2 NewcastleFive days after the Battle of Old Trafford, Arsenal kickstarted their Invincible season with a ding-dong win over Bobby Robson’s Newcastle. The winner wasteased softly down the middleby Henry. Maybe it was an unspoken message of defiance that Arsenal would continue to do things their own way. Maybe it meant nothing. Or maybe he was justtrolling Ruud van Nistelrooy.RSView image in fullscreenThierry Henry went full va-va-voom for his winning penalty against Newcastle.Illustration: Jamie McDonald/Getty ImagesMickaël Landreau, 2004Nantes 1-1 Sochaux (4-5 pens)For all the spot-kicks these keepers face, surely they’d understand the right and wrong way to disguise a Panenka.Not poor Mickaël Landreau. He had the chance to secure the 2004 Coupe de la Ligue final for Nantes, but his headlong dash failed to give his lob the requisite power. Sochaux ultimately flipped the result and won the cup.Jeff RueterLiam Lawrence, 2004Huddersfield 0-0 Mansfield (4-1 pens)Liam Lawrence scored 12 penalties, one short of Francis Lee’s English league record, to help Mansfield to the Third Division playoff final in 2003-04. When that game wheezed to a penalty competition, Lawrence was standing on the halfway line with his teammate Bobby Hassell (“a proper angry little fella”). Onthe Under the Cosh podcast, Lawrence remembered their exchange.double quotation markLLI’m gonna dink it.BHNo you’re not.LLI am, honestly. I’m gonna dink it down t’middle. He’s gonna dive; there’s no way he’s gonna stand there in a playoff final.BHLiam, don’t you fuckin’ dink that ball.He dinked that ball against the bar– “I got too much juice in my run-up” – to leave Mansfield 2-0 down after two penalties. “By the way,” Lawrence added, “the keeper did dive.”RSHelder Postiga, 2004Portugal 2-2 England (6-5 pens)Helder Postiga was a typical Tottenham signing of the era: a talent unfulfilled, sold at a loss after a single Premier League goal. His revenge on English football was to equalise in normal time of the Euro 2004 quarter-final and then send David James stumbling with Portugal’s sixth penalty,a kick so under-ampedit barely scraped over the line. Then Darius Vassell missed, the Portugal keeper Ricardo scored, and a tournament that England’s golden generation could have won had slipped from their grasp.JBPeter Crouch, 2006England 6-0 JamaicaThe then-Liverpool strikerscored an England hat-trickas part of World Cup preparations, yet many only remember him lifting the ballwell over the barfrom 12 yards. Arrogance certainly played its part, wanting to secure his treble in style, but he had to wait, earning the ire of the usually calm Sven-Göran Eriksson. “It was a golden opportunity to practise for a penalty shootout, but he made a joke out of it,” the head coach spewed. “He’s apologised.”Will UnwinView image in fullscreenJudging by his expression, Peter Crouch knew he’d got his penalty wrong as soon as he hit it.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesArtem Milevskiy, 2006Ukraine 0-0 Switzerland (3-0 pens)You’re excused if you don’t remember this one: it cameafter 120 minutesof the most soporific footballever played.RSZinedine Zidane, 2006Italy 1-1 France (5-3 pens)The nerve to do it in a World Cupfinal.The scene was nothing new for Zidane. He’d already bagged that brace eight years earlier against Brazil; it had to be him, in his last game, dinking it off the crossbar,past Gianluigi Buffon. It was going to be the dream sendoff – untilMarco Materazzi and the anger took over.Taha HashimView image in fullscreenZinedine Zidane steps up…Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen… and beats Gianluigi Buffon all ends up.Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Archive/PA ImagesYann Kermogant, 2010Cardiff 2-3 Leicester (agg: 3-3; 4-3 pens)To miss a Panenka is to embrace infamy. To do so in a Championship playoff is to be consumed by notoriety. In a shootout, with the decisive kick? Insanity. Kermogant, a useful French striker who found his home in England’s second tier,dollied his kickinto the body of the grateful Cardiff keeper, David Marshall. Kermogant is remembered for this moment above all others, possibly for eternity. He even hashis own Bonnie Tyler adaptation.JBSebastián Abreu, 2010Uruguay 1-1 Ghana (4-2 pens)If we were picking a Panenka XI, Sebastián Abreu would be one ofthe first names on the team sheet, so it’s apt that he administered one at a World Cup.A tumultuous quarter-final, best remembered for Luis Suárez’s handball and Asamoah Gyan missing a penalty in the last minute of extra-time, ended with the softest of executions.RSAndrea Pirlo, 2012England 0-0 Italy (2-4 pens)When England somehow prolonged their Euro 2012 quarter-final against Italy to penalties, and with his team leading 2-1 after two goes each, Joe Hart bounced and laughed, seeking to put Andrea Pirlo off … then plunged towards the corner as the ballwafted gently above him and in. “He felt I was too charged not to dive,” Hart reflected on a mood-switching moment. England missed their next two kicks, with two Italian successesfinishing them off. “I saw [Hart] making strange movements, so I hit it like that,” Pirlo confirmed afterwards.DHView image in fullscreenAndrea Pirlo icily dinks his penalty over a fired-up Joe Hart.Illustration: Matthias Schräder/APSergio Ramos, 2012Spain 0-0 Portugal (4-2 pens)For such a tactile defender, Sergio Ramos was surprisingly partial to a tender Panenka. His most important came in the Euro 2012 semi-finalagainst Portugal. Bruno Alvesmissed Portugal’s next kickand Spain went on to demolish Italy in the final.RSMaicosuel, 2012Udinese 1-1 Braga (agg: 2-2; 4-5 pens)The one that cost €20m. Maicosuel had just joined Udinese from Botafogo when his Panenkawas savedin a Champions League playoff against Braga. It was the only miss of the shootout. Udinese, coached by Francesco Guidolin, dropped into the Europa League and the big payday went to Braga. “I still can’t get it out of my head,” said Guidolin six years later. “It stalks me.”RSGraziano Pellè, 2012SC Heerenveen 2-2 Feyenoord (6-7 pens)Sudden death, the last 16 of the cup. You’re the seventh-choice penalty-taker, you have to score or it’s over, and you have the chutzpahto try aPellènka?RSRogério Ceni, 2013São Paulo 0-0 Corinthians (3-4 pens)No surprise that one ofthe great goalscoring keepersshould beat his opposite number with a Panenka. His reaction after scoring in this Campeonato Paulista semi-final shootout carried a simple message: it’s not personal, it’s strictly business. His São Paulo team lost anyway; Ceni thought he had kept them alive with a save from Alexandre Pato, but he wasfractionally off his line. Pato scored the retake emphatically.RSAlexandre Pato, 2013Gremio 0-0 Corinthians (3-2 pens)Five months later, Pato had to score to keep Corinthians in their Copa do Brasil quarter-final against Grêmio. It was an inopportune time to takeone of the worst Panenkas ever seen.RSAlexis Sánchez, 2015Chile 0-0 Argentina (4-1 pens)It’s impossible to top the historic significance of the definitive Panenka, but Alexis Sánchez came closer than anyone.His swaggering penalty, which barely left the ground, won Chile their first Copa América – andunlike Czechoslovakia in 1976,they were the hosts. The playful nature of Sánchez’s winning moment only added to the nationwide euphoria.RSAaron Ramsey, 2017Serbia 1-1 WalesThe Wales team of Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey and co regularly made history. In a World Cup qualifier in 2017, Ramseyunwittingly did soby scoring a Panenkaat the same endof the same ground in Belgrade where it all began. “I didn’t know,” he said, “but that is quite a nice touch.” In more ways than one.RSView image in fullscreenAaron Ramsey does a Panenka more completely than most.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/ReutersGeorge Calintaru, 2017Juventus Bucuresti 1-2 Steaua BucurestiA Panenka can seriously damage your health. When George Calintaru fluffed the chance to equalise for newly-promoted Juventus Bucuresti against Steaua with the last kick of the game, his teammates set upon him in frustration. He then punched a table in the dressing room and broke a finger.RSFedor Smolov, 2018Russia 2-2 Croatia (3-4 pens)Russia’s shock run to the 2018 World Cup quarter-final was soundtracked by raucous support. The crowd in Sochi met the occasion as a shootout with Croatia was all that stood between them and a semi-final. Pedants may contend thatFedor Smolov’s opening attemptlacked enough lob to qualify as a Panenka, but his tame prod up the middle made Danijel Subasic’s job easy to open the sequence in Croatia’s favour.JRLionel Messi, 2020Barcelona 2-2 Atlético MadridIf you’re going to bring up 700 career goals in an empty stadium,you might as well do it in style.RSView image in fullscreenLionel Messi’s penalty record is suprisingly human, but he got the one that gave him his 700th goal right.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty ImagesFara Williams, 2020Reading 3-1 Aston VillaThis unusual penaltyfrom Fara Williams might not satisfy the Panenka purists. But we’ve included it because it captures a recurring sub-genre: an all-time-great using the Panenka as an expression of undeniable superiority.RSAdemola Lookman, 2020West Ham 1-0 FulhamDuring his time at Fulham, Ademola Lookman attempted a Panenka against West Ham with the last kick of the gamebut his feeble chiplanded straight in the arms of Lukasz Fabianski. “I’m disappointed and angry,” said his manager Scott Parker in a rare momentof post-match honesty. “You can’t take penalties like that and he knows that.”Yara El-ShabourySanti Cazorla, 2021Al-Gharafa 0-2 Al SaddNot many players score orthodox penalties with their left and right feet, never mind Panenkas. Santi Cazorla is a member of the latter club – right footagainst Newcastle in 2014, left foot against Al-Gharafa in 2021.RSSergio Agüero, 2021Man City 1-2 ChelseaCity were set to secure the Premier League title but, in front of zero fans during Covid, Sergio Agüero did not feel the pressure. He decided tochip down the middle; Édouard Mendyalmost fell for itbut had enough time to get up and claim the ball. Chelsea went on to win, and Agüeroissued a public apology.WUView image in fullscreenSergio Agüero’s Panenka attempt almost, but crucially only almost, fools Édouard Mendy.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/AFP/Getty ImagesMarta, 2022France 2-1 BrazilBirthday gifts can be a pain to give, especially when the celebrant seems to have given themself the perfect present. Such was life if Marta was on your gift-giving list in 2022, with the Brazilian legend opening that day’s friendly against Francein sublime fashion.JRKarim Benzema, 2022Manchester City 4-3 Real MadridA moment of mischiefat the end of a pulsating and painfully serious match. Eight days later, Benzema scored a more orthodox penalty to put Madrid into another Champions League final.RSView image in fullscreenReal Madrid’s improbable run to winning the 2022 Champions League included Karim Benzema coming up clutch – again.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAchraf Hakimi, 2022Morocco 0-0 Spain (3-0 pens)If you’re going to put your country into their first World Cup quarter-final,you might as well do it in style.RSGaëtane Thiney, 2023Real Madrid 0-1 Paris FCWe can’t say for sure thatthisis the first Panenka in the Women’s Champions League, but it’s definitely the first to knock Real Madrid out of the competition.RSAntoine Mille, 2024Les Herbiers 2-2 Châteauroux (3-4 pens)In which the Les Herbiers goalkeeper Téo Hamelin is so affronted that, after savingone of the more pitiful Panenkasever taken, he flings the ball straight back at the unfortunate Mille.RSMarta, 2025Orlando Pride 2-1 San Diego WaveIf you have already missed your penalty, but opponents’ encroachment has given you a second chance, just how bold do you have to be to attempt a Panenka from the retake? That’s what Marta did in the NWSL for Orlando Pride in 2025,chipping in off the underside of the crossbarto secure a 2-1 victory over San Diego Wave, and remind everybody of her ageless class and skill.Tom GarryAlexia Putellas, 2025Roma 0-4 BarcelonaEven the greats fluff their efforts sometimes. Alexia Putellas, one of the best women’s footballers of all time, clipped a Panenkaharmlessly over the crossbarduring a Champions League victory for Barcelona when her team were only 1-0 up. She redeemed herself from the spot later in the match – that time, tucking safely into the bottom corner.TGTiaguinho, 2025Brazil U17 0-0 Paraguay U17 (5-4 pens)A Panenka is a dishbest servedcold.RSBrahim Díaz, 2026Morocco 3-0* SenegalBrahim Díaz had the chance to become a Moroccan hero when he won and then took a stoppage-time penalty that could have ended his country’s 50-year trophy wait. Instead, after a 16-minute delay caused by Senegal’s protests, his Panenkawas easily caught by Édouard Mendy. “He had a lot of time before taking the penalty, which must have disturbed him,” said the Morocco manager Walid Regragui. No kidding.Then again…YE-SView image in fullscreenBrahim Díaz’s miss saw Morocco squander their chance to win the Afcon. Or so we thought…Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesMohamed Salah, 2026Australia 1-1 Egypt (2-4 pens)Sixty-one penalties were taken at the 2026 World Cup. The surprise is thatMo Salah’s Panenka for Egypt in their shootout against Australiawas the only one. Fifty years after it came straight outta leftfield, the Panenka is now firmly part of the mainstream.RS

title: Vincent Pastore obituary | US television | The Guardian
description: American actor best known for his role as Salvatore ‘Big Pussy’ Bonpensiero in the US TV crime drama series The Sopranos
Author: Michael Carlson
Headline: American actor best known for his role as Salvatore ‘Big Pussy’ Bonpensiero in the US TV crime drama series The Sopranos
Content: Vincent Patsore, left, with James Gandolfini as Tony Soprano in a 2000 episode of The Sopranos.Photograph: HBO/Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenVincent Patsore, left, with James Gandolfini as Tony Soprano in a 2000 episode of The Sopranos.Photograph: HBO/Everett/ShutterstockUS televisionObituaryVincent Pastore obituaryAmerican actor best known for his role as Salvatore ‘Big Pussy’ Bonpensiero in the US TV crime drama series The SopranosMichael CarlsonMon 3 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe character actor Vincent Pastore, who has died aged 80, made Italian mobster roles his speciality, most notably playing Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero, one of the capos in The Sopranos. Although the character’s nickname came from his early career as a cat burglar,in a recent interviewPastore said the Soprano’s creator,David Chase, had written the part “for an actor who could play a tough guy but also could be sensitive. I saw Big Pussy as a man with a big heart.”In the show, Pastore’s Pussy balanced the violent intensity ofTony Sirico’s Paulie Walnuts. “It was like sharing the camera with an elephant,” Pastore joked about the much smaller but intense actor.View image in fullscreenVincent Pastore, third left, in The Sopranos, 2000.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyOne of The Sopranos’ most touching, if surreal, moments was centred on Pussy – and his demise. This came in the finale of series two, when Tony Soprano (played by James Gandolfini), in a fever dream while suffering food poisoning, realises who has been ratting the family out. Pussy, speaking to him as an eight-pound fish selling for four dollars a pound, confesses to Tony, and points out that the fish next to him are “sleeping”. As Pastore’s voice speaks, Tony says, “Don’t even say that,” as he realises agonisingly he will have to make Pussy sleep with the fishes too. The episode ends with Tony and two others (including a vengeful Paulie) shooting Pussy on Tony’s boat and tossing his body overboard.Pastore himself was born in the Bronx, but grew up in what he described as the “true Italian” neighbourhood in the Westchester suburb of New Rochelle, inNew York, where his father, John, was a school caretaker and his mother, Natalie (nee Santadonata), cooked part-time for the Italian men’s social club over which they lived. It was not a mob setting. “We saw bookies and loan sharks, but to play these parts you don’t rely on memories,” he said. “You use your own personality.”After high school, during the Vietnam war, he enlisted in the US navy, then studied drama at the Westchester campus of Pace University. He worked as a bouncer in nightclubs, and as a limo driver, eventually buying his own club in New Rochelle. His first break came when he drove the actors Matt and Kevin Dillon, also from Westchester. They came to his club, saw him in local theatre, and were impressed. Kevin offered support, but as Pastore began to land roles, the actorDanny Aiellobecame his mentor.In 1988 he made his film debut in the Canadian horror movie Black Roses. He played small parts in films, some of them very good, almost all of them involving crime. Between 1990 and 1995 he was in 15 movies, including an uncredited part inSidney Lumet’s Q&A.But the nature of his parts are reflected in his billing: “Man With Coat-rack” in Goodfellas, “Fat Tony” in Backstreet Dreams, “Tony Clams” in Who’s the Man, and “Copa Wiseguy” – from the Copacabana nightclub – in Carlito’s Way. His TV debut came in 1990, on the short-lived combined emergency services show H.E.L.P. withJohn Mahoneyand Wesley Snipes. Like many New York actors, including other Sopranos cast members, he played in four episodes of Law and Order. Pastore’s breakthrough role came in a comedy crime vehicle, The Jerky Boys (1995), as Tony Scarboni, right-hand man toAlan Arkin’s crime boss, who is crossed by the eponymous comedians.In 1996, he played a similar role in the HBO film Gotti, playing Angelo Ruggerio, the loyal No 2 to the New York crime boss John Gotti, played by Armand Assante, with whom he had worked on Q&A.View image in fullscreenVincent Pastore in New Jersey. 2014.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APIn 1997 he acted with Aiello in A Brooklyn State of Mind (with the future Sopranos cast member Jamie-Lynn Sigler), and in 1999 he was in the Hugh Grant comedy Mickey Blue Eyes.The Sopranos debuted the same year, and in 2000 he won a Screen Actors Guild award for outstanding performance in an ensemble drama. Though Big Pussy was killed off at the end of season two, his career took new turns.He had participated as a celebrity on the quiz comedy Hollywood Squares, but was soon in demand on the reality TV circuit. He was the host of Repo Men: Stealing for a Living, and lost 13kg on Celebrity Fit Club. He withdrew from Dancing With the Stars after a week, but his time on Celebrity Apprentice was marked by a feud withPiers Morgan. “Reality producers … to bring out the best or worst … place you in a bad improvisation scene with someone you genuinely don’t like,” he said.In 2007 he made hisBroadwaydebut in Chicago; the following year he also joined the cast of the daytime soap opera General Hospital. Pastore longed to do comedy; in 2009’s Oy Vey! My Son Is Gay! he was the father of the Italian boyfriend whose Jewish partner’s parents are more worried their son is with a non-Jewish boy than that he is gay.Still he was landing roles such as “Don Vito Perspirino” in Pizza With Bullets (2010) or “Amadore Condimento” in Made in Chinatown (2021). He returned to Broadway in Woody Allen’s Bullets Over Broadway: The Musical in 2014, and that year led the Columbus Day parade in the Bronx.He played recurring parts in Hawaii 5-0, Wu-Tang: An American Saga, and Gravesend, and had another leading role in the 2022 film The Black Caesar. He started a theatre company in 2021; his revival of the play Lamp Post Reunion starred Aiello. A new film, Bad News on the Doorstep, starring Chazz Palmintieri, Robert Davi, their sons Dante and Nick, respectively, and Sylvester Stallone’s daughter Sistine, has yet to be released.Pastore lived alone in City Island in the Bronx. His marriage to Nancy Berke ended in divorce; he is survived by their daughter, Renee.Vincent Dominic Pastore, actor, born 14 July 1946; died 1 August 2026Explore more on these topicsUS televisionThe SopranosTelevisionNew YorkBroadwayTheatrePiers MorganobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Finally, we have a PM for the digital age. But real change requires more than just being good on camera | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Connection with voters on screen only pays off when it’s matched with bold policies in the real world – as it has for Zohran Mamdani in New York, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Connection with voters on screen only pays off when it’s matched with bold policies in the real world – as it has for Zohran Mamdani in New York, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Andy Burnham taking a selfie during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield, 31 July 2026.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham taking a selfie during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield, 31 July 2026.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamFinally, we have a PM for the digital age. But real change requires more than just being good on cameraNesrine MalikConnection with voters on screen only pays off when it’s matched with bold policies in the real world – as it has for Zohran Mamdani in New YorkMon 3 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.03 EDTShareAndy Burnham is having a good time. I can’t remember the last time a prime minister (or indeed any high-profile British politician) actually looked as though they were enjoying what they were doing. I saw a clip the other day in whichBurnham rememberedarguing with his dad about the point of an English degree, quoted poetry and discussed the importance of mastering words. It was almost enough to make you feel sorry for Keir Starmer. In his entire time as leader of the Labour party and then the head of the government, Starmer delivered not a single unprocessed moment. No natural sentiment escaped the carapace. And here is his successor, practically oozing it.It matters. It’s good and healthy to have a leader who looks as though they want to be where they are. Whose approach isn’t that of a scold or a receiver who has taken control of the premises, or someone whose sole aim is to tenaciously clamber up to the top job and hold on for dear life.I hadn’t fully realised, until Starmer cleared off, how much his premiership gave off the sense that the public were doing a bad job. That it was somehow their fault Starmer wasn’t as popular as he thought he should have been. As though it were the public’s job to deliver stable government and stop being so restive and fickle; stop having feelings and opinions on your prime minister that show up in the polling. Poor Starmer,some said, smashed fatally against the rocks by the waves of the roiling, insentient electorate of an ungovernable country.Burnham’s approach restores the basic principle, lost for so long, that you have to woo people and establish a connection. Over the past two weeks, it looks as though it has been easier to get a replyfrom his X accountthan for business executives toestablish contactwith his team. The videos he is posting on social media are, by any measure, a remarkable departure from the old way of doing things. They collectively have a voice, an almost salesman-like pitch. They say “just hear me out”. If anything, Burnham’s posts on everything from the importance of learningpractical skillstoranking pub snacksshow how late British politics is to the game. My first sense of it all wasn’t of how revolutionary it was, but why on earth it took so long.The answer, of course, is that no one had the taste for it. The personalities of our last few prime ministers were not, to put it mildly, those of digital natives. Their styles were “cop”, “sidekick bully” and “Liz Truss”, rather than public-facing politicians keen to communicate via the platforms they actually use.Burnham’s performances may sometimes be perilously close to shtick, but he has an undeniable flair and energy for the sort of modern direct-to-camera address that could give him an edge in a media environment where the parameters have for too long been set by an overwhelmingly rightwing traditional media.Burnham knows all of this. A little too much, perhaps. The bar is in hell and so is the discourse. It takes very little to break through the grim record of the past few years and outdo stale TV and radio formats. It would be easy enough to post some good, sharp stuff on your own social media and call it a day. And if it continues that way – that is, an approach to communication which does not tackle the positions that made the atmosphere so fetid in the first place – then it will all soon become background noise, and then an irritant.Because digital political success is not just about being good on camera. Burnham’s style has been compared with that of the obvious originator of the model, Zohran Mamdani. But Mamdani shows that having aflair for direct communicationis only the first stage, the part where you get people on board. (His videos speaking in differentlanguagesduring the election campaign were gold.) You then have to keep at it and show you are new in both style and practice. That you are a strong advocate for people. And, most importantly, that you are a cheerful, unflappable threat to their enemies. “When I ran for mayor, I said I was gonna tax the rich,” Mamdani saysin a recent video. Then he comes up close, knocks the camera. “Well, today we’re taxing the rich.” His pied-à-terre tax, he told New Yorkers, will be levied on properties like the one he’s standing under, a penthouse belonging to the hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham the crowd-pleaser knows how to make friends, but he’ll be defined by how he makes enemies | Andy BeckettRead moreBurnham has already done some tangible good by starting out with policies focused on people’s pockets – on bills and bus fares and VAT relief – and with an evocative drive todevolve powerfrom London. He promises “a new political model and a new economic model”. Them’s fighting words. Or should be. But his narrative lacks a clear articulation of what actually separates the needy from the predatory. Yes, at this point it is revolutionary just to name the problems, let alone do anything about them. But it will not be enough.Burnham seems satisfied with figuring out what he can get away with without that epic fight; with broadly gesturing to how bad Thatcherism and neoliberalism are, but not actually slaying them. He won’t target the under-taxed wealthy because he doesn’t want to “create new divisionsand pitch people one against another”. He is willing to keep in place the punitive immigration regime of the previous administration (whilevalorising the foreign workerswho care for his father). And while it’s early days on foreign policy, things look to be business as usual, suggesting Burnham has little appetite for resetting international relations in a period of historic flux. Even though heapologised for Labour’s stance on Gaza, he continues the previous government’spermission for the US to use some UK bases for air strikes on Iran, and is entertaining, at leastaccording to Trump, friendly discussions on “North Sea Oil, Trade, the Military Alliance, Demining of the Hormuz Strait”. There looks to be no necessary reckoning afoot with the US’s calamitous actions in the Middle East.First you change the political culture, then you can change the political model. That culture is style and presentation and some policy, yes, but to really capture lightning in a bottle, you must show that intellectual and moral barriers are being redrawn. If there is any lesson to be gleaned from our age of short-lived prime ministers, it is that all ostensible advantages – landslides, huge polling leads, mandates to deliver Brexit – dissolve under the harsh light of insincerity born from timidity. Authenticity comes from congruence. Burnham might be able to get away with a lot of the effect and some of the substance for a while, but he will only be the revolutionary prime minister he promises he is – people will onlybelievethat he is – if he breaks something other than the fourth wall.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionZohran MamdaniSocial mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: The most dynamic countries are surging ahead with high-speed rail. Others, like Britain, are stuck in the station | Christian Wolmar | The Guardian
description: Around the world, these trains have boosted economies, development and prestige. The costs of missing out are high, says transport writer and author Christian Wolmar
Author: Christian Wolmar
Headline: Around the world, these trains have boosted economies, development and prestige. The costs of missing out are high, says transport writer and author Christian Wolmar
Content: High-speed trains depart from sidings at Nanjing South railway station, China, 30 June 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHigh-speed trains depart from sidings at Nanjing South railway station, China, 30 June 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesOpinionRail transportThe most dynamic countries are surging ahead with high-speed rail. Others, like Britain, are stuck in the stationChristian WolmarAround the world, these trains have boosted economies, development and prestige. The costs of missing out are highChristian Wolmar is the author of Fast Track: The Extraordinary Story of High-Speed RailMon 3 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTShareWith all our grumbling about trains – and it is close to a national pastime – it is easy to forget the successes. There is a tale to tell, for example, about high-speed trains, that goes beyond theendless wrangling over HS2.If you look at the history around the globe, as I have, you find that high-speed trains saved the railways. An industry that was gradually sinking into oblivion, thanks to motorways and aeroplanes, has been revitalised by a technological revolution that means trains travel faster, more safely and more comfortably.Over time, beautiful but inefficient steam engines and their dirty diesel successors have been replaced by sleek modern trains that shrink distances and provide a service that their rivals on either land or in the air cannot compete with. Train travel that had been in declinehas become the preferred mode of transportfor many journeys previously dominated by aviation.But this is a revolution that almost didn’t reach Europe. In 1964, Japan became the pioneer, creatingthe Shinkansen, known worldwide as the bullet train, in effect the first motorway on rail, with dedicated tracks, a small number of stops and an at the time unprecedented top speed of 210 km/h (130mph). Nowadays trains often run at 190mph and they mayroutinely reach 250mph before the decade is out.View image in fullscreenThe world’s first maglev passenger train in Shanghai, 11 August 2002.Photograph: China Photo/ReutersBut as Japan surged ahead, 1960s Europe had fallen out of love with trains.Beeching-type cutswere the order of the day across the continent and a new invention seemed in the 1980s to be about to supersede the iron road. This was levitation technology, with trains being elevated by air or magnetism and pushed forward at great speed by rocket propulsion or magnets. Tests in France of the Aérotrain saw it reach speeds of almost 270mph, while the German government was promotingmaglev technology, funding a line running between Hamburg and Berlin.Trains were 19th century, it was said, while maglev was a technology for the 21st. But then, just as with the hyperloop,Elon Musk’s recent failed reinventionof the maglev technology, the plans for maglev fell apart, as costs soared and the practicalities of developing a whole new system running into crowded city centres proved insuperable. A 2006 disaster on the German test trackkilling 23 peopleput paid to any hopes of reviving the idea.This victory of the railways over its rivals guarantees that trains will be operating across the world in the 22nd century. The victory by rail meant high-speed rail systems emerging first in France and then across Europe in Germany, Italy and Spain. In addition, 25 countries in the rest of the world, ranging from Morocco and Turkey to Taiwan and Uzbekistan, have high-speed rail systems or are developing them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAn anti-HS2 campaigner in Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire, 19 May 2021.Photograph: Maureen McLean/Rex/ShutterstockThe rewards are great, but the subject is always controversial because the route to high-speed rail is never easy. These are megaprojects costing sums with more zeros than any other government projects except possibly defence and space travel, and to see them through needs consistent government support, a clear understanding of their purpose and a long-term budget.In all the high-speed rail schemes across the world that I examined for my book, it was a struggle to find any that were completed on time and on budget. Most achieved one of these – the UK’s HS2 and the California high-speed project being the exceptions,failing miserably on both counts– and by and large they have been successful in attracting passengers and in many cases seeing off domestic flights on their routes. Who now flies between London and Paris, or indeed Barcelona and Madrid, or Rome and Milan? Mostly only people who are interlining, that is, transferring to another flight. The sensible choice for most people will usually be a pleasant train ride with fewer security hurdles to overcome and city-centre to city-centre travel.New high-speed lines have generally been designed to relieve congestion on the busiest existing railway routes, such as Paris-Lyon or Tokyo-Osaka. But high-speed rail has also been used as a catalyst for a wider modernisation scheme, notably in Spain, which surprisingly hasEurope’s most extensive high-speed rail network,with about 2,500 miles of line, as a result of a clear government strategy to use trains to create better connections between regions and the capital, Madrid. The Spanish government, noting the success of its initial line built for the Seville Expo between Madrid and Seville, then embarked on a national programme that revived a dying rail system and changed the image of the country from a poor relative of its European counterparts to that of a self-confident, dynamic nation. High-speed rail can help do that.But for the world leader,look to Chinawhich has built 70% of the world’s mileage of high-speed lines in under 20 years. The figures are so extraordinary that they seem almost unbelievable. There are now about 31,000 miles of high-speed line with about 10,000 services carrying an average of 10 million people daily.Here, too, though, it is more than just a railway. The officials I talked to while travelling around China on its stunning network were clear about this. Many of the early lines were built between the largest cities but now the system, which they hope to increase by at least 10,000 miles by 2040, is being expanded to smaller towns and cities to create a genuinely national network. This remarkable project is seen as a way of uniting the country in the same way the railways in Germany and Italy created nations out of these fragmented countries in the 19th century.That was the original concept in the UK when HS2 was first conceived andits progenitor, Andrew Adonis, registered HS3, HS4 and HS5 as companies. We can but dream that this will ever be realised. For the story of high-speed rail I found was of go-ahead nations embracing the future, while others, including alas Britain, are being left behind.Christian Wolmar is the author of Fast Track: The Extraordinary Story of High-Speed RailExplore more on these topicsRail transportOpinionTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: The right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen again | Ruben Andersson | The Guardian
description: The EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerable, says Ruben Andersson, professor of social anthropology
Author: Ruben Andersson
Headline: The EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerable, says Ruben Andersson, professor of social anthropology
Content: Spanish army infantry members speak with migrants near Ceuta’s border post, 2 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSpanish army infantry members speak with migrants near Ceuta’s border post, 2 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionSpainThe right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen againRuben AnderssonThe EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerableMon 3 Aug 2026 09.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTShareFor the European hard right and the White House, it seemed almost too good to be true: left-liberal Spain punished with a migration crisis of its own making.The histrionics came right on cue. As thousands of mainly Moroccan citizensstreamed into the tiny Spanish enclave of Ceutaat the tip of north Africa, Spain’s far-right party Vox decried a migrant “invasion”, blaming Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’sregularisationand leftist politics. The Trump administration did the same. A senior Israeli diplomat goaded Madrid over its “colonial” territories while Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area. Denmark and Finlandbacked Italy’s moveand, by the weekend, 22 EU leaders had penned aletterpointing an implicit finger at Madrid over its presumed failure to “relentlessly combat illegal migration”.But what these self-ascribed doyens of border control don’t want to understand is that it’s their panic and politicking over migration that has brought us here.Ceuta is hardly a poster-child for Spain’s otherwise liberal migration policy. Rather, since the 1990s it has been the prototype for Europe’s relentless border security battle. Drones, heat detectors, motion sensors, digital watchtowers, Moroccan Auxiliary Forces: Ceuta’s border is so thoroughly militarised that it puts even Trump’s barrier-building – let alone that of Greece, Poland or Finland – to shame.The paradox, as civil guards told me when I last visited in 2023, was that this militarisation had involved ceding control. “Rabat knows it can destabilise Spain with migration,” one chief said, as he reflected on themass entry of Moroccans in 2021, after Madrid had angered its partner by taking in Brahim Ghali, the leader of Western Sahara’s Polisario movement, for urgent healthcare. The heavily guarded fences have become a perfect foil for staging a migration crisis.While Morocco is usually tight-lipped about its intentions, at times its ministers have bluntly said it won’t play the “gendarme” of Europe unless its partners support its economic and political aims. The quiet at the border since 2021 had little to do with the aggressive security hardware, and everything to do with Madrid’s 2022 endorsement ofRabat’s planfor occupied Western Sahara. So why the latest crisis? While the facts and motives are still being established, it’s unlikely to be a coincidence that, only recently, Sánchez announced a “new phase” in relations with Algeria – Rabat’s arch-rival and supporter of Polisario.View image in fullscreenA man attempting to escape the police, Ceuta, 2 August 2026.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersSánchez blames the mass entry on people smugglers and misinformation about a recent Spanish supreme court ruling that prevents authorities from summarily expelling migrants who attempt to swim by sea to Spain’s territories in Africa. The official line from Morocco’s government is that the surge was due to “criminal organisations” and that cooperation with Spain is still “exemplary”. Yet blaming criminal organisations makes little sense: most of those who made it across were quietly returned within the day – unthinkable, if they had lost their life savings to pay smugglers. The social media rumour mill did mobilise people to cross; but crucially – according toSpanish intelligence– Moroccan law enforcement stopped controlling the border while its intelligence services failed to notify Spain about the online campaigns. Video clips and accounts from border crossers in numerous media outlets further suggest that law enforcement actively encouraged people to cross.It’s clear to anyone who knows the Ceuta border that nothing dramatic happens there without the Moroccan authorities letting it happen. Yet Spain is unable to call outMoroccoas it desperately depends on it. Instead, both Madrid and Brussels showered Rabat with praise this past week. This is the corner the EU has painted itself into: dependent on repressive and often undemocratic regimes that use migration threats for their own purposes.This has been a favoured tacticfor yearsacross the external EU borders, fromMuammar Gaddafi’s threatstoAnkara’s antics. And it’s all the more attractive to them thanks to the European obsession about unwanted migration – the higher the stakes, the bigger the rewards.The geopolitics are looking unfavourable to the EU. Since theAbraham accordswere signed in 2020, Morocco has strengthened its hand internationally through close alliances with the Trump and Netanyahu administrations. And those two governments see Spain as their arch-foe in Europe. This January, Rabat deepened its militarycooperationwith Israel. In April, a US House of Representatives committeestatedthat Ceuta and the other Spanish enclave of Melilla were “in Moroccan territory”. Israeli and Republican figures have made increasingly frequentnoisesof this kind. Recently, Morocco named ahighwaythrough Western Sahara after Trump.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreWhat all this points to is not necessarily some grand conspiracy. Rabat may well have sought to benefitopportunisticallyand then lost control of events. But it does suggest that what occurred in Ceuta was a geopolitical game with people as its pawns, leavingmore than 70 dead.European leaders have become so obsessed with “security” that they can’t see their own best interests clearly. Notably, one of the governments waving the threat of Schengen suspension was Denmark, which should know something about geopolitical blackmail against Europe. Coercive migration pressure,evidence shows, works best when destination regions are politically divided and prone to slanging matches. This is exactly what the far right and government leaders are now indulging as they nervously blame Spain and raise the spectre of another 2015 migration crisis.Having shown their hand to “partner” states and unfriendly regimes alike, these leaders will know exactly which button to push for maximum impact. Through their reaction, EU politicians are not only undermining Europeansolidarity– they are actively encouraging more crisis-generation, while abetting the anti-European forces in the White House and further afield.We need a different kind of migration politics that de-escalates panic instead of inviting it, that prioritises frank diplomacy over one-eyed “combat”, and that weakens the hand of hardmen and smugglers. European leaders could make a start on shifting this dynamic by not turning themselves into useful idiots at the first opportunity.Ruben Andersson is professor of social anthropology at the University of Oxford and author ofAge of Security: The Rise of a Global Obsession(William Collins) out 13th AugustDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
