title: AstraZeneca should stick to its winning formula. It doesn’t need a $400bn US mega-merger | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: The Anglo-Swedish drugmaker’s flirtation with a grand combo with US group Bristol Myers Squibb is baffling
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: The Anglo-Swedish drugmaker’s flirtation with a grand combo with US group Bristol Myers Squibb is baffling
Content: The strategy of AstraZeneca’s chief executive, Pascal Soriot, to supplement the company’s own development drugs with smart licensing and partnerships is a proven winner.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe strategy of AstraZeneca’s chief executive, Pascal Soriot, to supplement the company’s own development drugs with smart licensing and partnerships is a proven winner.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/ReutersNils Pratley on financeAstraZenecaAstraZeneca should stick to its winning formula. It doesn’t need a $400bn US mega-mergerNils PratleyThe Anglo-Swedish drugmaker’s flirtation with a grand combo with US group Bristol Myers Squibb is bafflingAstraZeneca shares fall 8.9% over merger talks with US cancer drug firmMon 3 Aug 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 14.49 EDTShareSir Pascal Soriot, chief executive of AstraZeneca, starts with huge credit in the bank, obviously. His long tenure has been a triumph, starting withthe against-the-odds victory over Pfizer’s charmless accountants in 2014.The $39bn (£29bn) purchase of Alexion in 2021looked a little over-priced at the time, but you could see how it sat well with Soriot’s sermons on the importance of backing science. The deal got AZ into the field of medicines for rare diseases, which should offer decades of growth.A flirtation witha grand combo with US group Bristol Myers Squibb(BMS), by contrast, looks baffling. What’s the big idea here? Why bet the farm on a $400bn (£300bn) mega-merger? The first challenge would be how to rip out a few billions-worth of costs to justify the takeover premium. Soriot has normally viewed such corporate exercises as anti-patient. And why do it now?In the absence of a statement by AZ – not even to confirm the basic accuracy of the FT’s initial report of talks with BMS – one must assume we’re in the territory of discussions that could end up being quietly ditched. One hopes that will be the outcome because the 67-year-old Soriot risks spoiling his legacy if a high-risk financial adventure goes wrong.A calamity must be a possibility since the acquisition of a $133bn (£99bn) rival would inevitably come with a large helping of debt. “If there is one company that doesn’t need financial engineering it’s AZ in our view,” commented Jefferies’ analyst. Quite.The only guarantee in buying BMS is that AZ would inherit the target’s patent cliff challenge that will see sales of its blockbuster Opdivo cancer treatment plunge between now and 2030. Expiries of major drugs can feel smaller if shared within a bigger group, so you can see why BMS would be minded to seek shelter, but it’s hard to understand why AZ would volunteer to pay for the umbrella.The theoretical appeal, perhaps, is the prospect of building a market-beating global colossus in oncology, the field that is also AZ’s greatest strength. But Soriot’s strategy of supplementing AZ’s own development drugs with smart licensing and partnerships, especially in China, is a proven winner. Why mess with the formula? US competition regulators may also have something to say about two leading oncology franchises being welded into one. Approval would be a long, and probably distracting, process.Plan A, by contrast, has the virtue of simplicity. It was only last week thatSoriot said he was “absolutely confident” of hitting AZ’s 2030 target for annual revenues of $80bndespite the failure of a heart disease drug in late-stage trials. He gave a typically bullish performance: investors should know the drug business involves the odd hiccup in the labs, so put one blemish in the context of the “20 high-value readouts due over the next 18 months”.The worry in the background is that Soriot’s enthusiasm for US risk-taking and innovation has somehow led to the conclusion that AZ needs to join the pharmaceutical establishment in the world’s largest market, never mind the fact that it is alreadyinvesting $50bn in US research and development and manufacturing.Last autumn, AZ“harmonised” its listing on the New York Stock Exchangeto give it equal status with the ones in London and Stockholm. “A global listing for global investors in a global company,” the corporate spin declared, but you didn’t have to be overly cynical to see how a new listing structure would make US deal-making simpler.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut not all US deals are alike. The thumping near-9% fall in AZ’s share price on Monday spoke volumes: shareholders of all stripes struggled to see the sense in a mega-deal with BMS.Viewed through patriotic British eyes, one can worry about AZ’s transatlantic drift or applaud the unusual sight of a UK-based company (for now, at least) being in the driver’s seat. Either way, though, the commercial logic has to add up. This idea just looks wholly out of character for AZ. It is best dropped.Explore more on these topicsAstraZenecaNils Pratley on financePharmaceuticals industryMergers and acquisitionsDrugscommentShareReuse this content

title: Liechtenstein’s archaic abortion laws need to be modernised. But a prince is standing in the way | Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel | The Guardian
description: Substantial hurdles are faced by women who have to travel abroad to access abortion, but Hereditary Prince Alois says he will veto any changes, says writer and campaigner from Liechtenstein Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel
Author: Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel
Headline: Substantial hurdles are faced by women who have to travel abroad to access abortion, but Hereditary Prince Alois says he will veto any changes, says writer and campaigner from Liechtenstein Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel
Content: Hereditary Prince Alois speaking at Liechtenstein's National Day celebrations in Vaduz, 15 August 2024.Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHereditary Prince Alois speaking at Liechtenstein's National Day celebrations in Vaduz, 15 August 2024.Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockOpinionAbortionLiechtenstein’s archaic abortion laws need to be modernised. But a prince is standing in the wayGabriella Alvarez-HummelThe hurdles for women who have to travel abroad to access abortion are considerable, but Hereditary Prince Alois says he will veto any changesMon 3 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.16 EDTShareThe first person Maria* called when she found out she was pregnant was her doctor. The second person was a lawyer. The single mother of one was in shock, and considering terminating the pregnancy. But she first had to make sure that she wasn’t about to do something illegal, because all she knew was that abortions were forbiddenwhere she lived. “On top of the emotional mountain that was already there, I also had to deal with this,” Maria told me.She also knew she wouldn’t get any information about abortions in her own country – that’s illegal too. After making her decision, she drove to a clinic across the border. It was a stressful, if short, 45-minute drive, at the end of which another hurdle was waiting: “Oh, you’re fromLiechtenstein?” the receptionist said, according to Maria. “Then you have to pay immediately – 680 Swiss francs (£620) please.” She was taken aback and asked: “What if I can’t pay that right now?” The receptionist replied: “Then you’ll have to come back tomorrow.”Liechtenstein has one of the strictest abortion laws in Europe. This is probably not something you know about my “micro-state” – you might think of its banks, of Alpine scenery and castles fit for a Netflix romance. But in between them live real people with real lives, and every year, anestimated 40 womenwho wish to terminate their pregnancy on their own terms cannot do so in their country.But if you ask Liechtenstein’s regent, Hereditary Prince Alois, our prime minister, or random people on the street, many will tell you the same thing: there is no problem at all. Since 2015, women arelegally permittedto have an abortion outside the country, and the external border is never more than a 15-minute drive away. And anyway, it is allowed if the woman was raped or if her health is at risk, so what more could you ask for?What I, and others who are part of a new people’s initiative aresimply askingfor is what is already standard in most European countries: decriminalisation of abortion up to 12 weeks, repeal of the national ban on information about abortions, and for the procedure to be covered by health insurance. Arecent poll showsthat 62% of voters would be in favour of it if a vote were held. It should be a done deal. But no matter what the people say: the hereditary prince has already announced that he would veto any change in the law, long before a single vote has been cast.Liechtenstein is not your typical European monarchy, and theprince’s poweris anything but ceremonial. Alois can veto any bill, dismiss the government or individual ministers, appoint judges, and propose changes to the law. He usually exercises this power with restraint, and has never actually used his veto. He has only threatened to use it once, in 2011, which was the last time a popular initiativetried to legaliseabortion. With the prince’s veto looming over the vote, it was rendered effectively pointless, leading to a historically low turnout, and a52% vote against.A national debate over the monarchy’s role ensued, culminating in a vote in which more than 76% chose to preserve the prince’sveto power. This happened though after Alois and his father, Prince Hans-Adam II, had threatened to leave the country if the vote didn’t go in their favour – a move that would have plunged our nation into a severe crisis.This is why it continues to be the case that speaking out in favour of legalising abortion is regarded as speaking out against the monarchy.Alois says that the present laws are there to protect unborn life, even though he acknowledges that the abortion bandoesn’t actually preventany abortions. And our prime minister, Brigitte Haas, says she’s pragmatic anddoesn’t see a problemwith sending women across the border. I have one question: have they ever spoken to a single woman who had to cross the border for an abortion? Because if they had, they would know that the abortion ban is indeed harming those affected in several ways.Since 2022, I’ve conducted more than a dozen interviews with women from Liechtenstein who had to seek abortion care outside the country. Their stories have several things in common.Just like Maria, Liechtensteiners who seek abortion care are completely on their own. A ban on information – the last one of its kind inEurope– prevents local groups and professionals from giving advice about procedures and where to go. Pressured for time by the 12-week limit for abortions in Switzerland and Austria, they have to make phone call after phone call to find the right clinic, for which they have to pay in advance, up to 2,500 Swiss francs (£2,360). They fear legal consequences, because many don’t realise that under Liechtenstein’s law only doctors are criminally liable. And they feel stigmatised by a law telling them to deal with their problems elsewhere. As Maria puts it: “You feel so awful when you want to do it, because it’s so taboo in this country. You feel like you’re a monster.”Alois’s veto announcement may have been intended to discourage people from signing the initiative or to demotivate us campaigners. The opposite has happened: many people felt even more motivated to sign, and in a country of about 41,000 people (only around 21,000 with voting rights), we received 4,970 signatures, the second-largest tally of signatories for a popular initiative in the country’s history – equivalent to 10.5m signatures in the UK or 13.8m in Germany.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA few weeks ago I went collecting some of those signatures in the streets of Vaduz. A dad with his two kids told me he had already signed, and his young daughter asked what we were doing. I said we were collecting signatures for a cause, and if we collected enough of them, all the people in the country could vote on it. Her father added: “Well, one person has already cast his vote.”There is only one man we have to convince. We hope a very clear vote might do the trick.Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel is a campaigner and journalist from Liechtenstein, focusing on reproductive rightsDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The right hates The Odyssey because of its ‘wokeness’ – but it missed an even bigger threat to its worldview | Peter Swallow | The Guardian
description: The new film extols the value of a rules-based world order. That’s far more radical than any casting decision says Labour MP and classicist Peter Swallow
Author: Peter Swallow
Headline: The new film extols the value of a rules-based world order. That’s far more radical than any casting decision says Labour MP and classicist Peter Swallow
Content: In Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, civilisation is collapsing as raiders defy Zeus’s law.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreenIn Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, civilisation is collapsing as raiders defy Zeus’s law.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesOpinionThe OdysseyThe right hates The Odyssey because of its ‘wokeness’ – but it missed an even bigger threat to its worldviewPeter SwallowThe new film extols the value of a rules-based world order. That’s far more radical than any casting decisionPeter Swallow is Labour MP for Bracknell, and the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on classics. Before his election, he was a classics teacher and academicMon 3 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTShareFor years, a small but vocal corner of the extremely online right has looked to the ancient world to justify its polluted brand of politics. The classicist Donna Zuckerberg (sister of Facebook founder Mark) wrote a book about it way back in 2018 calledNot All Dead White Men– a deep dive into the corners of the internet where misogynists pretend ancient philosophy can justify their hatred of minorities.You would think that these self-appointed guardians of the ancient world would be excited about a blockbuster retelling one of its greatest pieces of literature, the Odyssey. Especially when Christopher Nolan’s film has been getting rave reviews, “the vast majority … written by men”, as the Guardian’sCatherine Shoard has pointed out. The Odyssey is an action-packed thriller with a fight scene every five seconds. In many ways (and I don’t mean this as a criticism of Nolan; I loved the film for all its flaws), it’s a movie designed to appeal to their tastes. And yet.Many rightwing commentators have been railing atthe film’s perceived “wokeness”for months – since well before it hit cinemas. Nolan’s biggest crime seems to have been castingLupita Nyong’o, a black woman, as Helen of Troy, the entirely mythical daughter of Zeus. In other versions of her myth, she was born out of a swan’s egg alongside her mortal sister Clytemnestra and her two brothers, who were either gods or mortals depending on which one you read. I can see why they’re worried about inaccuracy …There have been plenty of other criticisms from keyboard warriors concerned about a lack of historical accuracy in a film adaptation of an entirely fictional myth. Having a PhD in classics means I agree with them that Corinthian helmets aren’t historically accurate to the film’s bronze age setting; having a sense of proportion and an understanding of artistic licence means I don’t really care.Elon Musk has, perhaps predictably, emerged as the loudest critic, even calling Nolan an “anti-White racist” and suggesting he might use Grok to create an AI-powered Odyssey movie “that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer”. But as ridiculous as that all is, the right shouldn’t hate Nolan’s Odyssey for its inaccuracies. They should hate it because of what it has to say about the very real, very Homeric concept ofxenia.Xenia, which Nolan translates as “Zeus’s law”, was an ancient custom that governed how people were supposed to treat strangers. Zeus’s law is absolutely original toHomer. In fact, it’s a pretty fundamental part of the poem. When I taught GCSE students about the Odyssey,xeniawas one of the first concepts I’d teach them. In Homer’s Odyssey, as in Nolan’s film, it drives how different civilisations and cultures are supposed to interact with one another in society. People (and monsters such as the Cyclops) who break Zeus’s law are punished; those who uphold it (such as Odysseus’s son, Telemachus) are rewarded.But Nolan’s take onxeniais unmistakably modern. To me, it feels like an allegory for the fraying, rules-based international system. Whether it’s state sovereignty being undermined by Russia, international maritime law under threat from China or Donald Trump’s disdain for global multilateral cooperation on everything from trade to defence to the climate crisis, the rules-based order established after the second world war is under threat.At the end of the movie – spoilers – Odysseus and Penelope see their entire bronze age Greek civilisation collapsing. This is based on an actual historical event, the Mycenaean collapse. In Nolan’s retelling, it happens because the people of the sea are raiding and warring, breaking Zeus’s law.The message for a modern audience is, again, not subtle: society will collapse if we abandon our rules-based international order. If Nolan’s film really is “woke”, this is why – because it’s fundamentally a film about the value of multilateralism produced for an increasingly nationalistic world. Musk and co seem to have missed this message. But it’s the real reason why they should hate the film. It pushes back against everything the hard right are trying to achieve and instead makes clear that a commitment to international diplomacy isn’t a nice-to-have – it’s a prerequisite to civilisation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd, yes, for all those complaining, that’s not in the original poem. Nolan’s film is a reimagining. But here’s the truth about classics. Nobody gets to decide how all those wonderful ancient stories get retold, rewritten for new times or redeployed to make new arguments or share new perspectives. No one person gets to own the ancient world. Especially notElon Musk.Peter Swallow is Labour MP for Bracknell, and the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on classics. title: My olive oil is uncool, apparently. Welcome to the world of microsnobbery | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: Social media has supposedly ramped up our impulse to judge each other on the most trivial grounds – but is this really a new thing, asks Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: Social media has supposedly ramped up our impulse to judge each other on the most trivial grounds – but is this really a new thing, asks Emma Beddington
Content: It may be tasty, but does it have astory?Photograph: Very Good/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt may be tasty, but does it have astory?Photograph: Very Good/Getty ImagesOpinionSocial etiquetteMy olive oil is uncool, apparently. Welcome to the world of microsnobberyEmma BeddingtonSocial media has supposedly ramped up our impulse to judge each other on the most trivial grounds – but is this really a new thing?Mon 3 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTShare‘Are we living in an “era of microsnobberies”? Writing inthe Washington Postlast week, the lifestyle influencer Victoria Wolff asserted that we are, claiming that the fragmentation of American taste facilitated by, and expressed through, social media had created a new phenomenon of “hundreds of tribes” judging each other on highly specific sets of status signifiers.Wolff cited a few–“your children’s lunch boxes, whether your roses are native and if your olive oil has a story”– thatleft me feeling like a grubby little peasant with my narratively inadequate oil, but also relieved not to live in Amagansett in the Hamptons, as she does. It sounds like a Nancy Meyers meets Edith Wharton hellscape. Indeed, I was reminded of reading earlier this year about the tiny-batch$80 (£60) fruit piesyou’re supposed to bring as a “hostess gift” in those parts (etiquette specialists advise Hobnobs remain an acceptable hostess gift in the eastern suburbs of York).I’m not convinced microsnobberies are new. If anything, when communities were more insular and less connected, surely the sets of rules they established were even more exacting and specific, the markers of difference in social status even more microscopic?I’ve just read Julian Barnes’The Man in the Red Coat, which paints “narcissistic and neurotic” belle époque Paris as a bitchy hotbed of microsnobberies, with incestuous social circles writing about trivial transgressions in place of today’s Substacks and Instagram posts. I bet even in the most austere 12th-century contemplative order, some unhappy monk was silently judging a novice’s “not quite us” stockings. It’s human nature, not a product of internet social atomisation – the impulse to judge each other, and feel judged, on minutiae is eternal.What’s Kylie’s favourite masking tape? How does Lena Dunham train pigs? It’s all out there – and I’m loving it | Emma BeddingtonRead moreThe only real escape I ever found was in living abroad. During 12 years in Brussels, I internalised the broad-brush macrosnobberies – the “right” areas; the (vital) hierarchy of chocolatiers; the holiday destinations of the most chic neighbours – but remained happily oblivious if I was introducing myself gauchely or buying beyond-the-pale condiments. Man, it was mentally restful and I miss it – I could be tempted to move somewhere new just to be blissfully socially clueless again.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on funerals: the law must change following Robert Bush’s crimes | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: An undertaker’s trial has exposed a regulatory blind spot. The public, as well as trade bodies, should be involved in shaping reform
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: An undertaker’s trial has exposed a regulatory blind spot. The public, as well as trade bodies, should be involved in shaping reform
Content: Karen Dry (centre), who used Legacy’s services for her parents’ funerals in 2016 and 2018, and other families involved in the case, speak to the media outside Hull crown court.Photograph: Scott Heppell/PAView image in fullscreenKaren Dry (centre), who used Legacy’s services for her parents’ funerals in 2016 and 2018, and other families involved in the case, speak to the media outside Hull crown court.Photograph: Scott Heppell/PAOpinionCrimeThe Guardian view on funerals: the law must change following Robert Bush’s crimesEditorialAn undertaker’s trial has exposed a regulatory blind spot. The public, as well as trade bodies, should be involved in shaping reformMon 3 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareThere are few more vulnerable moments in life than the days before and after the loss of a loved one. The rituals of farewell surrounding a funeral matter deeply. Hence the horrified public reaction to thecrimes of Robert Bushin Hull. Bush was sentenced last week to 20 years in prison for 67 offences including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.When his business, Legacy Independent Funeral Services, was searched, police found multiple bodies decomposing on racks. Bush had returned the wrong ashes to families, stolen money donated to charities and spent more than £42,000 on holidays over 12 years. In court, relatives revealed the distress caused; David Gorbutt, who scattered a stranger’s ashes in place of his wife’s, described feeling “abused”.The Competition and Markets Authorityproposed tighter regulationof the funeral industry in 2020. The independent inquiry into David Fuller – who abused the bodies of more than 100 women and girls in hospital mortuaries – includedregulation of undertakersamong its recommendations. Now, a year after that report was published, ministers have decided that they agree. New laws, which should be expected to include a licensing scheme, minimum standards and provision for inspections, are on the way.View image in fullscreenCourt artist drawing of Robert Bush.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAThis is the right call. It is a peculiar blind spot in UK law that a service as sensitive and essential as that provided by undertakers is unregulated; the Scottish government, recognising this, introduced its own system last year. And while Bush’s case is by far the most extreme of several recent ones, he is not the only undertaker to have beenjailed. Last year, another funeral director,Amie Upton, was banned from NHS mortuaries and maternity wards in Leeds after the BBC uncovered complaints about Florrie’s Army, a baby-loss service that she set up. Ms Upton has not been charged with any crime. But the Labour MP Mark Sewards has argued, rightly, that his constituents’ disturbing experiences with Florrie’s Army point to theneed for new laws.An enhanced role for local government would be in keeping with the government’s devolution push, and would require funding. Trade organisations have proposed a model in which they would play a part alongside the Human Tissue Authority. But while all options should be looked at, regulation must not be mistaken for a panacea. As in other situations where a position of trust has been abused, opportunities to intervene inHullappear to have been missed.About 65% of the more than 500,000 funerals that take place in the UK each year are handled by small, independent businesses. Regulation must be protective of them as well as of families who want to prepare bodies for cremation or burial themselves. Undertakers do a difficult job;those paying for their servicesare often extremely vulnerable. The likely increase in thecost of funerals, following tighter regulation, must also be taken seriously. Many people already struggle to afford them. It is vital to find out what the public, as well as the industry, want.It may be that laws concerning dead bodies require a widerreview, as the Law Commission believes. But the priority must be to find an effective, proportionate way to prevent rogue operators from setting up funeral businesses, and to identify any who already have. Grieving people ought to be able to have confidence in those they entrust with the bodies of relatives.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on events in Ceuta: chaos and tragedy are weaponised by the far right | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Instead of finger-pointing at Spain, mainstream EU leaders should be showing solidarity with its prime minister, Pedro Sánchez
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Instead of finger-pointing at Spain, mainstream EU leaders should be showing solidarity with its prime minister, Pedro Sánchez
Content: Migrants in Ceuta are escorted by Spanish soldiers towards the border with Morocco on Sunday.Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APView image in fullscreenMigrants in Ceuta are escorted by Spanish soldiers towards the border with Morocco on Sunday.Photograph: Bernat Armangué/APOpinionSpainThe Guardian view on events in Ceuta: chaos and tragedy are weaponised by the far rightEditorialInstead of finger-pointing at Spain, mainstream EU leaders should be showing solidarity with its prime minister, Pedro SánchezMon 3 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareAt least 72 people are believed to have died late last week, most of them drowned or crushed as theyjoinedtens of thousands of others in attempting to swim from Moroccan waters to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. Yet the scale of that human tragedy has barely registered, as Donald Trump has decried an “invasion” while European politicians exploit the crisis to serve their own agendas. If further evidence were needed of the way that the radical right increasingly distorts the terms of the migration debate in the EU, the last few days have furnished it.More needs to beunderstoodabout the drivers behind a shocking episode. Misinformation on social media – orchestrated or otherwise – appears to have played a big part, following a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily turned back. Moroccan authorities seemingly did little to prevent the chaotic exodus, which echoed previous smallerincidentsand focused international attention on a territory whose sovereignty Rabat contests. If there were online indications that such an incursion was a possibility, no alarm was sounded.The Spanish government, distracted by the need to combat ongoing wildfires, was utterly unprepared. But the vast majority of the 60,000 or so who crossed into Ceuta returned voluntarily across the border within 48 hours, some having aired grievances toreportersat the lack of work, decent wages and prospects available to them at home. The dangerous recklessness of their actions underlined the pressure-cooker levels of frustration beyond Europe’s external borders, particularly among the young.Pedro Sánchez.Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPASubsequently, the response of leaders such as Italy’s Giorgia Meloni has been predictable but deeply dispiriting. In a performative overreaction, Ms Meloni sought to demonstrate her hard line on irregular migration by temporarilysuspendingRome’s Schengen agreement with Madrid, though Ceuta has never been included in Schengen, and Italy and Spain share no border. Along with Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, she was also among 22 signatories to alettersent to the European Commission, suggesting that the liberal migrationpoliciesof the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – which, again, have no application in Ceuta – are undermining Europe’s security.Such posturing is largely intended for a domestic audience. Mr Merz, for example, faces a major challenge from the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in three imminent stateelections, while Ms Meloni is dealing with theemergenceof a new party that threatens her own right flank. The zeal of such forces to weaponise the immigration issue was shown by the speed with which the AfD’s leader, Alice Weidel,claimedthat the “likely destination” for most of those entering Ceuta was Germany.Hyperbolic rhetoric and finger-pointing will only undermine solidarity between European nations, and hamper attempts to deal effectively with the challenges of migration. It is impossible to cross from Ceuta into mainland Spain and the Schengen zone without passing through a checkpoint. It is also worth noting that the number of irregular border crossings into Europe in factdeclinedby 40% in the first half of 2026 compared with last year, partly as a result of better-coordinated preventive strategies. Instead of rounding on Mr Sánchez, mainstream European leaders should be pledging their cooperation in helping Spain to minimise the possibility of such a tragic incident ever happening again.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The best way to protect NHS patients’ data | NHS | The Guardian
description: Letter: A genuinely competitive market would prevent any single company’s decisions from putting the system at risk, says Prof Erika Denton
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: A genuinely competitive market would prevent any single company’s decisions from putting the system at risk, says Prof Erika Denton
Content: ‘Systems holding patients’ most sensitive data keep ending up with a small number of large suppliers.’Photograph: Lankowsky/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Systems holding patients’ most sensitive data keep ending up with a small number of large suppliers.’Photograph: Lankowsky/AlamyNHSLettersThe best way to protect NHS patients’ dataA genuinely competitive market would prevent any single company’s decisions from putting the system at risk, saysProfErika DentonMon 3 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.29 EDTShareYour article on the TPG/Optum UK deal, over the patient record system used by most GP practices in England, highlights a specific issue that is symptomatic of a much bigger problem (Alarm at NHS patient records being put under control of US private equity firm, 27 July). I’ve spent years working across the NHS, both in clinical radiology and in national policy roles, and this deal follows a pattern. Systems holding patients’ most sensitive data keep ending up with a small number of large suppliers.The real opportunity now is to build on the progress already under way, so that ownership of any single system carries less risk regardless of who holds it. NHS England’s own steps, from guidance on AI-enabled tools to the health bill’s proposed provisions on the single patient record, point in the right direction. What should follow on from that is straightforward: data hosted in the UK, a clinician signing off before anything changes in a patient’s record, and an audit trail that regulators and patients can actually check.The deeper opportunity is in the market itself. A genuinely competitive market needs suppliers working on open, standards-based systems, so that patient records aren’t trapped behind one vendor’s walls, and information is captured as structured, checkable data.TheNHShas already begun building accountability like this into how it works with suppliers, and there’s real value in going further, applying that same standard consistently to every supplier, wherever they are based, on open interoperability and clear governance. That’s what keeps any single company’s decisions from putting the whole system at risk. I’d rather see energy go into growing that choice, so that the NHS is never again this dependent on so few hands.Erika DentonHonorary professor of radiology, University of East Anglia; clinical adviser to AI care partner, HeidiExplore more on these topicsNHSEnglandHealth policyHealthData protectionlettersShareReuse this content

title: The buzz about fly infestations this summer | Insects | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article on the swarms of houseflies people are having to cope with in hot weather
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article on the swarms of houseflies people are having to cope with in hot weather
Content: ‘Any foodstuffs left out on a counter would immediately attract a variety of coloured flies within seconds.’Photograph: HHelene/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Any foodstuffs left out on a counter would immediately attract a variety of coloured flies within seconds.’Photograph: HHelene/AlamyInsectsLettersThe buzz about fly infestations this summerReaders respond to an article on the swarms of houseflies people are having to cope with in hot weatherMon 3 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.52 EDTShareMy experience of flies is that during the past 20 years or so there has been a significant decline in numbers – Highland midges not included of course (‘It makes you feel you’ve got a really dirty house’: what’s behind the UK’s plagues of flies?, 30 July).Memories of childhood summers in the 1950s and 60s are of endless sticky flytraps, typically placed near doorways in the house. Any foodstuffs left out on a counter would immediately attract a variety of coloured flies within seconds.Summer picnics could be a constant tussle against flying insects, including wasps. Sandwiches, even wrapped, presented a challenge that flies and wasps couldn’t resist. Pints of beer would encourage wasps to take up swimming until they became intoxicated. The swarms of butterflies this year are a different matter – and delightful sight to see.Mal JonesCardiffWhile I do not diminish the efforts of the people behind Buglife and the expertise of Erica McAlister quoted in your article, as we do need insects, I found the ideas presented to ameliorate fly infestations quite out of touch with a large number of people suffering from this plague.What about those of us who live in flats with no access to a garden to create a wildlife pond? Or those without the means to turn their outside space into a haven for wildlife? Placing a bucket on the veranda might work for those with the space, but those of us in flats must suffer without resolution.Jonathon MoloneyLeighton Buzzard, BedfordshireThe best solution is to fit permanent insect screens to all windows and doors. It can be expensive, but it’s a one-off cost. A major benefit is that it allows windows to be open at night for ventilation, while still preventing insects, especially mosquitoes, from entering. A problem in the UK is that most windows open outwards, so while screens can easily be fixed to the outside frame of the inward-opening windows here in Switzerland, the same would not be true in the UK.Let’s hope some smart, enterprising people can come up with a solution for UK windows.Dr Janet DawsonBennwil, SwitzerlandHere in the French Basque Country, our house is next to a sheep farm where several hundred sheep are housed, largely indoors, and in the summer we are usually beset by dozens of flies indoors. We have several barn swallows’ nests in our barn, which I carefully protect, but despite the swallows’ best efforts, the number of flies has always been annoying – until this year when we have had very few flies. The (inhumane) fly papers hanging in the kitchen are almost bare of prey. My first reaction was one of relief, although this was relatively short-lived as it was not long before I saw the decline in the fly population as an indication of the enormous and worrying decline in the overall insect population.Phil RuslingSaint-Jean-le-Vieux, FranceHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Radio presenters were 1966 World Cup heroes too  | World Cup | The Guardian
description: Letter: Andrew Keeley will never forget Brian Moore and Alan Clarke’s commentary on BBC radio
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Andrew Keeley will never forget Brian Moore and Alan Clarke’s commentary on BBC radio
Content: Bobby Moore is carried shoulder high by his teammates holding the World Cup trophy in 1966.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenBobby Moore is carried shoulder high by his teammates holding the World Cup trophy in 1966.Photograph: APWorld CupLettersRadio presenters were 1966 World Cup heroes tooAndrew Keeleywill never forgetBrian Moore and Alan Clarke’s commentary on BBC radioMon 3 Aug 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTShareGarry Richardson (England’s 1966 World Cup heroes were fun, humble and unlike today’s stars, 30 July) appears to make the assumption that everyone watched the 1966 World Cup final on television with Kenneth Wolstenholme’s iconic commentary. As a football-mad 10-year-old, I had the misfortune on the day of the final to be on our family summer holiday in the then sleepy village of Goathland, staying in a house with no TV.Hope rose when my dad was invited to watch the final at a neighbour’s who had one of the few TVs in the village and he asked if he could bring his children. When the neighbour learned that there were seven of us, he not surprisingly drew the line at a still very generous three, but as the fourth in line I missed out.Instead, I sat in the kitchen along with my mam and three younger sisters listening to the rarely mentioned but equally brilliant Brian Moore and Alan Clarke’s commentary on BBC radio. To this day, I still haven’t seen the match but nevertheless, like Garry, cherish my happy memories of it.Andrew KeeleyWarrington, CheshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Science funding cuts will harm Britain’s global standing  | Science policy | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial about the threat to research funding, including plans to close the Jodrell Bank Observatory
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial about the threat to research funding, including plans to close the Jodrell Bank Observatory
Content: An exhibition space inside Cern, Geneva. ‘Withdrawing previously secured funding has shocked international partners.’Photograph: Stefan PangritzView image in fullscreenAn exhibition space inside Cern, Geneva. ‘Withdrawing previously secured funding has shocked international partners.’Photograph: Stefan PangritzScience policyLettersScience funding cuts will harm Britain’s global standingReaders respond to an editorial about the threat to research funding, including plans to close the Jodrell Bank ObservatoryMon 3 Aug 2026 11.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTShareYour editorial rightly criticises the decision to cease funding the Lovell telescope from March 2028 (The Guardian view on the Lovell telescope: budget cuts to physics are bad science and worse politics, 31 July). There are additional reasons why this decision is so shortsighted. Modern astronomy is no longer simply physics. It brings together physics, chemistry, biology and computing to understand how the universe evolved and where we came from. The universe is an inexpensive laboratory in which we can study the interaction of physical, chemical and biological processes under conditions that can never be reproduced on Earth. Understanding how galaxies formed and evolved requires complementary observations across the radio, optical and infrared spectrum. The whole is greater than the sum of its parts.As a PhD researcher at Jodrell Bank in the 1960s, I saw first-hand how its innovations transformed radio astronomy. Jodrell played a pioneering role in the development of long-baseline radio interferometry, which links separate telescopes together to create virtual telescopes thousands of miles across. Removing the Lovell telescope from this network would weaken its ability to produce pictures of the radio universe with a sharpness comparable to that achieved by billion-pound space observatories such as Hubble.The Lovell telescope still plays a role in science diplomacy and it has long been a symbol of UK scientific leadership and hope. Ministers should think again.George Kildare MileyEmeritus professor of astronomy, Leiden University, the NetherlandsThe shortsighted attitude to science funding goes back to Margaret Thatcher. In the late 1980s I was briefly the economic adviser to the chief scientist, working in the Cabinet Office. The policy was to rate research funding on objective criteria such as the number of peer-reviewed publications and citations, and also to focus funding on research expected to have economic benefits in the near term. It was assumed that, as an economist, I would be a primary advocate for this approach. I argued that there was no methodology for assessing which research would turn out to be economically beneficial. There still isn’t.I also argued that the attempt to quantify research success by counting publications was leading to counterproductive effects – pressure to publish too much and too soon, multiple authors on every paper and a high-stress atmosphere that is fundamentally counterproductive to good research.I also found myself the sole advocate in the Cabinet Office for supporting research for its own sake – to advance human knowledge. We are made far poorer culturally as well as economically if we close the spaces in which talented people are given the time and funding to follow wherever their creativity leads them.Mick FosterChelmsford, EssexThe UK Research and Innovation budget is expected to rise to £10bn by 2030. However, UKRI consists of research councils (which mostly fund fundamental science) plus Innovate UK. The latter funds only companies, and only itsbudgethas risen. That for research councils has plummeted, by 40%-50% in real terms since 2011. As universities also grab a higher proportion of grants in “overheads”, the amount of actual science being funded is even lower. The flow of postdoctoral fellows needed to work in innovative industries is consequently being choked.Douglas KellOxfordThank you for an excellent editorial on the devastating cuts to major projects and research facilities, announced in a year when UKRI received a record budget settlement. The Large Hadron Collider beauty (LHCb) upgrade, a top priority of the European Strategy for Particle Physics, endorsed byCern Councilwith UK support, has been particularly hard hit. The announced withdrawal of funding risks cutting off a generation of UK scientists from the future of one of Cern’s four flagship experiments.The UK’s leadership in LHCb was built through decades of sustained investment. The UK should now reap the returns: graduates skilled in AI and data science; advances in semiconductors, materials and technology; students who are attracted to science by the opportunity to work at a world-leading laboratory; and, crucially, a reputation as a trusted partner capable of participating in and hosting major international projects.Withdrawing previously secured funding has shocked international partners. It undermines UK leadership, drastically reduces opportunities for PhD students and postdocs, and damages technological development.This investment represents less than 0.05% of the UK’s £10bn annual research budget. We hope that it will be swiftly restored.Paula CollinsLHCb deputy spokesperson, CernHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
