title: Yoga, kabaddi and the cut-price plan for Commonwealth Games survival | Commonwealth Games | The Guardian
description: Glasgow proved that a streamlined programme could hold the key to reviving the prospects of a seemingly doomed event
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Glasgow proved that a streamlined programme could hold the key to reviving the prospects of a seemingly doomed event
Content: Glasgow proved a popular Games with 87% of tickets sold.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGlasgow proved a popular Games with 87% of tickets sold.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth GamesYoga, kabaddi and the cut-price plan for Commonwealth Games survivalSean IngleGlasgow proved that a streamlined programme could hold the key to reviving the prospects of a seemingly doomed eventMon 3 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareHow good are you at judging a sun salutation or scorpion pose? I ask because yoga is under consideration as a sport at the nextCommonwealth Gamesin India. Less surprisingly, so is kabaddi. But if Amdavad 2030 really wants to find experts in landing seemingly impossible manoeuvres, or holding their breath in tricky situations, they should take the next flight to Scotland.Let us be frank. Glasgow 2026 has saved the Commonwealth Games, at least for now. AfterVictoria pulled out in 2023, the event was in limbo. Some feared it would never find a way out. Then Glasgow stepped in, less a knight in shining armour, more one that was a little dented and rusty, to put on an event from scratch in barely 20 months.‘Ready for next 100 years’: Glasgow 2026 chief hails revamped Commonwealth GamesRead moreIt didn’t help that the BBC did not televise it, but that is not the Commonwealth Games’ fault. The BBC offered a derisory sum, which left organisers with little option but to go with Warner Bros Discovery. For many, it was out of sight, out of mind. But those in Glasgow will testify these were a fun Games, full of heart and surprise.There were fears that few fans would show up. In the end, 434,000 of the 500,000 tickets were sold, putting the Games at 87% capacity. There were great stories too, such asJosh Kerr’s raw power in the mileandEmily Campbellthrowing the weight of a couple of beer kegs above her head like they were beer cans.It was so busy I never got the chance to write up one of my favourite interviews, with the South Africa swimmer – and Commonwealth medal record holder – Chad le Clos. At one point we asked after his father, Bert, who became famous at London 2012 for his celebrations, his beard andhis larger‑than‑life chats with Clare Balding, but has had cancer since.“He’s lost about 40kg,” Le Clos said. “He was 138kg. He weighs 99kg now. You won’t recognise him because he walks every day. But he still says: ‘This is my boy. He’s won 18, 19, 20, 21 medals. And he’s going to break the world record now.’ But people are like, ‘No, you’re not him. He’s the big old man, the Cookie Monster from the telly.’”Even at the end, Glasgow was flying by the seat of its pants. Usually, the closing ceremony is practised on stage until everything is honed to perfection. This one had to be rehearsed at a compound at the back of the Hydro, because the netball was on, before Simple Minds closed the show with Alive and Kicking.The Games is still that, all right. But for how much longer? We can all agree India will be spectacular. The opening ceremony is expected to be staged at the Narendra Modi Stadium, which seats 132,000. Many facilities are also already in place. India wants to stage the 2036 Olympic Games. It will not skimp on the trimmings.Katie Sadleir, the chief executive of Commonwealth Sport, says Amdavad will stage between 15 and 17 sports – up from Glasgow’s 10 – from three buckets: core, optional and traditional.The 10 core sports include athletics, swimming, gymnastics, boxing, netball and bowls. The five optional sports will be drawn from a list that contains cricket, triathlon and hockey. India can pick two traditional sports, which is where kabaddi and yoga may come in.However, Sadleir cautions that the traditional sports have to be played around the Commonwealth, have a recognised international federation and be World Anti‑Doping Agency compliant.That explains why she is more positive about kabaddi’s chances. Even if the possibility of yoga brings up the intriguing prospect of someone being asked for a sample while in a lotus position.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAlive and Kicking? Simple Minds perform at the closing ceremony for Glasgow 2026.Photograph: Steve Welsh/PABut the trickier question for the Commonwealth Games is what happens after 2030. Durban pulled out in 2017 as the 2022 host because the finances did not stack up and while Birmingham stepped in it lost a fortune. Glasgow was cheaper, but it was funded by the AUS$380m fine paid by Victoria when it withdrew. So can the Games really survive?Sadleir recalls a recent sports conference where she was sitting near the IOC president, Kirsty Coventry, and someone from the Brisbane 2032 Olympics. “I went right after Brisbane said they were going to raise $5.2bn. And I said, have I ever got a story to tell? We’ve gone from an £800m event to a £160m event because we’ve listened and we’ve learned.Top 20: Tom Jenkins’ best Commonwealth Games photographsRead more“The only way we can continue is by resetting, reimagining, and making the Games affordable. Glasgow is a proof of concept with that in terms of cost and using existing facilities.”But addressing the problem is one thing. Making enough to keep the Games going, quite another. While many remain sceptical, Sadleir is admirably indefatigable and optimistic.She points out that Glasgow raised £30m in sponsorship and commercial revenue in a short space of time. She also promises to look at ways to attract more big names, including using the Commonwealths as a qualifier for world championships. Certainly something needs to be done. If Keely Hodgkinson, Summer McIntosh and Julien Alfred don’t want to show up, then why should the rest of us?Sadleir says five countries are interested in 2034, including New Zealand and Nigeria, and to avoid another situation like Durban and Victoria, governments will have to be a bid underwriter in future. Abuja in eight years’ time anyone?Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth GamesCommonwealth Games 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Benjamin Nygren edges Celtic past Dundee for winning start to title defence | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Benjamin Nygren’s second-half header edged champions Celtic to a 1-0 home victory against Dundee in their Scottish Premiership opener
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Benjamin Nygren’s second-half header edged champions Celtic to a 1-0 home victory against Dundee in their Scottish Premiership opener
Content: Benjamin Nygren heads in what proved to be Celtic’s winning goal against Dundee.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenBenjamin Nygren heads in what proved to be Celtic’s winning goal against Dundee.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAScottish PremiershipBenjamin Nygren edges Celtic past Dundee for winning start to title defencePA MediaMon 3 Aug 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 20.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Nygren was quickly back on the goal trail as Celtic began the defence of their Premiership title with a 1-0 home win overDundee. Before the game, Celtic fans cheered as the captain, Callum McGregor, unfurled the flag which confirmed again a 14th title win in 15 seasons.It was all a bit flat in a first half with Martin O’Neill’s side struggling to get into their stride as the visitors posed problems. However, the Sweden midfielder Nygren, so prolific last season with 21 goals, struck with a close-range header in the 52nd minute and the goal proved enough to keep the three points in Glasgow as a new season got up and runningfor the champions.Scottish Premiership: Aberdeen’s late double stuns Hearts, St Johnstone edge thrillerRead moreCeltic supporters continue to call for new recruits to the squad but Camilo Durán, the Colombian striker signed from Qarabag reportedly for £5.5m, and Kasper Høgh, the Denmark forward who cost a club-record £11m plus add-ons from Bodø/Glimt, made their debuts.Alistair Johnston and Arne Engels, both attracting transfer interest, also started for the champions while the Dundee goalkeeper Owen Goodman came in for his debut.Høgh fired wide in the ninth minute after being set up by Nygren, then the Dane redirected an effort from Nygren past a post. Moments later at the other end, as the ball bounced around Celtic’s penalty area, Dundee’s Charlie Reilly hit the side netting with a shot from 12 yards.View image in fullscreenCeltic's Kasper Høgh (left) reacts after a missed chance against Dundee.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PASteven Pressley’s well-drilled outfit were finding joy with the high ball, either crosses or throw-ins and in the 33rd minute defender Owen Bevan got his head to the ball in the box but the Celtic goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo gathered comfortably.Five minutes later, Engels missed the best chance of the match to that point, unmarked in the visitors’ box, he headed a cross from Kieran Tierney past a post, before the Celtic left-back drew a fine save from Goodman with a close-range drive.The home side faltered at the start of the second half but when Tierney curled in a cross from the left, Nygren headed past Goodman from inside the box and the growing anxiety subsided.Quick GuideCeltic to play LASK in Champions League playoffShowCeltic will face LASK in the Champions League playoffs.Martin O’Neill’s side were drawn out first against the Austrian champions. The Linz-based club won the Austrian Bundesliga for the second time last season, finishing two points ahead of the defending champions Sturm Graz.The Hoops avoided a potential rematch with Kairat Almaty, who knocked Celtic out on penalties at the same stage last season following a goalless 210 minutes of action.The first leg will take place on 18/19 August, with the second leg the following week.PA MediaWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.O’Neill’s side probed with more purpose, the fans got more excited and the noise levels increased while Dundee’s attacks were more sporadic and less convincing, although the pace of Joe Bevan was cause for concern for the Parkhead defence. In the 67th minute Goodman threw himself down to his right to save a long-distance drive from forward Yang Hyun-jun.Celtic remained in control but as the second goal refused to arrive and the clock ticked on, some nerves returned. In the 82nd minute, Sinisalo pulled off a terrific save from the Dundee substitute Ashley Hay’s glancing header.Høgh missed another chance when he slid a shot past a post from six yards before McGregor cracked the upright with an effort from inside Dundee’s penalty area; James Forrest bent the rebound wide of the target.Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipCelticDundeematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Emma Raducanu to miss US Open with leg injury in latest fitness setback | Emma Raducanu | The Guardian
description: Emma Raducanu will miss the US Open because of the stress fracture in her right leg that she sustained during the grass-court season
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Emma Raducanu will miss the US Open because of the stress fracture in her right leg that she sustained during the grass-court season
Content: Emma Raducanu has not played since her defeat in the final at Queen’s Club in June.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenEmma Raducanu has not played since her defeat in the final at Queen’s Club in June.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAEmma RaducanuEmma Raducanu to miss US Open with leg injury in latest fitness setback2021 US Open champion out with stress fracture in legRaducanu also missed Wimbledon through injuryPA MediaMon 3 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmma Raducanu will miss the US Open because of the stress fracture in her right leg that she sustained during the grass-court season and forced her to pull out of Wimbledon.It is understood that following consultation with her medical team, Raducanu has concluded she will be unable to play in New York this month.Pat Rafter: ‘Why aren’t we producing players like Spain? I don’t know’Read moreWhile the news comes as no surprise given the nature of the injury and the fact Raducanu has only recently taken her first tentative steps back on court wearing a protective boot, it is another blow to the 23‑year‑old.Having made positive progress last summer, including winning her first matches at Flushing Meadows since lifting the trophyfive years ago, it has been a frustrating 12 months for Raducanu with more persistent physical issues.After a foot injury severely hampered her pre-season training, Raducanu spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness after initially falling unwell in early February. She finally returned for the end of the clay-court season having rehired Andrew Richardson, the coach who guided her to the US Open title, but the pair’s time on court together has been limited.Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career by reaching her biggest final since New York at Queen’s Club in Junebut it was that effortthat triggered her latest setback.She was not among the players named in Great Britain’s team for the Billie Jean King Cup finals in September and there must be question marks over whether Raducanu, who will slide from her current ranking of 49, will compete again in 2026.Raducanu did post an upbeat message on Instagram on Sunday from a break in Switzerland, calling it the “best reset ever”.Explore more on these topicsEmma RaducanuUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Vinícius Júnior to Arsenal doesn’t make sense. That’s why it may work | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta’s team and the Brazilian star could be a perfect match. It also could be a risk that ends in disaster
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: Mikel Arteta’s team and the Brazilian star could be a perfect match. It also could be a risk that ends in disaster
Content: Mikel Arteta, Vinícius Júnior and José Mourinho.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta, Vinícius Júnior and José Mourinho.Composite: Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonSoccerVinícius Júnior to Arsenal doesn’t make sense. That’s why it may workMikel Arteta’s team and the Brazilian star could be a perfect match. It also could be a risk that ends in disasterJonathan WilsonMon 3 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes what is needed is something different.There is a long history in football of counterintuitive thinking being successful, of the benefits of creative tension, of adding grit to the oyster to generate the pearl, but even so, the news that talks betweenVinícius Júniorand Arsenal on personal terms are progressing comes as something of a shock. Mikel Arteta’s great followers of a blueprint adding a free spirit like the Brazilian? Really?Vinícius returns toReal Madridthis week after the World Cup with movement on his future expected relatively soon. He has 12 months remaining on his contract and Madrid are keen either to tie him down to a new deal or to sell him while he will attract at least some kind of fee. As their squad rebuild goes on under José Mourinho, Madrid’s position is readily understandable. They have already signed Bernardo Silva, Denzel Dumfries, Marc Cucurella and Ibrahima Konaté this summer; removing Vinícius’s £420,000 a week (about $30m/year) basic wages significantly increases their financial headroom.The five big beasts are gone: who will be the Premier League’s next alpha manager? | Jonathan WilsonRead moreThere’s been a sense since Kylian Mbappé joined Madrid two years ago that having him and Vinícius together left the squad unbalanced. Why would you need two rapid forwards who both prefer to cut in from the left, particularly when Rodrygo, who tended to be consigned to the right before tearing his ACL in March, would also prefer to play from the left? Yan Diomandé is likely to confirm his move to Real Madrid from RB Leipzig this week. Although the Ivorian has said he would rather play on the right, he too has spent much of his career on the left.More broadly, Vinícius does not seem a natural Mourinho player. His pace and technical excellence are undoubted, but he has never been the most diligent at fulfilling his defensive responsibilities. Mourinho likes a forward who can improvise, and worked successfully with Cristiano Ronaldo at Madrid, but it’s difficult to see how he could indulge more than one such player at a time, and Mbappé will take precedence.But those concerns about tracking, about the willingness to stick to a gameplan, about the capacity to retain possession are just as relevant to Arteta as they are to Mourinho – arguably more so, as Arteta believes far more in structured attacking planning than Mourinho. Is Vinícius, after years of freedom at Madrid, really going to accept those rigid structures?It’s been fairly clear since the second half of last season thatArsenalwould be looking to strengthen their left side. The sale of Leandro Trossard to Beşiktaş did not come as a huge surprise. The 31-year-old is reliable and played a valuable role last season, starting 21 of the 38 league games and coming off the bench on a further 10 occasions, but there is not much stardust about him. Gabriel Martinelli started 11 league games and came off the bench 19 times, and his pace can be a great asset, but it’s no longer clear that he is at his best on the left. The signing of Eberechi Eze last summer looked like an attempt to add creativity from that flank but his tendency to drift infield when Arteta needs his left-sided forward to stay wide meant that by the end of the season he tended to be used centrally behind a striker.Vinícius would give Arsenal greater attacking thrust. At his best, under Carlo Ancelotti, he could transform a game in seconds. His pace, dribbling ability and finishing mean that no matter how stale a game seems to have gone, no matter how under pressure his team may be, they are never more than seven or eight seconds from a potential goal. It’s easy to see why Arsenal are tempted by him. He would immediately be their highest-profile player, adding a sense of direction to a summer that, at least from a recruitment point of view, has seemed to be drifting. Arsenal missed out on Morgan Rogers, who joined Chelsea, while Julián Álvarez, who would seem a much more natural fit on the Arsenal left, appears more likely to go to Barcelona, if sufficient financial levers can be pulled.But the fact Vinícius is not a natural fit may be part of the attraction. It was, after all, the season after signing Erling Haaland, far from a typical Pep Guardiola player, that Manchester City won the treble. A player who does not quite fit, who kicks against the general philosophy, can make a process team less predictable. The friction can produce valuable sparks.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaaland, it’s fair to say, is a different personality from Vinícius and, as a center-forward, there was never a worry he was going to leave his full-back exposed. Vinícius is a bigger risk. He would certainly be an expensive one, not just in terms of his own salary but the inflationary pressure that could have on wages at the club more generally.But he would also add a dash Arsenal have lacked that would make the accusation of being dead-ball plodders hard to sustain. And with Trossard gone, there is a left-sided hole that needs filling.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsFootballSoccer with Jonathan WilsonPremier LeagueArsenalReal MadridVinícius JúniorfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sigrid Haugset stuns Tour de France Femmes favourites by storming to stage win | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Sigrid Haugset, the Norwegian national champion, shocked the established order in the Tour de France Femmes by breaking away to take the overall lead
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Sigrid Haugset, the Norwegian national champion, shocked the established order in the Tour de France Femmes by breaking away to take the overall lead
Content: Sigrid Haugset enjoys the biggest success of her career after her dominant stage win.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenSigrid Haugset enjoys the biggest success of her career after her dominant stage win.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersTour de France FemmesSigrid Haugset stuns Tour de France Femmes favourites by storming to stage winNorwegian breaks clear in stage three to take overall leadHaugset: ‘I never thought it was possible, it’s unreal’Jeremy Whittlein PolignyMon 3 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSigrid Haugset, the Norwegian national champion, shocked the established order in theTour de France Femmes, breaking away alone for 90km, to take the overall lead after winning stage three to Poligny.“I never thought it was possible,” she said, after realising she had taken the biggest success of her career and the overall lead in the sport’s biggest race. “It’s unreal. I was so dizzy at the end. I know my boyfriend would be so angry at me for not celebrating, but I couldn’t. I could not lift my arms off the bike. It was impossible.”Tadej Pogacar will ride Vuelta a España in bid to complete Grand Tour trebleRead moreHaugset’s spectacular solo effort surprised the peloton’s leading teams and on the eve of the 21km individual time trial, from Gevrey‑Chambertin to Dijon, she leads by 2min 2sec from Kim Le Court.“I was thinking about all my teammates and everyone cheering from home, so I had to give it my all,” she said. “All done in the Norwegian champion’s jersey, too – it’s fantastic.We had looked at this stage and it was the goal for this Tour. I told my father I’d get some flowers today. Tomorrow is the time trial, but I haven’t worked on it this year so I will just enjoy it.”Haugset is the first Norwegian rider to wear the yellow jersey in the Tour Femmes. The 27-year-old’s lone effort began at the foot of the second‑category Col de la Savine and was marked by an intense pursuit from the former world road race champion Lotte Kopecky, winner of the points classification in all three Grand Tours.“I thought Kopecky would catch me,” Haugset said. “I can’t believe that she didn’t, but I kept on. The team car was amazing, pushing me.”Although, in what became an epic duel, Kopecky got as close as 10sec to Haugset, she was not able to find the power to finally close the gap and the Norwegian moved clear again to win the stage by almost a minute and a half.Temperatures in the high 30s made it yet another suffocating and stifling day on the route, with the ever-present iced drinks and ice socks passed up to the riders throughout the 156km stage.As the sweat-streaked Haugset held on to win, the first sparring match between the race favourites came on the Côte de Chaux‑Champagny, 25km from Poligny, where Le Court accelerated and temporarily left her rivals in disarray. But as the narrow climb went on, with brief tentative accelerations from Kasia Niewiadoma and Demi Vollering, the main contenders regrouped and with Tuesday’s potentially pivotal time trial looming large, a truce was called.There is some uncertainty over how well the defending champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, will fare in the winding test through the Routes des Grand Crus, which includes the sharp climb of the Lacets de Marsannay.View image in fullscreenSigrid Haugset is the first Norwegian to wear the Tour de France Femmes yellow jersey.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters“It’s a real challenge for me,” she said, acknowledging her lack of time‑trialling experience, certainly compared with Vollering and Le Court. The double Olympic gold medallist said she has spent several months working to improve her time trialling, but accepts that she will have to “limit the damage” against the clock.“We made sure to put me in a more correct position on the time‑trial bike. We also set out to do quite a few aerodynamic tests on the track, and to try to find the fastest outfit.”Even so, she appears to accept she will be on the back foot as the peloton heads into the Rhone valley on Wednesday. “It’s a possibility,” she said. “I don’t know how much time I will lose, but I will give my best to lose the least possible.”Ferrand-Prévot is not the only rider worrying about time losses, after the pre-race favourite Vollering crashed early in stage three, on the climb of the Col de la Faucille. The 2023 winner remounted and was active later in the stage, but her team carried out medical checks on an injured knee on Monday evening.Much of the south-east of France, which will host the summit finish to Mont Ventoux on Friday and the Côte d’Azur stages on Friday and Saturday, remains under elevated risk of wildfires.While the climb of the Ventoux scheduled for stage seven is expected to remain intact, the current routing of the stage through the Ventoux’s foothills could be affected.In a statement, the Vaucluse prefecture asked the Tour de France Femmes organisers to consider an alternative route. The prefecture is planning a risk assessment on Tuesday and has said that an “alternative route will be implemented should the wildfire risk be considered extreme”.Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maguire survives missed cuts and controversy to headline Solheim Cup wildcard picks | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: Leona Maguire has retained her place in Europe’s Solheim Cup team despite a disappointing 2026, with the Irish golfer one of four wildcard picks
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Leona Maguire has retained her place in Europe’s Solheim Cup team despite a disappointing 2026, with the Irish golfer one of four wildcard picks
Content: Leona Maguire’s strong record for Europe at the Solheim Cup counted in her favour.Photograph: David Dermer/APView image in fullscreenLeona Maguire’s strong record for Europe at the Solheim Cup counted in her favour.Photograph: David Dermer/APSolheim CupMaguire survives missed cuts and controversy to headline Solheim Cup wildcard picksIrish golfer one of four wildcard picks for EuropeRookies Ramirez, Nadaud and Rhodes also selectedEwan MurrayMon 3 Aug 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeona Maguire has retained her place in Europe’sSolheim Cupteam despite a disappointing 2026, with the Irish golfer one of four wildcard picks named on Monday by Anna Nordqvist.Maguire joins three rookies – Julia López Ramirez, Nastasia Nadaud and Mimi Rhodes – in completing the Europe side who will attempt to reclaim the trophy in the Netherlands next month.A missed cut for Maguire in the Women’s British Open last week meant the 31-year-old had failed to play in the closing 36 holes of four from a possible five majors in 2026. In the one where she made the cut, the Women’s PGA Championship, Maguire tied 53rd. She started this week ranked 83rd in the world.Kuwaki wins Women’s Open after Henseleit’s unlucky break off marshal’s leg in playoffRead moreThese numbers are striking for a player who was tipped for greatness at a young age. There is also the matter of the controversy that surrounded Maguire at the 2024 Solheim Cup when she admitted her limited play under the captain Suzann Pettersenproved a “bitter pill to swallow”. Maguire has enjoyed positive experiences in this arena in the past, however, having starred for Europe in the Solheim Cups of 2021 and 2023. The Irish golfer has also claimed eight and a half points from a dozen Solheim Cup matches.“I would rather play alongside her than against her,” Nordqvist said of Maguire. “She is such a fierce competitor and will do anything for you on the team. I had the honour of playing with her in Spain [at the 2021 Solheim Cup]. Her matchplay record, as an amateur too, definitely helps. I’m excited to see what she can do.”Maguire’s experience was clearly key to Nordqvist’s decision. Another blunt reality is that European options were not especially strong. “I love the Solheim Cup,” Maguire said. “It brings the best out of my game and I love being part of the team.”Ramirez said she is “living the dream” after her maiden call-up. The 23-year-old from Málaga is yet to win a professional event. Nadaud did taste victory, at the Ladies European Tour event in Andalusia late last year. England’s Rhodes was the LET’s rookie of the year in 2025, when she won three times. Nordqvist hailed Rhodes as a “fierce competitor”.View image in fullscreenEsther Henseleit will bring form into the event after losing in a playoff at the Women’s Open.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PACharley Hull, Esther Henseleit, Lottie Wood, Maja Stark, Linn Grant, Céline Boutier, Carlota Ciganda and Nanna Koerstz Madsen sealed Europe’s automatic berths. Albeit more than a month has to pass until the Solheim Cup gets under way at Bernardus Golf, Nordqvist will have high hopes for Henseleit. The German was beaten to the Women’s Open titlein a playoff on Sundayby Shiho Kuwaki. In the second and defining extra hole at Royal Lytham and St Annes, Henseleit’s drive rebounded from the leg of a marshal and to the bottom of a gorse bush. Henseleit had no idea what had transpired when watching from the tee.“I thought it was further left to be honest,” Henseleit said. “It must have gotten some kind of bad bounce. At least I still had a shot and could kind of get a good angle going into the green. I didn’t have to take an unplayable or something. But, probably a bit unlucky there. That’s just links golf.”Angel Yin and Jennifer Kupcho secured spots in the US Solheim Cup team at the Women’s Open conclusion. Nelly Korda had already done likewise. Angela Stanford, the US captain, will name three captain’s picks after their qualification period ends in late August.Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupWomen's OpenGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Black Foils on crest of a wave in fight against destructive marine trawling  | Sport | The Guardian
description: New Zealand sailing team combine racing with campaigning for environmental and social impact
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: New Zealand sailing team combine racing with campaigning for environmental and social impact
Content: New Zealand's Black Foils achieve lift off during the Great Britain Sail Grand Prix in Portsmouth.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenNew Zealand's Black Foils achieve lift off during the Great Britain Sail Grand Prix in Portsmouth.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAThe HotspotSportBlack Foils on crest of a wave in fight against destructive marine trawlingNew Zealand sailing team combine racing with campaigning for environmental and social impactGeorge TimmsMon 3 Aug 2026 06.24 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Sailing on the Solent was awesome, but our racing … not quite perfect,” says Blair Tuke, co-chief executive of the Black Foils, New Zealand’s SailGP team, after finishing fifth at last month’s Great Britain Sail Grand Prix. It was only the team’s second competitive outing of the season after the boat had to be “pretty much rebuilt” following a big crash in Auckland in February, which forced them to miss four races.But the team’s work off the water hasn’t stopped in the boatyard. Before the race in Portsmouth, which coincided with the beginning of National Marine Week in the UK, the Black Foils were awarded the Better Planet award in SailGP’s Impact League that rewards teams for environmental and social impact alongside racing.The team won the award after Live Ocean – the marine conservation foundation Tuke founded with Black Foils co-chief Peter Burling – supported the Swim4TheOcean campaign. This saw the ultramarathon swimmer Jono Ridler complete an unprecedented 1,367km staged swim down the east coast of New Zealand’s North Island after 90 days and 468 hours in the water. Tuke describes Ridler’s swim as “one of the greatest endurance feats of all time”.Some 5,000 people gathered in Wellington to give Ridler a hero’s welcome in April, many walking with him to parliament where he delivered a petition with 73,647 signatures demanding an end to bottom trawling in New Zealand, a destructive fishing practice dragging weighted nets across the seabed.View image in fullscreenPeter Burling co-founded Live Ocean – the marine conservation foundation – with Blair Tuke.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PANew Zealand is the only country that still bottom trawls seamounts in the South Pacific ocean, underwater mountains that are among the ocean’s most productive and ecologically important habitats. Research shows that bottom trawling causes devastating damage to seamount ecosystems.Polling commissioned by WWF-New Zealand and published in April found that 47% of New Zealanders identify bottom trawling as the greatest threat to the marine environment, with 90% supporting limiting the practice. In the UK, the government outlined plans in June 2025 to ban bottom trawling in 41 Marine Protected Areas, butrejected an outright banin September 2025.“Single trawls can destroy corals and crustaceans that have taken hundreds or thousands of years to grow and you can destroy them in minutes,” says Tuke.After witnessing ocean degradation while competing around the world with Burling, becoming 2016 Olympic gold medallists and 2017 America’s Cup champions in the process, Tuke says the duo began Live Ocean in 2019 after realising “the power of sport” and wanting to compete for more than just winning races. The 37-year-old describes his passion for the ocean as “natural”, rooted in coming from a country that is guardian to the fourth-largest ocean space on the planet.Tuke has “pushed really hard” over the past two years to make Swim4TheOcean happen because he believed in its power to create genuine change. Previous Live Ocean projects, such as protecting the Antipodean albatross, have proved “the power of what you can do by pulling all levers to create change”.Ridler’s route down the coast included multiple stopovers, creating opportunities to connect with coastal communities and share the mission’s message. “People love following people doing hard stuff,” says Tuke, who swam a couple of support legs alongside Ridler.View image in fullscreenThe ultramarathon swimmer Jono Ridler swimming New Zealand’s North Island east coast for the Swim4TheOcean campaign.Photograph: Joshua McCormackThe 35-year-old swimmer’s endurance and conviction carried an emotional charge that science and policy alone cannot match, making tens of thousands not only feel something about an invisible crisis happening beneath the ocean’s surface, but also do something about it by signing the petition and moving bottom trawling into New Zealand’s national conversation.SailGP Impact League judges praised the Black Foils for their advocacy aspect of the campaign, along with its community and political elements. But while the Impact League is designed to spur teams into social and environmental-centred action, Tuke says the Black Foils “look where we have the most impact” first before thinking about the Impact League.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEvery SailGP team has an ocean conservation charity partner, but what makes the Black Foils unique is Tuke and Burling are at the helm of both. “Live Ocean is in our DNA,” the former says. “With Peter and I, we’re wearing both hats the whole time.”Despite all the momentum generated by Ridler to end bottom trawling in New Zealand, the country’s government recently renewed a permit for a vessel to continue bottom trawling seamounts. Tuke explains these permits are issued on a yearly basis and the process to grant them was already underway as Ridler’s swim gained momentum.On the back of the decision, Live Ocean has called for new trawling permits on seamounts to be banned – which Tuke says “is the easiest place to start” – fully protected New Zealand seamounts by 2027, and a government-led transition to move the fishing industry away from bottom trawling entirely.New Zealand’s prime minister Christopher Luxon argued the environmental impacts of bottom trawling need to be balanced with its economic benefits, but deep ocean seamount trawling represents less than 7% of New Zealand’s deepwater fisheries exports.Tuke believes the general election in November will be influential for the future of marine protection in New Zealand. Despite the recent permit setback, continuing the Swim4TheOcean campaign remains a chief focus alongside regaining momentum on the water during SailGP’s European swing: “We are committed to seeing it through and getting policy change in New Zealand,” he says. “You don’t want to just stop now with the work half done.”This is an extract from our newsletter, The Hotspot. title: US states sue Trump administration over new tariffs on 60 trading partners | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Coalition of 25 states asks US Court of International Trade to halt tariffs and declare them them unlawful
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Coalition of 25 states asks US Court of International Trade to halt tariffs and declare them them unlawful
Content: Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during the ‘Make America Wealthy Again’ event at the the White House on 2 April 2025.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during the ‘Make America Wealthy Again’ event at the the White House on 2 April 2025.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsUS states sue Trump administration over new tariffs on 60 trading partnersCoalition of 25 states asks US Court of International Trade to halt tariffs and declare them them unlawfulTrump imposes fresh tariffs on dozens of trading partnersEdward HelmoreMon 3 Aug 2026 18.35 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 17.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA coalition of 25 US states sued the Trump administration on Monday overnew tariffspegged at 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners, calling them a pretext for replacing import taxes struck down by the supreme court in February.The states are asking the US Court of International Trade to halt the tariffs, declare them unlawful and order refunds of duties that have already been paid.According to the states involved in the action, tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union imposed last month account for 99.4% of US imports. TheTrump administrationofficials have charged that the countries have not done enough to crack down on imports produced by forced labor.“After losing at the Supreme Court, the administration is once again trying to illegally raise taxes on families and businesses with a new round of tariffs,” New York attorney general Letitia Jamessaid in a statement.“No matter how the administration tries to justify it, the law and our Constitution are clear that the president does not have the power to impose sweeping tariffs on whatever countries he wants,” James added.In addition to New York, the states joining the action are Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Vermont, Washington and Wisconsin, along with the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania.The new tariffs went into effect in July after “Liberation Day” tariffs wereruled unconstitutional in Februaryand a new set of temporary tariffs expired.The latest proposal for tariffs uses Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a federal law meant to target countries that use forced labor. The new tariffs affect major trading partners including the UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, Taiwan and China.The lawsuit follows aseparate suitfiled by the Liberty Justice Center on behalf of two US small businesses who argue that Trump exceeded his executive authority with the new tariffs.“The United States is using its lawful authority to obtain the elimination of unreasonable acts, policies, and practices that burden US commerce,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said. “A foreign country’s failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor is unreasonable and burdens US commerce, including American workers, and must be addressed. Section 301 tariffs have proven to be a legally durable tool since the President’s first term, and they remain so now.”The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, and the state attorney general argue that the administration’s tariffs based on “a supposed investigation into countries’ efforts to combat forced labor do not satisfy the requirements of Section 301”, they said in a statement.They said that the administration is using “forced labor” as an excuse to continue its policy of indiscriminately enacting damaging tariffs on a wide range of countries that lead to higher prices for their constituents.“President Trump’s illegal tariffs are nothing more than a tax on hardworking families, driving up the cost of groceries, household essentials, building materials, and countless everyday goods that New Yorkers rely on,” Hochul said. “The Supreme Court has made it clear that this administration cannot ignore the law to impose sweeping tariffs.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsTrump administrationTariffsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Vampire-obsessed man detained after dumping animal corpses outside churches in New Forest | Hampshire | The Guardian
description: Benjamin Lewis, who believed drinking blood would prolong life, will be kept in hospital for treatment
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Benjamin Lewis, who believed drinking blood would prolong life, will be kept in hospital for treatment
Content: Benjamin Lewis admitted religiously aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress and the theft of lambs.Photograph: Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary /Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary/PAView image in fullscreenBenjamin Lewis admitted religiously aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress and the theft of lambs.Photograph: Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary /Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary/PAHampshireVampire-obsessed man detained after dumping animal corpses outside churches in New ForestBenjamin Lewis, who believed drinking blood would prolong life, will be kept in hospital for treatmentSteven MorrisMon 3 Aug 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man fascinated with vampires and graveyards who apparently believed he would live for ever if he drank blood has been detained in hospital after being caught dumping animal corpses outside churches in a British forest.Benjamin Lewis, 48, left the bodies of sheep and deer on the doorsteps of churches in the New Forest inHampshire, frightening parishioners and upsetting farmers whose livestock he stole and slaughtered.‘It’s upset us all’: New Forest residents unnerved by man leaving animal carcasses by churchesRead moreAs part of the operation to trap Lewis, police officers carried out surveillance on ecclesiastical sites on significant dates in the satanic calendar.Lewis was finally arrested after traces of his DNA were found on a lamb’s remains. He admitted causing religiously aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress and the theft of lambs.During an earlier court appearance, Lewis, of Totton, Southampton, answered “Count Dracula” when asked to identify himself.Judge William Mousley KC said he would be detained for treatment unless and until either a mental health tribunal or the justice secretary considered it safe for him to be released.After his sentence, Lewis, who appeared via video link from hospital, apologised to his victims and said he bore no grudge towards the police who had caught him.View image in fullscreenSt Theresa’s church in Totton, one of the churches Benjamin Lewis targeted with the remains of animals.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianSpeaking outside court, PC Jessica Surman of Hampshire police said it was the most unusual case she had worked on. “It’s one where you think you have reached the end of the bizarreness and then something else happens and throws a curveball into the mix.”Lewis believed drinking blood would prolong his life, Surman said. “And if he drinks it enough he won’t go to hell, he won’t die and he will become a vampire.”Police began investigating when dead animals – lambs stolen from farmers and deer killed on roads – started being found at churches.Surman said police began to see a pattern in his offending. “We were almost able to predict when he was going to be striking.” They consulted satanic calendars, posting officers at churches on significant days.People connected to the churches Lewis focused on were very concerned. “We have had people who were so upset and frightened by it, they couldn’t go to church,” Surman said. One woman was too scared to visit the church where her son was buried.View image in fullscreenParsonage Farm, which had three sheep stolen.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianLaura Deuxberry, prosecuting, told Southampton crown court that lambs and deer were left by Lewis outside and inside churches, sometimes with an inverted cross nearby. A tarot card was also left near one.A lamb was put on a cross on top of a church and a second close to a statue of Jesus’s mother, Mary. Another lamb was left in a church pulpit on a cross taken from the altar. On one occasion children saw what had happened and were very distressed.One vicar said it made him angry – as if the “opposition” had left a signature. Another said: “It’s an insidious way to make a point.”A church warden said she was “on edge” when she went to one of the churches Lewis targeted. She said he was trying to cause fear and unrest. A churchgoer said she felt someone was sending a “sadistic message”.Deuxberry said one of the incidents centred on a community mental health facility close to Lewis’s home. A deer’s head and an inverted cross were left on the gates. The person who found the head said she was shocked and afterwards feared the culprit was watching her.When police searched Lewis’s home they found sketches of vampires, notes about rituals and references to sucking blood.Deuxberry said the offences he had been charged with took place between February and August last year but there had been concerns over him for a number of years.The woods and heaths of the New Forest national park are the setting for all manner of tales of witches, pixies, cursed souls and rituals, and even today are a magnet for those fascinated by the otherworldly.The village of Burley was the home of the “white witch” Sybil Leek, who wrote books on witchcraft and was famed for strolling around with her pet jackdaw.But Lewis’s actions were quite different. Livestock owners that Lewis stole from were very disturbed. “It’s a terrible thing to do,”saidMyra Noyce, one of the people Lewis took lambs from.View image in fullscreenThe road between Parsonage Farm and St Peter’s church in Bramshaw, where Lewis dumped one of the stolen sheep.Photograph: Peter Flude/The Guardian“It’s upset us all, made us feel very uncomfortable. This is a lovely part of the world and to think of someone going around doing something like that is horrible.”Sarah Harrison, a New Forest farmer Lewis stole black lambs from, said: “It’s pretty awful – there are some silly people around. One of her lambs ended up outside St Peter’s church in the village of Bramshaw, another draped over a finger post. “I suppose it’s to do with his beliefs but it’s scared some people.”In her victim personal statement, Harrison said she had been scared to walk alone at night and had thought about leaving the New Forest, though her family had lived there for generations. “I’m wondering what will it be next. When I hear a sound outside I think is that him.”She said the lambs would have suffered when he cut their throat and he put the bodies on show as if they meant nothing. She said the incidents had put the flock on alert.The consultant psychiatrist Dr Gauruv Malhan told the court Lewis had “complex mental health difficulties” and had recently been moved from a low- to medium-secure hospital.He said at the age of 13 Lewis had left a dead frog on a cross in church and the psychiatrist said he feared he could harm humans as well as animals. In hospital he had assaulted other patients and attempted to assault Malhan when he visited him and had to be restrained.Andrew Price, defending, said Lewis was sorry and recognised he had done wrong.Lewis’s conviction is not his first brush with the law. In 2003 he wasjailed for terrorising a vicar and his familynear his home by claiming to be a vampire. He and another man made abusive and frightening phone calls, set off fireworks and posted obscene pictures on the church noticeboard.Explore more on these topicsHampshireEnglandCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple launches legal challenge against UK government demand to access data | Apple | The Guardian
description: The Home Office has made a fresh request for ‘back door’ access to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: The Home Office has made a fresh request for ‘back door’ access to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users
Content: Apple launched the complaint after the UK government made a second request to access encrypted data.Photograph: ymgerman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenApple launched the complaint after the UK government made a second request to access encrypted data.Photograph: ymgerman/Getty ImagesAppleApple launches legal challenge against UK government demand to access dataThe Home Office has made a fresh request for ‘back door’ access to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British usersRachel HallMon 3 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple has launched a new legal challenge against a UK government demand to access its customers’ highly encrypted data, a year after theHome Officeagreed to abandon its previous request.The US tech company launched the legal complaint last month at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT), an independent court that has the power to investigate claims that the UK intelligence services have acted unlawfully.The UK government had made a second request toAppleto grant it a “back door” to encrypted iCloud data belonging to British users, according to an order issued by the court.Britain backed down on its original demand for access to data from UK and US customers last year, after a heated transatlantic tussle over encryption between London and Washington.UK authorities subsequently issued a new “technical capability notice” (TCN) to Apple that did not apply to American users.Apple is seeking to challenge the British government’s powers to issue TCNs under the UK Investigatory Powers Act, according to the details of the new legal case first reported by the Financial Times.The legislation compels companies to provide information to law enforcement agencies working on cases including terrorism and child sexual abuse. This can include forcing companies to provide the UK security services with access to customer data, even if such information is protected by secure encryption.The court sent an order giving notice of the new Apple complaint to the human rights group Privacy International, which, alongside fellow campaigner Liberty, had previously launched a separate complaint against TCNs at the IPT.Among the submissions made by the campaigners were requests for Apple’s claims to be held in public given the public interest in the matter, and a complaint “disputing the lawfulness, necessity and secrecy of the purported Apple TCN and the legal regime underpinning TCNs in general”.A case management hearing to discuss how the parallel complaints should be handled had been scheduled for next month, Privacy International said.A spokesperson added: “We are happy to learn that Apple is once again challenging the UK’s regime of secret orders. While we don’t know the substance of Apple’s claim, if it relates to the previously reported orders aimed at undermining the security of Apple’s iCloud storage, then Apple’s claim, alongside ours and Liberty’s, is crucially important to preserving all of our privacy and security.”Neither Apple nor the Home Office responded to requests for comment. Both are legally restricted from discussing TCNs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe original TCN issued last year asked Apple for the right to see users’ encrypted data protected by its advanced data protection (ADP) programme in the event of a national security risk.Apple said the removal of the tool – which not even it can access – would make users more vulnerable to data breaches from bad actors and other threats to customer privacy. Creating a “back door” would also mean all data was accessible by Apple, which it could be forced to share with law enforcement possessing a warrant.As a result, ApplewithdrewUK customers’ access to its ADP programme in January 2025.The Home Office has maintained that the Investigatory Powers Act, under which such orders are issued, contains robust safeguards and is used only when absolutely necessary.Explore more on these topicsAppleData protectionHome OfficeLabourComputingUK security and counter-terrorismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sunday Times and Sun columnist Rod Liddle dies aged 66 | Rod Liddle | The Guardian
description: Tributes paid across industry to provocative journalist who died after short illness
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Tributes paid across industry to provocative journalist who died after short illness
Content: Rod Liddle died in hospital on Sunday evening.Photograph: Lorenzo Dalberto/AlamyView image in fullscreenRod Liddle died in hospital on Sunday evening.Photograph: Lorenzo Dalberto/AlamyRod LiddleSunday Times and Sun columnist Rod Liddle dies aged 66Tributes paid across industry to provocative journalist who died after short illnessMichael SavageMedia editorMon 3 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe writer and broadcaster Rod Liddle, a prominent columnist for theSunday Timesand the Sun, has died after a short illness. He was 66.Liddle, whose provocative style attracted praise and criticism, also wrote for the Spectator magazine and earlier in his career edited BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.Liddle worked as a speechwriter for the Labour party in the 1980s, but his later writing often critiqued and criticised the left.Tributes to Liddle were paid by Piers Morgan, the former Sunday Times editor Andrew Neil and the Today programme presenter Justin Webb, who described Liddle as brilliant, kind and funny.The former Sun editor David Yelland said Liddle “morphed into a brilliant and gifted writer who I could rarely agree with but always turned to first”.He said: “It was because he was so talented he was able to behave so badly and write so (it has to be said) abhorrently on many occasions. And he knew this. It was his essence. RIP Rod.”View image in fullscreenRod Liddle (right) with the then Conservative party leader, David Cameron, campaigning with his home affairs spokesperson, David Davis.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianLiddle died at the James Cook university hospital in Middlesbrough on Sunday evening. His children, Wilder, Tyler and Emmy, said in a statement: “We’re all very saddened and shocked at the sudden passing of our wonderful father.“He raised us much as you might imagine, to be inquisitive, brave and always humorous. Even in hospital in the last few weeks, he consistently held the room and never let the awful situation show.“He has left a legacy that we are all incredibly proud of, he will always be our guide on how to live an extraordinary life.”View image in fullscreenRod Liddle at the Spectator summer party in 2011 with his second wife, Alicia Monckton.Photograph: Alan Davidson/ShutterstockLiddle was no stranger to controversy. In 2010 he became the first blogger to be censured by thePress Complaints Commission, for incorrectly stating in a Spectator piece that the “overwhelming majority” of violent crime in London was carried out by young African-Caribbean men.Liddle left as editor of Today in 2002. At the time, it was reported that his departure followed a disagreement with the BBC’s then director general, Greg Dyke, about a regular column he wrote for the Guardian.In one column Liddle had criticised Countryside Alliance marchers as “Mill on the Floss extras” and “those who own the countryside, or run it, together with a forelock-tugging menagerie of their better-paid servants”.View image in fullscreenRod Liddle during his time as producer of BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianIt was during his tenure at Today that Liddle hired Andrew Gilligan, the journalist whose 2003 report claimed the UK government had “sexed up” its dossier on Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction. Liddle left the BBC before Gilligan’s report was broadcast.Liddle also presented a programme about infidelity, arguing that men were genetically pre-programmed to be unfaithful. His former wife had written about his adultery in a series of newspaper features.Rebekah Brooks, the chief executive of News UK, which publishes the Sunday Times and the Sun, said everyone at the company had been “deeply shocked and saddened” to learn of his sudden death.“Rod was an inimitable journalistic force, brilliant, provocative and immensely talented, whose sharp wit and uncompromising voice graced our pages and airwaves for decades,” she said. “He challenged conventional thinking and left an indelible mark on British journalism.”Ben Taylor, the editor of the Sunday Times, said: “Rod Liddle had a wonderful way with words and used his unique talent to speak for the readers, highlighting the cant and absurdity that bedevils modern life. He was also supremely entertaining and for years his column was the first that many turned to every Sunday. We will miss him desperately.”Victoria Newton, the editor-in-chief of the Sun, said: “A champion of press freedom, no topic was off-limits, and his writing – as funny as it was excoriating – was simply exceptional. A terrific observer of the frailties of our political class, he will be remembered for his razor sharp wit and for his huge intellect.”Explore more on these topicsRod LiddleSunday TimesThe SunNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesNational newspapersRadio 4newsShareReuse this content

title: Driver jailed for four years after faking brake failure on motorway | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Nathan Owen drove his electric Jaguar at up to 86mph and lied to police it was malfunctioning and out of his control
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Nathan Owen drove his electric Jaguar at up to 86mph and lied to police it was malfunctioning and out of his control
Content: Nathan Owen collided with a police car 31 times as officers attempted to stop him.Photograph: Merseyside Police/PAView image in fullscreenNathan Owen collided with a police car 31 times as officers attempted to stop him.Photograph: Merseyside Police/PALiverpoolDriver jailed for four years after faking brake failure on motorwayNathan Owen drove his electric Jaguar at up to 86mph and lied to police it was malfunctioning and out of his controlMark BrownNorth of England correspondentMon 3 Aug 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 13.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man who drove his electric Jaguar at up to 86mph on motorways falsely telling police the car was malfunctioning and out of his control has been jailed for four years and three months.Nathan Owen fabricated not being able to brake in a “frighteningly stupid” ploy to avoid paying car finance,Liverpoolcrown court heard.In a statement,Jaguar Land RoverUK (JLR) said the firm had spent an extra £50m in marketing to try to counter the publicity from the false allegations, which they said generated 180 pieces of adverse media coverage.Owen, 33, collided with a police car 31 times as officers attempted to stop him after he phoned emergency services to tell them his vehicle was accelerating and there was nothing he could do.He drove at speeds of up to 86mph on the M58, M57 and M62 inMerseysidefor about 35 minutes, over a distance of about 38 miles, during the incident on 6 March 2024.The Jaguar I-Pace eventually came to a stop near junction 12 of the M62 when the battery ran out.Sentencing him, Judge Ian Unsworth KC said: “You set in train a course of conduct which caused a significant police traffic operation to be deployed, undoubted alarm to the public and very substantial loss and disruption to others.”The judge said police officers placed themselves in danger because they believed they were dealing with a genuine emergency.Addressing Owen, he added: “You, meanwhile, sought to profit from a lie.”Police said that an extensive investigation with JLR revealed the car was functioning correctly and data showed that Owen did not press the brakes at any point.He was arrested on 13 March and denied making it all up for financial gain. But police discovered Owen had a high level of personal debt and multiple missed payments on the vehicle finance.Eric Lamb, prosecuting, said Owen, of Prestatyn, had about £5,000 left to pay to a car finance company and, on the day of the incident, attempted and failed to borrow money from a loan company.Footage of police pursuit of Nathan OwenMinutes after being turned down for the loan money he called 999 claiming his car would not brake and he had no control over the vehicle, which he said was accelerating.Lamb said: “In fact, his car was stationary at the time of that call.”Footage of the police pursuit of Owen was played in court, along with the audio from his 999 call, in which he was heard telling an operator he was “shaking” and the car had “gone crazy”.When the car was eventually brought to a stop the brake lights could be seen turning on.Owen contacted the finance company 40 minutes after the incident.He was later paid £300 by the Sun and £500 by the Daily Mail for his story, the court heard.Daniel Travers, defending, said Owen’s actions were “frighteningly stupid”.Travers said Owen, who had no previous convictions and came from a “successful, stable family”, had been described by his father as a Walter Mitty character who “lives in a fantasy world”.He added: “He had grand ideas and things just went wrong.”Owen pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and two counts of fraud in June.He was banned from driving for a period of five years after his release from custody.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolEnglandJaguar Land RoverMerseysidenewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish seabird hunt cancelled for first time in 400 years | Scotland | The Guardian
description: NatureScot refuses licence for hunt on Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir in which up to 2,000 gannet chicks are killed
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: NatureScot refuses licence for hunt on Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir in which up to 2,000 gannet chicks are killed
Content: During the guga hunt, up to 2,000 gannet chicks are killed over 10 days on the uninhabited Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir, 40 miles north of Lewis and Harris.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAView image in fullscreenDuring the guga hunt, up to 2,000 gannet chicks are killed over 10 days on the uninhabited Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir, 40 miles north of Lewis and Harris.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAScotlandScottish seabird hunt cancelled for first time in 400 yearsNatureScot refuses licence for hunt on Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir in which up to 2,000 gannet chicks are killedRobyn VinterMon 3 Aug 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA controversial Scottish seabird hunt will not go ahead for the first time in 400 years, in what campaigners have called a “victory for common sense”.In the annual guga hunt, up to 2,000 gannet chicks are killed over a 10-day period on the uninhabited Hebridean island of Sula Sgeir, 40 miles north of Lewis and Harris.NatureScot, which is responsible for licensing, refused to allow this year’s hunt to go ahead, citing a potential “adverse impact” on gannet populations according to new modelling.Wildlife and animal rights organisations have long protested against the killing of the birds, which is part of a tradition that some say goes back to the Vikings, when the birds were hunted for food.MapThe hunters, known as the Men of Ness, take the chicks from their nests in the nature reserve of Sula Sgeir with a noose on a long pole and kill them with a blow to the head.The birds are then gutted and salted on the island and eaten as a delicacy in the Western Isles – though the taste has been described as“absolutely revolting”, “between rotten leather and fishy beef” and “without doubt the most disgusting thing”.In a statement, NatureScot said: “After assessing the application against the legislation and using the most recent scientific evidence, our board’s decision is to refuse a licence.View image in fullscreenA candidate stood for the Holyrood seat of Edinburgh Central in protest against the hunt.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“We have used the latest information available and commissioned an updated population model to help predict the effect of the guga hunt on the gannet population. As a result, we have concluded an adverse impact is possible, both at the applicants’ requested application limit of 2,000 juvenile gannets, and at a reduced limit of 500.”However, the organisation, which is part of the Scottish government, criticised some anti-hunt activists, saying the police had been called over the “aggression and intimidation tactics of some anti-guga hunt protesters [which] comes at significant personal cost to our expert and dedicated staff as they try to do their day-to-day jobs”.Two men dressed in gannet costumes were arrested and charged in March after spending several days on the roof of Great Glen House, NatureScot’s Inverness headquarters. In separate incidents, the building was tagged with graffiti and had windows smashed. In May, a candidate stood for the Holyrood seat of Edinburgh Central in protest against the hunt.People from Ness, in the north of Lewis, accused the activists of a campaign of bullying. Ahead of NatureScot’s board meeting, Murdo MacRitchie, of the Save Our Guga Harvest group, said: “People in Ness will understandably feel that this recommendation risks rewarding a campaign in which members of a small island community have been bullied and abused and publicly owned property has been vandalised.”Apetition to the Scottish government to end the practiceattracted more than 100,000 signatures, while a separate petition from the anti-hunting charity Protect the Wild surpassed 250,000.Devon Docherty, the Scottish campaigns manager at Protect the Wild, said the decision was a “victory for compassion, for science and for common sense”. She said: “Thousands of young seabirds have been spared from a brutal death because NatureScot chose to follow the evidence rather than simply rubber-stamp another licence to kill.”The decision does not prevent the Men of Ness from getting a licence in future years for the hunt, which is recognised in law under the Wildlife and Countryside Act.Explore more on these topicsScotlandBirdsWildlifeHuntingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wildfires rage across Washington as drought and heat fuel painful summer: ‘It’s not normal’ | Washington state | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of structures damaged as firefighters battle to contain 15 major wildfires amid extreme heat and drought
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Hundreds of structures damaged as firefighters battle to contain 15 major wildfires amid extreme heat and drought
Content: The remains of a home burned in the Old Trails fire in Spokane on Monday.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe remains of a home burned in the Old Trails fire in Spokane on Monday.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersWashington stateWildfires rage across Washington as drought and heat fuel painful summer: ‘It’s not normal’Hundreds of structures damaged as firefighters battle to contain 15 major wildfires amid extreme heat and droughtDani AnguianoMon 3 Aug 2026 14.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 15.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirefighters inWashington stateare battling wildfires that have forced 60,000 people to flee and destroyed hundreds of buildings as drought and extreme heat fuel an “extraordinary” fire season in the Pacific north-west.Fifteen major blazes are raging across the state, David Upthegrove, the head of Washington’s department of natural resources, told reporters over the weekend.“It’s not a normal season,” he said. “A confluence of weather conditions, a confluence of fires throughout the west, are stretching our resources and challenging the individuals in this response.”Spokane, a city of 230,000 in north-eastern Washington near the Idaho border, has been particularly hard hit, with three fires burning in the area. While no deaths have been reported, officials confirmed that at least 600 structures had been damaged or destroyed and that none of the fires are contained.The fires around Spokane forced rapid evacuations and prompted officials to open emergency shelters to support some of the 60,000 people displaced.“Driving around looking at the homes – it’s just one of the most heartbreaking things I’ve ever seen in my life,” Geoff Beadles, a Spokane resident who evacuated with his fiancee and dogs, told AFP.Light winds and lower temperatures were expected to aid firefighters before warmer weather arrives later in the week.Even before the fires exploded around Spokane, state officials had warned that the year had already been one of the busiest wildfire years on record.“Our firefighters are already stretched thin across the state, and with more heat and wind expected this weekend and for the rest of the summer, any new spark on our tinder-dry landscapes can lead to another devastating wildfire,” Upthegrove said on Saturday.The National Weather Service last week issued a “particularly dangerous situation” red-flag alert and noted that eastern Washington was facing extreme weather risk.Bob Ferguson, Washington’s governor, declared a state of emergency on Saturday due to drought, unusually high temperatures and high winds “exacerbating our record-setting wildfires”, and banned most burning in the state through September.The state is in the midst of a record-setting fourth consecutive statewide drought, Ferguson noted in his announcement.The governor has requested federal assistance to respond to the wildfires and said he had been in contact with Donald Trump and other administration officials.It has been a challenging fire season across the Pacific north-west, with Oregon already nearing its largeston record.AFP contributed to this storyExplore more on these topicsWashington stateWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: French boy thrown from Tate balcony has ‘smile back’ after hospital release | UK news | The Guardian
description: Family update on GoFundMe page says child, who was six when badly injured in 2019 incident, is now back at school
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Family update on GoFundMe page says child, who was six when badly injured in 2019 incident, is now back at school
Content: Tate Modern by the Thames in London, where the six-year-old was seriously injured in a 30-metre fall.Photograph: Imagebroker/AlamyView image in fullscreenTate Modern by the Thames in London, where the six-year-old was seriously injured in a 30-metre fall.Photograph: Imagebroker/AlamyUK newsFrench boy thrown from Tate balcony has ‘smile back’ after hospital releaseFamily update on GoFundMe page says child, who was six when badly injured in 2019 incident, is now back at schoolPress AssociationMon 3 Aug 2026 11.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA boy thrown from the viewing balcony in London’sTate Modernart gallery has a “smile back on his face” after being discharged from hospital, his family have said.The French youngster, whose name remains undisclosed for privacy reasons, was six when he was badly hurt in an attack by then teenager Jonty Bravery at theLondonattraction on 4 August 2019.The child, who was on holiday with his parents, survived a 30-metre (100ft) fall but suffered life-changing injuries, including a bleed on the brain and numerous broken bones.Almost seven years on from the incident, his family, who call him “notre petit chevalier” (our little knight) reported via an update on a GoFundMe page that he was able to return to school briefly before the summer holidays.They said: “We wanted to let you know that our little knight has finally left the hospital!“His hospital stay was kept as short as possible because, despite our daily presence and encouragement, our son was becoming deeply disheartened and kept asking when he could go back to class and see his friends.“It was a great joy for him to return to school shortly before the summer holidays; since the lessons were well-tailored to his needs and challenges, he was able to start learning again, and reuniting with his teachers and classmates put a smile back on his face.”In April this year, his family reported that his recovery had taken a “sad step backwards”, but this newest message appeared to be a lot more positive.The GoFundMe page was set up by nurse Vicky Di Placito from Surrey, whose own brother was paralysed in an incident overseas.The crowdfunding initiative, which aims to cover the medical costs of the injured French boy’s family, has so far raised more than £500,000.The boy continues to undergo intensive rehabilitation, including physiotherapy, speech therapy and neuropsychology.To celebrate the end of his hospital treatment, his family are treating him to a tandem paragliding flight, and a seaside getaway with friends.He also plans to resume his adaptive swimming lessons along with maths tutoring to catch up on the school he has missed.His family said: “It will certainly be a busy summer. We are going to try to fully recharge his batteries (and our own) before the start of the school year, and to get back to a family routine as normal as possible.”View image in fullscreenJonty Bravery pleaded guilty to attempted murder after the attack.Photograph: Metropolitan Police/PABravery, now 24, was in supported accommodation at the time of the attack but allowed out unsupervised.He intended to select and kill someone, a court was later told.Bravery, who was 17 at the time, pleaded guilty to attempted murder and was handed a life sentence with a minimum term of 15 years.He was jailed for 16 weeks in January after being found guilty of assaulting two nurses at Broadmoor, a high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire, in September 2024.In 2020, he was given a 14-week jail sentence after admitting to attacking staff at the same hospital.Explore more on these topicsUK newsFranceCrimeTate ModernLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: July was driest month in southern England since records began  | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: England and Wales provisionally record driest July in nearly 200 years, Met Office says
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: England and Wales provisionally record driest July in nearly 200 years, Met Office says
Content: A lone ice cream van is surrounded by parched grassland at Blackheath Common in London, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenA lone ice cream van is surrounded by parched grassland at Blackheath Common in London, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAExtreme heatJuly was driest month in southern England since records beganEngland and Wales provisionally record driest July in nearly 200 years, Met Office saysPippa NeillEnvironment reporterMon 3 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJuly 2026 was the driest month in southernEnglandsince records began nearly 200 years ago, the Met Office has said.England andWalesalso provisionally recorded their driest July since records began in 1836. Wales had its joint warmest July on record for mean temperature, and England recorded its second warmest July.The Met Office said the “remarkable conditions” this year came amid a summer marked by multiple heat records.The heatwaves have been made more intense and more likely by the fossil fuel-driven climate crisis. The heatwave that affected western Europe at the end of June was themost severe and widespread ever.View image in fullscreenPeople use umbrellas to shelter from the sun as they visit Trafalgar Square in central London.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAJuly was the sixth consecutive month this year to have had above average mean temperatures, with only January so far experiencing mean temperatures below average.Dr Amy Doherty, a science manager at the Met Office, said: “The combination of record-breaking dryness, exceptional warmth and unprecedented sunshine has delivered one of the most notable summer months in our historical records.”The Environment Agency said the conditions were affecting farmers, wildlife and the amount of water available for public and business use.Half of England and the whole of Wales were last week declared to beofficially in drought. In England, 40% of the population are under ahosepipe ban.The National Farmers’ Union haswarnedthe punishing drought could lead to shortages of certain foods in Britain.A series of huge wildfires, supercharged by the climate crisis, has torched large parts of Europe this summer.Greece is battlingone of the worst seasons of wildfires of the past decade and in France, thousands of evacuees were allowed to return home or to holiday accommodation on Monday after the country’s largest wildfire on record.View image in fullscreenCattle on Dorney Common, Buckinghamshire graze on parched grassland.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockRivers in Europe are facing extremely low flows. TheDanube’s water flow has fallen to 1,500 cubic metres a second in Romania, less than a third of its July average.The Met Office said on Monday England had its driest July on record, with only 6.5mm of rainfall.
