That is only 10% of its long-term meteorological average for the month, and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.Wales has also had its driest July on record, with 9.3mm of rainfall – only 9% of its long-term meteorological average for the month.View image in fullscreenGolfers play at the North Wales Golf Club as a drought continues across in Llandudno, Wales.Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty ImagesNineteen counties recorded less than (or equal to) 1mm of rainfall in July. These were: Berkshire, Dorset, East Riding of Yorkshire, East Sussex, Essex, Gloucestershire, Greater London, Herefordshire, Isle of Wight, Kent, Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Northamptonshire, Nottinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Rutland, Surrey, Warwickshire and West Sussex.The Environment Agencysaid last monthwater reserves “should be enough for the coming months until the next period of sustained rainfall”.While rain is forecast for some parts of England, the Met Office said south-east England would continue to experience little rain.Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatDroughtEnglandWalesWater industryClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge orders return of alleged victim of trafficking sent to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Ruling quashes Home Office policy to refuse asylum seekers’ right to have trafficking claims reconsidered after initial rejection
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Ruling quashes Home Office policy to refuse asylum seekers’ right to have trafficking claims reconsidered after initial rejection
Content: People detained under the UK's ‘one in, one out’ deal with France, in Dover, Kent.Photograph: Home Office/PAView image in fullscreenPeople detained under the UK's ‘one in, one out’ deal with France, in Dover, Kent.Photograph: Home Office/PAImmigration and asylumJudge orders return of alleged victim of trafficking sent to France under ‘one in one out’ schemeRuling quashes Home Office policy to refuse asylum seekers’ right to have trafficking claims reconsidered after initial rejectionDiane TaylorMon 3 Aug 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA high court judge has ordered the Home Office to bring an alleged victim of trafficking forcibly removed to France under the“one in one out” schemeback to the UK.It is the first ruling of its kind and could lead to more people affected by the “one in one out” policy being brought back to the UK.The judge, Mr Justice Sheldon, has quashed aHome Officepolicy change to refuse asylum seekers the right to have their trafficking claims reconsidered after an initial rejection. “I have quashed it so that it is as if it never happened,” he said.The “one in one out” policy forcibly removes some people who cross the Channel in small boats in exchange for bringing a similar number from northern France legally to the UK.The government hopes the scheme will deter small boat crossings. They have reduced by more than 40% compared with this time last year, but in the last week more than1,000 peoplehave arrived and on Thursdayfour people diedattempting the journey.Asylum seekers returned to France now have a right to have trafficking cases that were initially rejected reconsidered. It is unclear how this will work in practice as many of those forcibly removed to France who have previously claimed to have been trafficked have now disappeared.Some have gone underground after being threatened by smugglers in northern France. Others have fled France after being threatened with removal to their home country or to another EU country where they were previously fingerprinted on their journey seeking asylum.The man whom the judge has ordered the Home Office to bring back from France was forcibly returned there on 27 November 2025. Reasonable grounds have been identified that he is a victim of trafficking. He is an asylum seeker from Sudan, a survivor of torture, and one of five people who challenged the home secretary’s policy change.A second asylum seeker sent to France by the Home Office, who was also involved in the legal challenge, will have his trafficking case reconsidered in France, and depending on the outcome he too may be brought back to the UK.The high court has granted the Home Office and the asylum seekers permission to appeal on various points in the judgment.Emily Soothill, of Deighton Pierce Glynn, welcomed the judge’s decision. She said: “Our client is a vulnerable victim of trafficking and torture who has suffered significantly as a result of the Home Office’s unlawful decision-making. We are delighted that the court has rightly recognised that his removal to France was unlawful and that he must therefore be brought back to the UK.“This is a highly significant decision; for our client, for other victims of trafficking who may have been unlawfully removed to France and for ensuring that the rule of law is upheld.”Elizabeth Cole, a solicitor at Duncan Lewis, also welcomed the decision. Her asylum seeker client in France, who took part in the legal challenge, now has a right to reconsideration.“The court’s decision calls into question the lawfulness of previous removals under the UK-France treaty where a negative reasonable grounds decision was made or reconsideration was denied,” she said. “We hope that this will allow a broader cohort of cases who have been removed to France unlawfully under the treaty to obtain justice and potentially return to the UK.”Home Office sources say they are carefully considering the judgment, including their options for appeal.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficenewsShareReuse this content

title: Children using social media at younger age appear to do worse in school tests | Science | The Guardian
description: Pupils who open accounts aged 11 to 12 score lower in some subjects than those who wait a few years, study finds
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Pupils who open accounts aged 11 to 12 score lower in some subjects than those who wait a few years, study finds
Content: One of the best predictors of the performance gap was how often children picked up their phones throughout the day and night.Photograph: True Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne of the best predictors of the performance gap was how often children picked up their phones throughout the day and night.Photograph: True Images/AlamyScienceChildren using social media at younger age appear to do worse in school testsPupils who open accounts aged 11 to 12 score lower in some subjects than those who wait a few years, study findsIan SampleScience editorMon 3 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChildren who open social media accounts at the start of secondary school appear to perform worse in tests than those who delay, with researchers suspecting that the constant checking for updates is a major distraction for many students.Pupils who opened their first social media account aged 11 to 12 scored lower in mathematics and reading tests than those who waited a few years, with scores at age 16 differing between the groups by the equivalent of about six months of learning, the study found.The work does not prove social media is to blame, but the researchers took account of many other factors that could skew the results, such as the students’ academic performance before they had social media, their family structure and parents’ education.“I think we now know there is a problem and that it’s a complex problem, to do with how these platforms are built,” said Dr Marco Gui, the first author on the study at the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy. “Our research shows that at least during pre-adolescence, these social media are problematic.”Gui and his colleagues analysed surveys on the social media habits of more than 5,000 Italian schoolchildren and their results in standardised maths, Italian and English exams. When tested at age 13 to 14, those who had opened their first social media account at 11 or 12 scored worse than those who waited until at least 14 years old. The score gap at age 15 to 16 remained the same for Italian and widened for maths.Writing inNature Human Behaviour, the researchers say the difference in scores is roughly equivalent to the early adopters falling behind by six months of schooling. Put another way, the benefit to those who delayed social media was about half that achieved with intensive and costly tutoring.While a performance gap was evident for maths and Italian, there was no impact on English, which the students were learning as a foreign language, possibly because so much social media is in English, providing “incidental exposure and practice”, the researchers said.One of the best predictors of the performance gap was how often children picked up their phones throughout the day and night, suggesting that constantly checking social media was at least partly to blame.“We speculate that one of the mechanisms is the continuous state of alert that social media used on a smartphone exerts on minors’ lives. The continuous need to check messages, to see if something is happening in the online world, why you are engaged in something in the physical world you have around you,” Gui said. “This means being less present in the physical space of the family or the house. And from a cognitive point of view, it could mean being less engaged in something that takes time, as homework can for a student of that age.”The study comes as the UK is poised to introduce asocial media banfor under-16s, following Australia which brought in its own ban last year. While Gui favours an age limit on social media, he said a ban was an “emergency policy” and that work was needed to make the platforms themselves safer and less addictive. “For pre-adolescents we have to work on diminishing the social relevance of these environments,” he said.Dennis Ougrin, a professor of child and adolescent psychiatry at Queen Mary University of London, said the work added to growing evidence that the age at which young people first engaged with social media may affect their educational development. “The message for parents, educators and policymakers is not necessarily to ban social media, but to support young people in developing healthy habits when interacting with social media,” he said.Explore more on these topicsScienceSocial mediaSocial media banSocial media bansChildrenSchoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claims | Russia | The Guardian
description: Seven people, including three children, dead after ‘drone debris’ strike beach in seaside town, says Russian taskforce
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Seven people, including three children, dead after ‘drone debris’ strike beach in seaside town, says Russian taskforce
Content: Arkhipo-Osipovka is a resort town near Gelendzhik on the Black Sea shore in Russia.Photograph: Andrey Khrobostov/AlamyView image in fullscreenArkhipo-Osipovka is a resort town near Gelendzhik on the Black Sea shore in Russia.Photograph: Andrey Khrobostov/AlamyRussiaUkrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claimsSeven people, including three children, dead after ‘drone debris’ strike beach in seaside town, says Russian taskforcePjotr SauerandAngus ThomsonMon 3 Aug 2026 18.04 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 06.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkrainian drone attacks on a Black Sea resort and the annexed Crimea peninsula killed 11 people, Russian officials said after blamingUkrainefor another explosion that killed five people in a Moscow restaurant.Seven people, including three children, were killed when “drone debris” struck a beach in the seaside town of Arkhipo-Osipovka, the crisis taskforce for Russia’s southern Krasnodar region said on social media.Social media videos, verified by Reuters and the BBC, showed tourists in the water and on the shore watching on as what appeared to be a drone slammed into a busy beach.View image in fullscreenSocial media footage of a drone strike on the holiday resort of Arkhipo-Osipovka, Russia, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Twitter/XAnother four people were killed in a Ukrainian strike on the illegally annexed Crimea, the Moscow-installed governor, Sergey Aksyonov, said in a post on Telegram.Both Crimea and the Black Sea coast are popular holiday destinations for Russian tourists during summer.Earlier, Russia blamed Ukraine for a bombing at a restaurant in central Moscow that killed five people, amid growing speculation that a senior Russian military commander was the intended target.The explosion occurred on Saturday evening near the entrance to an upmarket Italian restaurant in one of the city’s seven Stalin-era skyscrapers on Kudrinskaya Square.Russian prosecutors said an unidentified woman carrying an improvised explosive device had attempted to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard.The device detonated moments later, killing five people and injuring 19 others.View image in fullscreenAccording to Russia’s national anti-terrorism committee (NAC), an improvised explosive device detonated outside the entrance to the ‘Balzi Rossi’ restaurant in Kudrinskaya Square, on 1 August 2026.Photograph: Sergei Ilnitsky/EPAIn a statement on Sunday, Russia’s foreign ministry accused Kyiv of carrying out the attack, saying: “The bloody tentacles of [Volodymyr]Zelenskyy’s terrorist gang have reached the Balzi Rossi Italian restaurant in Moscow.”Russian authorities have not identified the intended target or named the victims.However, pro-Kremlin military bloggers and several independent Russian media outlets reported that the attack may have been aimed at Col Gen Alexander Chaiko, the commander of Russia’s aerospace forces, who was reportedly attending a private banquet at the restaurant to celebrate his 55th birthday.Photographs and videos that appeared online shortly after the bombing, purportedly from the private event, showed a stage with the words “Aleksandr 55” displayed in the background.Chaiko is one of Russia’s top military commanders, having led the failed assault on Kyiv in early 2022 before later being promoted to command the Russian air force.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Telegram channel VChK-OGPU, which is known for publishing leaks from within Russia’s security services, reported that Chaiko escaped unharmed. According to the channel, his daughter, Maria, was seriously injured in the blast, while her husband, Daniil Peredriy, was killed. They were outside on the restaurant’s terrace when the explosion occurred.The Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that investigators believed the woman carrying the explosive device may not have known she was transporting a bomb, suggesting it was detonated remotely by another person, killing her.Among the other reported victims was a member of Russia’s elite Federal Protective Service (FSO).Kyiv has not yet commented on the incidents. Both sides have repeatedly said they do not target civilians in the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.In Ukraine, one person was killed and dozens more injured when Russian planes launched a 90-minute bombing blitz on residential districts in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, the regional chief, Ivan Fedorov, said on Monday.Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have targeted dozens of senior Russian military officers and Russia-installed officials, accusing them of involvement in war crimes.Ukrainian intelligence services have previously employed a range of tactics, relying on both willing saboteurs and unwitting civilians to carry out bombings.They have succeeded in killing at least four Russian generals and several other senior military figures, as well as pro-war activists deep inside Russian territory, although some operations have missed their intended targets. In 2022, a car bomb killed Darya Dugina, the daughter of the ultranationalist Russian ideologue Aleksandr Dugin, in an attack widely believed to have been intended for her father.Explore more on these topicsRussiaEuropeUkrainenewsShareReuse this content

title: Romania blasts rock to divert water from drought-hit Danube to nuclear reactor | Romania | The Guardian
description: Hungary and Romania face energy crisis as record-low river levels force atomic power plants to reduce output
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Hungary and Romania face energy crisis as record-low river levels force atomic power plants to reduce output
Content: 0:38Romanian navy blows up rock in Danube to redirect water to nuclear plant – videoRomaniaRomania blasts rock to divert water from drought-hit Danube to nuclear reactorHungary and Romania face energy crisis as record-low river levels force atomic power plants to reduce outputLorenzo Tondoand agenciesMon 3 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRomanian naval forces carried out a controlled explosion to help redirect vital cooling water from the drought-hit Danube to the country’s last working nuclear ⁠reactor, while neighbouringHungary​said it may be able to eke out two more days of power from its only atomic plant.Hungary and Romania have beenforced to shut down nuclear reactorscooled by the Danube for the first time, as record-low water levels deepen fears of an energy crisis across the region.Romania has declared a nationwide state of emergency throughout August stemming from a decline in electricity productionafter record low Danube river levelsled to the shutdown at the Cernavodǎ nuclear plant.The Danube operation used 180kg of explosives, the Adevărul newspaper reported, to move a large rock restricting the flow of water in a blast that sent a tower of water ⁠into the air. The extraordinary measure underlined the scale of the crisis inEurope, where heat and drought have lowered river levels and raised concerns about water supplies, river transport and power generation.“Any day past Wednesday or Thursday that the nuclear power plant functions is a gain,” Romania’s defence minister, Radu Miruțǎ, said on Monday. “A day of it functioning is three times more efficient than the costs of this operation.”View image in fullscreenThe drought forced the shutdown of a reactor at Romania’s only nuclear plant at Cernavodǎ.Photograph: Andreea Alexandru/APExperts said the controlled explosion would allow authorities to build a temporary dam, diverting more water into the channel serving Cernavodǎ’s remaining reactor.With both countries’ sole nuclear plants at reduced ⁠capacity, Hungary and Romania are increasingly relying on expensive power imports as heatwave conditions increase demand for electricity. Both countries use water ​from the Danube as coolant for their reactors.At Paks, Hungary’s Soviet-era nuclear power station, output has been reduced. The 44-year-old plant, which normally generates almost half of the country’s electricity, is operating at less than half its capacity. Authorities ‌earlier said they might have to ‌shut Paks as early as Sunday, but later said it could operate at its reduced capacity until Monday ‌or Tuesday, offering a small reprieve for the power supply.Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, said the plant was expected to be fully shut down next week. With the Danube forecast to remain too shallow for the reactors’ cooling systems, the closure could last for several weeks.“An energy crisis situation could arise beginning Monday,” he posted on X. “Coordinated steps and restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences. We are counting on everyone!”He added: “Today and maybe tomorrow the last turbine producing 240 megawatts can keep working. This is very good news, as the complete shutdown of the plant can be avoided on one of the days with the ‌highest consumption.”View image in fullscreenThe partially dried-up Danube outside the Paks nuclear plant in Hungary.Photograph: Bernadett Szabó/ReutersMagyar earlier said voluntary ​cuts in power usage had reduced ​demand by 700MW on Sunday, significantly easing pressure on the grid.Adding to voluntary cuts by other companies, the pharmaceuticals company Richter said on Mondayit would reduce its electricity consumption by more than 50% in the next three weeks.In Serbia, record-low Danube levels have pushed the country’s key hydroelectric plant to operate with only 20% of its capacity, prompting the prime minister, Djuro Macut, to preside over an emergency meeting on Monday focusing on energy problems.Water levels are not expected to rise on the Danube in the coming days or even weeks as no significant rainfall is forecast. The river passes through 10 countries. In some stretches it has fallen to levels never previously recorded. The river’s retreat has revealed rocks, shipwrecks, a second world war bomb and theremains of a woolly mammoth.The prehistoric bones were discovered on the exposed riverbed by a resident of Ryahovo, a village in northern Bulgaria. Experts from the regional history museum in the nearby city of Ruse were sent to examine the rare find.Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsRomaniaHungaryEuropeDroughtClimate crisisRiversnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anti-war politician flees Russia amid pre-election crackdown on dissent | Russia | The Guardian
description: Boris Nadezhdin, who gained prominence after standing against Putin in 2024, says he is now in France
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Boris Nadezhdin, who gained prominence after standing against Putin in 2024, says he is now in France
Content: Boris Nadezhdin in court in Dolgoprudny, Russia, last month after he was briefly detained and accused of a minor administrative violation.Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/ReutersView image in fullscreenBoris Nadezhdin in court in Dolgoprudny, Russia, last month after he was briefly detained and accused of a minor administrative violation.Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/ReutersRussiaAnti-war politician flees Russia amid pre-election crackdown on dissentBoris Nadezhdin, who gained prominence after standing against Putin in 2024, says he is now in FrancePjotr SauerMon 3 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prominent Russian anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin has fled to Paris as Moscow tightens its grip on dissent before parliamentary elections later this year.Nadezhdin, a veteran liberal politician, gained international prominence during Russia’s 2024 presidential election when his long-shot campaign against Vladimir Putin unexpectedly gathered momentum before electoral authoritiesbarred him from running.Since his presidential campaign, Nadezhdin, 63, has remained one of the last well-known Russian public figures to publicly oppose the war in Ukraine. That made him an increasingly uncomfortable figure for the Kremlin.“Good news: I’m alive and free. Unfortunately, I’m not in Russia for the time being,” Nadezhdin said in a video filmed in front of the Eiffel Tower. He added that he needed “to look around and figure out life going forward”.Last month, less than three weeks after registering to run in September’s parliamentary elections, he was briefly detained and accused of a minor administrative violation in what was widely seen as an attempt to intimidate him and undermine his candidacy.The same month, the justice ministry designated Nadezhdin a “foreign agent” – a label that carries onerous reporting requirements, increased government scrutiny, and a powerful stigma in Russia.The designation, combined with a conviction on an extremism-related administrative charge, barred him from running in September’s parliamentary elections, which are widely expected to be tightly controlled by the Kremlin.In an interview with the Russian independent outlet Meduza last month, Nadezhdin said he and his family were considering leaving Russia as pressure from the authorities intensified. While he said he wanted to remain in the country and run in the parliamentary elections, he acknowledged that the growing risk of imprisonment was becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.Following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian authorities launched an unprecedented crackdown on dissent, targeting independent media, human rights groups, civil society organisations and critics of the war. Hundreds have been imprisoned and thousands more have fled the country.Putin’s ruling United Russia party is seeking to preserve its dominance in the lower house of parliament in September’s state-managed elections, in which no genuine opposition is allowed to take part. The vote comes amid signs of growing public fatigue with the war in Ukraine, as fuel shortages and mounting economic pressures weigh on Russians, leaving the Kremlin increasingly unwilling to tolerate even token opposition.Explore more on these topicsRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Designer John Galliano to get unvarnished Met retrospective in May | John Galliano | The Guardian
description: Decision to stage solo exhibition comes 15 years after conviction over racist and antisemitic remarks
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Decision to stage solo exhibition comes 15 years after conviction over racist and antisemitic remarks
Content: John Galliano at the end of his autumn-winter 2010-2011 show for Dior in Paris.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersView image in fullscreenJohn Galliano at the end of his autumn-winter 2010-2011 show for Dior in Paris.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersJohn GallianoDesigner John Galliano to get unvarnished Met retrospective in MayDecision to stage solo exhibition comes 15 years after conviction over racist and antisemitic remarksChloe Mac DonnellMon 3 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe controversial designerJohn Gallianois to get an unvarnished retrospective at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute in New York next May.Galliano, who is widely considered to be one of the most influential designers of the past four decades, was exiled from the industry in 2011 after he was filmed making a series of racist and antisemitic comments. He was fired from his position as creative director of Dior, a post he had held for 15 years, condemned by the media and laterconvicted and finedby a French court.At the time it was questioned whether the British designer would ever be able to redeem himself in the fashion industry.The decision by the Met to spotlight Galliano with his own fashion blockbuster, which will be only the third time it has given a living designer a solo exhibition, suggests that perhaps, he has reached the pinnacle of his rehabilitation. The exhibition will be kicked off by the annualMet Galared carpet extravaganza, making it one of the biggest events on the fashion calendar.“The fashion business has a short memory,” said Dana Thomas, the author of Gods and Kings: The Rise and Fall of Alexander McQueen and John Galliano. “It is also remarkably forgiving of bad behaviours.”Olya Kuryshchuk, the founder and editor in chief of the platform1 Granary, described it as “refreshing” to see the celebration of a living artist rather than a typical thematic exhibition.“Few designers have left a mark on fashion as profound as John Galliano,” she said. “He fundamentally changed the way fashion communicates emotion, fantasy and storytelling and influenced generations of designers.”Thomas describes Galliano as having “worked hard to earn the industry’s forgiveness”.A documentaryin 2024 by Kevin Macdonald delved into this redemption as the designer recalled how he spent time in rehabilitation for alcohol addiction and met prominent Jewish leaders to seek forgiveness. Within three years of his outburst, Galliano was appointed the creative director of Maison Margiela, a post he held for a decade and where he was widely lauded.View image in fullscreenA model presents a creation John Galliano for Maison Margiela in 2015 in Paris.Photograph: François Guillot/AFP/Getty ImagesSince then his reintegration into the fashion industry has stepped up even further. In January, he sat front row at Jonathan Anderson’s debut show for Dior. In March, it was announced Galliano was embarking on a “two-year creative partnership” with Zara on a series of collections, the first of which hits stores in September.According to theNew YorkTimes, the Met has held several meetings with Jewish leaders over the past year to discuss the event. In May, the Costume Institute’s head curator, Andrew Bolton, Vogue’s global editorial director and Met trustee, Anna Wintour, along with Galliano, attended a closed-door meeting met “a handful of the most influential rabbis and Jewish leaders in New York City”.According to a press release, the exhibition, which is split into three parts, “will address the derogatory conduct that fundamentally altered his career and public reception. In doing so, the exhibition will consider how artistic achievement should be understood alongside ethical accountability.”View image in fullscreenKate Moss takes to the runway in John Galliano’s breakthrough spring-summer 1994 show in Paris.Photograph: ARNAL/PAT/Gamma-Rapho/Getty ImagesWintour has championed Galliano since his graduate collection show at Central Saint Martins in London in 1984. She helped him secure financial support for his collections including his breakthrough spring-summer 1994 Paris show, which featured Kate Moss as a runaway bride, and championed him for roles at Givenchy and Dior. Insiders said a Met exhibition was originally planned for 2024 but was postponed after some board members voiced concerns.Writing on Vogue.comWintour said: “There is no one more deserving of an exhibition of this scale than John Galliano. He’s a great designer and his career isn’t defined by a moment – something that he will live with for the rest of his life. The exhibition won’t shy away from any of the darkness in John’s past. It’s part of what has shaped him. The show will take in the full arc of his career and grapple with all of it.”View image in fullscreenAnna Wintour, pictured with John Galliano at the Dior show in Paris last year, has championed the designer since 1984.Photograph: WWD/Getty ImagesThe exhibition John Galliano: Horizons will feature garments, accessories, sketches and research books with the aim of revealing “how Galliano brings places, histories, artistic traditions, narratives, and identities into unexpected relation and transforms these encounters into imaginative garments”.As the Costume Institute is the holder of the largest collection of Galliano’s work in the world, the exhibition is expected to include pieces from his earliest collections alongside examples from his more recent tenures.Bolton said the exhibition would trace “how images become ideas, ideas become material, and material becomes emotion”. It would also explore “both how Galliano has remapped the world through fashion and how his conduct, its consequences, and changing cultural values have reshaped our understanding of his work”, Bolton added.The show will begin by showing how Galliano’s collections relate to broader cultural events. The museum said this was where the exhibition would “directly address the rupture caused by his antisemitic, racist, and anti-Asian conduct in 2010 and 2011”.View image in fullscreenJohn Galliano poses at the end of the presentation of the Dior spring-summer 2010 show.Photograph: Jacques Brinon/APHowever, rather than “presenting a conventional narrative of disgrace and redemption, the gallery will examine how memory, experience, cultural values, and historical circumstances continually reshape the reception of a designer’s work. It will invite visitors to consider how aesthetic achievement, ethical accountability, and institutional recognition intersect.”Sarah Gresty, the course leader of the fashion BA at Central Saint Martins, said Galliano was still an inspiration for many of its students. “Lots of students admire the skill and aesthetic ambition of Galliano so I am not surprised by the news. The museum obviously have decided his work merits that platform.”Thomas added that the retrospective would show whether the public had forgiven Galliano too, or whether “extraordinary talent” ultimately outweighed even “extraordinary transgressions”.Explore more on these topicsJohn GallianoMuseumsMet GalaNew YorknewsShareReuse this content

title: UK manufacturing growth picks up as Trump tariff chaos eases | Economics | The Guardian
description: Factories in upbeat mood despite fears over economic impact of US war on Iran, poll finds
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Factories in upbeat mood despite fears over economic impact of US war on Iran, poll finds
Content: The S&P Global purchasing managers’ index dipped in July, but maintained a run of nine months of expansion.Photograph: David Levenson/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe S&P Global purchasing managers’ index dipped in July, but maintained a run of nine months of expansion.Photograph: David Levenson/AlamyEconomicsUK manufacturing growth picks up as Trump tariff chaos easesFactories in upbeat mood despite fears over economic impact of US war on Iran, poll findsBusiness live – latest updatesPhillip InmanMon 3 Aug 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK manufacturers ramped up production last month for the fourth consecutive month and at the fastest pace in almost two years, according to a leading survey of the industry.The S&P Global poll of manufacturers found them in upbeat mood in July, though anxious about the prospect of a long war in the Middle East that would block supplies of oil and gas, and raise the cost of production.Uncertainty about the outcome of the war meant the S&P Global purchasing managers’ index (PMI) dipped in July, but maintained a run of nine months of expansion. The PMI, which tracks activity in the sector, fell back to 51.9 in July, down from 52.5 in June, despite the rise in manufacturing output growth. A reading above 50 denotes a period of expansion.UK economy faces recession if strait of Hormuz remains closed, EY warns - business liveRead moreThe figures come after a torrid two years for the manufacturing industry after the election ofDonald Trumpand the president’s “liberation day” tariffs that took effect in the spring last year. The industry received a second big blow last autumn when a hack of the computer system at Jaguar Land Rover brought production at the UK’s largest car manufacturer to a halt.The report said the latest increase in production was strongly linked to “rising intakes of new business from both domestic and export clients”.Total new orders rose for the eighth successive month, with some companies noting an improvement in the functioning of global supply chains after the chaos caused by US tariffs in 2025.It said new export orders flowed from the US and Canada, the EU, mainland China, India and South Korea.However, the recovery has led to only a small increase in employment. “Uncertainty about the future dragged on the labour market in July. Although staffing levels increased for the fourth successive month, the rate of growth eased to near-stagnation and was the weakest during the current upturn,” the report said.Rob Dobson, the director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said July brought “further encouragement for the UK manufacturing sector”, as rates of growth in output, new orders and new export business all accelerated.He said a moratorium on new hiring in July was likely to be short-lived after the influx of new business caused backlogs of work, which should prompt companies to take on more staff.“This would be assisted if business optimism recovers from its current subdued level. Hopefully progress relating to geopolitics, global trade tensions and the direction of the new UK government’s industrial and tax policies will aid, and not hinder, this process,” he added.Ginni Cooper, the manufacturing partner at the accountancy firm MHA, said: the manufacturing sector had proved resilient amid yo-yoing commodity prices that had seen the cost of many basic manufacturing goods rise and fall sharply in recent months, including oil and gas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Manufacturers are by their nature positive and adaptable to change and these past few months have tested both,” she said.She said many companies in the industry had welcomed the initiatives announced by Andy Burnham after becoming prime minister, includingvocational training in schools.Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the consultancy the Item Club, was more downbeat about the prospects for the rest of the year.He said: “We expect the sector to endure a difficult period in the latter half of this year. The conflict in the Middle East is the key wildcard, but the breakdown of the ceasefire has led to a resurgence in oil and gas prices, as well as increasing business uncertainty.“Higher energy prices will filter through into higher business costs while demand will be hit by the squeeze on disposable incomes from rising inflation and weakening wage growth.”Explore more on these topicsEconomicsManufacturing sectorManufacturing dataTariffsTrump tariffsDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: AstraZeneca shares fall 8.9% over merger talks with US cancer drug firm | AstraZeneca | The Guardian
description: Proposed $400bn tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb would create world’s fourth-largest drugmaker but analysts question rationale
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Proposed $400bn tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb would create world’s fourth-largest drugmaker but analysts question rationale
Content: AstraZeneca is the second-biggest listed company in the UK, with a market value of nearly £196bn.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAstraZeneca is the second-biggest listed company in the UK, with a market value of nearly £196bn.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianAstraZenecaAstraZeneca shares fall 8.9% over merger talks with US cancer drug firmProposed $400bn tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb would create world’s fourth-largest drugmaker but analysts question rationaleJulia KolleweMon 3 Aug 2026 12.32 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 03.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than £17bn was wiped off the value of Britain’s biggest drugmaker,AstraZeneca, on Monday after a report that it was in discussions to take over its US rival Bristol Myers Squibb in a deal that would create a near $400bn (£300bn) pharmaceutical group.AstraZeneca, run by Pascal Soriot, its longtime chief executive, had been worth nearly £196bn before the news broke. BMS, headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and known for its cancer treatments, was worth $133bn (£98bn).A tie-up would be one of the biggest ever pharmaceutical deals and would create the world’s fourth largest drugmaker by market value.AstraZeneca boss urges western drugmakers to move at ‘Chinese speed’Read moreAstraZeneca’s FTSE 100-listed shares plunged by 8.9% to close at a low of £115 in London as investors reacted to news of the talks, which werefirst reported by the Financial Times.That pushed AstraZeneca’s value down to about £178bn, as it lost the title of the second-biggest listed company in the UK to Shell.BMS’s shares rose 1.7% after Wall Street opened, before reversing and losing those gains by midday in New York.While talks have been held in recent months, there is no certainty that a deal will be concluded, according to sources.A deal would expand AstraZeneca’s presence in the US, where it is alreadyinvesting $50bn in research and manufacturing by 2030. It completed a direct listing of its shares on the New York stock exchange in June, and a deal with BMS could revive fears of a shift away from the UK.The news surprised analysts, who questioned the rationale behind a tie-up and noted that any deal would be closely scrutinised by regulators, given the overlap of the companies’ oncology portfolios.Analysts at Jefferies, led by Michael Leuchten, said: “‘Why’ is perhaps not yet clear to us: we suspect that most people will focus on the potential to establish an even bigger oncology powerhouse, with the resultant portfolio likely the broadest in the industry. However, beyond the regulatory hurdles we would argue that pipeline assets could be sourced elsewhere, as AstraZeneca has been doing, particularly in China.”Chris Beauchamp, a chief market analyst at the investment platform IG, said: “Though a rare example of a big UK firm buying a smaller US firm is something to warm the cockles of the British heart, it risks the departure of yet another national champion, and in any case the pair’s large cancer divisions are a major hurdle to a successful deal. BMS has struggled since 2023, and some Astra shareholders will wonder at the need to do expensive M&A when their shares are doing so well.”Some shareholders were also sceptical. “The only advantage for AstraZeneca in this rumoured combination with BMS seems to be to accelerate its US footprint and sales,” said Lucy Coutts, an investment director at JM Finn, an AstraZeneca shareholder. “On balance, BMS shareholders would be the winners of any combination with AstraZeneca and so this news will undoubtedly be received coolly by AstraZeneca shareholders,” she told Reuters.A major shareholder told the Guardian: “Bold potential move, but not yet any real detail to get our teeth into.”Lukas Leu, a portfolio manager at the AstraZeneca shareholder ATG Healthcare Investments, said a deal could boost margins through cost synergies and expand reach in neuroscience and cell therapy, but he questioned how a combined firm would position competing drugs. “I am not a big fan of mega-mergers, it kills innovation and agility,” he said.AstraZeneca, headquartered in Cambridge, England, was formed in 1999 from the merger of the Swedish company Astra AB and the UK company Zeneca Group. Zeneca had been spun off from Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI) five years earlier.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAstraZeneca’s share price has more than quadrupled during Soriot’s leadership, when it overtook its UK rival GSK in size.Under Soriot,the company fended off a hostile bid from its US rival Pfizerin 2014 that valued AstraZeneca at almost £70bn. He then successfully rebuilt the company’s drug pipeline with cancer immunotherapies – drugs that harness the body’s immune system to fight tumours – and other treatments.A week ago, AstraZeneca said it was confident of hitting its growth targets for 2030, by which time itexpects to achieve $80bn (£60bn) in annual sales, up from $59bn last year, despite the surprise failure of Wainua, one of its leading heart disease drugs in development. Soriot saidthe company must move at “Chinese speed”to ensure it did not fall behind competitors.A few days later, BMS beat Wall Street expectations with its second-quarter results and lifted its 2026 outlook. It made revenues of $12.97bn during the quarter, up 5% on a year earlier, excluding currency movements.The US company employs about 800 people in the UK. Its UK research team of 250 people isbased at Moreton on the Wirral peninsulanear Liverpool, while its commercial head office for the UK and Ireland is in Uxbridge, west London.John Murphy, a senior pharma analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said a deal made “limited strategic sense” for AstraZeneca. “Their growth outlooks are very different – double-digit earnings gains are forecast at Astra through 2030, with Bristol set for continued declines, due to multiple patent expiries – and, while both are focused on developing promising pipelines, history suggests such mega-mergers hamper pipeline progress.“Major cost savings via eradication of overlapping infrastructure is one obvious benefit but would suggest reduced confidence at Astra in its pipeline and growth outlook. A link-up in certain disease categories may be a possible area of future collaboration,” he added.AstraZeneca declined to comment. BMS was also contacted.Explore more on these topicsAstraZenecaPharmaceuticals industryMergers and acquisitionsnewsShareReuse this content
