title: ‘Trumpeters? We think we’re the kings of the orchestra’: Wynton Marsalis prepares to blow the Edinburgh festival away | Wynton Marsalis | The Guardian
description: It has 12 movements, 200 musicians and aims to unite America. The great US trumpeter and composer talks about his All Rise symphony, his jazz great mentors – and learning humility from his wife
Author: John Lewis
Headline: It has 12 movements, 200 musicians and aims to unite America. The great US trumpeter and composer talks about his All Rise symphony, his jazz great mentors – and learning humility from his wife
Content: ‘I was one of the youngest in the orchestra. Now I’m probably the oldest’ … Marsalis.View image in fullscreen‘I was one of the youngest in the orchestra. Now I’m probably the oldest’ … Marsalis.Wynton MarsalisInterview‘Trumpeters? We think we’re the kings of the orchestra’: Wynton Marsalis prepares to blow the Edinburgh festival awayJohn LewisIt has 12 movements, 200 musicians and aims to unite America. The great US trumpeter and composer talks about his All Rise symphony, his jazz great mentors – and learning humility from his wifeMon 3 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt Heinz Hall in Pittsburgh,Wynton Marsalisis hard to spot. When he first played this venue, in 1984, he was the prodigious 22-year-old soloist out front, blowing Haydn’s trumpet concerto under the baton of Lorin Maazel. Tonight he is embedded in the machinery: half-hidden behind ranks of strings and woodwind, a black-suited figure in the heart of his own symphony.It’s a strange way for a composer to behave – especially one whose public persona has long been associated with certainty, polemic and the upright authority of a man who can make any argument sound like a moral law. Yet Marsalis seems almost pleased by his disappearance. “It’s my piece,” he says, as we talk in his hotel room the next morning, “but it’s not my show.”double quotation markWhen you hang out with old people, you stay 19 for everThe piece is All Rise, Marsalis’s first symphony, written in 1999 – a mammoth hybrid for a 15-piece jazz band, a 50-piece orchestra and a 100-piece choir, premiered at the turn of the millennium by the New York Philharmonic with Kurt Masur. Across 12 movements, Marsalis paints a sprawling civic canvas whose building blocks are American – marches, blues, dance rhythms – and whose aspiration is almost embarrassingly large: to sound like pluralism.This year’s Edinburgh international festival has built its artistic theme around the piece: on the opening night at Usher Hall, Marsalis and hisJazzat Lincoln Center Orchestra will join the Royal Scottish National Orchestra and massed choirs. That’s more than 200 performers in total. Edinburgh has had no shortage of big opening statements over the decades, but this is a particularly pointed choice: a work first conceived as a celebration of integration, now revived in a moment when the very idea of common culture has begun to look quaint.View image in fullscreenMassed ranks … jazz band, orchestra and choirs on stage in Pittsburgh.Photograph: Gilberto Tadday/Jazz at Lincoln CenterIn the past, Marsalis could be confrontational: a man with a rulebook and a relish for battle. Today he’s mellower: quick to credit others, reject ego and talk more about collaboration than correction. He’s keen to puncture the myth that a symphonic work is the solitary utterance of genius. “All Rise was a collaborative exercise. James Oliverio, a soundtrack writer, was teaching me how to orchestrate while I was doing it. I had Milan Turković, the great Austrian bassoonist, helping me with the woodwind. But the main man was the late conductor Kurt Masur. He was always goading me to write something for him. ‘Are you afraid to write for the New York Philharmonic?’ he’d say. Kurt saw a segregated New York, and wanted a piece that brought people together.”Masur – East German, Beethovenian, exacting – was conscripted into the German army as a teen in the final months of the second world war. “I remember he told me then, ‘You think that nazism is unique to Germany? It can happen here.’ Kurt said nazism didn’t happen because people were poor: it happened because lots of Germans wanted to behave like that. And, coming from the south, I could relate to that.”For some, All Rise is exhilarating: a large-scale attempt to make American music sound like an argument worth having. For others, it feels like an impossible negotiation: two institutions – orchestra and big band – asked to behave like one. Marsalis has always been furiously outspoken about what he sees as the malign role of “fusion” in jazz, and is equally wary of the limits of fusing jazz and symphonic music. “I wanted to draw from American mythology and find intersections. Because with some music, there is no common ground.”For instance? “You’re not going to hear a jazz version of a Beethoven symphony. It’s too many chord changes.” Marsalis’s first symphony is instead built on the dance music shared by Americans. “It’s about the relationship between tango and choro; between ragtime and Anglo-Celtic fiddle music; between New Orleans marches and European band counterpoint. But you have to be aware of certain things. In classical music, the basses don’t play all the time. In our music, it plays all the time. And in classical music, the percussion is accent, but in jazz and Latin music, it’s everything.“So you have to find the common ground that you intersect with. Because if you’re not on that ground, there’s no intersection. John Coltrane said he was looking for a universal coefficient. It’s like the word mama. You say mama, it has a universal sound and feeling to it.”He talks a lot about seeking links with other musics – about what he’s learned from the Iraqi oud virtuoso Naseer Shamma, Ghanaian percussionist Yacub Addy, Irish-American violinist Mark O’Connor, and about his enduring friendships with Willie Nelson and Paul Simon. “I meet up with Paul as much as I can – we talk a lot about the relationships between African-American and Anglo-Celtic music, how that is the foundation of pretty much everything we all do.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s my piece but it’s not my show’ … Marsalis on stage in Pittsburgh.Photograph: Gilberto Tadday/Jazz at Lincoln CenterUnlike some of Marsalis’s other large-scale pieces, All Rise is not a polemic. “If you want to know how I think jazz can help democracy, listen to [2020 album] The Ever Fonky Lowdown. If you want to hear what I say about government corruption – and how our government has always been corrupt – listen to my song Super Capitalism, on [the 2007 album] From the Plantation to the Penitentiary. But All Rise is different, it’s about bringing people together.”Drawing from spirituals, gospel music and European devotional sources, All Rise is also full of God. Has his faith changed since writing it? “No. I always had a very strong spiritual faith that was not denominational, even as a kid. I came from very spiritual people. I spent a lot of time with my great uncle, who was born in 1883. He was a stonecutter for the cemetery. If you are around death that much, you become religious.“But I never believed in the dogma. I always noticed the contradictions in Christianity: the saviour was poor, the church is rich. The saviour took a vow of poverty and said, ‘Love people.’ But a lot of religious people don’t love people who aren’t into their religion. So my libretto constantly counterstates that. I draw from the Muslim call to prayer as much as the Bible.”Marsalis, now 64, is fascinated by such ecumenical statements: he remembers his father telling him to read Autobiography of a Yogi when he left high school. “That book was hard work. My dad told me to carry a notebook and write down the name of each swami. When you want to make connections, you have to really work at it.”One connection he’s worked at is his marriage. Marsalis recently married Scottish violinist Nicola Benedetti, who also happens to be director of the Edinburgh international festival. They have a daughter, Elise, born in May 2024. Their relationship is largely long-distance at the moment – lengthy FaceTime chats and phone conversations. Would he ever move to the UK? “I’m going to have to plead the fifth on that one, I’m afraid,” he says with a chuckle, but also dismisses the prospect of Benedetti joining him in New York. “She’s not going to do that,” he says with a resigned smile.View image in fullscreen‘I fell in love with Nicola when I wrote her a violin concerto’ … Marsalis’s wife Nicola Benedetti.Photograph: Andy ParadiseBenedetti, 26 years Marsalis’s junior, has been a frequent collaborator. “What really made me fall in love with Nicola was when I wrote a violin concerto for her,” says Marsalis. “After the first run-through, she sent me a list of about 40 notes. First I laughed. Then I read them. And each of them were tiny things she thought I should change. Her detail was quite incredible. ‘If you put the violas on beat one of the 58th bar, that will save us 20 minutes of rehearsal time. Maybe put the bassoon’s entry at the end of bar 112, on the four of the bar rather than the two. Maybe stress the first beat of that passage in 5/8 time.’ And so on.“I was amazed that she was able to notice all of this while playing the piece. I have so much respect for her, the time she spends practising, her dedication to the humility of study, the desire to learn, to get better. And she is completely collegiate in the way she deals with ensembles.” Has he learned humility from her? “Maybe. Trumpeters, we think we’re the kings of the orchestra, there to blow down the walls of Jericho. We think the piece only starts when we start playing. We know the strings are doing something but we can’t figure out what the hell they’re up to. Maybe I’m less like that now …”I suggest that people will already expect young Elise, with such parentage, to grow up as a virtuoso musician. “She’s a hell of a singer,” he says. “But you can’t determine what your children do. I’ve got three sons – only one is a musician. He’s mainly a visual artist, but he makes music as part of his practice. One teaches track and soccer. Another teaches literature. I never put them in any direction – I just wanted to make sure they have integrity.”How is he coping with late fatherhood? “You know, I always used to hang out with older people. All my mentors were older men – not just my father, but Clark Terry, Dizzy Gillespie, Sweets Edison, Elvin Jones, August Wilson, Romare Bearden, Ralph Ellison. And, when you’re hanging out with old people, you stay 19 for ever. But I’ve always enjoyed hanging with young people too. It’s a privilege when people come up after gigs, teenage kids with their parents, asking for advice. It takes a village to raise a child. We’re all raising the same kid.”‘I saw Herbie Hancock play with D’Angelo, and got my head blown off!’: the festival keeping alive jazz’s golden ageRead moreWhen Marsalis began running the jazz orchestra and jazz programme at Lincoln Center – New York’s pre-eminent arts complex – he was just 26. “I was one of the youngest in the orchestra, alongside legends who had worked with Ellington and Basie. Now I’m probably the oldest.” He recently announced that he will be stepping back from his executive leadership role after nearly four decades, while remaining involved artistically for a transition period.It’s easy to imagine Marsalis as an Alex Ferguson-type spectral presence, presiding warily over anyone who takes up the reins. “No, I’m not going to be like that. There are so many talented people in the band now who could carry on what I’m doing. The bassist Carlos Henriquez, the alto saxophonist Sherman Irby, tenor saxophonist and clarinetist Dan Block – all amazing professionals. But it’s not my choice: there’s a whole executive board at the Lincoln Center who will be making that decision.”Maybe stepping away from the Lincoln Center has altered his angle of vision. For decades it was his pulpit for declarations; now he sounds more interested in how musicians learn one another’s language – happy to defer, amused by his own ego. “I think about Copernicus and Galileo, about how they both observed that the Earth was not the centre of the solar system. They realised that, every time you discovered a new body, the equation became more complicated, until you stopped clinging to the old ways of looking at the universe. Maybe we all need to do that.”All Rise opens theEdinburgh international festival on 8 August. The UK premiere of Marsalis’s Concerto for Orchestra is at theBBC Proms on 13 AugustExplore more on these topicsWynton MarsalisClassical musicJazzEdinburgh festivalEdinburgh festival 2026FestivalsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day: new characters, new flaws, new tech and brain-exploding future consequences – discuss with spoilers | Movies | The Guardian
description: Now you’ve seen the new Spidey, let’s talk about new baddies (or are they goodies?), X-Men alumni, painful relationships and a potential Spidey-pig
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Now you’ve seen the new Spidey, let’s talk about new baddies (or are they goodies?), X-Men alumni, painful relationships and a potential Spidey-pig
Content: Holding on by a thread … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Sony PicturesView image in fullscreenHolding on by a thread … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Sony PicturesNow you've seen itMoviesSpider-Man: Brand New Day: new characters, new flaws, new tech and brain-exploding future consequences – discuss with spoilersNow you’ve seen the new Spidey, let’s talk about new baddies (or are they goodies?), X-Men alumni, painful relationships and a potential Spidey-pigThis article contains spoilers for Spider-Man: Brand New DayBen ChildMon 3 Aug 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a danger thatSpider-Man: Brand New Daymight amount to little more than a palate cleanser between the multiversal excesses of No Way Home and the all-star chaos ofAvengers: Doomsday. Why not just keep it small: a more grounded tale of New York crime-fighting, to keep the Marvel machine rolling before the inevitable return of world-ending stakes? Instead, the studio, once again in partnership with Spider-Man rights holder Sony, has produced a gamechanging comic book epic whose effects will continue being felt for years to come.The film’s biggest twist is significant enough on its own, but Brand New Day keeps widening the implications long after the initial shock has started to wear off. Characters who seemed to exist for one purpose gradually reveal another. Throwaway conversations acquire unexpected significance. New gadgets, strange abilities and apparently routine subplots all hint at much broader shifts taking place beneath the familiar web-slinging adventure. By the time the credits have rolled, the film has answered some longstanding questions, raised several more, and left audiences with a surprisingly clear idea of where theMarvelCinematic Universe (MCU) could be heading next.So if you walked out of the cinema this weekend wondering why certain revelations felt so important, what some seemingly innocuous scenes were really setting up, or whether one particular post-credit tease might have enormous implications for the years ahead, here is what the film may have been trying to tell us.Something very strange is happening toSpider-ManView image in fullscreenPeter Parker (Tom Holland) peers through a web in Spider-Man: Brand New DayPhotograph: CTMG/PAThe Peter Parker we re-encounter at the beginning of Brand New Day is in a bad place. Yes, he has locked up enough New York City supervillains to recreatethe Sinister Sixseveral times over, but he lives a lonely existence without his dear departed Aunt May, his girlfriend MJ or his best friend, Ned, and the last two don’t even remember who he is thanks to Doctor Strange’s spell at the tail end ofNo Way Home. As if loneliness weren’t awful enough, Spidey also finds himself struggling to control strange new powers: the organic web shooters could be useful if they can be controlled but the hypersensitive Spider-sense is a problem, while all that extra arachnid aggression only serves to increase the chances of our friendly neighbourhood hero accidentally taking down innocent bystanders. The question remains whether the hero really is falling apart or just evolving into something new.A Jean Grey for the Marvel Cinematic UniverseJust when Spidey is at his weakest, he is faced with an antagonist whose powers far outstrip those of the street-level crims he has been swatting away. At first, Sadie Sink appears to be portraying a common-or-garden body-swapping baddie who is out to hurt MJ if Parker doesn’t do what she says. But it quickly emerges, in one of the most significant moments in the series, that this is the MCU’s version of Jean Grey, a telepath with extraordinary powers whose presence means we are now firmly in the Marvel mutant era.Damage Control isnot what it wasIntroduced inSpider-Man: Homecomingas a sort of handy clean-up gang who zoom in to put everything back in its rightful place after Loki and his mates have smashed up another cityscape, the Department of Damage Control initially looks like just another one of Spider-Man’s allies in the battle against supervillain chaos. Yet it soon emerges that something more sinister is going on. All Jean wants is to rescue her sister Sara, who is being held against her will at the organisation’s secret complex – or at least she was, until scientists killed her while trying to learn how her telepathic powers worked. Led by Bill Metzger (Tramell Tillman), this new take on Damage Control seems to be transforming into the MCU’s version of the comic books’ Mutant Response Division. Then the younger Grey is trapped at the complex, effectively taking her dead sister’s place.Did Peter Parker just invent the mutant restraint collar?View image in fullscreenMJ (Zendaya) watches Spider-Man at workPhotograph: CTMG/PAHere we need to roll the plot back a little, to the chapter in which Peter approaches Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner – now happily teaching at Empire State University and sporting a decidedly less green complexion – to ask how he has managed to stop transforming into the Hulk and flattening half of Manhattan every five minutes. It turns out he has been using an inhibitor chip, whose underlying technology Peter realises could also help stabilise his own increasingly erratic mutation. Being a scientific genius in his own right, Parker builds his own version (with the help of MJ), taming those organic web-shooters, dialling back the hair-trigger aggression and regaining control of his wayward powers.Only later does the breakthrough acquire much darker significance. Peter adapts Banner’s technology into a universal inhibitor and uses a second chip to suppress Jean’s abilities during their confrontation at Damage Control. Jean ultimately overwhelms the device but its broken remains are left behind. What looked like a powerful tool against unwanted mutation could therefore become something akin to the power-dampening restraints that have long haunted the X-Men comics. Peter has probably solved his own problem – in fact, by the end of the movie, he decides he doesn’t even need the chip – but may also have invented the MCU’s first truly effective anti-mutant weapon.How manyX-Menare already out there?The question now is whether the MCU has its own (presumably youthful) versions of Charles Xavier, Wolverine and Cyclops waiting in the wings, or whether we won’t get to see them until the original 20th Century Fox-era versions have yet another swansong in the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. The New Avengers’ Yelena Belova, who spends much of Brand New Day sitting in a Russian bathhouse on Zoom, later begins decoding Damage Control’s redacted files, suggesting that the conspiracy may stretch beyond what Peter and Jean have uncovered. We no longer need ask whether mutants exist in the MCU, but rather how many the bad guys already know about, and what else Metzger has been doing to them.Ned, MJ and getting the old gang back togetherIt was inevitable Peter would reacquaint himself with the two people who matter most to him, even if neither initially has the faintest idea why the nervous young man hovering at the edge of their lives seems so familiar. The trio’s gradual reconnection risks softening the wonderfully bleak ending of No Way Home, in which Parker chose to keep his friends safe and ignorant rather than risk putting them in the sort of danger that eventually killed Aunt May. But Brand New Day does not simply reverse Doctor Strange’s spell, or restore the previous status quo at the flick of a mystical switch. Instead, it suggests Peter may have to earn his comrades’ friendship all over again. Spidey is not quite getting the old gang back together – he is being offered the much more awkward prospect of meeting them for the first time again.Exactly whichSpider-Mandid the Spider-tracker find?One of Brand New Day’s most amusing conceits is Ned’s 8-bit-style Spidey-tracker, which seems to be able to pinpoint the location of the nearest wall crawler with remarkable accuracy. It is never made particularly clear how it works, but the film’s post-credit scene suggests that the faux retro tech might have a more potent long-term use than just helping Peter’s best friend keep tabs on him. It appears to detect aSpider-Manbeyond Earth’s atmosphere, raising the obvious question of which version of Spider-Man is out in the cosmos.Given that the post-credits scene ofThunderbolts*showed the Fantastic Four’s rocket ship heading towards the MCU version of Earth, the temptation is to imagine an alternate-reality version of Spidey entering the solar system just in time to play a pivotal role in Avengers: Doomsday. The problem is that there are so many possible candidates: Tobey Maguire Spidey; Andrew Garfield Spidey; Miles Morales; Spider-Noir; Spider-Gwen; or perhaps even that weird little Spider-pig from the animated films. Then again, maybe Ned’s machine is simply on the blink after he spilled one too many caffeine drinks on it.Explore more on these topicsFilmNow you've seen itSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayTom HollandZendayaSpider-ManMarvelSuperhero moviesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A gentle poetry in the everyday’: why The Straight Story is my feelgood movie | David Lynch | The Guardian
description: The latest in our ongoing series of writers picking their most beloved comfort films is a tribute to David Lynch’s gentlest movie
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our ongoing series of writers picking their most beloved comfort films is a tribute to David Lynch’s gentlest movie
Content: Richard Farnsworth in The Straight Story.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenRichard Farnsworth in The Straight Story.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMy feelgood movieDavid Lynch‘A gentle poetry in the everyday’: why The Straight Story is my feelgood movieThe latest in our ongoing series of writers picking their most beloved comfort films is a tribute to David Lynch’s gentlest moviePatrick SmithMon 3 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat was your gateway into the Lynchian empire? Maybe it was the elliptical horror of Mulholland Drive, with its labyrinth of dream and deceit. Perhaps it was the small-town banality of Twin Peaks or Blue Velvet, the gee-whiz vernacular and cherry-pie dispositions hiding a malice so pure behind those white picket fences. Or was it Wild at Heart, that nightmarish road movie where oddballs and deviants lurk at every bend, Nicolas Cage and Laura Dern tearing through America with unbridled passion and violence?‘The plane movie I’ll watch anytime’: why Up in the Air is my feelgood movieRead moreWeirdly, it was none of those for me. In fact, my introduction toDavid Lynchcontained not one drop of sexual depravity or grisly malevolence. The film was The Straight Story and I was 15. Released in May 1999, it tells the real-life tale of Alvin Straight, a 73-year-old second world war vet who rode a lawnmower 300 miles across the midwest to reconcile with his ailing brother. While the title obviously names the main character, it also invites you to take Lynch at his word: that this is that fabled chronicler of the demented and the macabre playing it straight(ish). Think of it as Lynch does Disney: a family-friendly hymn to Americana, sparse and only a little bit strange, finding a gentle poetry in the everyday.My love for this Homeric tale deepened around a decade ago, when I was commissioned to write about the making of the film. I spoke to Mary Sweeney – Lynch’s longtime editor, producer and then partner – who told me how she’d come across the story in the first place, reading about Straight’s odyssey in the New York Times. Charmed by the man’s plucky attitude, she optioned the rights, wrote the screenplay with a childhood friend, John Roach, and brought it to Lynch.Cast in the lead role was Richard Farnsworth, a stuntman turned Oscar-nominated actor for 1978’s Comes a Horseman. A picture of stoic defiance in his red plaid jacket and cowboy hat, he nails Straight’s contradictions: stubborn yet tender, infirm yet unstoppable. There is a flinty gravitas to his work, and a low-key dignity too, shimmering in the ice-blue pools of his rheumy eyes. That he knew this was his swan song, terminally ill as he was during the shoot, means his grizzled face becomes a canvas on to which ache and acceptance paint themselves. He was 79 and lost to Kevin Spacey at the 2000 Oscars. He died later that year.The film around Farnsworth, scored with a blend of mournful Spanish guitar and folksy fiddle by Lynch stalwart Angelo Badalamenti, cruises along in perfect harmony with his talents. Serving up succour for the soul, it drifts from scene to scene with a hushed profundity, alighting on the various exchanges with people Straight meets on the road: a pregnant runaway, a woman hysterical after hitting a deer, a pair of squabbling twin mechanics and a retired John Deere employee who lets Alvin camp in his back yard. Most poignant of all, though, is a tavern scene in Iowa, where Straight, sipping a glass of milk, opens up to a fellow veteran. “That is one thing I can’t shake loose,” he laments. “All my buddies’ faces are still young. And the thing is, the more years I have, the more they’ve lost.”Throughout that sequence, Freddie Francis, the film’s venerable cinematographer, holds his lens on Farnsworth’s face, the subtle twitches saying as much as the dialogue itself. It was the final film for Francis too, and equally Oscar-worthy, though not nominated: amid sweeping vistas, crops harvested in a wash of magic-hour light and roads stretching into the infinite distance, each shot is as evocative as that one creased, weather-beaten visage.Watching it now, sinceLynch’s own death in January 2025, carries an added pathos. In his final years, he too found walking difficult, then impossible, his lungs ravaged by decades of smoking, much like Straight’s. Acclaimed though the film was, it made just $6.2m at the US box office – less than its $10m budget – and remains a relatively unknown gem. Whenever I’ve watched it with someone, though, their verdict has always been the same: that it’s deeply moving.The exquisite last scene belongs to Harry Dean Stanton, an actor who knew a thing or two about laconic devastation, having spent Wim Wenders’s Paris, Texas (my favourite movie) saying almost nothing at all. “Did you ride that thing all the way out here to see me?” says Stanton’s Lyle, glancing at the lawnmower, lip quivering, years of resentment dissolving in a single frame. “I did, Lyle,” comes the reply. It’s a flawless ending. Emerging untouched is just about inconceivable.The Straight Story is available on Disney+ and the Criterion Channel in the US, to rent digitally in the UK and on Mubi in AustraliaThis article was amended on 3 August 2026 to clarify that Richard Farnsworth died after the 2000 Oscars, not before.Explore more on these topicsDavid LynchMy feelgood movieDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: This Tempting Madness review – watchable psychological suspense offers Mexican standoff of gaslighting | Movies | The Guardian
description: Pleasingly potboilerish tale of a woman trying to make sense of a traumatic fall that left her comatose slightly loses track of its toxic mind games
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Pleasingly potboilerish tale of a woman trying to make sense of a traumatic fall that left her comatose slightly loses track of its toxic mind games
Content: Frock horror … This Tempting Madness.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenFrock horror … This Tempting Madness.Photograph: Publicity imageMoviesReviewThis Tempting Madness review – watchable psychological suspense offers Mexican standoff of gaslightingPleasingly potboilerish tale of a woman trying to make sense of a traumatic fall that left her comatose slightly loses track of its toxic mind gamesPhil HoadMon 3 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is fair to say that spending your time doodling ouroboroses and picking open your surgical scar probably indicates you are not in a fantastic frame of mind. These are coping mechanisms for Mia (Simone Ashley) after she wakes up, at the start of this capable psychological thriller, from a coma resulting from falling several storeys of an airport building. A safety net is luckily there to catch her – but she remains in mental freefall. Assaulted by stray fragments of memory, she is unable to say whether husband, Jake (Austin Stowell), who is currently in jail, was the one who pushed her over the parapet.As Mia tries to piece together shattered body and mind, her family, led by solicitous brother Ajay (Suraj Sharma), try to persuade her to cut Jake loose. But she dithers, held back by guilt about how seriously she took his own unravelling, the spiralling paranoia that made him quit his job as a New York actuary and led them to start a new life in Los Angeles. When she finally visits him in jail, is Jake gaslighting her – intent on further manipulation – when he suggests that Ajay is gaslighting her for his own ends by pushing her to break up with him? Or she gaslighting herself by giving him the benefit of the doubt in the first place? This is a Mexican standoff of gaslighting.Pulling this claustrophobic knot satisfyingly tight, director Jennifer E Montgomery occasionally snags a Vertigo-like sense of concertinaed time as she explores Mia and Jake’s troubled past. There’s a kind of mnemonic rapture in the recurring snapshot of her tumbling down the atrium in her tangerine dress, and with the circle motif omnipresent in her drawings and elsewhere, in the suggestiont that this cycle of abuse must be broken.Lurching into the past, or into Mia’s fugue states, every other minute, This Tempting Madness is heavily plot-driven without exactly being scrupulously plotted. It sometimes loses its grip on Mia’s inner state, and what may be prompting a particular spinout at a given moment. Culminating in a jarringly rough ending, it doesn’t quite have an astute enough grasp of these queasy personalities for true Hitchcockian finesse (Ajay, especially, ends up underused). But Montgomery brings visual poise to a pleasingly potboilerish wallow in toxic co-dependency.This Tempting Madness is on digital platforms from 10 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Ribbon Hero review – do-gooder princess battles giant flying earwigs in update of classic yarn | Movies | The Guardian
description: Yûki Igarashi’s adaptation of Osamu Tezuka’s influential manga is a conservative (if impressively animated) reimagining that dulls the source material’s pioneering elements
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Yûki Igarashi’s adaptation of Osamu Tezuka’s influential manga is a conservative (if impressively animated) reimagining that dulls the source material’s pioneering elements
Content: ‘Haute Euro-pageantry placed against striking 2D backdrops’ … The Ribbon Hero.Photograph: ©Twin EngineView image in fullscreen‘Haute Euro-pageantry placed against striking 2D backdrops’ … The Ribbon Hero.Photograph: ©Twin EngineMoviesReviewThe Ribbon Hero review – do-gooder princess battles giant flying earwigs in update of classic yarnYûki Igarashi’s adaptation of Osamu Tezuka’s influential manga is a conservative (if impressively animated) reimagining that dulls the source material’s pioneering elementsPhil HoadMon 3 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst-time director Yûki Igarashi should hit the jackpot here: the first big-screen adaptation for decades of Princess Knight, a seminal postwar manga series from Astro Boy genius Osamu Tezuka. But this very loose reworking is an anticlimax: conservative in solely concentrating on the girlishly feminine side of its protagonist, Sapphire (voiced by Saya), where the gender-flipping original was heralded by many as pioneering; and bland in its vanilla characterisation and dull adherence to battle-anime norms.The owner of the most prominent hair bow since Minnie Mouse, Sapphire is a princess forced into exile when a Nergal – a kind of gargantuan flying earwig – lays waste to her home kingdom of Silverland. Wandering with her lady-in-waiting Zirco (Mayumi Shintani), she takes refuge in neighbouring Goldland and, in need of cash, bags a job working in the mines that supply crystals to placate the Nergal. When another one attacks, she falls into a crystal pool that activates her head ribbon and transforms her into Princess Knight, who is capable of trouncing the interdimensional critters. Local noble Velvet (Seiran Kobayashi), keen to slip free of the Nergal yoke himself, is paying close attention.It’s understandable that Igarashi might want to pay fan service to Tezuka’s more innocent era of entertainment. But surely that should have been manageable while carving out fresh terrain for Princess Knight? Instead he simply serves up a saccharine do-gooder, always bleating about helping other people (something which proves contagious among her forgettable posse). Nor are the contractually obliged sky brawls livened up by a madcap array of special powers showcased in the likes of One Piece or My Hero Academia.The animation can’t be faulted though, encompassing an impressive array of different styles that place haute Euro-pageantry against striking 2D backdrops, along withchibi-style emotional meltdowns, and dumbshow and shadow play interludes among the mayhem. It displays the creative intrepidness in short supply elsewhere; failing to capitalise on Tezuka’s more far-out impulses means this adaptation merely registers as run-of-the-mill girl-power puff.The Ribbon Hero is on Netflix from 8 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmAnimeMangaComics and graphic novelsJapanScience fiction and fantasy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCSO/Järvi/Kavakos review – virtuosic violinist makes fiendishly light work of Tchaikovsky | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: The intricate concerto was paired with the world premiere of Dani Howard’s likable Concerto for Brass and a lush Scriabin symphony, all admirably led by Paavo Järvi
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The intricate concerto was paired with the world premiere of Dani Howard’s likable Concerto for Brass and a lush Scriabin symphony, all admirably led by Paavo Järvi
Content: Breathtaking … Paavo Järvi and Leonidas Kavakos at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenBreathtaking … Paavo Järvi and Leonidas Kavakos at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCProms 2026ReviewBBCSO/Järvi/Kavakos review – virtuosic violinist makes fiendishly light work of TchaikovskyRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe intricate concerto was paired with the world premiere of Dani Howard’s likable Concerto for Brass and a lush Scriabin symphony, all admirably led by Paavo JärviClive PagetMon 3 Aug 2026 08.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon will be seeing a lot more of Paavo Järvi when the Estonian conductortakes the reins at the London Philharmonic in 2028. Here, on the podium with the BBC Symphony Orchestra, he proved a model of calm, control and clarity as well as the most sensitive of accompanists, shepherding a breathtaking account of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto by Leonidas Kavakos.The Russian composer struggled for three years to find a soloist brave enough to take on the work’s premiere, yet Kavakos was clearly undaunted. The Greek violinist’s exceptional dexterity and pinpoint intonation at the very top of the range made light of fiendish passagework that has foxed some of the finest. The first movement’s intricate variations were exquisitely decorated, while the intensity of his playing drew spontaneous applause mid-cadenza. Järvi, for his part, was alert to the soloist’s generous rubato, keeping the orchestra in soft-shoed lockstep. As the simple eloquence of the canzonetta gave way to a helter-skelter finale, Kavakos let fly, his bow skimming the strings with unerring accuracy. A Bach encore was dispatched with similar poise and precision.View image in fullscreenPacked an emotional punch … Paavo Järvi conducts the BBC Symphony Orchestra.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCThe Tchaikovsky came hot on the heels of the world premiere of Dani Howard’s Concerto for Brass. Its subtitle, Signal, is a nod to a time when brass instruments were frequently employed as a means of communication. It opened with a buzz of violins and a view hallooing of horns in perfect fifths, the concerto’s signature interval, before the rest of the section joined the hunt. Bright, celebratory and eminently likable, the music shimmered and frothed, its energetic outbursts crowned with fluttering trumpets and underpinned by sonorous bass trombone and tuba.Generally sumptuous, if occasionally turgid, Scriabin’s Second Symphony eschews the harmonic instability of his later works, preferring to plough a lush, late-Romantic furrow. Järvi let it unfold naturally, the internal architecture rendered admirably clear. And yet, where needed, his interpretation packed a brooding emotional punch: the melancholy strivings of the opening movement, for example, or the central enchanted garden episode with its percussive climaxes. The composer himself dismissed the quasi-bombastic finale as “banal”. Perhaps – though Järvi moved heaven and earth to convince us otherwise.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicBBC Symphony OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Exhibition by Alex Hyde review – an elegiac love letter to the YBA era | Fiction | The Guardian
description: London’s 90s art scene forms the backdrop to this tale of a complex relationship between two artists whose identities become entangled in their creative collaboration
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: London’s 90s art scene forms the backdrop to this tale of a complex relationship between two artists whose identities become entangled in their creative collaboration
Content: Melancholic reflection … Alex Hyde.Photograph: Matthew DyasView image in fullscreenMelancholic reflection … Alex Hyde.Photograph: Matthew DyasFictionReviewExhibition by Alex Hyde review – an elegiac love letter to the YBA eraLondon’s 90s art scene forms the backdrop to this tale of a complex relationship between two artists whose identities become entangled in their creative collaborationKeiran GoddardMon 3 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor all the wrong reasons, Damien Hirst’s Shark (The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living) has a claim to being the most prescient British artwork of the last half-century: a grim parable of neoliberalism. In 1991, it was still possible to mistake the predatory violence of that system for a kind of animal vitality. But today, open-mouthed, dead-eyed and decayed, it speaks only of a regime preserved far beyond its natural lifespan, lauded exclusively by institutions that can profit from its ugliness.Alex Hyde’s second novel, an elegantKünstlerromanwhich plays out during a lightly fictionalised version of the YBA explosion, explores the resonance of that particular cultural inflection point: a moment when the collapse of the postwar cultural settlement, municipal culture and public institutions was transfigured decisively and ubiquitously into individualised, confessional artistic capital.It tells the story of Rabble Stone, a working-class photography student who moves to London and falls into the orbit of a moneyed, cosmopolitan artistic set who are alternately impressed, baffled and alienated by the seriousness of both her manner and her work. Among them is the unnamed artist, now deceased, to whom the novel is primarily addressed through a series of elegiac reminiscences, unpicking their entanglement as friends, muses and occasional antagonists.double quotation markQuestions of self-authorship and plagiarism are handled well enough, but will feel overfamiliar to many readersCentral to this relationship are the ways in which their respective selfhoods become intertwined and distorted via their ongoing artistic collaboration. Rabble begins to photograph the artist, a series of intimate, confrontational portraits that are eventually physically incorporated into the artist’s figurative drawings and paintings. Hyde’s descriptions of the work strongly evoke Tracey Emin, as does its subsequent journey from localised art-world curio to highly valuable, globally exhibited market commodity.Thematically, there is an air of predictability in how this all plays out. Questions of self-authorship, doubling, co-option, plagiarism and the quasi-erotics of display and representation are handled well enough, but will feel overfamiliar to many readers. There are also occasions where the language is imprecise and hesitant in ways that appear to be stylistic lapses rather than stylistic choices. Hyde leans heavily on superposition; needs are “base and noble at the same time”, faces are “ugly and beautiful at the same time”, characters feel “something and nothing at the same time”. And just as frequently, the prose lapses into a hazy self-correction that reads less as an evocation of the unreliability of memory and more as syntactic hesitance.The novel also contains passages of precise and inventive writing. Hyde is especially admirable on a rhythmic level, demonstrating comfort with the staccato and fragmentary as well as the more languid and expansive descriptive work she uses sparingly but to great effect. She writes particularly well and tenderly about bodily exhaustion, both among the working-class communities of Rabble’s youth, and the struggling artists she later encounters in New York, both made brittle by virtue of their position in the economic value chain. Similarly, the character of Duncan, an effervescent aesthete who succumbs to the ravages of addiction, is handled with delicacy, a lightness of touch that captures the horror of chasing ghosts until you finally become one.Also commendable is Hyde’s willingness to grapple with the issue that plagues ekphrastic writing in practically all of its forms. To write about images is to render things that are fundamentally spatial, relational and simultaneous into sentences that are necessarily sequential, disaggregated and hierarchical. The standard way out of this dilemma for a novelist is to focus the description such that it tells us less about the artwork than about the sensibilities and feelings of the character viewing it. In Exhibition, however, Hyde repeatedly goes a step further and engages directly with the theoretical challenge at hand, allowing Rabble to talk at length about composition, the role of the lens, the function of framing; how photographs “are not taken … they are made”.And that Rabble is a photographer, rather than, say, a sculptor or a painter, hints at what appears to me to be the novel’s central philosophical concern; namely remembrance, nostalgia and preservation. It is photographs we turn to, after all, to re-narrativise our lives, to reflect on distances travelled and the alternate turns we might have taken along the way. That feeling of melancholic reflection, of abundant futures concertinaed into the inevitability of the present, suffuses Exhibition and is its primary achievement. For just as Rabble is left mourning lost friends and collaborators, we as readers are left mourning the loss of something larger and more significant, an entire structure of possibility. Exhibition is a eulogy for a world of livable rents, radical art schools, free higher education and opportunities for working-class artists, for a society in which a life like Rabble’s, spent making beautiful things out of the people and places she loved, was not seen as a risible pipe dream or as the gate-kept preserve of the select few.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The August Coup by Robert Service review – the drink-soaked collapse of the Soviet Union | History books | The Guardian
description: This brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully
Author: John Simpson
Headline: This brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully
Content: A soldier in Red Square, Moscow, during the attempted coup in 1991.Photograph: Peter Turnley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA soldier in Red Square, Moscow, during the attempted coup in 1991.Photograph: Peter Turnley/Getty ImagesBook of the dayHistory booksReviewThe August Coup by Robert Service review – the drink-soaked collapse of the Soviet UnionThis brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifullyJohn SimpsonMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarxist-Leninist rule inRussialasted 74 years, and in August 1991 it effectively collapsed in just three days: clear evidence of how hollowed out it had become. In the period that followed, Russia tried parliamentary democracy and unalloyed capitalism, then sank back into autocracy. Now it’s struggling under a wholly unnecessary war against its neighbour and former possession, Ukraine.Why did the system of Lenin, Stalin, Khrushchev and Brezhnev vanish so fast, without a fight? Because that’s how regimes fall in Russia: look at tsarism in 1917. (It almost happened again in June 2023, when the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin’s men marched on Moscow largely unopposed; Vladimir Putin might have gone the way of Nicholas II had he not made some pretty wholesale promises to Prigozhin, then allegedly blown him up two months later.)Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in 1985 with the intention of saving the USSR. Instead, he oversaw its death. He was a charming, decent man but no visionary, and the two medicines he brought to the patient’s bedside,perestroika(restructuring) andglasnost(openness), proved to be wholly ineffective. The brief coup of August 1991 against him, headed by Vladimir Kryuchkov, the boss of the KGB, was the kneejerk response of a bureaucracy that knew things were going wrong but had absolutely no idea what to do about it. It failed quickly, and Gorbachev was back at his desk within days, but the coup had damaged him fatally. Four months later, at the end of 1991, he was bundled out of power by the tough, brutal, boozymuzhik,Boris Yeltsin.Robert Service, author of The August Coup,is the English-speaking world’s foremost historian of 20th-century Russia and Bolshevism. His biographies of the three major Soviet leaders, Lenin, Stalin and Trotsky, are outstanding, even in that crowded field. In writing about the death of the system that these prodigies and monsters helped to create, Service has displayed a remarkable grasp of the vast sources, and a delightfully clear writing style which makes even the complexities of Soviet bureaucracy easy to understand. Compared with his earlier subjects, the story of the coup against Gorbachev and the collapse of the USSR is moderately simple; but Service guides the reader through the chaos of the collapsing system and the machinations of the coup leaders with ease and grace.double quotation markThe acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire dayAfter the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 and the loss of the various Soviet satrapies in eastern and centralEurope, the USSR was falling apart, and Gorbachev, as its president, was shedding power and influence. No one knew how many Soviet republics would break away, and Gorbachev’s plan for running the rump of the union was bitterly contested. Yeltsin was the president of the Russian Republic, the largest, richest and most effective part of the old USSR. The two men were in angry contention. The coup leaders didn’t support either of them: they wanted to go back to a system which would restore as much Soviet power as possible. The assumption at the time was that the KGB had led the coup to protect its own interests, but Service demonstrates that Kryuchkov, the KGB boss, was much more concerned about the overall collapse of the Soviet system. And anyway, many KGB officers refused to join the coup.I was lucky enough to be in Moscow during those extraordinary days. Service captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully. The coup leaders lost their faith in what they were doing almost immediately, and many of them didn’t have much to begin with. They argued, betrayed each other, or were paralysed by fear or torpor. Most of the people involved left some account of what happened, so the records available to Service were particularly rich. He provides us with a graphic description of the fatal press conference that the plotters gave at 5pm on the first day of the coup. The acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire day and his hands were visibly shaking. The press conference was broadcast live on state television, so everyone could see the condition he was in. After that, failure was certain.The basic reason it collapsed, though, was that the plotters didn’t manage to get hold of Yeltsin. It was easy enough to imprison Gorbachev at his palatial residence, Zarya, on the Crimean coast, where he was holidaying with his wife Raisa and their daughter; but Yeltsin remained free, and had use of the Russian republic’s Moscow headquarters, known as the White House. You might expect communist plotters to be good at cutting communications and taking over the media, but no one stopped Yeltsin from phoning allies and friends around Russia and across the world. Nor did they try to prevent him making his famous speech from a tank in front of the White House, condemning the coup and pledging to support democracy. It was a good speech, and the television coverage of it was seen worldwide. Again, no one pulled the plugs. Journalists like me were able to broadcast live throughout the coup. Yeltsin stayed inside the White House, mostly protected by a small crowd of unarmed demonstrators whose numbers dropped as the first night wore on and the rain came down.Yet Yeltsin suffered from the same weaknesses as many of the plotters. In the lobby of the White House I begged to be allowed to go up to his office and interview him, but was told he was too busy speaking to world leaders and organising the opposition. Later, the former Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze arrived to see him. When he came out of the building an hour afterwards, he announced that Yeltsin had told him he would defend Russia’s freedom to the last drop of blood in his body. Stirring stuff. Three years later I reminisced with Shevardnadze about it all. He laughed. “When I got into Yeltsin’s office, he was lying unconscious on the floor with a couple of empty vodka bottles beside him.” But what about him fighting to his last drop of blood? “What do you think would have happened if I’d come out and told you I couldn’t speak to Yeltsin because he was dead drunk?”Such was the chaos and absurdity surrounding the death of the Soviet Union. In the days that followed no one had any idea where authority lay. The famously brave and entrepreneurial cameraman Rory Peck and I marched into KGB headquarters, the Lubyanka, and filmed in Kryuchkov’s own office. After that we even filmed among the ultra-secret KGB files. The next day Rory offered to buy the contents of the Central Museum of the Revolution for a million dollars. Only the fact that the official in charge couldn’t find a bank prepared to accept that much cash stopped the deal going through. We tend to forget the details of this pivotal episode. Perhaps Russia’s troubled history since 1991 has wiped them from our memories. Now Service has brought his magnificent grasp of Soviet history to the task of chronicling the ludicrous way it ended: not with a bang, but with the clink of vodka bottles.John Simpson is the BBC’s world affairs editor. His programme, Unspun World, returns to BBC Two in September. The August Coup: The Destruction of the Soviet Union and the Making of New Russia 1985-1991 by Robert Service is published by Picador (£30).
