title: The end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online games | Games | The Guardian
description: Online multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or later
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Online multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or later
Content: A sense of mourning spoken and unspoken … Halo 3.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosView image in fullscreenA sense of mourning spoken and unspoken … Halo 3.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosGamesThe end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online gamesOnline multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or laterNicole CarpenterMon 3 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNevan Hagarty had an idea. If he and otherHalo3 players stayed online the night of 13 January 2022, they could delay the impending server shutdown. Players knew this was coming: it had happened to Halo 2when its Xbox Live servers were turned off in 2010, and a group managed to stay logged into the multiplayer serversfor weeks.And so, players gathered online before the server shutdown to pay homage and to mourn the game they loved so dearly. And, maybe, to keep it online for a little longer. “I must have played ’til about 4am the night of the shutdown, trading stories with so many players about their love of the game and their experiences over the last 15 years,” says Hagarty, 22. “It was a really wholesome experience I won’t forget.”A sense of mourning went both spoken and unspoken. Thirty-year-old fan Jimi hadn’t played Halo 3in a while but logged on to the game on shutdown day to experience the original servers just once more, later posting a video onReddit.“My team was losing really bad,” he says, “I saw a few of the other team’s people standing in the middle, and our guy standing in the middle, and everybody’s just looking at each other. I shot up once in the air, and then everybody just starts going crazy.” Someone threw a shield down, others threw grenades in the air and launched rockets. It looked almost like fireworks. “There were no people on the voice chat. There wasn’t any mutual agreement on this. Everybody just felt it and knew.”View image in fullscreenA person dressed as a character from the game at the UK launch of Halo 3.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianWhen online multiplayer came to video games in the late 90s, it meant that players from across the globe could interact with people they’d never otherwise meet. This changed the trajectory of video games, bringing people together in ways that games hadn’t before – to play, and to mourn, when their virtual worlds are doomed to die.Games go offline all the time, and people have got used to saying goodbye to their favourites. The increasing popularity of online-only live service games means more reliance on servers to host these experiences. And those servers cost money to run and maintain; in the case of recent flopHighguard, developer Wildlight Entertainment couldn’t afford to keep the game online for more than a few months.Over twenty gameshave shut off their servers already in 2026.View image in fullscreenGoing down fighting … Highguard.Photograph: Wildlight Entertainment, Inc.“People really hold on to the idea of place,” says UX and games researcher Evan Conaway, who holds a PhD in anthropology. “That we create community online at all is really remarkable. When you find it and you have it and it’s real, you have an emotional connection to it. Wanting to hold on to it is only human.”Conaway says this happens a lot in the real world, when the corner bar shutters, or a local skatepark is torn down. His research delved into the ways people commemorate online spaces, with a focus on the massively multiplayer online role-playing gameWorld of Warcraft(WoW). People play together on separate servers – or instances – which all run contained copies of WoW, and each server has its own culture created by the community. When the game changes, the culture can change, too. WoW has persisted for decades, and the game is no longer the same as it was when it was released – it’s hardly the same game it was just a few years ago.Though people still have access to WoW, they are often “gradually mourning”, says Conaway. They know that this version of the game is ephemeral. It won’t stay the same – it can’t, by design. In exchange for new content, players must accept that the spaces they inhabit online will find new forms. “The quests are different, the way things are worded is different,” he says. “The way I felt while playing it, and wandering around by myself or exploring the world, all of that is part of this meaning-making for people – just the raw experience of it.”Part of Conaway’s research centred on a group of people who wanted to literally hold on to those memories and meanings. When Blizzard Entertainment was changing its servers in 2011, it auctioned off the old server blades withautographed placardsdisplaying which server they held. It was important for some players, he says, to have a physical representation of that moment in time. He points to one server in particular, Proudmoore, which was an unofficial queer server: “For a gay person or queer person who was playing World of Warcraft at that time on that server, it does feel a little bit like a skatepark brick, like they can take home a piece of a thing.”View image in fullscreenStrength in numbers … characters from World of Warcraft, which has an online community of five million.Photograph: Blizzard EntertainmentWhen World of Warcraftplayers in China were faced with server shutdowns in2023, they were at the mercy of both Blizzard Entertainment and its Chinese partner NetEase.Games in Chinamust be published with a local company, so when Blizzard Entertainment and NetEase had a dispute, it hit the players. Millions lost not just the server but the whole game, and there was no date set for its return. It could have been months, years. Maybe never.Naturally, players wanted to gather in their servers on the day of the shutdown, 24 January 2023, to pay their respects. To do so, people started preparing – and logging in – days in advance, according to City University of Hong Kong PhD student and games researcher HongLan Xu, who joined them to document the last days.“I encountered hundreds of players, but there are millions,” says Xu. “Everybody thought it could be at least several years. They don’t know when the server will be back. It’s profound. It’s real. The shutdown is very real for them, so they gathered in the game to say farewell to their avatars, like it’s the last time.”View image in fullscreenA Chinese gamer plays World of Warcraft at an internet cafe in Beijing in 2024.Photograph: Jade Gao/AFP/Getty ImagesChinese players’ grief was mixed with anger, too, says Xu. Many in the Chinese market felt disrespected, as if Blizzard Entertainment didn’t care about them: “From a Chinese player’s perspective, the main takeaway is sometimes the capitalism of the western gaming companies [leads to] distrust.”WoW opened back up to Chinese players in August 2024. Returning players were glad to have it back, of course, but there was an unease underneath that excitement. This could happen again; they knew what it felt like to lose it all. “Virtual life attachment and this sense of loss is deep, profound,” says Xu. “It can be completely vulnerable and very uncertain.”Losing your forever-game is a uniquely sad experience. Players make a very real investment into these spaces – time, money, friendships, stories, characters, creativity. As one playerput it, “What gets me is that people poured themselves into these games. Not just cash, but actual time, actual friendships built inside them, characters they spent months on. And then one day a studio decides the numbers don’t work any more and everything just disappears.”Explore more on these topicsGamesHaloWorld of WarcraftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Never felt so scared’: the Cats obsessive who’s created a feral dance version of the purr-fect musical | Stage | The Guardian
description: Drew McOnie skipped school to audition for the original. It launched his astonishing career. Now he’s getting his claws into a no-pussyfooting version of the classic hit
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Drew McOnie skipped school to audition for the original. It launched his astonishing career. Now he’s getting his claws into a no-pussyfooting version of the classic hit
Content: Tails at the ready … the cast rehearse for the show at Regents Park Open Air theatre.Photograph: Mark SeniorView image in fullscreenTails at the ready … the cast rehearse for the show at Regents Park Open Air theatre.Photograph: Mark SeniorStageInterview‘Never felt so scared’: the Cats obsessive who’s created a feral dance version of the purr-fect musicalLyndsey WinshipDrew McOnie skipped school to audition for the original. It launched his astonishing career. Now he’s getting his claws into a no-pussyfooting version of the classic hitMon 3 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the age of 17, Drew McOnie was so determined to be in the musicalCatsthat he snuck out of school to audition. Four days later, he was on a flight to Germany to join the international production. (Luckily, he was at a performing arts school and they forgave him.) It was a life-changing moment: at that point, McOnie’s stellar career as a dancer, Olivier award-winning choreographer and director began – and, 23 years later, it’s all about to come full circle. McOnie has created his own version of the musical he’s been obsessed with since childhood.For any dancer growing up in the 1980s and 90s, Cats wasthemusical: dance wasn’t just an accompaniment, but instrumental to the show. Gillian Lynne’s original choreography is iconic – much copied by local dance schools and student shows of the era. Lynne was a force of nature, still doing the splits at 88, four years before she died in 2018. For McOnie, artistic director at Regent’s Park Open Air theatre and famed for his blazing choreography in Jesus Christ Superstar, it takes some nerve to remake it.double quotation markThere are a lot of kittens in the cast. My task is to make each one light up“I don’t think I’ve ever felt so scared,” he says. Not because he doesn’t think he can do it, but “because I was in the original and I adore Gillian Lynne. The challenge is to honour her with the amount of rigour she put in – to match that ferocity of spirit, that ambition.”View image in fullscreenThe energy is buzzing … McOnie and cast in rehearsals.Photograph: Mark SeniorWe might now think of Cats as a “glorious celebration of the 80s”, says McOnie, but we shouldn’t forget how original and contemporary it was when it first came out. He wants his version to feel the same to audiences today. That means movement that brings in current influences from street and commercial dance, as well as jazz and classical, “while also staying within that world of being a cat”.As I enter Studio 1 at Regent’s Park, the energy’s buzzing, the moves are sensual, low slung and slinky, earthier than the original, but with bursts of wild, joyful energy. Then the dancers suddenly go full pelt. It’s more feral than you might expect. “I don’t think many of our cats are house cats,” says McOnie.Because his youthful experience on Cats was so formative, McOnie deliberately went in search of standout student dancers to add to the mix. “There are a lot of kittens in the cast,” he says. The young dancers are so effortlessly cool, he tells me, not like Tiggerish McOnie was at their age, bouncing off the walls. But in rehearsals, he started digging beneath their inscrutable exteriors, letting them loose in solos. “One lad just completely lit up and I was like, ‘OK, there’s the teenager.’ I said, ‘I like the version of you bounding about with your eyes on fire.’ My task is to make each one of them light up.”Cats isn’t known as a particularly “cool” show, but McOnie thinks we forget how impressively out-there Andrew Lloyd Webber’s musicals can be. “They’re extraordinarily off the wall, completely form-busting and brave,” he says. He has nothing but praise for Lloyd Webber. “Honestly, my time with Andrew over the last year, with the combination of Jesus Christ Superstar and Cats, has been utterly thrilling. He’s incredibly funny. He’s very witty, he’s very sharp, and he’s really, really rigorous.” McOnie is awed by Lloyd Webber’s ability to see the big picture. “He’s like a musical architect,” says McOnie, able to glean how every detail fits into the larger show. “There’s definitely a magic about what he can hear.”View image in fullscreenWonder and joy … Gary Wilmot as Gus the Theatre Cat.Photograph: Mark SeniorMcOnie does admit Cats is a bit weird, though. Based on the TS Eliot poems in Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats, with portraits of Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer, Macavity and Skimbleshanks, it doesn’t exactly have a strong narrative. “It sort of levitates somewhere between a choreo-poem, a ballet, a song cycle, a piece of vaudeville and a kind of pagan ritual,” he says.What it isn’t is a bunch of cute talking animals. In this production, the costumes won’t be fully formed cats, and they’re not masked. McOnie sees it as “a ritual that endows the performer with an animal form through which they can express deeply human emotion”. There’ll still be some “great glittery numbers” though, don’t worry. “Its core themes are wonder and joy.”‘I wasn’t ambitious until I was 60!’ Gary Wilmot on comedy, panto, musicals – and his Beckett-style new playRead moreI have to ask McOnie briefly about themuch-maligned Cats film. It turns out he loved a lot of things about it but thinks it was doomed from the start. “It just isn’t a filmic idea,” he says. “Cats is one of the most extraordinary expressions of theatricality of all time,” he says. “Capital-T theatre – because so much of it hangs in the imagination. You have this mass of bodies giving all of their soul to that music, with that exchange of energy live in the room.”It all comes back to Gillian Lynne’s legacy. She trusted dancers and the power of what they could do. McOnie has exactly the same animal instinct.Cats is atRegents Park Open Air theatre, London, until 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageMusicalsAndrew Lloyd WebberCatsAnimalsTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ring Cycle review – AI staging dispenses with drama to create banal bric-a-brac  | Opera | The Guardian
description: For the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless mess
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: For the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless mess
Content: Unexplained, mindless scrolling … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathView image in fullscreenUnexplained, mindless scrolling … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathOperaReviewRing Cycle review – AI staging dispenses with drama to create banal bric-a-bracBayreuth festival theatre, BayreuthFor the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless messFlora WillsonMon 3 Aug 2026 09.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnveiled the same week in which tech company Anthropic admitted that itsAI model Claude had gone rogue during testing, Bayreuth festival’s new AI-generated staging of Wagner’s four-partRing of the Nibelungenis at least timely. But anyone who assumes that the cycle’s obsession with knowledge, power and possession might make it an ideal forum for reflection on AI as a major contemporary frontier will be disappointed, as will anyone hopeful about AI’s creative potential within opera.Commissioned to mark the festival’s 150th anniversary, the production is “curated” – emphatically not “directed” – by a team led by German stage directorMarcus Lobbes. He apparently spent weeks in dialogue with AI models about possible interpretations of the Ring. According to the programme book, “power structures, capitalism, mythology, gender roles, nationalism”, all came up. So far, so mainstream Wagner reception. But if these human-machine exchanges were revelatory, you wouldn’t know it from the resulting staging, which uses AI “as an extension of a cultural memory that is never complete”.In plainer English: the AI system is allowed to roam archival materials from 150 years of Ring cycle productions at Bayreuth as the starting point for constantly spooling visuals projected on to a screen that is stretched the full width and height of the proscenium arch. Lobbes also asked the system to incorporate imagery chronologically, from a political or social event every year of the festival’s history as a plausible conversation topic for that season’s audience. Each scene begins with a source from the cycle’s 1876 premiere, but what happens next is determined by the system in real time during the performance.View image in fullscreenGrotesque … Bayreuth festival’s 2026 Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathThe good news is that anyone who attends another of this production’s outings definitely won’t see the same selection of visual bric-à-brac that I did. The bad news is that the principle of rapid machinic free-association will remain.So, I assume, will the constant grotesque morph and flow of visual objects. Das Rheingold and Die Walküre involved countless hands that warped horribly, producing extra fingers and nails. (Did someone adjust the settings ahead of Siegfried and Götterdämmerung, I wonder? The visual tic disappeared mid-cycle as suddenly as it emerged.) Faces appeared, only to go instantly out of focus. Some were very famous (Adolf Hitler, Queen Elizabeth II, JFK) but I struggled to identify most. Watercolour rocks became bodies became other bodies. There were rapid swings between the entirely inscrutable and the totally obvious. Alberich’s transformation into a toad triggered various mutant amphibians, there were bears when Siegfried brought one in, a rainbow for the rainbow bridge to Valhalla.double quotation markThe singers stood behind a vast projection screen like budget Star Trek monsters rooted to the spotBut there were also endless picture-library bland photos of scrap metal, creeping greenery, water droplets, abandoned rooms. I spotted design elements from various past Bayreuth Ring productions but was mostly – inevitably – unable to keep pace with the AI system’s connection-making. One low point: the appearance of a historical photo of emaciated African youths – as unexplained as everything else, but picture the results of an image-search for “European colonialism” – which flashed past during Die Walküre. This is not engaging with the complex, problematic history of Bayreuth or the Ring. It’s just another form of mindless scrolling.You’ll be wondering where the singers fitted in. Forget Wagner’s notion of the inescapably multimediaGesamtkunstwerk: this Ring presents the sonic and the visual as separate tracks, with theatrical drama kept to a minimum. Over four nights, some of today’s leading Wagnerians stood behind – yes, behind – the vast projection screen, all wearing subtle variations on a single costume design like budget Star Trek monsters. Mostly they were rooted to the spot. Recently murdered characters simply walked off; at erotic climaxes, lovers held hands; Siegfried discovered Brünnhilde despite being alone on stage.View image in fullscreenTheatrical drama is kept to a minimum … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring Cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathMichael Vollewas a magnificent, stately Wotan and Wanderer, his power unforced.Klaus Florian Vogtwas by turn Loge, Siegmund and Siegfried, in each case supple and darkly luminous with compelling diction.Elza van den Heever’s Sieglinde got better and better, blossoming in her love duet in Die Walküre.Camilla Nylund’s Brünnhilde was often wild and sometimes ungainly, but her impassioned lyricism and most intimate moments were deeply moving regardless.Mika Kares’s Hunding was all iron and velvet, his Hagen unleashing mighty, smooth torrents of sound – evil rarely sounds better.Gerhard Siegel(Mime) and Jochen Schmeckenbecher (Alberich) were more old-school baddies, respectively wheedling and raw.Peter Rosewas a rather muddy Fafner andChrista Mayerwobbly but forceful as Erda and Waltraute. The Rhinemaidens, Valkyries and Norns were exquisitely balanced and as characterised as they could be without acting.double quotation markForget Wagner’s notion of the Gesamtkunstwerk – this Ring keeps theatrical drama to a minimumConductorChristian Thielemanndrew playing from the orchestra that was occasionally poorly tuned and even scrappy, but which at its best should have been captivating: details were finely balanced and tutti passages blistering, the brass rising like an immense wave from the pit or splatting nastily for the bad guys. Tempi were often brisk (only in Siegfried did this cause coordination problems, with Vogt left struggling to keep up) but there were also precious moments of spaciousness. Yet even the silence that Thielemann left in Wotan’s devastating monologue couldn’t stop the onscreen hyperactivity that instantly dispersed all dramatic tension.There are numerous criticisms you could levy against this production from all manner of perspectives; there is, after all, something for everyone to dislike. But the most dismal was perhaps how unmoving it was – and how difficult it became to care.The Ring Cycle continues at theBayreuth festivaluntil 16 August.Explore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicAI (artificial intelligence)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Now You See Me Live review – magic so bombastic it may be visible from space | Stage | The Guardian
description: A quartet of conjurors, calling themselves the Horsemen, perform fine feats of escapology and mentalism that are undermined by smoke, lasers and pomposity
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A quartet of conjurors, calling themselves the Horsemen, perform fine feats of escapology and mentalism that are undermined by smoke, lasers and pomposity
Content: It could scarcely be more pompous … (left to right) Enzo Weyne, Andrew Basso, Rafferty Coope, Gabriella Lester and Matthew Pomeroy in Now You See Me Live.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenIt could scarcely be more pompous … (left to right) Enzo Weyne, Andrew Basso, Rafferty Coope, Gabriella Lester and Matthew Pomeroy in Now You See Me Live.Photograph: Johan PerssonStageReviewNow You See Me Live review – magic so bombastic it may be visible from spaceLondon ColiseumA quartet of conjurors, calling themselves the Horsemen, perform fine feats of escapology and mentalism that are undermined by smoke, lasers and pomposityBrian LoganMon 3 Aug 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs there an opposite of close-up magic? If there is, it would look a bit like the magic in Now You See Me, which must be visible (and audible) from space. This new spectacle, heading later this year to its spiritual home of Las Vegas, spins off fromthe movie franchise of the same nameand features a quartet of conjurors (identifying, rather awkwardly, as “the Horsemen”) performing feats of escapology, mentalism and even time travel amid much bombasticsonetlumièreand self-promotion.It could scarcely be more pompous – but happily, there are plenty of entertaining tricks to keep pomp-phobes like myself onside. The Italian Andrew Basso has arguably the stoppiest showstoppers, including his recreation of Houdini’s water torture stunt, and another where he extricates himself from padlocked chains while harbouring something very undesirable in his mouth. His French counterpart Enzo Weyne delivers an arresting number with a paper bag and a lightbulb, and there’s a fine audience participation set piece inviting us all to shred, shuffle then – as if by magic! – reassemble the playing cards we were given on the way in to the theatre.Does any of this benefit from the noisy theatrics and inflated self-regard? (For the latter, see MC Matthew Pomeroy’s boast that this show is reversing magic’s historic gender inequalities, despite only one of the show’s seven acts being female.) Far from it – on more than one occasion, the estimable skills on display are undermined by the smoke and lasers, while the self-aggrandising sets expectations that not all these tricks can meet.View image in fullscreenQuickfire cameo … Eden Choi.Photograph: Johan PerssonHow much more impressive would these feats be if staged sparsely? Just ask seven-year-old audience volunteer Elektra, who cited as her favourite act the ex Britain’s Got Talent semi-finalist Eden Choi, whose quickfire cameo, a silent but deadly card manipulation sequence, requires no embellishment. It’s one of several adroit set pieces in a show that proves there’s life yet in the ancient arts of wriggling out of a straitjacket and squeezing oneself into a dynamited safe – even if I found myself wishing pestilence on the four horsemen’s overblown style.AtLondon Coliseum, until 6 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageMagicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Benjamin Alire Sáenz, first Latino winner of PEN/Faulkner award, dies aged 71 | Books | The Guardian
description: Celebrated writer, poet and novelist for young adults drew upon his sexuality and life on US southern border
Author: Abené Clayton
Headline: Celebrated writer, poet and novelist for young adults drew upon his sexuality and life on US southern border
Content: Benjamin Alire Sáenz in this 2016 picture.Photograph: Larry D MooreBenjamin Alire Sáenz in this 2016 picture.Photograph: Larry D MooreBooksBenjamin Alire Sáenz, first Latino winner of PEN/Faulkner award, dies aged 71Celebrated writer, poet and novelist for young adults drew upon his sexuality and life on US southern borderAbené ClaytonMon 3 Aug 2026 17.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Alire Sáenz, an award-winning fiction writer and poet who drew upon his sexuality and his life on the southern border, has died at age 71. He was the first Latino to win the PEN/Faulkner prize.Sáenz, who produced a story collection that won the PEN/Faulkner prize and a young adult novel that received acclaim from readers and reviewers and condemnation from censors, died on 28 July in El Paso,Texas, after a lengthy illness, according to a spokesperson for Simon & Schuster.Sáenz, born in Old Picacho, New Mexico, was an ordained Catholic priest who eventually left the order and came out as gay. Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe, the story of two Mexican American boys falling in love, was published in 2012 and received a pair of citations for outstanding LGBTQ+ literature: a Stonewall book award and the Lambda literary award.Ina tribute postedto the late author’s Instagram account on Saturday, Sáenz is described as a writer whose words ensured visibility and belonging among people who have been pushed into the margins of society.“Ben believed that words could build bridges where walls once stood. He believed that every life mattered, every story deserved to be told, and every soul longed to be seen,” the post reads. “He wrote of lonely boys who discovered they were worthy of love. He wrote of deserts, rivers, family, memory, grief, forgiveness, and hope…But more than anything, he wrote toward the light.”This sentiment was echoed by playwright Lin-Manuel Miranda, who narrated the audio edition ofAristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe, helped produce the 2023 film adaptation, and lent his voice to the audiobook for Sáenz’s sequel novel Aristotle and Dante Dive into the Waters of the World.“Heartbroken by the passing of [Benjamin Alire Sáenz]. Forever grateful he trusted me to narrate both audiobooks of Aristotle & Dante’s adventures…Condolences to his galaxy of friends and family. Rest easy, maestro,” Mirandawrote in an Instagram postthe day after Sáenz’s death.The film adaptation’s director, Aitch Alberto, also posted a tribute to the man whom she described as more than just an author.“He was a friend, a believer in me, and one of the greatest supporters of my work and my voice. He trusted me with Ari and Dante, with characters and a world that came from somewhere so deeply personal to him, and that trust changed the course of my life,” she wrote.Though Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe is considered a part of the LGBTQIA+ literary canon, the love story at its center led to its temporary removal from a school district in Granbury, Texas, and to bans in Russia and in Belarus.Sáenz’s other books included the poetry collection The Book of What Remains and such adult novels as In Perfect Light and Names on a Map.He received the PEN/Faulkner award in 2013 for Everything Begins and Ends at the Kentucky Club, a story collection set in El Paso, and across the border in Juarez, Mexico. Starting in the 1990s, he taught for decades at the University of Texas at El Paso, where he had received a master’s degree in creative writing.He served as chair of the school’s creative writing department before retiring in 2016.Next month, Simon & Schuster will publish When the World Was Happy, which draws in part upon the loss of his niece in 1990 in a bowling alley shooting in Las Cruces, New Mexico. Sáenz was reminded of that tragedy by the 2022 school shooting in Uvalde, Texas.“That was when I decided that this was not gonna leave me alone until I wrote about it,” he wrote in an author’s note shared by the publisher. “I wanted to write a book about how people survive and live through something as senseless as this.”Explore more on these topicsBooksUS-Mexico borderTexasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barbie sequel at risk as salary talks with Robbie, Gosling and Gerwig hit impasse | Movies | The Guardian
description: Warner Bros faces losing rights to the blockbuster sequel if deals with the film’s stars and director are not agreed by December
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Warner Bros faces losing rights to the blockbuster sequel if deals with the film’s stars and director are not agreed by December
Content: Jeopardy … Ryan Gosling, Margot Robbie and Greta Gerwig on the set of Barbie in 2022.Photograph: Jaap Buitendijk/APView image in fullscreenJeopardy … Ryan Gosling, Margot Robbie and Greta Gerwig on the set of Barbie in 2022.Photograph: Jaap Buitendijk/APMoviesBarbie sequel at risk as salary talks with Robbie, Gosling and Gerwig hit impasseWarner Bros faces losing rights to the blockbuster sequel if deals with the film’s stars and director are not agreed by DecemberLaurence PhelanMon 3 Aug 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe comedy mega-hit Barbie made an estimated $1.5bn (£1.1bn) at the box office, was nominated for eight Academy Awards and – alongside the biopic Oppenheimer – dominated the culture during the summer of 2023. A sequel had seemed a foregone conclusion. However, the development of Barbie 2 has stalled over salary negotiations, putting the entire project in jeopardy, according toa report in the New York Times.Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, the first film’s stars, and its director and co-writer Greta Gerwig, are yet to agree on terms. Gosling, who was nominated for a best supporting actor Oscar for his performance as Barbie’s boyfriend Ken, is reportedly asking for $20m (£14.8m) to return to the role. All three are represented by the same talent agency, CAA.The film rights to Barbie are due to revert to Mattel, the toy company that manufactures the doll, ifWarner Brosdoes not get deals in place with all three of them by December. The film studio’s co-chairs, Pam Abdy and Michael De Luca, said in a statement: “We have a rights deal with Mattel in place and have made a series of big offers to try and finalise deals to make the next Barbie film. Unfortunately, we have been unable to reach an agreement thus far.”If the rights were to return to Mattel and it wanted to make anotherBarbiefilm with a different studio, it would be unable to incorporate any original story elements from the first film, and Robbie, Gosling and Gerwig could not be involved.As well as being the biggest hit of 2023, the highest-grossing live-action comedy ever and the 18th highest-grossing film in history, Barbie is also Warner Bros’s best-performing film. However, the studio only signed a one-movie deal with Gerwig and did not require the stars to commit to any sequels. “We didn’t build it to be a trilogy or something … We put everything into this one,” Robbietold Associated Pressat the time. But Gerwig and Noah Baumbach, her writing partner and husband, have now said they do have an idea for a sequel, and are ready to begin writing if terms can be agreed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome of Warner Bros’s more recent high-budget productions, including the DC Comics filmSupergirlandThe Bride, a feminist reworking of Frankenstein, underperformed at the box office this year and failed to recoup their costs. The studio also had its planned merger with Paramountput on holdlast month, after a group of 12 US states won a temporary injunction in their efforts to block the deal.Explore more on these topicsFilmBarbieGreta GerwigRyan GoslingMargot RobbieNoah BaumbachFilm industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Justin Hardy, director of Wicker Man sequel, dies three weeks before its premiere | Movies | The Guardian
description: Hardy, a Bafta-nominated film-maker, has died aged 61, having completed a sequel to the cult 1973 folk-horror made by his father Robin Hardy
Author: Laurence Phelan
Headline: Hardy, a Bafta-nominated film-maker, has died aged 61, having completed a sequel to the cult 1973 folk-horror made by his father Robin Hardy
Content: Film-maker Justin Hardy.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenFilm-maker Justin Hardy.Photograph: Family handout/PAMoviesJustin Hardy, director of Wicker Man sequel, dies three weeks before its premiereHardy, a Bafta-nominated film-maker, has died aged 61, having completed a sequel to the cult 1973 folk-horror made by his father Robin HardyLaurence PhelanMon 3 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 13.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish film-maker Justin Hardy, the son ofThe Wicker Mandirector Robin Hardy, has died aged 61. He had recently completed Wrath of the Gods, a second sequel to the fondly regarded folk-horror film, inspired by a story idea discovered in his father’s archives.In a statement, the director’s family said they are “devastated to share that Justin Hardy passed away [on Friday]. He was so full of life right to the end, and incredibly energised to be working towards premiering his latest film this month. We are all so proud of him and heartbroken he won’t be with us at his premiere. He was a man of family, of boundless creativity and of devotion for everyone he held dear.”The BBC reportedHardy died after a heart attack.View image in fullscreenDominic Hardy, left, and Justin Hardy, co-writers of Wrath of the Gods, at a Wicker Man anniversary screening in 2023.Photograph: Vianney Le Caer/ShutterstockHardy had a varied career and his 45 directing credits include dramas, documentaries and romcoms for the cinema and television. He was nominated for a Bafta for 2007’s The Relief of Belsen, a feature-length television drama about the liberation of the concentration camp, starring Corin and Gemma Redgrave.In 2024 he made Children of the Wicker Man, a documentary based on a book of the same name which he co-wrote with his brother Dominic, about their father’s making of the 1973 film, the uncredited part their mother played in its production, and the toll it took on their family.The Wicker Man stars Edward Woodward as a devout Christian police officer who investigates a disappearance on a fictional Scottish island lorded over by a pagan priest played by Christopher Lee. In 2010, the Guardian ranked it theNo 4 best horror film of all time, and when it was rereleased for its 50th anniversary in 2023, the paper’s film criticPeter Bradshaw wrotethat “it is so much better and more distinctive than any film that comes under the folk-horror heading … it’s virtually a one-movie genre in itself”.Robin Hardy wrote and directed a sequel,The Wicker Tree, released in 2011. Wrath of the Gods, which completes the trilogy, was written by Justin and Dominic Hardy after the story concept was found amongtheir father’s archivesin the attic of their former family home.Filmed in Shetland, it stars Norwegian actor Christiane Schaldemose as a woman who returns to a North Sea island to bury her husband after his suicide. When children start going missing, she is cast out by the eccentric locals for being a symbol of bad luck and evil.On Monday, Dominic Hardy paid further tribute to his brother, saying: “He aimed to use film on his own terms, to tell stories from original sources.” And describing Wrath of the Gods, he said: “I feel it is personal, a distinctively new creative statement from so seasoned a film-maker … When I last saw him, on 17 July, he was looking forward to a future in which writing scripts could be his exclusive focus, bringing him, along with the form’s inbuilt challenges, generous measures of joy.”Wrath of the Gods has itsworld premiereat the horror film festival FrightFest in London on 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe Wicker ManHorror filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Phil Collins details serious alcoholism: ‘People were coming to say goodbye’ | Phil Collins | The Guardian
description: Pop and rock legend tells Sunday Times of drinking problem and ill health after final Genesis tour in 2021
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Pop and rock legend tells Sunday Times of drinking problem and ill health after final Genesis tour in 2021
Content: Phil Collins performing in 2019.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAView image in fullscreenPhil Collins performing in 2019.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAPhil CollinsPhil Collins details serious alcoholism: ‘People were coming to say goodbye’Pop and rock legend tells Sunday Times of drinking problem and ill health after final Genesis tour in 2021Ben Beaumont-ThomasMon 3 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePhil Collins has said that he suffered life-threatening alcoholism in recent years.Speaking to the Sunday Times, the pop and rock legend, 75, said that his drinking began after he stopped taking Antabuse, a drug that causes illness if alcohol is consumed, which he had been using since an earlier period of alcoholism.Collins describes drinking wine at breakfast time, and says his extensive alcohol intake led to him being hospitalised in November 2023, for seven months, with damage to his pancreas and kidneys.“There were some decisions to be made about ‘Do we keep Phil on life support?’ kind of thing,” he said. “My kidneys were packing up, my organs were just seizing up. People were coming to say goodbye. But I don’t remember them coming, I didn’t have no idea this was going on. They were all worried that they wouldn’t see me again. It could all have gone so terribly wrong.”He added: “I was very lucky to have come out of that. Needless to say, I haven’t had a drink since.”In 2015, Collins described a period of alcohol abuse after his 2006 divorce from third wife, Orianne Cevey. “It left me with a lot of time on my hands to think about what happened,” hetold Rolling Stone. “I went through a few bits of darkness; drinking too much. I killed my hours watching TV and drinking, and it almost killed me. But I haven’t had a drink in three years.”Collins has experienced a series of other health issues in recent years, including problems with his neck and spine that required surgery, and which mean he is no longer able to play the drums: his role on theGenesisreunion tour in 2021 was restricted to vocals. In 2016 he announced he had been diagnosed with diabetes.Ahead of the Genesis concerts in 2021, Collinstold the Guardian: “Of course, my health does change things, doing the show seated changes things. But I actually found on my recent solo tours, it didn’t get in the way; the audience were still listening and responding. It’s not the way I would have written it, but it’s the way that it is.”Genesis review – rock’s most unlikely stars go out with a bangRead moreCollins is one of the most commercially successful musicians in British history. After taking over vocal duties in Genesis from Peter Gabriel, he helped to turn them from prog darlings to mainstream hit-makers, scoring five back-to-back UK No 1 albums in the 1980s and early 1990s. His solo career was just as illustrious, with another four UK No 1 albums across the same period, featuring hits such as Against All Odds, Easy Lover and In the Air Tonight.His most recent solo album is 2010’s Going Back. Collins retired for four years after its release, but returned in 2015, telling Rolling Stone: “My kids are now 10 and 14 and they want to see what their dad does. They were in nappies when I was last on the road. They love my music and I’d like to take them out so they can enjoy it.”Explore more on these topicsPhil CollinsPop and rockAlcoholAlcoholismGenesisnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Am I 68? 69?’ Irvine Welsh on growing old, getting clean, bashing out his new novel – and flirting with guns | Irvine Welsh | The Guardian
description: Three decades after he channelled his heroin addiction into the cult classic Trainspotting, the Scottish author has discovered the joys of yoga, breathwork and standing desks. But is he quite as ‘Zen’ as he claims?
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: Three decades after he channelled his heroin addiction into the cult classic Trainspotting, the Scottish author has discovered the joys of yoga, breathwork and standing desks. But is he quite as ‘Zen’ as he claims?
Content: ‘Everything is going too fast for us to control’ … Irvine Welsh in London, July 2026.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian. Photographer’s assistant: Flora LunaView image in fullscreen‘Everything is going too fast for us to control’ … Irvine Welsh in London, July 2026.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian. Photographer’s assistant: Flora LunaThe big interviewIrvine WelshInterview‘Am I 68? 69?’ Irvine Welsh on growing old, getting clean, bashing out his new novel – and flirting with gunsPaula CocozzaThree decades after he channelled his heroin addiction into the cult classic Trainspotting, the Scottish author has discovered the joys of yoga, breathwork and standing desks. But is he quite as ‘Zen’ as he claims?Mon 3 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy rights,Irvine Welshought to be photographed somewhere gritty, looking grumpy, he says: “That’s the brand.” Beside a graffitied wall or at the docks, with a beanie pulled low, and definitely not smiling. But here he is, clear-skinned and wholesome in shorts and a T-shirt, drinking tea and – it’s hard to think of anything more off-brand – talking about the health benefits of yoga. Given his reputation for having lived in the worlds his books portray, he should or could look a lot worse. He guffaws at this, eyes a delighted blue, and repeats the phrase as if he’s found a new personal tagline: “Could look a lot worse!”Over the three decades since his cult debut,Trainspotting, was published in 1993, Welsh’s fiction has explored with humour the darker side of life. Drugs, clubs, alcohol, violence … often alongside psychological or social deprivation. Despite being 17 novels and four short-story collections into his career, selling more than 6m books globally, he remains best known for his first. It achieved, he says, “what most writers want to achieve in a lifetime – the big zeitgeist book that goes into the culture”.View image in fullscreenRobert Carlyle(left)and Ewan McGregor in Trainspotting, 1996.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyWelsh’s new book, Can Nothing Save Us?, is a big American novel and applies the same sharp-eyed realism that Trainspotting brought to working-class Edinburgh to Trump’s US. Set in the scorching heat of Las Vegas, it’s a multigenerational thriller in which, as one character puts it: “Everyone is dissatisfied. Democracy over. A confused citizenry reduced to helping rich egomaniacs build fiefdoms.” Sound familiar?Welsh, who grew up in Muirhouse, north Edinburgh, has spent swathes of the past 20 years in the US, after marrying his second (now ex-) wife, Beth Quinn, who’s American, in 2005. He still has a home in Miami (and in London and Edinburgh). “I was there when Obama first got elected and I was there when Trump first got elected,” he says. In the run-up to Trump’s presidency, Welsh wasn’t too worried. The professional, educated women he knew barely gave him a thought, focusing instead on his rival. “Clinton,” he says. “She was the one that brought on the real seethe. She was [seen as] an enabler of the worst kind of guy – the liberal sex pest in sheep’s clothing.”Trump remains an unarticulated presence in Welsh’s novel, an orange glow emanating from a fictional TV. Did Welsh fear litigation? “I wanted to show real people. I didn’t want to get into the politics of those wankers because they’ve got too much to say for themselves already,” Welsh says. Instead, in the midst of an affordability crisis, climate crisis, health crises and complex family relationships, all the novel’s characters are searching for the moral heart of their story.View image in fullscreen‘My mother could be very critical of my books.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianCan Nothing Save Us? is published this month, but it has a long back story. Welsh originally thought he was collecting material foran HBO pilot on the superstar DJ– this was in 2014 – with his friendCalvin Harris. (Welsh also DJs and co-ownsa record label.) From the DJ boxes of Vegas, he’d look out at “this ugly scene where middle-aged sleazy guys grind up against young women who’ve been comped for the clubs” – but the project stalled and Welsh realised he had the makings of something different: “A novel about modern America.”He gave the draft to his editor and some writer friends. “And they all said the same thing. ‘This is shit!’”Welsh re-read it. “Fuck, they’re right,” he thought.Rejection must be unfamiliar to a multimillion-selling novelist. But Welsh did manage to sell the screen rights, and while he watched the writers’ room work through his pages, he became “a voyeur of my own material” and understood how to fix his novel.By now, Welsh had seen his friend Jake Chapman’s filmAccelerate or Dieand he’d read the work of the accelerationists Nick Land and Sadie Plant – broadly speaking,accelerationismis the idea that technology and capitalism must speed up if humanity is to reach a better place. In Welsh’s novel, time flips forward and lurches back.“People have got that existential crisis. Everything is going too fast for us to control,” he says.View image in fullscreenWelsh returns briefly to Leith, Edinburgh, where he was born.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianSo what can save us?“What does save us is the inherent insanity and unworkability of the system,” Welsh says, crashing down his tea.His proofs of “unworkability” includethe decline of social media usage(“If you argue with someone on social media, you’re basically saying you haven’t got a sex life”), thedimming of the lights in Las Vegas(“You watch Vegas sneeze and the rest of America is catching cold”), “enshittification”, the climate crisis, the “radicalisation of the centre” in British and US politics, and the internet in general.This last “was supposed to be this big zone of freedom, and now it becomes self-made manacles. It does somethingtous rather thanforus. We’re policing each other through our bizarre politics and our nosiness …”The novel strings a path through all this from the My Lai massacre in Vietnam in 1968 to modern mass shootings and, true to brand, climaxes in spectacular carnage.Welsh doesn’t own a gun, but he had a transformative experience at the Lock & Load shooting range in Miami. It’s “massively seductive”, he says, “when you start shooting at things”.He thought he’d be “skittish”. But no. “I was a stone-cold assassin. I really enjoyed it. I was feeling the power of it.”He got to thinking: “How would it be for a dispossessed kid who’s got no money and can’t get into the system and you’re told that you’re rubbish, and suddenly you’ve got this thing in your hand …”When Welsh left Lock & Load, “I wanted to shoot live prey,” he says. “To shoot something that’s moving. To hunt something down. I thought: ‘Fucking hell! What’s going on with me?’ This is a drug. You know? I went twice and I thought: ‘I’m liking this too much. I’ve got to stop.’”Welsh is practised at monitoring his proclivities, drawing the line and sticking to it. His addiction toheroin in his early 20s, “living in a Velvet Underground album, basically”, is well documented (he used notes and diaries from this timeto draft Trainspotting). He tried rehab but it was just a chance “to detox [to] start again with a clean slate, get some pills in”, so he went cold turkey. Was it hard?“Not once I decided that I really wanted to,” he says. “The worst part is the psychological thing. Once [drug use] is in your emotional vocabulary as your get-out – ‘I can stop feeling crap by doing this’ – you have to reorder your thinking.”View image in fullscreenLas Vegas, where Welsh’s new novel is set.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesReordering thoughts isn’t always easy, but, for Welsh, making the decision seems tantamount to its execution. He has a sort of self-applied strictness, which implies he is his own master, but also gives the impression of having to countermand his compulsions.It’s not just the gun he’s recently overruled, but also sitting down. “Sitting down is the new cigarettes,” he says. As far as demonised lifestyle choices go, being sedentary is not the one typically associated with Welsh, but these days he writes at a standing desk. The other week, he took the train from Edinburgh to Guildford in Surrey for a rehearsal ofTrainspotting the Musical– and the next day he was in agony.“I was fucked from sitting all day,” he says. “I quite liked it.”Liked the pain?“The idea that it has become something that makes me feel bad, so I don’t do it any more.”Perhaps not surprisingly, given the grim pleasure he took from the way his body registered dissent, he is geekily disciplined about wellbeing.He takes the Zapply nutritional supplement favoured by boxers – he has boxed since childhood, when his parents sent him to toughen him up. He also attends breathing workshops – “Everything is better afterwards: your digestion, your sleeping” – and practises pilates and yoga.View image in fullscreenTrainspotting the Musical, at Theatre Royal Haymarket, London, July 2026.Photograph: Alan West/Hogan Media/ShutterstockEspecially yin yoga – or “lazy bastards’ yoga”, as he calls it, because poses are held for several minutes. “You feel yourself opening up … Your shoulders, back, hips … It makes you calmer, basically.”With his shiny head and straight mouth, I can’t help picturing Welsh briefly in an alternative career as a wellbeing guru or monk. Especially when he says: “I’m more Zen now than I used to be.”Just before Christmas he was atthe funeral of Mani, the bass player for Primal Scream and the Stone Roses. Once upon a time, Welsh would have been drinking with the best of them. But instead he microdosed and was “off my tits” on Guinness zero and a cup of mushroom chocolate. “Then bang! You’re sober … You go to bed feeling happy and clean … Everybody else is wrecked.”Maybe the decisively slow yoga practice, the strict drawing of lines, is a way to counteract his own frenzy. For someone so relentlessly productive, it’s notable that his favourite bit of writing – “the best thing that I like most” – is to write “The End”. He always types the words.It’s possible Welsh is on his own accelerationist trajectory, because this is his third novel in three years. He’s already written the next novel – a return to the Trainspotting cast – and started the one after that.“Banging them out!” he says cheerfully, pretend-typing with hands bunched into fists, as if he’s punching the keyboard. Maybe he does. He goes to Miami each January, stays for three months, and between the gym and yoga, “easily” amasses 90,000 words.“I’m just playing, basically,” he says. “You know when you’re a kid and you line up your soldiers on the carpet? I’m doing the same thing.” An only child, he always prized the “luxury” of his own room.Sometimes, his wife –Emma Currie, an actor;they married four years ago – yells up. “‘You’ve got real friends down here that have come for dinner! Come and talk to them instead of your imaginary friends!’” he says. “‘You’re talking to people that don’t exist! You’re a nutter!’”I wonder how it felt to write a multigenerational novel of complex family dynamics as an only child with no children of his own (though he is stepfather to three). Welsh was close to both parents, but his dad, a former dockworker and carpet salesman who died when Welsh was 22, “was my best mate”, and the relationship with his mother, a waitress, “more fractious”.She was “very loving, but never into having kids”. She often told him: “You were an accident, son. A lovely accident, but an accident.” “She was quite tough, my mother,” he says. “She could be very critical of the books.“She hated Trainspotting at first. ‘You’re hanging your dirty washing in public! Bringing shame on me again! I’m embarrassed!’” His parents “weren’t massively drug-literate” and didn’t know when Welsh was using heroin, beyond the sense that “it was more than other drugs”.View image in fullscreen‘Sitting down is the new cigarettes.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBut Trainspotting grew on Welsh’s mother. “When it started to make money, she was like: ‘I want new windows, son.’ I bought her council house and got the windows double-glazed and a new door. She was all right with it after that.‘My laddie’s written a book and it’s a bestseller!’” he says in a Scottish accent stronger than his own. “I do miss her.” She died in 2023.“She got a bit frail in her last couple of years. I felt it put me in a strange position because she could besocutting. We had these brilliant jousts. Then suddenly she got a bit slower and frail, and I felt I was bullying her if I tried to get involved in the cut and thrust of our jousts … But I felt I was patronising her if I didn’t.”They did find peace. “Me and my mum, we said everything to each other. We put it all out on the table emotionally and talked about how we loved each other, and how we were friends, and how we’ve been through this and been through that together.” In a funny way, he says: “We did that too early. We were twiddling our thumbs for the last five years.”Certainly, family love comes through in the novel as an important remedy. As to political answers, Welsh has previously said he’d like to dissolve the monarchy and the House of Lords, institutions that are “not really serving any function in the lives of most citizens”. He’d have “as much devolution as Britain and England wanted or needed”.More personally, he believes that as people “become fed up with the system”, they will switch off. He’s noticed this switching off in himself.“The office now posts all my stuff on X. This thing here,” he says, tapping his phone, face down on the table. “I’ve started going out without it. After about an hour, you’re anxious. Then you feel so liberated.’” He won’t touch AI, even for research.View image in fullscreen‘I stopped celebrating birthdays when I got to 30’ … Welsh in 1999.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianOne of the problems of the internet, he says, is that it strips the context from everything – including Welsh himself. At events in college towns, “there’ll all be young people in the audience and they expect me to be young. ‘Who is this old fucker? That can’t be Irvine Welsh!’”Yet there is something ageless about him, even if these days he gets “the young team” – friends’ and cousins’ children – to check his younger characters’ dialogue for him.“Tell that to the mirror!” he says.He hasn’t counted his age in years. Does he even know it?“Sixty … eight? Sixty-nine?” he asks. (The internet says 67.) “I stopped celebrating birthdays when I got to 30. I was really depressed. I thought: ‘I’m not doing this again.’”It sounds like ageing, measuring age – or maybe growing up – is another practice he’s drawn a line under. But he doesn’t fear what follows. He recently abandoned lifelong atheism, aftera trip on the psychedelic drug DMT. “Now I just don’t know,” he says. “I’m quite excited … You do look at life in a more positive way.”Can Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh(Jonathan Cape, £20) is published on 13 August. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges might applyDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
