title: Whey to go! Could the cheese byproduct heat our homes and fuel our cars? | Cheese | The Guardian
description: British cheesemakers have struggled to find a use for the 95,000 tonnes of salty whey they produce every year. But researchers may have come up with a solution
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: British cheesemakers have struggled to find a use for the 95,000 tonnes of salty whey they produce every year. But researchers may have come up with a solution
Content: Whey: what is it good for?Photograph: JulieAlexK/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhey: what is it good for?Photograph: JulieAlexK/Getty ImagesCheeseWhey to go! Could the cheese byproduct heat our homes and fuel our cars?British cheesemakers have struggled to find a use for the 95,000 tonnes of salty whey they produce every year. But researchers may have come up with a solutionMon 3 Aug 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Whey.Age:As old as milk.Appearance:Translucent, yellow-tinged.What isit?Whey is what remains after you’ve made cheese: the milk curdles, the curds are strained and the whey is left over.Yeah, but what’s in it?About 75% to 93% of it is water. The rest is lactose, protein and fat. Salty whey, produced when cheese curds are salted early in the process, also contains a lot of salt –as much as 10%.What is it used for?Whey can be used to produce more cheese and cheese-style foods – ricotta, manouri and the caramel-like Norwegian spread brunost are made from whey – and the protein can be extracted for nutritional supplements. But salty whey is generally considered a waste product.How much waste are we talking about?Britain produces95,000 tonnes of salty whey annuallyand disposing of it presents an environmental challenge, in part because it’s so salty.Surely technology can meet the challenge. Can’t weput the whey on a rocket andcrash iton to the moon?We may not have to. Researchers at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, working with the space tech company Take Root Bio, have devised a method forturning salty whey into fuel.Actual fuel?Yes – it could heat homes or power your car.Will my exhaust smell like cheese?No word on that yet.How do they do it?The sugars in the whey are subjected to a “bio-based” process.What a weird idea.Not, however, a new one. In 2021, the then Prince Charles burnished his green credentials by running his Aston Martin onbioethanol made from whey and surplus wine.All the whey up! How a dairy byproduct became the star of the ‘proteinmaxxing’ boomRead moreSurplus wine? That sounds like a royal family problem.Bioethanol has fallen out of favour as a green fuel since. The salty whey research is about adding value to byproducts that “still contain valuable components but can be challenging to manage”, according to Heriot-Watt’s Dr Jane White.So is whey the cheap petrol of tomorrow?Whey ispretty expensive. High demand forprotein supplements– largely driven by their recommendation to patients on weight-loss drugs – has pushed up the price of whey-protein concentrate. Some suppliers have already sold out for the rest of the year.Wine surpluses, whey shortages – what crazy times we live in.I’ll admit it, I did not see any of this coming.Do say:“To transform whey – something regarded as waste – into something of value can provide real benefit to cheese manufacturers and the environment.”Don’t say:“Drive caerphilly, your majesty.”Explore more on these topicsCheeseFood (global)Food (Environment)MilkFood scienceBiofuelsFood wastefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rukmini Iyer’s quick and easy Thai-style cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodles – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Enjoy this big bowl of refreshing noodle soup with turmeric and coconut milk spiked with a kick of chilli
Author: Rukmini Iyer
Headline: Enjoy this big bowl of refreshing noodle soup with turmeric and coconut milk spiked with a kick of chilli
Content: Rukmini Iyer's cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodles.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenRukmini Iyer's cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodles.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.Quick and easyFoodRukmini Iyer’s quick and easy Thai-style cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodles – recipeEnjoy this big bowl of refreshing noodle soup with turmeric and coconut milk spiked with a kick of chilliRukmini IyerMon 3 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is exactly what I want to eat when I’m under the weather: a big bowl of Thai-inspired, soupy noodles with turmeric and coconut milk, all spiked with chilli. It’s a soup base that adapts perfectly for vegetarians (add cubed tofu) or leftovers (shredded roast chicken). This makes alotof broth (hydration is important!), so serve it in your best ramen or soup bowls. The choice of noodles is yours: rice noodles (flat or vermicelli) work well for a gluten-free option, but I inevitably use my favourite straight-to-wok thick udon.Cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodlesWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appIf you’re using tofu or leftover shredded cooked chicken, add it with the pak choi, so it simmers for four minutes in total.Prep5 minCook15 minChill2 hr+Serves22tbsp neutral oil150g fresh shiitake or chestnut mushrooms1tsp sea salt400ml tin coconut milk150g packthick straight-to-wokudon noodles2 heads pak choi, finely sliced150g prawns, peeled and deveinedFor the base1 lemongrass stalk2 spring onions, trimmed2garlic cloves, peeled1 fat red chilli4cm piece fresh ginger, peeled1cm piece turmeric root, or ½ tsp ground turmericFinely grated zest and juice of 1 lime, plus wedges to serveFinely grate all the base ingredients bar the lime juice; alternatively, roughly chop the lemongrass and spring onions, then put them in a blender with the other base ingredients (again, bar the lime juice) and blitz to a rough paste. (Do not, as I have done in the past, put a whole stick of lemongrass in the blender: the blender will break and you will be sad.)Put the oil in a large saucepan on a medium to low heat, then add the chopped lemongrass-chilli-ginger paste and fry, stirring constantly, for three minutes. Add the mushrooms, fry, still stirring, for a further five minutes, then add the salt, coconut milk and 400ml of just-boiled water. Bring the broth to a boil, then take off the heat and leave to cool. Once cooled, chill for at least two hours. (Alternatively, for a hot version, once the broth is boiling, add the pak choi and simmer for two minutes. Taste the broth, adding salt as needed, then add the noodles and prawns, and simmer for two minutes, until they are cooked through.)Just before you want to eat, bring a pan of salted water to a boil, then drop in the noodles and pak choi. Boil for a minute, then add the prawns and simmer for a further minute until they turn pink and are cooked through. Drain well, then rinse under the cold tap. Arrange the noodles, pak choi and prawns in bowls, then pour the cold broth all over the top. Season with the lime juice and serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodQuick and easySummer food and drinkNoodlesVegetablesThai food and drinkShellfishSeafoodrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Pollock tacos and hake with saffron aïoli and butter beans: Andy Beynon’s summer fish recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Perfect for cooking in the heat, these light, fresh dishes that are bursting with flavour will have you falling hook, line and sinker
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Perfect for cooking in the heat, these light, fresh dishes that are bursting with flavour will have you falling hook, line and sinker
Content: Andy Beynon’s crisp polluck tacos with grilled sweetcorn jalapeno yoghurt and lime pickled cucumberPhotograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenAndy Beynon’s crisp polluck tacos with grilled sweetcorn jalapeno yoghurt and lime pickled cucumberPhotograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodPollock tacos and hake with saffron aïoli and butter beans: Andy Beynon’s summer fish recipesPerfect for cooking in the heat, these light, fresh dishes that are bursting with flavour will have you falling hook, line and sinkerAndy BeynonMon 3 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSummer is my favourite time of year to cook fish. There are so many fantastic seasonal species available and, so long as they’re properly fresh and of good quality, they need very little intervention. I often look for lightness, freshness and acidity to bring balance and lift to a summery fish dish, whether that comes from citrus, herbs or a sharp dressing, because those elements enhance the natural flavour of the fish, rather than masking it. These recipes are ideal for relaxed summer cooking: full of flavour, yet straightforward enough for a midweek meal.Crisp pollock tacos with grilled sweetcorn, jalapeño yoghurt and lime-pickled cucumberWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep15 minPickle20 min+Cook25 minServes4For the lime-pickled cucumber1 cucumber, trimmed, deseeded and thinly slicedJuice of 2 limes1 small handful fresh mint leaves1 tsp sugarSalt and black pepperFor the jalapeño yoghurt1 fresh jalapeño, deseeded (leave the pith and seeds in if you like more heat)1 small handful coriander leaves1 small garlic clove, peeled200g Greek yoghurtJuice of 1 limeFor the sweetcornTwo corn cobs, or 300g fresh kernels1 tsp olive oilFor the pollock75g plain flour1 tsp smoked paprika½ tsp garlic powder500g pollock fillets, cut into finger-width strips1 egg, beaten100g panko breadcrumbsVegetable oil, for fryingTo serve8 small corn tortillas, or flour tortillasShredded red cabbage(optional)Coriander leavesLime wedgesPut the sliced cucumber in a bowl with the lime juice, mint, sugar and ½ tsp salt, toss to combine, then leave to pickle for at least 20 minutes.Blend or finely chop the jalapeño, coriander and garlic, then mix with the yoghurt, lime juice and a pinch of salt, and chill until needed.Brush the sweetcorn with oil, grill until lightly charred, then cut the kernels off the cob and season.Mix the flour, paprika, garlic powder, salt and pepper in a shallow bowl. One by one, dredge the fish strips in the flour mixture, then dip them in the beaten egg and coat with the breadcrumbs.Put 1cm vegetable oil in a deep-sided frying pan on a medium-high heat, then, working in batches, if need be, fry the pollock strips for two to three minutes on each side, until golden, crisp and cooked through. Drain on kitchen paper and keep warm while you cook the rest of the fish.Warm the tortillas for a few seconds on each side in a dry frying pan.To serve, spread a spoonful of jalapeño yoghurt over one side of each tortilla. Top with a little shredded cabbage, if using, then lay the crisp pollock, grilled sweetcorn and drained pickled cucumber on top. Finish with coriander leaves and a squeeze of lime.Roast hake with saffron aïoli and crabby anchovy-roasted garlic butter beans with tarragonWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenPrep10 minCook1 hrServes4For the butter beans1garlic bulbOlive oil2400g tins butter beans, drained and lightly rinsed1long red chilli, finely chopped1 handfulfresh coriander leaves4 anchovy fillets, drained and finely chopped100g white crab meat1 tbsp lemon juice1 tbsp chopped fresh tarragon, plus extra to garnishSalt and black pepperFor the aïoli1 pinch saffron threads150g mayonnaise1 garlic clove, peeled and finely grated1 tsp lemon juiceFor the hake4 hake fillets– about 150-180g each1 tbsp olive oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Slice the top off the garlic bulb to expose the flesh inside, drizzle all over with a little oil, then wrap in tinfoil and roast for 40-45 minutes, until soft and caramelised.Meanwhile, soak the saffron in a tablespoon of warm water for five minutes. Once steeped, stir the saffron and its water into the mayonnaise, add the garlic and lemon juice, then season lightly and chill until needed.Put the drained butter beans in a roasting tray with a tablespoon of olive oil, add the finely diced chilli and picked coriander, and toss to combine. Roast alongside the garlic for the last 20 minutes, stirring once halfway, until lightly golden.Squeeze the roast garlic flesh out of the skins, then mash to a paste. Heat a tablespoon of olive oil in a frying pan, then gently fry the anchovies, stirring, for a minute or two, until they dissolve. Stir in the garlic paste, then fold the lot through the hot roast butter beans. Gently mix in the crab meat, lemon juice and tarragon, season to taste and keep warm.At least half an hour before you want to cook it, pat dry the hake and season generously – this will give the salt time to draw out any excess moisture and firm up the fish. Put an ovenproof frying pan on medium-high heat, add the olive oil, then lay in the hake skin side down, turn up the heat to high and leave to caramelise for a minute. Flip over the pieces of fish so they’re now skin side up, then transfer to the oven and roast for five minutes, until just cooked through (the cooking time will depend on the thickness of the fish).Divide the crabby anchovy butter beans between four warmed plates, top each portion with a piece of the roast hake and serve with a generous spoonful of saffron aïoli alongside. Garnish with extra tarragon, if desired.Andy Beynon is chef/owner ofBehind, London E8Explore more on these topicsFoodFishSeafoodShellfishBeans, pulses and legumesMexican food and drinkHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Karl, the tabby who went to college and learned to use a toilet | Life and style | The Guardian
description: He could seem judgmental, even moody. But the whole neighbourhood mourned when this remarkable moggy went to meet his maker
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: He could seem judgmental, even moody. But the whole neighbourhood mourned when this remarkable moggy went to meet his maker
Content: ‘A south London legend’ … Karl.Photograph: Courtesy of Nadya SmithView image in fullscreen‘A south London legend’ … Karl.Photograph: Courtesy of Nadya SmithThe pet I'll never forgetLife and styleThe pet I’ll never forget: Karl, the tabby who went to college and learned to use a toiletHe could seem judgmental, even moody. But the whole neighbourhood mourned when this remarkable moggy went to meet his makerNadya SmithMon 3 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen my cat Eric passed away from stomach cancer in 2001, I wasn’t sure I would ever be ready to have a pet again. But a few months later I was given another cat, Karl, by an old friend from Camberwell College of Arts in south London, who was moving back to Germany. I had known Karl when I was a student there, where he had been mates with Eric. Karl, an unassuming brown tabby with a judgmental glare, took me back to living in student halls in the 90s.Karl was perhaps the most average-looking tabby in south London, but on my quiet street he became a legend of sorts. He accompanied my children and me on school runs. He would walk ahead with his belly swinging and take us to the top of the road. There he would wait until I dropped off the children and escort me back home.During his time at college, Karl had learned how to use the toilet. He would climb on to the seat, lift his tail up and aim directly into the bowl. It was like a party trick he had picked up.He would sit in the front garden for “chats” with neighbours and passersby he recognised. My apparently moody cat had formed connections with neighbours I didn’t even know. He remembered their routines, so he knew when to be waiting for his daily pats.In 2008, I was awaiting the birth of my third child – a baby I knew that Karl would only tolerate at best. On the walls of the front garden Karl stood as the neighbourhood watch. It was also where he was killed.View image in fullscreenThe memorial plaque commissioned by Nadya and her partner Tim.Photograph: Courtesy of Nadya SmithKarl was sadly mauled by an unruly dog. Neighbours, who had played with him and talked to him all these years, rushed out to my desperate screams. They stood next to me as he died in my arms.My partner, Tim, had trained as a funeral director before deciding to become a chef and he decided that Karl needed a fitting send-off. We had a funeral that same night. Our neighbours attended and we played music as we lowered Karl and his shoebox coffin into our back garden.I was so caught up in my grief, I hadn’t realised how many people loved Karl outside my own home. I received more condolence cards for Karl than when my mother died. I could hear people walking past my house asking: “Where’s the cat?”Tim knew some stonemasons from his funeral director days so we had a plaque commissioned. We put it at cat height so people who had knelt to stroke Karl could see it. When I moved homes in 2019, I offered to remove it for the new tenants. Surprisingly, they refused. Nearly 20 years on, the memory of Karl the cat lives on in a quiet suburban street.As told to Faisa MohamedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe pet I'll never forgetAnimalsCatsPetsBereavementfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I was fined £500 after putting a coffee cup in a rubbish bag next to a full bin | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: Reader expresses consternation after enforcement officer issues penalty notice outside station in London
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: Reader expresses consternation after enforcement officer issues penalty notice outside station in London
Content: An enforcement officer told a reader they had violated the law and refused an offer to remove their cup. He asked for their details, including their passport.Photograph: Steve Speller/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn enforcement officer told a reader they had violated the law and refused an offer to remove their cup. He asked for their details, including their passport.Photograph: Steve Speller/AlamyConsumer championsConsumer affairsI was fined £500 after putting a coffee cup in a rubbish bag next to a full binReader expresses consternation after enforcement officer issues penalty notice outside station in LondonAnna TimsMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI was outside London Waterloo railway stationand was looking for a bin to dispose of an empty coffee cup.The only bin Icould see wascompletelyfull, but there was a plastic bag containing rubbish at the base.I put my cup in that bag and was stopped by an enforcement officer, who had been standing at a distance watching the bin. He told meI had violated the law and refused my offer to remove my cup. He asked for my details, including my passport.After printing out a penalty notice, he remained in the same spot watching the overflowing bin. It seemed like a set-up.I discovered I had been fined £500, payable within 28 days and reduced to £325 if paid within 14 days. There is no right of appeal, and failure to paycould result in prosecution and a £2,500 penalty. Can you advise me?CP,WinchesterI have been reporting – with mounting alarm – on the large fines being handed out by councils for littering. Deliberate littering, I accept, is a blight on our streets and is indefensible.What concerns me is that, in my view, the penalties are – in the cases I’ve seen – disproportionate. Enforcement can be heavy-handed, and councils’ interpretation of what constitutes littering is far wider than what most of us understand it to be.One reader wasfined for putting a cigarette butt in a refuse sack. In March this year,councils were given statutory powersto fine what the government called “litter louts” up to £500 – and many have opted to apply the full sum. This means a dropped receipt could cost you £80 in one London street and £500 in another.A penalty of £500 is five times the fine for jumping a red light or for allowing a dog to foul a playground. It’s a sum unaffordable to many people who, nevertheless, have to stump up at speed to avoid it quintupling. And, unlike parking penalties, the only way to contest the fine is to go to court.The same government guidance states that enforcement action should be proportionate and focused on the worst offenders rather those who have unwittingly littered. It was not unreasonable to assume that a plastic bag beside an overflowing bin (I have seen a photo) was the next-best option for your rubbish before you hurried into a meeting. It is also not unreasonable to expect councils to ensure their own rubbish disposal – including emptying brimming bins – is up to scratch.I asked Lambeth council why people who were evidently unaware they were committing an offence were not given warnings instead of fines. It said that to be “consistent and fair,” it fined everyone, and it justified imposing the highest allowable penalty as a deterrent.The south London councilreportedly issued the second-highest number of finesfor littering over a 12-month period. It outsources its enforcement to the parking company APCOA but says the company does not keep any of the revenue raised or receive incentives to issue tickets.It refused to cancel your fine. If you challenge it in court, you lose the early payment discount. So my advice to you is to pay up through gritted teeth and stick to official bins in future.Hazardous toys: an updateView image in fullscreenFive children’s toys on sale in Britain analysed in a Guardian investigation in May were found to contain asbestos.Photograph: Addictive Stock Creatives/AlamyFour months ago I bought a selection of children’s toys to be tested for asbestos – andfive came back positive. All were removed from sale when I shared the test results with retailers and the Department for Business and Trade (DBT). One small retailer issued a recall notice to customers within the hour. That was in mid-May.It took the government’s Office for Product Safety and Standards (OPSS) 47 days to issue a recall notice on its website.Two weeks after that, and two months after I alerted Amazon, I have received a recall notice from the Amazon marketplace seller, NicoToys, which had sold me one of the contaminated items, telling me to stop using it immediately.The delay means children could have been playing with a potentially hazardous toy for eight weeks.Four days later came a recall notice for the same toy from Amazon’s product safety team. I asked Amazon – with which I had shared the test results in May – how it justified such a dangerous delay. It replied that the OPSS had prescribed actions for the seller, not Amazon, and that the item had been removed from sale in May.The DBT, which oversees the OPSS, wrung its hands when I asked what steps it took to ensure customers were contacted immediately.“Our product safety laws are clear: businesses must ensure the products they sell are safe and are required to act without delay where a safety risk has been identified,” said a spokesperson. “If they fail to meet their legal obligations, regulators will not hesitate to take action to protect consumers.”Nico Toys was contacted for comment.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsConsumer championsLocal governmentRetail industryToysAsbestosChildrenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … a cold shower is the best way to cool down on a hot night? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Want to lower your temperature and drift off to sleep quicker? An ice-cold shower might seem the best solution, but the truth is more complicated
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: Want to lower your temperature and drift off to sleep quicker? An ice-cold shower might seem the best solution, but the truth is more complicated
Content: Illustration: Becky Barnicoat/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Becky Barnicoat/The GuardianIs it true that …Life and styleIs it true that … a cold shower is the best way to cool down on a hot night?Want to lower your temperature and drift off to sleep quicker? An ice-cold shower might seem the best solution, but the truth is more complicatedKate LloydMon 3 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s another sticky summer evening. You’re too hot to sleep. Surely an ice-cold shower is the best way to cool off and drift away quicker? Not really, says Mike Tipton, a professor of human and applied physiology at the University of Portsmouth.“If you’re trying to go to sleep, the last thing you want to do is go into a freezing cold shower,” he says. The shock of cold water immersion causes the body to produce adrenaline and cortisol, stress hormones designed to keep us alert. “That’s just about the last thing you want before you go to bed.”double quotation markTo cool down before bed, a tepid shower is most effective because it allows blood flow to the skin, where heat can be gently removedCold water immersion also affects blood circulation, one of the body’s main ways of regulating temperature. When we get too hot, blood vessels near the skin dilate, warm blood moves towards the surface and heat is released into the air.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs it true that … saunas can reduce your sperm count?Read moreVery cold water triggers the opposite response: the body defends its temperature by decreasing circulation and shutting down blood flow to the skin. “What you do then is you trap the heat inside the body.” Eventually it will come out, Tipton says, but transfer from the body’s core to the skin and then into the air takes longer.Freezing cold water is useful during severe heatstroke, when circulation has collapsed. “The best way to get heat out of the body then is by immersing somebody in very cold water,” he says. But for someone simply trying to cool down before bed, a tepid shower is more effective because it allows blood flow to the skin, where heat can be gently removed.The ideal temperature varies between people but is likely in the mid to high 20C range, whereas a freezing cold shower would be below 10C.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleIs it true that …Health & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 10 of Britain’s best piers for dining, nightlife and good old seaside fun | Beach holidays | The Guardian
description: From Blackpool to Bournemouth, these quintessentially British institutions celebrate a lot more than fish and chips and amusement arcades
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: From Blackpool to Bournemouth, these quintessentially British institutions celebrate a lot more than fish and chips and amusement arcades
Content: Worthing pier, opened in 1862, is fun for foodies.Photograph: Paul Mansfield Photography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWorthing pier, opened in 1862, is fun for foodies.Photograph: Paul Mansfield Photography/Getty ImagesTop 10sBeach holidays10 of Britain’s best piers for dining, nightlife and good old seaside funFrom Blackpool to Bournemouth, these quintessentially British institutions  celebrate a lot more than fish and chips and amusement arcadesRachel DixonMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerched in our glass-fronted eyrie, 300 metres out to sea, we watch a murmuration of starlings rise and fall and swoop around us. When the show is over, we turn our attention to the food. I have a bespoke vegan menu based on the best early summer ingredients: jersey royals, asparagus, strawberries. My boyfriend orders off the weekly changing à la carte: slow-cooked beef dumplings followed by butter-poached halibut.We are atEbb, a restaurant at the end of the pier in Worthing, West Sussex, which opened in May. Its art-deco design and fine-dining dishes are a far cry from the fish-and-chip shops and ice-cream parlours more commonly found on seaside piers. But traditionalists need not despair: downstairs atPerch on the Pier, fish and chips – as well as tofish (tofu) and chips – are always on the menu, with a knickerbocker glory to round things off in fine retro style.Worthing pier, which opened in 1862, is one of Britain’s surviving 19th-century pleasure piers. “The seaside piers around the coast of Britain stand as a powerful reminder of the achievements of Victorian engineers and entrepreneurs,” says theNational Piers Societywebsite. “However, of the 100 piers that once graced our coastline, only half survive, and several of these face an uncertain future.” The society campaigns to preserve the piers for everyone’s enjoyment, and has saved several that were at risk of demolition.Worthing may well be the foodiest pier in the UK, but they all have their charms. Here are 10 well worth a stroll out to sea.Best for overnight stays:Garth pier, Bangor, GwyneddView image in fullscreenThe Pier Master’s House at Garth Pier, to the right, is now a holiday let.Photograph: Maciej Olszewski/AlamyBangor’s 458-metre (1,500ft) pier stretches out halfway across the Menai Strait, backdropped by the Eryri mountain range (Snowdonia). To coincide with its 130th anniversary this year, the Pier Master’s House at the entrance has been turned into a holiday let (from£140 a night, sleeps six). The pavilion at the far end is now a cafe, and the smaller Victorian kiosks dotted along the pier house independent businesses selling gifts, artworks and local food. There is a programme of weekend events over the summer, from busking and children’s fun days to a dog parade.Best for adventure:Bournemouth pierView image in fullscreenThe world’s first pier-to-shore zip wire .Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Live NewsBournemouth pier (first opened 1856, current structure 1880) boasts the world’s first pier-to-shore zip wire, a 250-metre dual line starting from the end-of-the-pier tower. As well as thePierZip, it hasRockReef, an indoor climbing centre with 28 climbing walls, an aerial obstacle course, a vertical slide, a “leap of faith” and caving tunnels. The pier is the best place to watch Bournemouth’sFriday fireworks(10pm, until 28 August), and there is regular live music at itsKey Westrestaurant (until 28 August). The town’s other pier,Boscombe(opened 1889), is next to free bouldering obstacles and slacklines, and near the beach volleyball courts.Best for traditional seaside fun:Britannia pier, Great YarmouthView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Eye35.pix/AlamyBritannia pier won the coveted 2026Pier of the Yearaward, taking over from last year’s winnerLlandudno, and beating runners-upHerne BayandSwanage. The 250-metre pier was built in 1858, but as with many of the original Victorian piers, it has been damaged, demolished, rebuilt (in 1901), burned down and reconstructed over the years. The current owners bought it in 2022 and have spent £2.2m restoring and upgrading it. Its attractions include a theatre, fun fair, arcades, fish and chip shop, pub and nightclub. Holidaymakers can also visit the town’sWellington pier, further south along the seafront, which opened in 1853 and has a bowling alley, arcade and ice-cream parlour.Best for culture:Penarth pier, GlamorganView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Nigel Wiggins/AlamyWhile Penarth pier dates back to 1894, as a landing jetty for the steamships in the Bristol Channel, its art-deco pavilion wasn’t built until 1929. This former dancehall has recently been restored and is now a cinema and arts centre, with year-round film screenings, art exhibitions, live music, workshops and talks.Coming up this monthis a jazz brunch, a drawing workshop, and a knitting and crocheting social, alongside summer blockbustersThe OdysseyandMinions & Monsters. There is a cafe in the pavilion, and a coffee shop, ice-cream parlour and chippy elsewhere on the pier.Best for exploration:Roker pier, SunderlandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Paul D Hunter/AlamyRoker pier is distinctive for its red-and-white striped granite lighthouse, completed in 1903. After extensive restoration, and closures due to storm damage, pier and lighthouse are now open for guided tours (£14 adults/£10 children, to 27 August). Visitors walk the length of an underground tunnel to reach the lighthouse – the route the keeper used in bad weather – then climb to the top to take in the views. For post-tour refreshments, the pier’s former toilet block is now a gin bar,Tin of Sardines, with brunch and tapas menus served on the terrace in the summer.Best for beauty:Clevedon pier, north SomersetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: PhotoPlus Magazine/Future/Getty ImagesEngland’s only Grade I-listed pier opened in 1869 to receive paddle steamer passengers from Devon and Wales. It is made from discarded wrought iron railway lines shaped into eight arches, nearly 15 metres high. In 1980, during a campaign to save it from demolition, the then poet laureate John Betjeman described it as “the most beautiful pier in England”. “Clevedon without its pier would be like a diamond with a flaw,” he said. The pier was duly saved, and now its Victorian pagoda is a cafe, its toll house is a museum and gift shop, and there is a modern restaurant, the Glass Box. The sea view from the porthole room isstreamed live24/7.Best for nightlife:Royal pier, AberystwythView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Colin Burdett/AlamyThe oldest pier in Wales (1865) was designed by Eugenius Birch, a renowned seaside architect best-known for Brighton’s now-ruined West pier. Today, Royal pier is billed as “the number one destination for competitive socialising in Aberystwyth”, with three bars and a nightclub. There is a host of activities in the Billiard Bar, including shuffleboard, augmented-reality darts, footpool and interactive mini golf; the Upstairs Bar has seven pool tables; and the Inn on the Pier is a restored Victorian boozer, with stained glass and custom tiles. DJs play chill-out tunes in the pier garden over the summer, and the Pressure Nightclub is open until 4am on Fridays and Saturdays.Best for variety: BlackpoolView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesBlackpool is the proud home of three piers:Blackpool North(1863),Blackpool Central(1868) andBlackpool South(1893). The Grade II-listed north pier is the oldest surviving Birch pier, and has an art-deco theatre, a two-tier carousel, bars and an arcade. It was sold in June and is open until at least the end of the year before a promised £10m refurbishment. The central pier has Blackpool’s Big Wheel, a funfair and a show bar with live performances. The south pier has a more high-octane funfair, with a rollercoaster, a freefalling swing and a reverse bungee ride, and is next to Blackpool’s Pleasure Beach for more adrenaline-fuelled fun. Its many food and drink options include the Gin House and a loaded jacket potato stand.Best for history:Gravesend pier, KentView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ian Goodrick/AlamyGravesend’s pier opened on the Thames in 1834, and is the oldest surviving cast-iron pier in the world. It was once a hub for steam packets to London – more than 3 million passengers used it between 1835 and 1842 – and today there are still occasional summer sailings to the capital withUber Boat by Thames Clippers. Just by the entrance to the pier is the ancientThree Dawspub, which was licensed in 1565 as the Three Cornish Choughs and renamed in 1745. This old smugglers’ haunt, which has three underground tunnels, now hosts a summer beer and music festival (7-9 August) and an Oktoberfest (18 September).Best for rainy days:Sandown pier, Isle of WightView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Steve Hawkins/AlamyThe Isle of Wight once had an incredible 11 piers, and four still survive:Ryde(the second-longest in the UK, afterSouthend-on-Seain Essex), Sandown, Totland (for sale) andYarmouth. Sandown (1879) is a particular paradise for families, whatever the weather. There is the Aztec-themed Lost World indoor crazy golf, with lighting and sound effects; the Magic Island indoor adventure play area; and Superbowl 10-pin bowling. The end of the pier has rides such as dodgems and teacups (Easter to September only); there is a cafe, ice-cream kiosk and burger bar; and Scruffy Jacks bar shows live sport.Food was provided by Ebb and Perch on the Pier. Accommodation was provided bySleep Eco Hotel,Worthing (doubles from £120 room-only)Explore more on these topicsBeach holidaysTop 10sUnited Kingdom holidaysEngland holidaysWales holidaysPiersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The one change that worked: I learned to love my arms – after decades of hating and hiding them | Life and style | The Guardian
description: It took a heatwave to get me to shed my shame and my sleeves, but now there’s no stopping me. Life is cooler in every way
Author: Amy Annette
Headline: It took a heatwave to get me to shed my shame and my sleeves, but now there’s no stopping me. Life is cooler in every way
Content: ‘I’m still figuring out this new version of myself’ … Amy Annette.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’m still figuring out this new version of myself’ … Amy Annette.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianThe one change that workedLife and styleThe one change that worked: I learned to love my arms – after decades of hating and hiding themIt took a heatwave to get me to shed my shame and my sleeves, but now there’s no stopping me. Life is cooler in every wayAmy AnnetteMon 3 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Aren’t you hot in that?” was the question that plagued my summers as a teenager. I would never bare my arms; instead, I would cover up with a trusty black cardigan. Even T-shirts felt too revealing, too tight on the arm, too clinging to the body. I needed layers to feel comfortable. Well, comfortable isn’t the right word. I was never comfortable, despite telling everyone: “No, I’m not hot. I don’t really feel the heat.”In my 20s and 30s, I collected a hot-weather capsule wardrobe of T-shirt dresses in various sizes, all baggy and sleeved. But why? I’m someone who should know better. I’ve read the books, I’ve shared the memes. I know, from body-positivity activists, that you don’t have to deny yourself the joy of being at the beach or pool just because a magazine tells you you have to get yourself “beach-body ready”: slimmer, hairless, perfect.I’m also someone who understands logically that a cardigan may cover you, but it doesn’t hide your body shape. When I hide my skin, I don’t make myself magicallydisappear, but I do make myself smaller. I’m showing the world that I respect beauty norms and that I know I don’t meet them.View image in fullscreen‘I learned to hate my arms by listening to other women talk about theirs’ … Amy(standing, second from left)on holiday in Italy, 2018.Photograph: Amy AnnetteI learned to hate my arms by listening to other women talk about theirs. Arm hatred feels like a homegrown industry – by women for women. Arms don’t have the mainstream attention of beauty standards. Perhaps it’s because they aren’t sexualised. I don’t remember seeing a lads’ mag spread on “Barbara from Bradford’s biceps” when I was growing up.But last month it was my friend’s birthday. That day, the temperature was more than 30C in London. The idea of putting any real clothing on and leaving the house seemed impossible, but I had to be there. I looked at my small selection of heatwave-appropriate clothes. None of them were very celebratory. I looked through the hangers for something else.My eye was drawn to a white sleeveless shirt, bought in Austin, Texas, where theydress for the constant heat– I’d bought it thinking I’d wear it one day, probably with a jacket. At that moment, something shifted and, despite years of conditioning to hate my arms, my hatred for the heat won. I put the sleeveless shirt on. (I added a pair of navy culottes with a white band at the bottom that made me feel like a fancy little Victorian boy, if he had access to Asos.) At 37, outside a swimming pool, I was bare-armed in public for the first time.And, of course, it was fine. No one cared. If they did, they didn’t tell me. I haven’t been properly catcalled in years (I look too old not to yell back) and the revealing of my BCG vaccination scar didn’t change that. I can’t believe it took me this long.View image in fullscreen‘No one cared. If they did, they didn’t tell me’ … Amy sleeveless in London, June 2026.Photograph: Sasha BrownThe next day, I posted about it on Instagram. I have a video series called Diary of a Sweaty Girl, where I chronicle my life as, you guessed it, a sweaty girl. I shared thatthe climate crisishad overtaken sexist body standards and had somehow freed me from my besleeved burden. Others shared that they too were experiencing their “first year arms out no shame” because they “couldn’t be bothered any more”. That’s how I felt. Yes, it was lovely to have my arms out, but it wasn’t a celebratory feeling. It was more like waking up: a softer, quiet change.And did it make things cooler? Yes, it turns out you do keep a lot of heat in if you cover the upper arms and shoulders.The week after my heatwave brainwave, I went on holiday with a group of friends. The change stuck. Instead of always having some sort of cover-up to hand, I was happy to be in my swimsuit. During hot French evenings, I didn’t find a way to fashion a shirt over my outfit; I wore a sleeveless dress and danced the night away, getting more mosquito bites on my shoulders than ever before.Now, I’m reconsidering my wardrobe. I’m no longer letting my friends talk about their arms negatively in front of me. I’m trying to quell that inner voice that whispers: “But is it flattering?” I’m still figuring out this new changed version of myself. And if it gets any hotter, I’m wondering what other internalised standards I can sweat out.Amy Annette’s showSay What You Like About Meis at the Edinburgh fringe from 5-30 August at the Pleasance theatreDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Did you solve it? Are you a match for the world’s smartest teen? | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: The solution to today’s puzzle
Author: Alex Bellos
Headline: The solution to today’s puzzle
Content: Alex ChuiPhotograph: Alex ChuiView image in fullscreenAlex ChuiPhotograph: Alex ChuiAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleMathematicsDid you solve it? Are you a match for the world’s smartest teen?The solution to today’s puzzleAlex BellosMon 3 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier today I set you the following puzzle, suggested by Briton Alex Chui, the most successful ever candidate at the International Mathematical Olympiad.Last month Alex, who is a pupil at Tonbridge School in Kent, became the first person to win a medal at the olympiad for seven years in a row. Bravo!How many ways are there to fill a 3×3 grid with positive whole numbers such that the product of the numbers in each row and each column is 30?[Each of the nine cells in the grid has a whole number in it. When you multiply the three numbers in each row, and in every column, the answer is 30. The three numbers in each row or column do not have to be three different numbers.]Alex said: “I like this puzzle because the key idea is to look at the prime factors of the numbers and realize that the arrangements of each prime factor (2, 3, 5) can be considered independently. This clean separation into different parts is one of my favourite aspects about maths.”Solution216The first thing to notice is that 30 = 2 x 3 x 5.So, every row and column must include a 2, a 3 and a 5.There are six ways to have a single 2 in every row and column. (3 ways to choose the 2 in first row, 2 ways to choose the 2 in second row in a different column, and 1 way to choose the last 2 in the third row, so 3 × 2 × 1 = 6). Here they are:View image in fullscreenSimilarly there are 6 ways to choose the placement of 3s and the placement of 5s.Each full grid is a unique placement of 2s, 3s and 5s. Therefore there are 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 ways to fill the grid.For example, here is one way to combine 2s, 3s and 5s.View image in fullscreenThese placements produce the full grid below, which is constructed by placing each number in the correct cell. If there is more than one number per cell you multiply them, and if there are no numbers, you put a 1.View image in fullscreenThere are 216 ways to combine the 2s, 3s and 5s in this way.I hope you enjoyed today’s puzzle. Thanks to Alex and best of luck for in your mathematical career!I’ll be back in two weeks.I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one,email me.Explore more on these topicsMathematicsAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleShareReuse this content

title: Crossword editor’s desk: what would be the point of an AI puzzle? | Crosswords | The Guardian
description: Some reassurance that our puzzles are created by flesh-and-blood setters – and your clues for the name of Brockwell’s dog
Author: Alan Connor
Headline: Some reassurance that our puzzles are created by flesh-and-blood setters – and your clues for the name of Brockwell’s dog
Content: Imbued with humanity … a solver and her puzzle.Photograph: Burak Karademir/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenImbued with humanity … a solver and her puzzle.Photograph: Burak Karademir/Getty ImagesCrossword editor's updateCrosswordsCrossword editor’s desk: what would be the point of an AI puzzle?Some reassurance that our puzzles are created by flesh-and-blood setters – and your clues for the name of Brockwell’s dogAlan ConnorMon 3 Aug 2026 07.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world of crosswords is generally a happy and sensible place. The human mind being what it is, though, we are not immune to entertaining ideas that are less than true.Our equivalent of the conspiracy theory that humankind is being controlled by5G phone mastsis that puzzles are appearing that have not been created by people.Yes: we’re talking about artificial intelligence. Some solvers reckon that they can discern, from a sideways definition or a piece of punctuation, the kind of clue only an AI would generate.We’ve discussed here beforethe feeble efforts AI has so far offered wheninvited to create clues. But we last did so more than three years ago; I expect the efforts would be better now, but still subpar. And I expect the time will come when AI can spit out cryptic clues that are perfectly sound.Still, though: what would be the point? When a human plays a computer at chess, the challenge is to see whether a brain can produce better strategies than a machine and get to checkmate.In crosswords, though, there is no winner. The setter wants the puzzle to be solved. The solver wants to be entertained by the clever, amusing or devious choices a setter has made; a setter is more like a poet or a comedian than a chess player. And the idea of being entertained by code-generated witticisms and deceptions is frankly eerie.On the topic of slyness:in July’s Genius, the message hiding in the clues is CONTAIN SAME LETTER AS TODAY’S CRYPTIC. Once you find the overlap withthat day’s regular puzzle, you find the contents of the safe:View image in fullscreenGenius 277 merged with cryptic 30,051.I’ll include the actual normal answer grid below, but you can see that the goodies in the notional safe are a dagger, a diamond ring and fake ID.August’s Genius awaits you!View image in fullscreenThe solution for Genius 277.Thanks foryour clues for EDDIE. The audacity award goes to Wellywearer2 for the verse:double quotation markDo anything you wanna doHis Hot Rods might advise youTheir ‘leader’ might say as wellLosing me hurts like hell (5)The runners-up are a pair of tributes to the real Eddie who inspired the conference,Brockwell’s late yorkshire terrier: Matty36251’s “A little Yorkie I’d delighted over” and Schroduck’s “Recalled doggie I’d definitely embrace!” And the winner is bawdy: “Elegant head, big chest, incomparable wings … the Eagle?”Kludos to Gurkentruppe; please leave clues for EERIE below, along with any favourite clues or puzzles you have spotted.Alan Connor is the Guardian’s crossword editor. His book What Would Reacher Do? is published by Transworld(£16.99). To support the Guardian,order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says | European Union | The Guardian
description: European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people
Content: Members of the Moroccan navy patrol the Moroccan side of the floating barrier off the border with Ceuta.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersView image in fullscreenMembers of the Moroccan navy patrol the Moroccan side of the floating barrier off the border with Ceuta.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersEuropean UnionStronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen saysEuropean Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more peopleJennifer Rankinin BrusselsMon 3 Aug 2026 13.44 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”She praised the Spanish socialist leader’s swift handling of the crisis, after the vast majority of migrants left Ceuta and Spanish officials began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier at the border ‌withMorocco. “Order has been restored and the returns system in place worked,” she wrote in the letter.View image in fullscreenPeople arriving in Ceuta from Morocco last week.Photograph: Reduan Dris/EPASpain ⁠estimates that about 69,500 migrants ​have returned to Morocco over the past four days, exceeding initial estimates of 50,000 having arrived in the enclave in north Africa on Thursday. Authorities in Ceutareported that 88 people diedtrying to reach the territory, while at least 11 deaths have been recorded in Morocco.Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave, have the EU’s only land borders withAfrica. There are periodic surges in attempted crossings to both cities, although neither permits onward free movement to the EU as they are outside the border-free Schengen zone.EU interior ministers will hold emergency talks on Tuesday, which von der Leyen said would be a chance to draw lessons from the crossings.She said the EU should double down on five areas: strengthening cooperation with non-EU countries to prevent migration; stronger external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks; and boosting returns of people with no right to stay.View image in fullscreenPeople who arrived in Ceuta from Morocco sitting on the street.Photograph: Reduan/EPAItalian media reported that Giorgia Meloni’s government wanted to accelerate the opening of offshore migration centres, which Europe’s top human rights expert recently saidrisked becoming “human rights black holes”.The EUopened the door to offshore detention centresin June in an unprecedented departure from legal norms as part of a law aiming to increase the deportations of people with no legal right to stay.Amid heavy criticism of the EU’s divided response to the Ceuta border crossings, von der Leyen stressed that Spain could access EU funds as well as support from the Frontex border agency. So far Madrid has not requested the assistance of Frontex.The crossings – seized on by far-right politicians across Europe – have exposed deep divisions over migration that have left Spain’s leader isolated.Over the weekend, Sánchez criticised other governments for failing to support Spain, after Italy and Denmark led calls for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen zone. Sánchez said such an attitude was “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest” and contrary to European and humanitarian law “and the principles of solidarity that bind us together”.Italy and Denmark organised a letter signed by 20 other EU member states that appeared to blame the crisis on Sánchez’s decision toregularise the status of 500,000 migrants without documents. “We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration,” the 22 leaders wrote, arguing for the need to address “all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularisation of [a] very large number of irregular migrants”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez has criticised other governments for failing to support Spain.Photograph: Borja Puig de la Bellacasa/Moncloa Handout/EPAEU member states favouring a tough approach to migration are expected to raise the issue of “pull factors” on Tuesday. “There is some concern that the regularisation of 1.2 million people can be used to paint a picture that the door is open,” an EU diplomat said, referring to the approximate number of people whoapplied for regularisationunder the 2026 Spanish government programme.Academic research hasfound no evidenceof a pull effect from regularisation programmes on arrivals of irregular migrants.Michele LeVoy, the director of Picum, an umbrella group that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants, said regularisation programmes had been criticised by EU governments for the last two decades. “If an EU country offers regularisation possibilities, other member states believe that it may invite secondary movement [onward movement to other EU member states] – that is what EU member states don’t want and that explains most likely the harsh response.”Amidwidespread suspicion that Morocco helped fuel the crisis, von der Leyen described the country as “an important strategic partner”, especially in combating “illegal migration”.Officials said that before the Ceuta crossings, the European Commission was looking to upgrade the EU’s diplomatic relationship with Morocco to a “strategic and comprehensive partnership”. The EU already has similar wide-ranging agreements with Egypt and Tunisia, which include pledges to stem migration, but which have been heavily criticised by rights groups.Von der Leyen wrote: “On anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.”Rights groups said people seeking work or fleeing persecution needed routes to move safely. LeVoy said: “On Ceuta, political games are being played over the lives of people on both sides of the border – those who hope for a better life, and those who are made to fear a so-called ‘invasion’. But what happened in and around Ceuta is fundamentally the result of Europe’s inaction on decent work permits and other regular pathways and the dismantling of its asylum systems.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionSpainMigrationEuropeMoroccoAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing | Spain | The Guardian
description: Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity
Content: People sit in the shade of a tree on a beach in Ceuta on Monday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople sit in the shade of a tree on a beach in Ceuta on Monday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersSpainCeuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossingJuan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarityExplainer: why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint?Ashifa Kassamin Madrid,Okba Mohammadin Ceuta andLisa O’Carrollin LondonMon 3 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA growing chorus of voices has accusedMoroccoof helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”.Spanish officials ⁠said on Monday that an estimated 69,500 people who had arrived late last week in Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in northAfrica, had returned to Morocco in recent days. About 2,500 people who had made the crossing were believed to still be in Ceuta.The extraordinary influx hadoverwhelmedthe city of 84,000 people and set offa political crisisacross the EU as some member states laid blame on Spain.In Ceuta, leaders pointed to the broader picture of what had transpired. “It’s an atrocity,” said Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of the territory. “There are 88 bodies in the morgue, and there are more on the other side of the border.”How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The LatestRead moreHe said local people watched the events play out with a mix of sadness, worry and anguish. “People see this not as a migration crisis; it was fundamentally an attack, a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” Vivas told El País newspaper. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco.”He drew a parallel with May 2021, when Rabat loosened border controls,allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceutaover the course of two days, during a diplomatic standoff over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.This time around, analysts have suggested that Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s arch-enemy Algeria could have triggered a response from Morocco.View image in fullscreenPeople who crossed from Morocco sit on a street in Ceuta on Monday.Photograph: Reduan/EPASpeaking on Monday, Spain’s defence minister, Margarita Robles, also seemingly signalled Rabat’s involvement. “Neither Spain nor Morocco can look the other way when it comes to this tragedy,” she told reporters. “I ask the Moroccan government to fully investigate what happened.”The insinuation appeared to be backed by the preliminary assessment of Spanish intelligence services, who cited suspicions that the influx had not been planned by Moroccan authorities but concluded that Morocco had failed to stem the tide of people rushing towards the border and in some cases had even facilitated their passage.Intelligence sources told El País that the roots of the influx probably lay in a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported. As the hoax gained steam online, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum until it was completely lifted late last week, allowing tens of thousands of people to stream through.In Ceuta on Monday, hundreds of people continued to sleep rough on the beach or near Ceuta’s mosques. One local official told reporters that those who remained in the city included 862 unaccompanied minors.Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streetsRead moreAshraf, 28, said he had defied his mother’s warnings against crossing into Spain after spotting posts on social media that said the border had been opened. While he had made it to Ceuta, what had followed was a days-long ordeal as he scrambled to find food and shelter while fending off the memories of what he had lived through.“You might see me smile a little but inside I’m shattered,” the Moroccan national said as he recalled swimming past bodies to reach Ceuta. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you. The Moroccan police were pushing us toward the water and telling us ‘swim, swim’.”Others were desperately seeking loved ones who were missing. One mother said she had been roaming the streets of Ceuta for days, frantically searching for any sign of her children, aged 13 and 16.She had left Morocco alone, finding out later that her two children had followed her by plunging into the sea to make their way around the border.“I need help,” she said as she held up a photo of a smiling young boy flashing a thumbs-up sign. “Some migrants told me they had seen them in Ceuta, but I can’t find them.”10:29How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The LatestAcross the EU, the crisis in Ceuta had seemingly ushered in a moment of reckoning after a handful of EU countries responded to the crisis by calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Italy said it had suspended passport-free Schengen travel arrangements with Spain for one month, despite the fact that Ceuta is not part of Schengen.Before an emergency video meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday to address the crisis, Spain’s foreign minister said the country would demand solidarity from EU members after several had, in his view, “fallen short” of what was expected.“There was a synchronised reactionary international effort that very quickly amplified what was happening, spreading lies and fake news about the integrity of the Schengen area and about Spain’s actions,” José Manuel Albares told the broadcaster TVE. “Unfortunately, these falsehoods have even been amplified by some European governments.”What had transpired in Ceuta was “very unusual”, he said. “Spain currently has the lowest number of irregular entries on the Mediterranean route,” he added, while Italy “was the country with the highest number of irregular entries in Europe”.He said he had been in contact with Moroccan authorities throughout the crisis. “They showed a willingness from the very beginning to mobilise police forces to help stem the flow of migrants.”View image in fullscreenPeople wait outside Ceuta’s temporary migrant centre, which is at full capacity.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersUrsula von der Leyen, theEuropean Commission president, said in a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, that the Tuesday meeting would be a chance to draw lessons from what happened in Ceuta, and she commended Madrid for its swift handling of the crisis. “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points,” she said.At a meeting of member states on Saturday, the Guardian was told that while Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, had criticised Spain for what had happened, there was a strong suspicion that the crisis was not an accident but had been coordinated.There was widespread recognition that Spain could not simply pin the blame on Morocco, given the close cooperation needed to return those who had crossed and, in the longer term, for migration control and security, a source said.EU states also spoke about the threat of Russian disinformation and how it could exploit the crisis to heighten tensions across the bloc, the source added.The concerns came into public view late last week when Ukraine’s acting foreign minister said more than 1,500 publications regarding Ceuta had been identified in pro-Russian networks.“We have detected an intensive Russian propaganda campaign across Europe using pictures from Ceuta to sow destabilisation,” Andrii Sybiha wrote on social media. “This is not about the situation itself but about the way Russia tries to exploit any topic that can benefit its agenda.”Explore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoEuropean UnionEuropeAfricaMigrationMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Weather tracker: Austria breaks heat records as Japan braces for Typhoon Dolphin  | Environment | The Guardian
description: Soaring temperatures continue to sweep parts of Europe, while Okinawa faces powerful winds and storm surges
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Soaring temperatures continue to sweep parts of Europe, while Okinawa faces powerful winds and storm surges
Content: Soaring temperatures near Lake Zicksee, Austria.Photograph: Leonhard Föger/ReutersView image in fullscreenSoaring temperatures near Lake Zicksee, Austria.Photograph: Leonhard Föger/ReutersWeather trackerEnvironmentAnalysisWeather tracker: Austria breaks heat records as Japan braces for Typhoon DolphinEd Walton for MetDeskSoaring temperatures continue to sweep parts of Europe, while Okinawa faces powerful winds and storm surgesEurope live – latest updatesMon 3 Aug 2026 04.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.11 EDTShareUnbearable, record-breaking heat has dominated the summer of 2026 across much of Europe. New records were set in central Europe last week, with Wieselburg inAustriaregistering a new July peak of 40.3C (104.5F). This is particularly significant as it is just 0.2C behind the all-time high, set in the August of 2003.However, not all of the northern hemisphere has experienced extreme heat and aridity. Vancouver recorded its wettest July since 2016 and the third wettest since 2008, with 33.6mm of rain. While that total may not appear exceptional, it is only a touch above the 1991-2020 climate average, highlighting how unusually dry July has been in the Canadian city over the past decade.Meanwhile, Typhoon Dolphin has continued to barrel westwards across the Pacific Ocean towards Japan andTaiwan. It became the fifth category 5 tropical cyclone of 2026 and ranks third for wind speed, behind only typhoons Bavi and Sinlaku.Dolphin reached maximum sustained wind speeds of 175mph on Thursday, with a central pressure of 910mb. The storm intensified rapidly over just 36 hours. On 27 July, it was a tropical storm, however, exceptionally warm sea temperatures of about 30C fuelled its swift transformation into a super typhoon. Another contributing factor was its unusually compact structure, with hurricane-force winds extending only 52 miles from the centre. By comparison, a powerful typhoon such as Dolphin would typically have a hurricane-force wind radius of about 100 miles.As of Monday, Dolphin has been downgraded to a category 3 storm, with sustained wind speeds of 125mph. As it continues westwards towards the island of Okinawa, it is forecast to weaken further and make landfall as a category 1 or 2 typhoon.However, wind speeds of 80-100mph are still expected to affect the archipelago and remain strong enough to cause widespread damage and disruption.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlthough the overall wind speed of Dolphin is decreasing, its wind field is forecast to expand as it approaches land, shifting the primary threat from destructive winds to storm surge.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentWeather trackerJapanAustriaTaiwanCanadaAmericasAsia PacificanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Nauru officially changes its name to Naoero | Pacific islands | The Guardian
description: Pacific nation is latest country to signal a shift away from its colonial past with return to its traditional name
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pacific nation is latest country to signal a shift away from its colonial past with return to its traditional name
Content: Republic of Naoero national flags flying in the Pacific nation formerly known as Nauru.Photograph: Jason Oxenham/APView image in fullscreenRepublic of Naoero national flags flying in the Pacific nation formerly known as Nauru.Photograph: Jason Oxenham/APPacific islandsNauru officially changes its name to NaoeroPacific nation is latest country to signal a shift away from its colonial past with return to its traditional nameAssociated Press in WellingtonMon 3 Aug 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Pacific Island country ofNauruhas changed its name to the Republic of Naoero, its president said, matching the spelling and pronunciation in the national language.The country’s international code will change from NRU to NRO and its people will be known as dei-Naoero instead of Nauruan. Commonly known abroad by the pronunciation of Now-roo, the new name is spoken as Now-ero.The move returns the remote South Pacific island nation to its traditional name, a statement posted on the government’s Facebook account said. The country became known internationally as Nauru only because its local name was difficult for foreigners to pronounce and was a matter of convenience rather than choice, according to an earlier government statement.“This proposed change seeks tomore faithfully honour our nation’s heritage, our language, and our identity,” President David Adeang had said when he proposed the move to parliament in January. The suggested constitutional amendment has been endorsed by lawmakers in the requisite two rounds of voting, though it was not immediately clear if the document had been formally amended.With 12,000 residents, it is the world’s third-smallest country by population size, after Tuvalu and Vatican City. The tiny coral limestone atoll was colonised by Germany and later administered by Australia before becoming an independent republic in 1968.It has faced tumultuous circumstances, with phosphate mining creating huge wealth on the island in the 1970s before the industry collapsed, bringing it to the brink of economic ruin in the 1990s.Now, the atoll is one of the world’s most at risk from rising seas due to climate breakdown, prompting the government to seek overseas investment through a paid citizenship programme intended to fund the movement of people and infrastructure away from the encroaching ocean.The name change indicated “the beginning of renewed national pride”, Adeang said in his latest announcement. When his government last voted for the move in May, the president announced a referendum to confirm it.The government said in last week’s statement that after “extensive discussions”, lawmakers had decided a public vote was not needed.“While a referendum is intended to determine the will of the people, the name Naoero has never been lost, but rather waiting to be fully embraced,” the statement said.The designation “is already the identity of the people, is on the national coat of arms, and spoken in the community; and importantly is allowed by the constitution,” it added.The move makes the country the latest to signal a shift away from a colonial past by changing its name. The tiny African kingdom of Eswatinireverted its name from Swaziland in 2018. Other countries have sought the switch as a sort of rebrand, as Turkey did when Ankara asked the UN in 2022 to begin calling it Türkiye, as it had long gone by at home.Naoero’s decision will prompt the renaming of its national aircraft and ships. The government was already seeking to have other countries and international institutions recognise the shift, its statement said.The website of the UN records the country by its new name, noting the government had requested it be changed in June. Australia and New Zealand’s foreign ministries as well as the US and Chinese embassies in the region also designate the country as Naoero on their websites.Explore more on these topicsPacific islandsNauruAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yen hits three-month high after Trump helps prop up currency | Yen | The Guardian
description: US and Japanese governments confirm they carried out a rare joint intervention late last week
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: US and Japanese governments confirm they carried out a rare joint intervention late last week
Content: Japan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi met Donald Trump in March.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenJapan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi met Donald Trump in March.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersYenYen hits three-month high after Trump helps prop up currencyUS and Japanese governments confirm they carried out a rare joint intervention late last weekWhy has Trump stepped in to prop up Japan’s currency?Business live – latest updatesGraeme WeardenMon 3 Aug 2026 04.34 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe yen has hit its highest level in three months afterJapan and the USlaunched a combined operation to support the Japanese currency.The yen strengthened to ¥155 to the US dollar on Monday, its highest level since early May, after Tokyo and Washington confirmed they had carried out a rare joint currency intervention late last week.Tokyo’s finance ministry said on Monday the two governments had conducted coordinated yen-buying intervention and would not hesitate to take further action.Why has Trump stepped in to prop up Japan’s currency?Read moreThe intervention came after the yen had weakened to a 40-year low of almost ¥164 to the dollar last week.Donald Trump told reporters on Sunday: “They have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we’re always there forJapan.”The yen had weakened in recent months as Japanese borrowing costs remained lower than in other advanced economies. This disparity fuelled a so-called “carry trade”, in which investors borrowed cheaply in yen to buy higher-yielding dollar assets.The yen has also suffered from investors’ concern about Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to usetax and spending measures to stimulate the Japanese economy, and her criticism of the Bank of Japan setting higher interest rates, which have also pushed up the country’s borrowing costs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBessent ‘to-do’ list shows proposal for US to buy $5bn-$10bn of Japanese yenRead moreThe US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Washington “will not hesitate to ⁠participate in further joint intervention”, while repeating calls for further interest rate rises from Japan’s central ​bank. On Saturday,a photograph of Bessent’s notebook taken during a cabinet meeting showedthat his “to do” list included buying $5bn-$10bn ⁠worth of Japanese yen.However, the Financial Times reported that Washington had sold euros to buy yen, rather than using dollars – perhaps to avoid suggesting it wanted a weaker US currency.Bank of Japan data suggested Tokyo spent as much as $36.58bn last Friday to buy yen and strengthen the local currency, Reuters reported.This is the first collaboration involving Japan and the US since March 2011 when a joint intervention was made to weaken the yen after the March Tohoku earthquake and tsunami.Lee Hardman, a currency analyst at MUFG bank, said: “The threat of further joint intervention and a faster pace of BoJ hikes should provide more support for the yen, and discourage speculators from running elevated short yen positions.”The consultancy OxfordEconomicssaid the US-Japan coordinated intervention would not be enough to reverse the trend of yen weakness.“Despite rising market speculation about faster rate hikes by the Bank of Japan, we continue to assume the central bank waits until December because the intervention reduces the risk of a sharp yen depreciation and gives the BoJ more time to assess the impact of the Middle East conflict and past rate hikes on the economy,” it said.Explore more on these topicsYenEconomicsCurrenciesJapanAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Stop all outdoor activities’: South Korea records its highest ever temperature | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Authorities issue alert saying indoor spaces without airconditioning are ‘dangerous’ as temperatures pass 40C for fifth straight day
Author: Mark Saunokonoko
Headline: Authorities issue alert saying indoor spaces without airconditioning are ‘dangerous’ as temperatures pass 40C for fifth straight day
Content: Women use portable fans to cool off at the Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul in July. South Korea has recorded its hottest temperature and issued a heat alert.Photograph: Jade Gao/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWomen use portable fans to cool off at the Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul in July. South Korea has recorded its hottest temperature and issued a heat alert.Photograph: Jade Gao/AFP/Getty ImagesSouth Korea‘Stop all outdoor activities’: South Korea records its highest ever temperatureAuthorities issue alert saying indoor spaces without airconditioning are ‘dangerous’ as temperatures pass 40C for fifth straight dayMark SaunokonokoMon 3 Aug 2026 01.17 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Korea has registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, as authorities warned people to “immediately” stop all outdoor activities in affected areas.The south-eastern city of Yangsan saw the temperature reach 42.5C on Sunday afternoon, the Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said, the highest temperature reported since modern weather observation began in 1904.Yangsan has been the centre of an ongoing heatwave, where temperatures exceeded 40C for a fifth consecutive day on Sunday, while many other cities including Daegu and Busan are seeing temperatures climb into the high 30s.Will brutal wildfires force French leaders to take climate crisis seriously?Read morePeople gathered in airconditioned shopping malls or cafes to escape the blistering temperatures. Others sought relief under mist-spray zones set up in Seoul.
