Ju Dong-yeol, 27, took refuge from the heat in a Starbucks in the South Korean capital, along with his parents and told AFP “it is too hot to be outside doing anything”.“I can’t think of anything else to do other than stay in airconditioned places like home, shopping malls and cafes,” the office worker said.The city of Gyeongju, about 240km south-east of Seoul, reached 40.3C on Sunday, its highest recorded temperature in eight years.North Korea has also faced punishing heat, with temperatures soaring as high as 40C in some regions, state media reported on Monday. Residents in Pyongyang have endured a week of nights where the temperature has not dropped below 25C.More than 20 localities in South Korea were under emergency heatwave alerts on Sunday – a new warning category introduced this year to better address rising temperatures. An emergency alert is issued when areas experiencing a heatwave are forecast to hit perceived temperatures of 38C or an actual temperature of 39C for the day.View image in fullscreenWorkers harvest strawberries under parasols to protect against the scorching sun in Miryang, South Gyeongsang Province, South Korea.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAIssuing a heat warning, the weather agency urged people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities”, adding that “indoor spaces without air conditioning are dangerous”.“Move immediately to a cool place, such as a designated cooling centre or a shaded area, and stay hydrated while resting,” it advised.Fearing for those people most vulnerable to heat, the prime minister, Han Seong-sook, ordered local officials to strengthen safety checks on residents and to ensure a stable power and water supply was maintained.Easterly winds are expected to push the extreme heat further inland on Monday, with Seoul forecast to reach 37C. “Temperatures in South Jeolla and South Gyeongsang are expected to exceed 39C, bringing extreme heat at life-threatening levels,” the KMA said.View image in fullscreenPeople stand in a mist-spraying zone to cool off on a street in Seoul.Photograph: Jung Yeon-Je/AFP/Getty ImagesOfficials are also monitoring Typhoon Dolphin, which is now tracking towards China’s south-east coastal regions, south of the Korean peninsula, and could dictate how long the stifling heat persists.If the typhoon moves towards eastern China, it could increase humidity and potentially worsening the heatwave and tropical nights in Korea, the KMA said. But a path closer to the south of the peninsula could bring stronger winds, greater cloud cover and rain, temporarily easing the heat.KMA data show the average annual number of heatwave days in the country has more than doubled to 19 in the past five years.A heatwave day is defined as one with a maximum temperature of at least 33C.South Korea’s professional baseball league was forced to cancel one game in Changwon after the city’s temperature climbed to 39.5C, marking the second consecutive game cancellation in the city.“The decision was made with the safety and health of spectators and players as the top priority, as a severe heatwave warning remains in effect for the Changwon area,” said the Korea Baseball Organization in a statement.Scientists warn that extreme weather events such as heatwaves are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change.Adding to theextreme weather is the return this year of El Niño– a natural climate phenomenon that warms Pacific Ocean surface temperatures and typically occurs every two to seven years.With Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsSouth KoreaAsia PacificClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: New Zealand legislation recognising English an official language ridiculed as ‘pathetic’ | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Passing of bill technically gives English same status as Māori and sign language but, with it already spoken by 95% of country, critics call it ‘a pointless exercise’
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Passing of bill technically gives English same status as Māori and sign language but, with it already spoken by 95% of country, critics call it ‘a pointless exercise’
Content: The English language bill became law in New Zealand despite ministry of justice advice that there were no concerns about the status of the language.Photograph: Marty Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe English language bill became law in New Zealand despite ministry of justice advice that there were no concerns about the status of the language.Photograph: Marty Melville/ReutersNew ZealandNew Zealand legislation recognising English an official language ridiculed as ‘pathetic’Passing of bill technically gives English same status as Māori and sign language but, with it already spoken by 95% of country, critics call it ‘a pointless exercise’Eva Corlettin WellingtonMon 3 Aug 2026 00.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLegislation recognising English as an official language ofNew Zealandhas been passed by parliament, prompting derision from linguists and legal experts and a now-viral broadside from a Māori MP who called it “pathetic”.The English language bill became law on 30 July giving English, which is spoken by 95% of the country, the same official status as te reoMāori(Māori language) and New Zealand sign language. However, experts say it is already considered an official language as a result of usage and custom.The bill formed part of a coalition deal between the centre-right National party and the minor populist New Zealand First party, whose leader, Winston Peters, has longopposed affirmative initiativesfor Māori. National needed to strike deals with New Zealand First and another minor party, Act, in order to govern.Why is the New Zealand government cutting Māori words from some school books?Read moreMinistry of justice officials had recommended that lawmakers should not pass the bill, because there was “no evidence to support concerns about the use or status of English as an official language”. Te reoMāoriand New Zealand sign language had become official to protect linguistic minorities, they said.However, the coalition government and the major opposition Labour party voted in favour of the bill, with minor opposition parties the Greens and Te Pāti Māori against.During the debate, Green MP Tamatha Paul said the bill was “a pathetic waste of the responsibility of this house”, in aspeechthat has generated millions of views online.Paul said the coalition government were “snowflakes” who saw the word Aotearoa – the Māori name for New Zealand – and “shiver in their boots”.Speaking on behalf of New Zealand First during the final reading, MP Casey Costello denied the law was trivial or unnecessary. “This is a practical measure. It aligns the statute book with longstanding practice, and provides a clear statement about the status of English within New Zealand’s official framework,” Costello told the house.Peters, who is also the foreign affairs minister, haspreviously arguedthe bill was necessary because the use of Māori in public services was causing confusion.Labour, meanwhile,has previously saidit was against the law but had voted in its favour in order to move on from a “needless culture war”.New Zealand coalition votes to make English an official language as critics decry ‘cynical’ billRead moreDr Sidney Wong, a linguist and post-doctoral fellow at research centre Te Pūnaha Matatini, said official language status was given to languages in need of protection and services, but English was not under any threat.“The main reason why this bill was put in place was based on ideology – there was this perception that English was under threat, that it doesn’t have the prestige, and it needs that sort of legislative protection. But it doesn’t need that,” he told the Guardian.Wong said if the government was really interested in protecting English, it would be funding research into the way New Zealanders spoke English, but the law did not address this. “That’s where the money should be going. Not spending time on this 70-word legislation that’s not going to benefit anyone.”Very few English-speaking countries had made English an official language, the officials said, and where they had, it generally coincided with protecting another language – for example in Canada, where law established both French and English are to be used official contexts.Dr Dean Knight, a law professor at Victoria University of Wellington, said the legislation was “a pointless exercise” that made no difference legally or practically as English was already an official language by dint of custom and usage.“All the act does is spell out that status in legislation so folk can read in in the statute book.“Folk who got excited by this performative law-making will be disappointed to learn that, despite the dog-whistling and claims from its promoters within parliament, it does not mandate priority to the English language in government communications and elsewhere,” he said.“Like before, Aotearoa New Zealand will continue to have three official languages.”This story was amended on 4 August 2026 to clarify that English was already regarded as an official language because of its usageExplore more on these topicsNew ZealandNew Zealand politicsMāoriWinston PetersAsia PacificLanguagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Kmart sells out of low-cost rival to Meta camera glasses across Australia amid warnings of ‘privacy nightmare’ | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: Expert says people face being filmed without their consent as $89 Anko smartglasses sell out in stores and online
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Expert says people face being filmed without their consent as $89 Anko smartglasses sell out in stores and online
Content: The price point of Kmart’s Anko camera glasses is significantly cheaper than the Meta Ray-Bans, which sell from $337.Photograph: KmartView image in fullscreenThe price point of Kmart’s Anko camera glasses is significantly cheaper than the Meta Ray-Bans, which sell from $337.Photograph: KmartConsumer affairsKmart sells out of low-cost rival to Meta camera glasses across Australia amid warnings of ‘privacy nightmare’Expert says people face being filmed without their consent as $89 Anko smartglasses sell out in stores and onlineFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterMon 3 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 17.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKmart has sold out of Anko-branded $89 camera glasses across Australia, which a digital rights expert says presents a “privacy nightmare” as people face being filmed without their consent.As of Monday, the clear-lens, black-rimmed glasses, which can capture images and record high-definition videos, were sold out at Kmart stores across Australia and online.The price point at $89 is significantly cheaper than the Meta Ray-Bans that the Anko brand glasses are styled on, which sell from $337.The Anko glasses run on HeyCyan software, which allows the wearer to play music, answer calls, use an AI assistant, and transfer photos and videos from the device.‘More than just objects’: Australian booksellers raise alarm over ‘horrific’ destruction of rare titles to feed AIRead moreThe software is used in a range of low-budget camera glasses, from online retailers including Amazon and Temu. Reddit users report that the software is sluggish compared with the software in the Meta Ray-Bans.Meta has faced significant pushback from privacy advocates since launching the glasses – which some people have dubbed “pervert glasses” – for their ability to record people in public.Meta’s glasses have a light on to indicate the wearer is recording but there have beenreports of userscovertly recording in public andreports that moderators employedby Meta review intimate footage from the glasses, including of people using the toilet and having sex.The companylast month rolled out an updatethat disables the camera if the LED light is interfered with, and also reportedly beganremoving videosfrom its platform of wearers using the device to harass strangers in public.New York courts, the US air force and a hacker convention have allreportedly banned peoplefrom wearing the glasses.View image in fullscreenThe Meta chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, wearing the Meta Ray-Ban glasses.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersMeta has said it has sold more than 7m of its glasses worldwide, and has recruited celebrity Kylie Jenner for advertising to push the devices into the mainstream, but the Ray-Bans and the flood of cheap versions of the same technology have concerned privacy advocates.“Smartglasses with cameras are a privacy nightmare that illustrate how Australian privacy laws haven’t kept up with technology changes,” said Tom Sulston, head of policy at Digital Rights Watch.“We shouldn’t have elevated expectations of personal privacy when out in public, but we should have some.”Sulston said it was particularly problematic when in the hands of misogynist social media influencers who use the glasses to make content “of them harassing women – typically in places where we have higher expectations of more sensitive use of video cameras, like the beach”.A spokesperson for the office of the Australian information commissioner said the privacy regulator was aware of the community concerns and was monitoring the rollout of the new technology.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Organisations that collect, use or disclose personal information through products or services are subject to obligations under the act and the AustralianPrivacyPrinciples where the act applies,” the spokesperson said.“People concerned about being photographed or recorded by another individual may also wish to seek independent legal advice about whether other commonwealth, state or territory laws may be relevant in the circumstances.”A spokesperson for Kmart said the Anko glasses “are part of an established and increasingly mainstream category of wearable technology, with similar products available globally from major technology and eyewear brands”.I wore Meta’s smartglasses for a month – and it left me feeling like a creepRead more“As with any device capable of recording images, we expect customers to use the product responsibly, respectfully and in accordance with applicable laws and community expectations around privacy.”Sulston said that due to the ongoing privacy issues, including how the collected data may be used by the companies producing the glasses, the social backlash would likely continue.“The best way to lose friends and alienate people will be to be a public specs offender.”Onereviewer on TechRadar saidof the Meta glasses this week that, although it is his favourite tech of the year so far, he was afraid to wear them in public due to the growing backlash.“I haven’t been worried about going around wearing my Meta Ray-Ban and Oakley specs in the past, but with growing public anger over the way smart specs are being misused I have a genuine concern someone will see me wearing them and act violently towards me,” he said.Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsPrivacynewsShareReuse this content

title: Most Sydney road tolls to keep rising after Transurban accused of blocking reforms | Transport | The Guardian
description: Handful of tollroads to get one-off price cuts but WestConnex toll to keep rising at least 4% a year
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Handful of tollroads to get one-off price cuts but WestConnex toll to keep rising at least 4% a year
Content: The Westconnex, which alone accounted for 359,000 trips a day by the end of 2025, will not get a toll reduction.Photograph: NSW GovernmentView image in fullscreenThe Westconnex, which alone accounted for 359,000 trips a day by the end of 2025, will not get a toll reduction.Photograph: NSW GovernmentTransportMost Sydney road tolls to keep rising after Transurban accused of blocking reformsHandful of tollroads to get one-off price cuts but WestConnex toll to keep rising at least 4% a yearFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniMon 3 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 17.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cost of using Sydney’s biggest toll road will continue to rise at least 4% a year after the multinational private operator was accused of blocking the state government’s push for sweeping reforms.Only a handful of Sydney’s motorways will receive one-off toll cuts under a deal announced by the state Labor government on Monday, as the tolling bill footed by taxpayers surpasses $1bn.Eleven of Sydney’s toll roads are run by Transurban, a $47bn company with operations in Victoria, Queensland and the US, with most under contracts granting exclusive operating rights into the 2040s or later.The deal will see the state pay $850m to widen the M2-M7 tollway, boosting traffic flows, which Transurban expects will increase its toll revenue. The government will separately spend $143m to settle the deal, negotiated over two years.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUnder Monday’s deal, Transurban will cut some fares by 10% on the Lane Cove Tunnel and the M2 in July 2027 and the M7 in 2028. The cross-city tunnel toll will be cut by a one-off 20% in 2028 while the Eastern Distributor’s northbound fare will be cut and a southbound fare added.Those highways accounted for less than half of the 1m trips recorded each day on average across Transurban’s Sydney network, suggesting most tollway trips would not see a toll reduction.EVs and hybrids approach half of Australian new car sales amid ongoing fuel crisisRead moreThe WestConnex highway, which alone accounted for 359,000 trips a day by the end of 2025, and the NorthConnex will not get a reduction.The premier,Chris Minns, told reporters on Monday the government had failed to negotiate a deal for the excluded highways at an appropriate cost with Transurban.“We weren’t able to get the rate of the dollars that we wanted in exchange for, I guess, what we had to give up,” Minns said.“We need toll relief now and it’s better to have it at a lower base given the multiple increases that they have through the year.”Transurban’s chief executive, Michelle Jablko, told investors on Monday the state would have had to spend significant amounts to fund a WestConnex toll reduction.“Even a small change in WestConnex could cost taxpayers quite a lot,” Jablko said.Transurban data indicates the average Sydney customer spends nearly $650 a year on tolls. It costs $12.74 for a car to travel the full length of WestConnex and the motorway’s tollsincrease by at least 4%each year.Allan Fels, a former chief of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, led the state’s 2024 tolling review and called for thedifferent roads’ tolls to be standardisedso toll burdens would be balanced between Sydney’s west and its wealthier north and east. Jabklo on Monday said sweeping reforms could worsen congestion.Fels, who was not directly involved in the government’s negotiations, said Monday’s toll reductions represented a “good start”.But he said Transurban had blocked reform and put profits over public interest. The company declined to comment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGet in touchContact Guardian AustraliaIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact  Guardian Australia’s news teams using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don't need strong security you can write to a Guardian Australia journalist using the detailshere. Click on a person to see their details.For end to end encrypted email you can create a freeProton Mailaccount and emailgaus.contact@protonmail.com.Messaging appsYou can  use the encrypted messaging apps Signal or WhatsApp to message us at +61 490 758 250.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show more“It’s essentially a financial vehicle, that receives an enormous amount of money, and that’s what it’s all about,” Fels told Guardian Australia.“[Transurban’s demands] were excessive, completely out of the ballpark … Their whole approach to compensation ruled out some public interest reforms, including on WestConnex.”New South Wales taxpayers already pay Transurban more than $100m a year to cover Labor’s cap on tolls introduced in January 2024, covering the difference for motorists spending more than $60 each week.That figure will more than double to $211m in 2026-27 after the state budget temporarily lowered the cap to $50.Fels said commuter anger at growing toll bills would force the state to revisit the contracts in future.“The government deemed it was just too tough politically in the face of resistance by Transurban to deliver the whole package … [but] they hinted they might come back to this,” he said.Jablko did not directly answer when asked on Monday whether the government had promised it would not amend the contracts in future.“By working constructively with the government, we were able to deal into what was important to them today and protect the value of the contracts,” she said.“What government wants to do in the future is always going to be a question for them but it was really important for us to show up in the right way.”Explore more on these topicsTransportSydneyNew South WalesChris MinnsNew South Wales politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alan Jones argues ‘rivalry’ and ‘treachery’ but after decades wielding the sword of public opinion, he’s the one on trial | Alan Jones | The Guardian
description: His legal strategy was apparent from the very first. Jones will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the ‘credibility and reliability’ of his accusers
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: His legal strategy was apparent from the very first. Jones will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the ‘credibility and reliability’ of his accusers
Content: Alan Jones, centre, leaves the Downing Centre local court in Sydney on Monday.Photograph: Bianca De Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenAlan Jones, centre, leaves the Downing Centre local court in Sydney on Monday.Photograph: Bianca De Marchi/AAPAlan JonesAnalysisAlan Jones argues ‘rivalry’ and ‘treachery’ but after decades wielding the sword of public opinion, he’s the one on trialBen DohertyHis legal strategy was apparent from the very first. Jones will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the ‘credibility and reliability’ of his accusersFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMon 3 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 19.49 EDTShareAlan Jones has enjoyed decades as the centre of attention, as the wielder of power.The booming voice, the vast radio audience, the bully pulpit of an eponymous TV show, the great and the good on speed-dial, a staffer in the prime ministerial office dubbed the “minister for Alan Jones”: these were not ancillaries peripheral to the Jones empire, they were central to it.Alan Jones allegedly gifted cash and car to teenager he kissed after commenting on sprinter’s penis, trial hearsRead moreEven walking into court on Monday, at the centre of a glacially moving press pack, it was all about Alan.That evaporated as soon as he stepped inside the claustrophobic confines of court 3.1.Here he is simply “the defendant”.Stripped of his dominance, his control and his voice, Jones is forced instead to listen, as 22 separate allegations are detailed against him.Jones has pleaded not guilty. He is – as he has consistently asserted – entitled to the presumption of innocence.‘Credibility and reliability’At first, Jones sat not in the dock but behind his lawyers, with whom he quietly conversed and occasionally showed handwritten notes, recorded with a silver pen in a black notebook.At one point, Jones was asked to move to another seat across the courtroom.He would have been in the eyeline of the first witness – complainant J – and the court wanted Jones moved to a place where he could not be seen by the man who would be the first to detail his charges against him.Jones’s legal strategy was apparent from the very first. He will, it was explicitly stated, seek to undermine the “credibility and reliability” of those who accuse him.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” his barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, told the court, the first thundering sentence of her opening submission.“Rumours and innuendo have been thrown at Alan Jones for years.”Jones’s defence would expose, the court heard, “what [the complainants] did not tell the police, what they left out of their statements … but that we have discovered: concoction, contamination and reconstruction”.“Mr Jones since day one has said he was not guilty of all these charges,” Bashir told the court.“Mr Jones will have the opportunity to test the evidence in the prosecution case including the credibility and the reliability of the complainants.”This is a trial over 22 alleged indecent assault and sexual touching offences.In opening submissions, the prosecution argued a common thread emerged, of people too afraid, too indebted, too ashamed, to speak up in their own defence.View image in fullscreen‘Walking into court, at the epicentre of a glacially moving press pack, it was all about Alan. That evaporated as soon as he stepped inside the claustrophobic confines of court 3.1.’Photograph: Damian Shaw/AAPThe court heard that Jones had allegedly been financially supporting the family of complainant A. The then-17-year-old was invited to stay at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls property. There, in a bedroom, he alleges Jones forced himself on him, kissing him and grabbing his penis.The teenager told no one about it but 10 days later wrote, in a letter to his mother, “Someone in power did something they should not have and I was so worried because of all the help they had offered”, according to the prosecution’s opening.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlan Jones wielded huge power, but now the legacy of his four-decade career will be decided by four months in courtRead moreAnother teenager, a star schoolboy athlete from a similarly impecunious background, was given a weekly stipend by Jones, a mobile phone “to keep in contact” and, later, a car. Jones allegedly grabbed him on the penis as he drove Jones to his country property, the court heard.After an alleged incident in which Jones kissed him – un-consented, on the mouth “with a chomping motion … smothering” – Jones is alleged to have told complainant J “you’ve been a really good boy, I’m going to give you some more money”.Complainant C worked for Jones at a radio station and was repeatedly groped by Jones, the court heard. The court heard that, as C drove Jones home from work, Jones would grab C on the penis, rubbing his hand up and down.The prosecution alleged Jones would talk about C’s penis, “calling him ‘Donkey’ and saying things like ‘It’s not really that big is it?’ and ‘when can I see it?’”The court was told the prosecution would present as evidence text messages sent by Jones to C, commenting on the “size of his penis, dismay at never having seen C’s penis” and declarations of love.The court heard C did not invite, nor want to receive, the messages, but felt he had to reply, “concerned about his position in the media industry if he overtly rejected” Jones’s propositions.Complainant F, who was 17 when he alleges Jones squeezed his buttocks at a public event, told his mother of the assault, but did not report it to police because he “felt nobody would believe his word over the defendant’s”.The first witnessComplainant J was the first witness to take the stand. A record-breaking junior athlete when he fell into Jones’s orbit, he is now a middle-aged man but retains a sportsman’s build and singular focus.Asked to relive his allegations against Jones, J repeatedly took time to compose himself, closing his eyes and asking the court for a moment while he sought to replay in his mind the specifics of incidents, some of them more than two decades old.J told the court Jones grabbed and squeezed his penis as he drove Jones to his country property, the older man asking “does it feel good?”. In another incident at Jones’s Circular Quay apartment, J gave evidence Jones allegedly hugged him and kissed him without his consent. J’s coach was waiting downstairs in a car for him.Prosecutor Georgina Wright asked why J didn’t tell his coach what had just happened.“If I told someone … all of a sudden I would lose everything. I come from a small family, we struggled our whole lives, and I was getting everything handed to me, it was a wonderful life.“I thought if I told someone what was happening, I would lose everything.”J told the court he was conflicted by his friendship with Jones.Jones was generous and supportive, he says, Jones had given him a financial security he’d not known in his life. But there was a price to pay, J said.“I was fearful of him, but I was also accepting these things from him. And I didn’t want to lose those things.“The friendship, I would say, was tainted by the things that were going on.“For me it was a fearful relationship.”The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsAlan JonesAlan Jones trialAustralian lawanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claims | Russia | The Guardian
description: Seven people, including three children, dead after ‘drone debris’ strike beach in seaside town, says Russian taskforce
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Seven people, including three children, dead after ‘drone debris’ strike beach in seaside town, says Russian taskforce
Content: Arkhipo-Osipovka is a resort town near Gelendzhik on the Black Sea shore in Russia.Photograph: Andrey Khrobostov/AlamyView image in fullscreenArkhipo-Osipovka is a resort town near Gelendzhik on the Black Sea shore in Russia.Photograph: Andrey Khrobostov/AlamyRussiaUkrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claimsSeven people, including three children, dead after ‘drone debris’ strike beach in seaside town, says Russian taskforcePjotr SauerandAngus ThomsonMon 3 Aug 2026 18.04 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 06.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkrainian drone attacks on a Black Sea resort and the annexed Crimea peninsula killed 11 people, Russian officials said after blamingUkrainefor another explosion that killed five people in a Moscow restaurant.Seven people, including three children, were killed when “drone debris” struck a beach in the seaside town of Arkhipo-Osipovka, the crisis taskforce for Russia’s southern Krasnodar region said on social media.Social media videos, verified by Reuters and the BBC, showed tourists in the water and on the shore watching on as what appeared to be a drone slammed into a busy beach.View image in fullscreenSocial media footage of a drone strike on the holiday resort of Arkhipo-Osipovka, Russia, 3 August 2026.Photograph: Twitter/XAnother four people were killed in a Ukrainian strike on the illegally annexed Crimea, the Moscow-installed governor, Sergey Aksyonov, said in a post on Telegram.Both Crimea and the Black Sea coast are popular holiday destinations for Russian tourists during summer.Earlier, Russia blamed Ukraine for a bombing at a restaurant in central Moscow that killed five people, amid growing speculation that a senior Russian military commander was the intended target.The explosion occurred on Saturday evening near the entrance to an upmarket Italian restaurant in one of the city’s seven Stalin-era skyscrapers on Kudrinskaya Square.Russian prosecutors said an unidentified woman carrying an improvised explosive device had attempted to enter the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard.The device detonated moments later, killing five people and injuring 19 others.View image in fullscreenAccording to Russia’s national anti-terrorism committee (NAC), an improvised explosive device detonated outside the entrance to the ‘Balzi Rossi’ restaurant in Kudrinskaya Square, on 1 August 2026.Photograph: Sergei Ilnitsky/EPAIn a statement on Sunday, Russia’s foreign ministry accused Kyiv of carrying out the attack, saying: “The bloody tentacles of [Volodymyr]Zelenskyy’s terrorist gang have reached the Balzi Rossi Italian restaurant in Moscow.”Russian authorities have not identified the intended target or named the victims.However, pro-Kremlin military bloggers and several independent Russian media outlets reported that the attack may have been aimed at Col Gen Alexander Chaiko, the commander of Russia’s aerospace forces, who was reportedly attending a private banquet at the restaurant to celebrate his 55th birthday.Photographs and videos that appeared online shortly after the bombing, purportedly from the private event, showed a stage with the words “Aleksandr 55” displayed in the background.Chaiko is one of Russia’s top military commanders, having led the failed assault on Kyiv in early 2022 before later being promoted to command the Russian air force.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Telegram channel VChK-OGPU, which is known for publishing leaks from within Russia’s security services, reported that Chaiko escaped unharmed. According to the channel, his daughter, Maria, was seriously injured in the blast, while her husband, Daniil Peredriy, was killed. They were outside on the restaurant’s terrace when the explosion occurred.The Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that investigators believed the woman carrying the explosive device may not have known she was transporting a bomb, suggesting it was detonated remotely by another person, killing her.Among the other reported victims was a member of Russia’s elite Federal Protective Service (FSO).Kyiv has not yet commented on the incidents. Both sides have repeatedly said they do not target civilians in the conflict, which is now in its fifth year.In Ukraine, one person was killed and dozens more injured when Russian planes launched a 90-minute bombing blitz on residential districts in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, the regional chief, Ivan Fedorov, said on Monday.Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have targeted dozens of senior Russian military officers and Russia-installed officials, accusing them of involvement in war crimes.Ukrainian intelligence services have previously employed a range of tactics, relying on both willing saboteurs and unwitting civilians to carry out bombings.They have succeeded in killing at least four Russian generals and several other senior military figures, as well as pro-war activists deep inside Russian territory, although some operations have missed their intended targets. In 2022, a car bomb killed Darya Dugina, the daughter of the ultranationalist Russian ideologue Aleksandr Dugin, in an attack widely believed to have been intended for her father.Explore more on these topicsRussiaEuropeUkrainenewsShareReuse this content

title: Athens suitcase death: suspect admits hiding body but denies murder | Greece | The Guardian
description: Police are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killing
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Police are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killing
Content: Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body was found inside a suitcase in Athens.Photograph: FacebookElisabeth-Jane Ross’s body was found inside a suitcase in Athens.Photograph: FacebookGreeceAthens suitcase death: suspect admits hiding body but denies murderPolice are focusing on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s final hours in hope of discovering motive for her killingHelena Smithin AthensMon 3 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreek authorities are investigating what may have motivated a 26-year-old Afghan man to kill aScottish charity workerfound dead in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens last month.Inquiries have focused increasingly on Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s last few hours alive and police believe they hold the key to revealing why the 38-year-old was targeted.On Sunday the suspect, identified as Sharif Ahmadzai, was accused of intentional homicide after three days of questioning. He will appear before an investigating magistrate to be formally charged on Wednesday.George Kalliakmanis, the honorary president of the police officers’ association in Athens, told the Guardian the homicide division was now intent on discovering the motive behind “the murder” because the Afghan was continuing to deny any role in it, although he had confessed to hiding Ross in a suitcase.“He has admitted to carrying her body to the site. Police have CCTV footage of him doing this on the night of 16 July. He has also confessed to withdrawing €10,000 from ATMs using credit cards that belonged to her. But he has denied murder which police do not believe,” Kalliakmanis said.The Afghan, a professional boxer in the lightweight division, is believed to have arrived in Greece via the island of Lesbos as a child refugee at the height of Europe’s migration crisis 10 years ago.View image in fullscreenSharif Ahmadzai  and his wife, US citizen Alaina Hall. She is said to have played a ‘significant role’ in the investigation.Photograph: Twitter/XHe has been quoted as telling police he discovered Ross’s lifeless body in the first floor flat of an apartment block he helped manage in Exarchia, a bohemian district in downtown Athens popular among leftists, foreigners and NGOs.Ahmadzai, who married a US citizen and devout Christian, Alaina Hall, in 2023, had keys to the flat where their own refugee solidarity group, Love Every Nation, regularly met.Investigators have confirmed that Ross, a friend of Hall’s with similar volunteering experience and religious views, had moved to the apartment on 10 July after staying with Greek friends when she arrived in the Athens from Edinburgh on 26 June.Her last telephone call was made from her mobile phone on the night of 15 July – three days before her body was discovered by a homeless man in an abandoned building in Kypseli, about two miles away.Two possible scenarios in the run up to Ross’s death were being studied, police said. “We believe there was a confrontation,” said one source. “But was that spurred by Ross discovering the Afghan rummaging through her things and stealing her credit cards, or was it a case of sexual assault or the Briton spurning his advances?”View image in fullscreenSharif Ahmadzai arrived in Greece via the island of Lesbos as a child refugee. He has been accused of intentional homicide.Photograph: Twitter/XForensic scientists believe Ross was “likely asphyxiated” after an initial on-site postmortem, which showed there were no evident signs of injuries on her body. However, the autopsy was also deemed inconclusive because of advanced decay.Further toxicological tests and analysis of vital organs are expected to determine the exact cause of death in the coming days.Hall, who met Ahmadzai on Lesbos, is widely described as having played a “significant role” in the investigation.After allegedly becoming suspicious of Ahmadzai’s movements – and newfound wealth, the result of making cash withdrawals with Ross’s credit cards – she reportedly contacted the police, handed over cash he had given her and moved into a hotel.Adding to the mystery that has engulfed the inquiry, Ross’s phone was used for several days after her death, with text messages sent to family and friends. The messages were described as “deliberately misleading” by police, who believe they were sent in a bid to delay Ross being declared missing. One spoke of her “need to be alone”.“The Afghan’s partner was very helpful,” said Kalliakmanis. “From the day the victim was identified the investigation faced several challenges but thanks to the homicide division being so thorough they cracked it.”Police, who collaborated with the UK’s National Crime Agency and the Scottish service, combed through CCTV footage from cameras in the area where the suitcase was found and from banks where cash withdrawals were made before identifying the suspect.Explore more on these topicsGreeceEuropeScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anti-war politician flees Russia amid pre-election crackdown on dissent | Russia | The Guardian
description: Boris Nadezhdin, who gained prominence after standing against Putin in 2024, says he is now in France
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Boris Nadezhdin, who gained prominence after standing against Putin in 2024, says he is now in France
Content: Boris Nadezhdin in court in Dolgoprudny, Russia, last month after he was briefly detained and accused of a minor administrative violation.Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/ReutersView image in fullscreenBoris Nadezhdin in court in Dolgoprudny, Russia, last month after he was briefly detained and accused of a minor administrative violation.Photograph: Anastasia Barashkova/ReutersRussiaAnti-war politician flees Russia amid pre-election crackdown on dissentBoris Nadezhdin, who gained prominence after standing against Putin in 2024, says he is now in FrancePjotr SauerMon 3 Aug 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prominent Russian anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin has fled to Paris as Moscow tightens its grip on dissent before parliamentary elections later this year.Nadezhdin, a veteran liberal politician, gained international prominence during Russia’s 2024 presidential election when his long-shot campaign against Vladimir Putin unexpectedly gathered momentum before electoral authoritiesbarred him from running.Since his presidential campaign, Nadezhdin, 63, has remained one of the last well-known Russian public figures to publicly oppose the war in Ukraine. That made him an increasingly uncomfortable figure for the Kremlin.“Good news: I’m alive and free. Unfortunately, I’m not in Russia for the time being,” Nadezhdin said in a video filmed in front of the Eiffel Tower. He added that he needed “to look around and figure out life going forward”.Last month, less than three weeks after registering to run in September’s parliamentary elections, he was briefly detained and accused of a minor administrative violation in what was widely seen as an attempt to intimidate him and undermine his candidacy.The same month, the justice ministry designated Nadezhdin a “foreign agent” – a label that carries onerous reporting requirements, increased government scrutiny, and a powerful stigma in Russia.The designation, combined with a conviction on an extremism-related administrative charge, barred him from running in September’s parliamentary elections, which are widely expected to be tightly controlled by the Kremlin.In an interview with the Russian independent outlet Meduza last month, Nadezhdin said he and his family were considering leaving Russia as pressure from the authorities intensified. While he said he wanted to remain in the country and run in the parliamentary elections, he acknowledged that the growing risk of imprisonment was becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.Following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian authorities launched an unprecedented crackdown on dissent, targeting independent media, human rights groups, civil society organisations and critics of the war. Hundreds have been imprisoned and thousands more have fled the country.Putin’s ruling United Russia party is seeking to preserve its dominance in the lower house of parliament in September’s state-managed elections, in which no genuine opposition is allowed to take part. The vote comes amid signs of growing public fatigue with the war in Ukraine, as fuel shortages and mounting economic pressures weigh on Russians, leaving the Kremlin increasingly unwilling to tolerate even token opposition.Explore more on these topicsRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Paris prosecutor investigates alleged bullying in government departments after suicide attempt | France | The Guardian
description: Internal inquiries also opened after two suicides and two attempted suicides of staff in departments connected to PM’s office
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Internal inquiries also opened after two suicides and two attempted suicides of staff in departments connected to PM’s office
Content: A lawyer for the woman who attempted suicide said difficulties for staff had been compounded by the instability of governments – there have been four prime ministers in two years.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersView image in fullscreenA lawyer for the woman who attempted suicide said difficulties for staff had been compounded by the instability of governments – there have been four prime ministers in two years.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersFranceParis prosecutor investigates alleged bullying in government departments after suicide attemptInternal inquiries also opened after two suicides and two attempted suicides of staff in departments connected to PM’s officeAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 3 Aug 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Paris state prosecutor has opened a preliminary inquiry into alleged workplace bullying after the attempted suicide of a staff member in a department connected to the French prime minister’s office,FranceInter radio has revealed.The public radio stationreported on Mondaythat two government workers in different departments had ended their lives in the past year, and two others had attempted suicide. The radio station said complaints of alleged workplace bullying had been made.A complaint had been made by a staff representative to the Paris prosecutor in June over alleged bullying in certain government departments, the station said. The prosecutor has opened a preliminary inquiry. A document seen by France Inter and AFP said a complaint had been made that “presumed institutional bullying” had allegedly led a staff member to attempt to end their life.Three internal government inquiries have also been opened into specific cases and broader workplace wellbeing.The allegations of workplace bullying relate to a group of dozens of government departments and missions working under the umbrella of services of the prime minister.The staff member at the centre of the prosecutor’s preliminary inquiry worked in a service that handled issues related to correspondence for the prime minister’s office, France Inter reported.The woman’s lawyer, Christelle Mazza, told the radio station: “My client had been made [to feel] invisible. She was no longer invited to attend meetings, had been taken off the staff list, treated as if she was no one. She was mocked and jeered at as if it was playground bullying, [she was] ostracised.”The lawyer said difficulties for staff had been compounded by the instability of governments after Emmanuel Macron dissolved the national assembly and called a snap election in June 2024.In the two years from June 2024 to June 2026, there were four prime ministers: Gabriel Attal in a caretaker role,Michel Barnier,François Bayrouand Sébastien Lecornu.No wrongdoing was alleged of the prime ministers.In a statement, two senior officials in the department of services of the prime minister expressed full respect and support to colleagues and families after the suicides and attempted suicides. They said psychological welfare was “a constant priority” for the prime minister’s services and a specialist audit on workplace wellbeing would be conducted.One case of attempted suicide was investigated and found not to be connected to the government service, they said. Another case of attempted suicide was at the centre of an administrative inquiry after allegations of bullying. For the two deaths by suicide, “investigations are under way in close cooperation with trade union staff representatives”, they said.The officials added: “None of the people concerned worked directly with the prime minister or in his office.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: South-eastern Europe faces heatwave energy crunch as Romania detonates Danube rock to increase water flow – as it happened  | Hungary | The Guardian
description: Explosives used to move a large rock and let more water flow to cool nuclear power plant
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Explosives used to move a large rock and let more water flow to cool nuclear power plant
Content: 05.00 EDTRomanian army carries out controlled explosion to divert water, help cool nuclear power plantMeanwhile in Romania, the Romanian naval forces carried out a controlled explosion to divert a large volume of water to the Old Danube and the Cernavodă nuclear power plant to help with its cooling.The Romanian Navy detonates underwater explosives during a controlled demolition of submerged rocks to improve water flow to the Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant amid exceptionally low water levels on the Danube River, in Izvoarele, Romania.Photograph: Andreea Alexandru/APSome 180 kg of explosives were used today, Adevărulreported, to move a large rock restricting the flow of water.Acting defence ministerRadu Miruțăhailed the operation as a success, saying it will help with cooling of the plant and water transport on the river.Given the continuing extreme weather conditions, the Cernavodă plant may still have to temporarily suspend its operations at some point, but any extra day of its work is worth more than the cost of the explosion, he said.ShareUpdated at05.20 EDT

title: Trump claims strait of Hormuz could open ‘by tomorrow’ as Iran denies any talks taking place – as it happened  | World news | The Guardian
description: US president claims talks are ‘not very complex’ as he speaks at White House as Iran’s foreign ministry says there are no talks taking place with US
Author: Vivian Ho
Headline: US president claims talks are ‘not very complex’ as he speaks at White House as Iran’s foreign ministry says there are no talks taking place with US
Content: 14.13 EDTStrait of Hormuz could open 'by tomorrow': TrumpDonald Trump is speaking at an executive order signing at the White House, where he was asked where direct talks with Iran would take place.“You’ll find out today or tomorrow,” he said. “They’re going to go quickly one way or the other. It’s not very complex.”Trump said the strait of Hormuz could be open “literally by tomorrow”.“The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearisation,” he said. “That’ll take a little while, but … we’re very strong on it.”Vessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman.Photograph: ReutersShareUpdated at14.19 EDT

title: Fresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump says | Iran | The Guardian
description: US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington
Content: Donald Trump said on Monday he expected negotiations with Iran on reopening the strait of Hormuz to begin imminently.Photograph: Allison Robbert/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump said on Monday he expected negotiations with Iran on reopening the strait of Hormuz to begin imminently.Photograph: Allison Robbert/EPAIranFresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump saysUS president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with WashingtonPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 3 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” forIranto forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday.Trump said he expected negotiations to begin in the next day or two to reopen the strait of Hormuz and create a pathway for Iran to address the US’s concerns about its nuclear programme.“The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearisation,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “And that will take a little while.”Trump reiterated that he was running out of patience with Iran. “This is the last chance for them to sign a good document.”Iran has been in discussions withOmanabout the creation of a temporary route through the strait that would allow commercial shipping to resume, but is not yet reviving talks with the US, Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said earlier on Monday.Esmail Baghaei denied claims by Trump that talks between the two sides covering all the major disputes between them could restart as early as Monday. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” he said.Trump claimed he had held off from launching the biggest strike on any country “since world war two” over the weekend after Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, rang him to urge diplomacy. Trump said the cancellation was conditional on Iran reaching a deal quickly.Trump says Iran talks set for Monday as Tehran and Oman discuss strait of Hormuz dealRead moreIt is thought to be the 12th time in the war between the US and Iran that Trump has called off threatened strikes.On Monday, the US president called the Iranian leadership “unbelievably duplicitous” in a post on social media.“They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg’, talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’. They then go on to give their usual blather in saying, theStrait of Hormuzwill be operated powerfully by them, when it is already completely controlled by the United States Navy and our ‘Blockade’.”A middle route through the strait would represent progress. Iran is claiming full sovereignty over the strait and has been making demands over its routes and future management, including the possibility of charging fees in return for providing ships with maritime services.One proposal is to create a joint Omani-Iranian company that would provide all the services that insurance companies used to provide at high costs, but at lower prices, and with preferential tariffs for some countries.View image in fullscreenIran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said it was discussing with Oman the possibility of an intermediate route through the strait of Hormuz to be used temporarily.Photograph: ReutersUnlocking a mutually acceptable route through the strait is the precondition to unlocking all the other agreements laid out in the memorandum of understanding, the ceasefire document both sides signed on 18 June. Disagreements about the memorandum’s obligations has led to a resumption of the war, which has spread to the Red Sea and to Iraq.Last week, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said Tehran was demanding that ships entering the strait take a route to the north close to Iran, but that some ships could take a southern route. Iran rejected the traffic being divided evenly between the two routes, and also that a third country could start de-mining the routes.Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran: “We are now talking about a corridor that will have a round trip route, not two or three separate routes. This intermediate route is to be used temporarily until a decision is made on a fixed route.”He framed the route as an alternative to the transport separation scheme, the longstanding prewar route overseen by the UN’s International Maritime Office. He said maps had been exchanged by the two sides.Baghaedi said an agreement on a route would not solve all the problems, pointing to the continuing US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, and that unless the US approach changed, there would be no significant improvement in the situation in the strait.Recently there had been gloom in Omani circles about reaching an agreement with Iran on routes, leading to a revival of preparations for Oman’s European allies to start to clear the southern route of mines, a step that might have provoked direct conflict between Iran and European powers.In a sign of the pressure Tehran diplomats face, a statement from the Assembly of Experts, the body of clerics that elects the supreme leader, warned against investing any trust in the US, saying: “Hope for understanding and agreement with this bullying regime will lead nowhere.”However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he believed the “memorandum of understanding would prove to be the centre of gravity of our foreign relations in the future”.The Saudis’ intervention came in a week in which Riyadh attacked Iranian-backed forces inside Iraq and raised the temperature in its dispute with the Iranian-backed Houthis in northern Yemen, underlining the extent to which Saudi Arabia fears the consequence of an all-out US war against Iran spiralling out of control across the Middle East.Additional reporting by Associated PressExplore more on these topicsIranStrait of HormuzUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaOmannewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump meets his obstinate match in Iran’s hardball regime | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: US president reduced to bemoaning Tehran’s ‘unbelievable duplicity’ as he struggles to find solid negotiating ground
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: US president reduced to bemoaning Tehran’s ‘unbelievable duplicity’ as he struggles to find solid negotiating ground
Content: Time is of the essence for Trump as the clock ticks towards a global energy crisis and a painful midterm elections for him and his Republican party.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersView image in fullscreenTime is of the essence for Trump as the clock ticks towards a global energy crisis and a painful midterm elections for him and his Republican party.Photograph: Majid Asgaripour/ReutersUS-Israel war on IranAnalysisTrump meets his obstinate match in Iran’s hardball regimeAndrew RothUS president reduced to bemoaning Tehran’s ‘unbelievable duplicity’ as he struggles to find solid negotiating groundMon 3 Aug 2026 14.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 22.27 EDTShareThe Donald Trump doctrine has always contained a tenuous relationship with the truth. It was his mentor,the infamous New York lawyer Roy Cohn, who taught the young real estate mogul always to claim victory and never to admit defeat. Unfortunately for Trump, in Iran the US president has found a counterpart just as stubborn as himself.As Trump claims new negotiations are to begin with Tehran this week,Iranhas shown it can also reignite the conflict by lobbing ballistic missiles at US bases in the region and maintaining a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz, effectively taking initiative in the stalled peace process. And time is of the essence for Trump as the clock ticks toward a global energy crisis and a painful midterm elections for him and his Republican party.But as soon as his latest attempt to hammer out a peace deal was announced,it was denied by Iranand the US president was left fuming once again. “Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous!” he posted to his social media site, Truth Social, saying that Iran had begged for a meeting and talks had already begun. “Nothing gets through to Iran, unless we want it to, and nothing will get through, unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished.”Iran in talks with Oman over shipping but US negotiations on hold, says TehranRead moreTrump has suggested dozens of times since the beginning of the war that a deal with Iran is imminent, and his latest claim that new negotiations could produce a peace deal within days has shown the administration’s desperation to reopen the strait and find a road map out of the crisis. After promising to hit Iran “very hard”, Trump made a U-turn on Sunday and claimed that talks would continue and that the “perimeters of a deal” for the opening of Hormuz and the “denuclearization of Iran” had been agreed.Unfortunately, the Iranians don’t agree. In a statement on Monday, an Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson denied any peace negotiations were taking place. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” said Esmaeil Baqaei. “Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the strait of Hormuz.”That may result in an agreement. But that will not result in the return of the strait of Hormuz to its prewar status, Baqaei added, in effect keeping the waterway a political football for the foreseeable future. “We must ensure that the strait of Hormuz cannot be misused by parties that have committed aggression against Iran,” said Baqaei.Little has changed since the last round of negotiations. Iran remains capable of closing the strait of Hormuz and stifling shipping – including a fifth of global oil supply – through the crucial waterway. The US remains capable of inflicting devastating strikes on Iran – despite a shortage of key munitions that could be needed for a war against key rivals like China – but has a lack of meaningful targets that could force Iran to change its policy.The Trump administration has been signalling a desire to end the conflict since April and three ceasefires have come and collapsed since then. With just over three months left until the US midterm elections, in which the Republicans are expected to lose the House and possibly even the Senate, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll last week showed that fewer than a third of Americans support the war in Iran, and 69% believe that Trump has not “clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran”.For Iran, the strategic unpredictability has become a new weapon in a war that has counterintuitively strengthened its negotiating position, giving the regime new tools in slowing global oil supply and in attacking regional US allies in the Gulf.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIran has concluded that its best strategy is to “maximise the pain that they can impose on the United States and its partners in the region”, said Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute and an expert on Middle East security issues with a focus on Iran, during the institute’s podcast last week. The view there was that Trump “is not really yet ready for a deal with Iran, not a deal that would work for the Iranians anyway”.Iran is also facing a time crunch with a US blockade in effect halting trade out of the country.“They are now at a point where they don’t think just sitting back and having one round after another of diplomatic talks is the best way forward,” he added. “They’re trying to shake things up to try get Trump’s attention and see if they can get a different result.”Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpIranUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Abandoned by the US: Palestinian Americans trapped in a surge of Israeli settler violence | West Bank | The Guardian
description: After visits by US ambassador Mike Huckabee to the nearby Israeli settlement of Shilo, Palestinian Americans in Turmus Ayya have witnessed a terrifying rise in attacks
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: After visits by US ambassador Mike Huckabee to the nearby Israeli settlement of Shilo, Palestinian Americans in Turmus Ayya have witnessed a terrifying rise in attacks
Content: A US flag flies at a Palestinian home in the town of Turmus Ayya in the occupied West Bank. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianAfter visits by US ambassador Mike Huckabee to the nearby Israeli settlement of Shilo, Palestinian Americans in Turmus Ayya have witnessed a terrifying rise in attacksByAndrew RothandSufian Tahain Turmus Ayya, West Bank. Photography byQuique KierszenbaumMon 3 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo man’s land in Turmus Ayya lies where the US flags end and the Israeli flags begin. It is a few hundred metres of soil scorched by molotov cocktails where Israeli settlers have placed a boulder to tell the Palestinian villagers: this is our land now.On one side of that boulder are the white-stoned mansions where the Palestinian residents of Turmus Ayya live. About 80% of them are US citizens, members of the diaspora in New York, Chicago and Paterson, New Jersey, who return for the summers and bring their children here to experience Palestinian culture and learn Arabic. Many call themselves proud American patriots and fly the stars and stripes from their balconies.View image in fullscreenAn Israeli military Jeep patrols an illegal outpost built by Israeli settlers after they took control of private farmland owned by the people of Turmus Ayya.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianOn the other side is an illegal Israeli outpost of corrugated metal trailers and shacks staffed by young men who claim all of theWest Bankas Jewish land.The outposts radiate from Shilo, a hilltop settlement across the valley that has become a destination for Americans seeking Judaism’s first religious and spiritual capital before the first temple was built.Mike Huckabee, the US ambassadorto Israel, has visited Shilo, which the UNsays is a violation of international law,twice in the last two years.View image in fullscreenAshraf Rabi on the farm where he breeds Arabian horses in Turmus Ayya. He is worried that settlers attacking the village could harm his horses.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe irony is not lost on people here that the US has backed settlers claiming the West Bank as theirs, and that US dollars – through Jewish charities and the US budget to support the Israeli military – have helped finance the Israeli land grab. Given Shilo’s close ties to the US, they muse that some of those attacking Turmus Ayya could be fellow Americans.“Only inPalestinewill you find American citizens invading American citizens for land,” said Yaser Alkam, a semi-retired family law attorney from Turmus Ayya who for 35 years lived in Anaheim, California. He is now the head of this village’s council. “There is no fight. One side attacks and the other side defends with the limited means that we have.”View image in fullscreenYaser Alkam, the head of the village council, who lived in the US for 35 years, shows the ‘hot areas’ where radical settlers attack Palestinian landowners.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe violence is relentless.At night, settlers roam the village in off-road vehicles and intimidate people with gunshots, screaming and shining flashlights through the windows. In a recent attack against a family on the edge of the village, the settlers spray-painted the word “Revenge” on the side of the house.Among those accused of violence and intimidation is Amishav Melet, whose brother was killed in a clash when settlers marched into another Palestinian village last week. He has publicly declared that he believes Jews should retake all of the West Bank. He has denied claims that he is connected to settler violence.View image in fullscreenAmishav Melet has publicly declared he believes Jews should retake all of the West Bank and has been accused of violence and intimidation.“I have his pictures,” Alkam said of Melet. “And I’m sure he has my pictures and he has my name. He knows me and I know him … And he’s probably waiting for the time to get me.”While theTrump administrationis focused on Iran, Israel’s accelerating land grab in the West Bank has found an enthusiastic supporter in Huckabee. The US ambassador is an evangelical Christian who has supported Jewish claims on the occupied land that settlers call Judea and Samaria.Huckabee told residents in 2025: “President Trump loves this land. You are not alone. We stand with you, and so do many around the world. Those who do not stand with you do not stand with God.”Relatives mourn Palestinian American beaten to death by Israeli settlers: ‘He made everyone feel loved’Read moreWhen attacks take place, Alkam contacts Huckabee’s embassy for protection. Sometimes, he said, US officials have helped, most recently in late July when the Israeli military occupied a house owned by a doctor from Syracuse, who had hosted theDemocratic congressman Ro Khanna during his visitto Turmus Ayya earlier in the month. Alkam credited the US embassy with “playing a big role” in getting the military to leave, he said.But nine Palestinian Americans have been killed in the West Bank since 2022 by either settlers or the Israeli military, and the US is often unable to help or to restrain the settlers or military during violent attacks. A year after a Palestinian American from Tampa Bay wasbeaten to deathby Israeli settlers in the West Bank, settlers attacked his family members and friends, and even a CNN crew, who had gathered for a vigil.In response to questions from the Guardian, the state department said all US citizens in the West Bank had access to consular services, condemned violence “by any party in the West Bank” and said it was in “regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security”.“As the president has clearly stated, the United States does not support Israel annexing the West Bank,” the spokesperson said. “A stable West Bank keeps Israel secure and is in line with this administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region.”View image in fullscreenA US flag flies at a Palestinian home in Turmus Ayya.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe moments when the US has intervened have only convinced Alkam that Washington could be doing more to restrain the settlers and the Israeli government.“We thought we would never get to this point,” he said. “We never thought that American citizens in Turmus Ayya are going to be attacked under the eyes and the ears of the current administration.” Many of the residents even voted for Trump, he said, but lost faith when the administration quickly moved to remove violent settlers from sanctions lists drawn up under the Biden administration.Ghaith Odeh grew up in Queens, New York, and still spends most of his time in Paterson, New Jersey, but his wife and children moved to their family’s land in Turmus Ayya in 2021. They live on the border of the village near the settlers, and like others on the frontlines, they have shutters over their windows (plastic, not metal, he regrets). From there, he can scan the settler outpost below.View image in fullscreenGhaith Odeh was born in New York and has a business in  New Jersey, but his family moved to their land in Turmus Ayya in 2021.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe violence began before the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 and the launch of Israel’s war in Gaza, but has grown worse in the past year. “We’ve had multiple times where we were scared for our lives here, where we were actually in danger,” Odeh said, recounting the night that settlers burned down part of his parents’ house, the six Israeli military raids on his house, the regular gunfire near the village, and the time a rifle was pointed at his son, one of six children. He is especially scared when he is out of the house, he said.When Odeh contacted the US embassy about the attacks, he said he was given canned replies to report them to local law enforcement. Asked what message he felt he had received from the US government, he said: “It’s OK for an Israeli American to live over here, but not for an American Palestinian.”The violence has changed daily life in the village. Many fear bringing their children here and people have to rely on themselves for protection. The discussions in the village now revolve around security measures: whether to install barbed wire or hang more American flags to emphasise the village’s connection to the US.Pointing to a neighbour from Chicago who was installing a barbed-wire fence, Odeh said: “I don’t want to live in a prison,” adding that he wanted to set an example for his children of how to live without fear.“I’m born and raised in America,” he said. “We lived in freedom over there. And I’m not gonna live any other way.”View image in fullscreenMaisoon Ali points to the protective razor wire outside her home that now resembles ‘a prison’.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianBut people are scared for their lives. Last month, Maisoon Ali, a 60-year-old retiree, was at home in nearby Deir Dibwan when she looked up and saw three young men running up the driveway with bottles filled with a flammable liquid. She says it was only luck that she ran into her house, where she pulled down the metal shutters that put a barrier between her and them. After trying to pour the liquid on her, the settlers set fire to furniture and the building’s exterior while Ali sheltered inside.“Thank God I acted fast,” said Ali, who for decades lived in Vienna, Virginia, and whose children still live in the US.“If I didn’t do that, I would have been burned alive,” she said.View image in fullscreenBenches outside Ali’s home in Deir Dibwan that were set on fire in an arson attack.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianAli’s father foresaw trouble in the 1970s when he built the house and installed bulletproof glass.When he died, Ali’s father made her promise that she would not abandon the house. Now, she has turned the home into a “prison”, with fences around the house and the surrounding olive grove. She has abandoned her regular routine of travelling to Ramallah to see friends or swim at the local YMCA.“It would kill him to see this,” she said, gesturing toward the fortifications. “It makes me emotional because this is our land and I’m 60 years old and I decided to retire in my family home. And I don’t want to live like this, scared, and not doing my routine.”Meanwhile, the Israeli settlers camped nearby remain a constant threat. Dozens besieged the house again on 18 June, days after the first attack. One of the men has threatened her online, posting a video in which he is seen standing by a fence next to a basketball court behind Ali’s house. “The reality on the ground is shouting out what they already understand on their own: the homeowner has returned,” he says.The firebomb attack against Ali took place on 14 June, two days after Huckabee made a surprise visit to Shilo to back the settlers.Alkam, noting Huckabee does not address the Palestinian American community in the West Bank, said: “I’ve reached out at least four times asking for a visit to Turmus Ayya. He does not even consider that we exist.”Israeli prosecutors say they have charged six settlers with “acts of terrorism, arson, sabotage and violent rioting” in Deir Dibwan, although the cases are reportedly covered by a gag order and it is not clear if they are related to the attack on Ali’s house. After filing an initial report with the US embassy, she said she was told to report the case to local authorities.“If we were a Jewish Israeli American family who they had tried to burn alive, the American ambassador would have been here in two hours,” she said. “But I haven’t been contacted.”Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelMike HuckabeeTrump administrationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Red Cross visits Aung San Suu Kyi after Myanmar military pushed to prove she is alive | Myanmar | The Guardian
description: Meeting follows years of questions over wellbeing of detained former leader, who was ousted by coup in 2021
Author: Natasha May
Headline: Meeting follows years of questions over wellbeing of detained former leader, who was ousted by coup in 2021
Content: Aung San Suu Kyi with Arnaud de Baecque, resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross to Myanmar, in Naypyidaw.Photograph: Myanmar's Presidential Press and Information Bureau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAung San Suu Kyi with Arnaud de Baecque, resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross to Myanmar, in Naypyidaw.Photograph: Myanmar's Presidential Press and Information Bureau/AFP/Getty ImagesMyanmarRed Cross visits Aung San Suu Kyi after Myanmar military pushed to prove she is aliveMeeting follows years of questions over wellbeing of detained former leader, who was ousted by coup in 2021Natasha Mayin BangkokMon 3 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMyanmar’s detained former leaderAung San Suu Kyihas met a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the aid organisation has confirmed.The meeting on Monday ⁠followed years ofquestions over the wellbeing of the 81-year-old, whose whereabouts and health condition have been largely unknown since the elected civilian government she led was ousted by a military coup in February 2021.Little has beenseen or heard of Aung San Suu Kyi since late 2022. Myanmar’s military-backed administrations have repeatedly claimed she is in “good health”, even as international pressure has grown on the country’s ​government to allow independent verification.Aung San Suu Kyi’s son, Kim Aris, who had recentlydemanded the ruling junta provide proof of life,welcomed news of the meeting.
