He described it as “the first positive development concerning her in more than five years”, adding: “This is an important first step, but it must not be the last,.”In a social media post, Aris said he hoped the meeting would lead to “greater humanitarian access, direct contact with my mother, credible and independently verified information about her wellbeing, and ultimately her immediate and unconditional release, together with all political prisoners”.Leaked footage and prison logs reveal Aung San Suu Kyi’s life in detentionRead moreOn Monday, Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative of the ICRC ​to Myanmar, visitedAung San Suu Kyiin the capital, Naypyidaw, the government spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said in a post on Telegram.View image in fullscreenPhoto released by Myanmar’s government shows Aung San Suu Kyi cutting a birthday cake during her meeting with Arnaud de Baecque.Photograph: Myanmar President Office/APIn two of the four photographs provided by Khine Khine Soe, Aung San Suu Kyi – dressed in traditional ​Burmese attire – is seen with Baecque in a sparsely furnished, wood-panelled room containing only two chairs and a desk.In another photo, Myanmar’s former leader is seen cutting a birthday cake inscribed with her name. A clothes rack and storage boxes are visible in the background.A fourth image is a closeup of the cake, inscribed with “Happy Birthday Aunty Suu 19.6.2026”.In a statement released afterwards, the ICRC confirmed the visit had occurred and was carried out in accordance with its standards and procedures for visiting people deprived of liberty, including the opportunity to speak with Aung San Suu Kyi in private.“In line with the ICRC’s working methods, detention visits provide people deprived of liberty with the opportunity to exchange news with their families,” the statement said.“As is customary in the ICRC’s detention work, observations and recommendations related to the visit are shared exclusively and confidentially with the detaining authorities.”In late April, after amilitary-engineered electionthat allowed the former junta leader Min Aung ​Hlaing to become Myanmar’s ⁠president, authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi had beenmoved to house arrest.A photograph of the detained former leader was shown on military-controlled TV, however Aris told the BBC the image was taken years ago.While the election waslargely criticised as a sham, it has led to diplomatic re-engagement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).‘We feel like we are failing’: Myanmar doctor speaks out as health system teeters on ‘brink of collapse’Read moreFollowing a meeting between Myanmar’s foreign minister and counterparts from the regional Asean bloc in Bangkok in July, Thailand’s foreign minister, Sihasak Phuangketkeow,called for accessto Aung San Suu Kyi “so that we can be able to verify the claims” of her good health.But the new military-backed administration had so far been reluctant to provide access ⁠to Aung San Suu ​Kyi, includinga May request by the Philippinesto allow an Asean special envoy to visit her.Explore more on these topicsMyanmarAung San Suu KyiInternational Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)South and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: NHS radiographers report rise in overt racist abuse by patients | NHS | The Guardian
description: Survey reveals medics were called ‘monkeys’ and ‘dirty foreigners’, and patients refused to be seen by black or Asian staff
Author: Tobi Thomas
Headline: Survey reveals medics were called ‘monkeys’ and ‘dirty foreigners’, and patients refused to be seen by black or Asian staff
Content: The head of the NHS Race and Health Observatory said: ‘There must be a clear, consistently enforced zero-tolerance approach’ to racism across the NHS.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe head of the NHS Race and Health Observatory said: ‘There must be a clear, consistently enforced zero-tolerance approach’ to racism across the NHS.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianNHSNHS radiographers report rise in overt racist abuse by patientsSurvey reveals medics were called ‘monkeys’ and ‘dirty foreigners’, and patients refused to be seen by black or Asian staffTobi ThomasHealth and inequalities correspondentMon 3 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNHS radiographers are experiencing racist abuse by patients, who have called them “monkeys” and refused to be seen by black and Asian staff, according to a report.A survey of 381 members of the Society of Radiographers revealed a “noticeable” rise in instances of overt racism experienced and witnessed by radiographers across the health service over the past 18 months.Examples included staff being called “dirty foreigners”, patients complaining about the skin colour of those attending to them, and patients making comments in front of staff about “people coming over here and taking our jobs”.One patient made jokes about a radiographer’s headscarf and complained they couldn’t understand her; she speaks with a mild Yorkshire accent. Another patient waiting to be X-rayed refused to accept a black radiographer and said: “Black people frighten me.”The chief executive of the NHS Race andHealthObservatory, Prof Habib Naqvi, said such cases were a “sobering reminder of the racism, prejudice and hatred that persist in our society, and of the profound impact they have on healthcare staff and the communities they serve”.“They create real fear, trauma and anxiety among our diverse workforce, who continue to provide diligent, compassionate care to patients at some of the most vulnerable moments in their lives,” he said.“The NHS could not function without the skill, dedication and compassion of healthcare workers from across the world. We strongly condemn these reported racist incidents, and there must be a clear, consistently enforced zero-tolerance approach across the NHS, including in cases where patients display racist or otherwise unacceptable conduct.”Paul Awah, 39, a radiographer based in Bedfordshire who moved to the UK from Nigeria five years ago, has frequently experienced patients claiming they are unable to understand what he’s saying even though English is his first language.View image in fullscreenPaul Awah“Sometimes no matter how clear you’re speaking to a particular patient, a white patient, independent of whether the patient is sick or not, they just pretend not to understand,” he said.“They seem to understand people speaking with an Irish or a Scottish accent, but they claim to not understand me even though I am speaking clearly. Some patients also assume that we are not qualified.”For Awah, the current political climate and rhetoric about immigration from the far right has a part to play in the increase in racism experienced by NHS staff. “What used to be something people wouldn’t say, now the rhetoric has changed,” he said.“Immigrants are blamed for the cost of living, energy bills, the worsening situation in the country, and people feel it’s OK to say it.”Previous surveys have revealed the extent of racism directed at staff throughout the NHS. The Royal College of Nursing revealed in October that the number of racistincidents experienced by its members had risen 55%over a three-year period, while the latest NHS staff survey found thatone in five black and minority-ethnic staff had reported abuse, bullying or harassmentfrom patients or the public, compared with just one in 20 white staff.The chief human resources and organisational development officer at NHS England, Thomas Simonssaid: “Racist abuse towards NHS staff is completely unacceptable and has no place in our health service.“Our new national staff standards are clear that NHS organisations must take meaningful action to prevent and respond to racism, support affected staff and ensure there are clear consequences for patients who racially abuse or discriminate against NHS staff – including the option to refuse care in non-emergency situations.”Explore more on these topicsNHSRaceHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rapists, child abusers and groomers will not leave prison early, says PM | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until October
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Andy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until October
Content: About 6,000 offenders had been due for early release in September amid official predictions that prisons will be full in November.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenAbout 6,000 offenders had been due for early release in September amid official predictions that prisons will be full in November.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyPrisons and probationRapists, child abusers and groomers will not leave prison early, says PMAndy Burnham will also delay release of thousands of prisoners across England and Wales a month, until OctoberRajeev SyalandAlexandra ToppingMon 3 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will be excluded fromearly release plansto ease critical prison overcrowding in a major intervention by Andy Burnham.The prime minister said on Tuesday that he would delay the planned early release of thousands of prisoners acrossEnglandand Wales by a month until October.But he will still allow domestic abusers and killers to go free, including two men jailed for their role inthe death of PC Andrew Harper.The decision will put the lives of women and girls “at risk” and has “let down” serving police officers, a watchdog and a pressure group have warned.It follows the suspension of Keir Starmer’s plans to release up to 6,000 offenders from prison early in September amid official predictions that prisons will be full in November.Burnham suspended the schemein his second week as PM after coming under intense pressure from MPs, victims, campaigners and frontline prison officers to halt the early release of serious sexual and violent offenders.In a statement, Burnham said: “I asked for an urgent review of the prisoner release scheme. I fully understand the anger, anxiety and distress that’s been caused. I’ve heard that loud and clear. That’s why we’re making significant changes: offenders who have been sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and other grooming offences will be excluded from the changes.”The Ministry of Justice has declined to release the numbers of prisoners who will no longer be freed as a result of Burnham’s intervention.It has also declined to say when its own internal modelling predicts that prisons will be full again, and if there are already plans for further early release schemes.The domestic abuse commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, said the decision to exclude those who have abused their partners was “wrong” and “puts victims’ lives at risk”.“As I told the lord chancellor just last week, the danger perpetrators pose to their victim should not be underestimated. These are individuals who are fixated on their victim and will stop at nothing to control and cause harm.“Measures that will keep domestic abuse victims safe still appear to be an afterthought.”Andrea Simon, the London victim’s commissioner, said the failure was concerning, given a shortage of probation officers with experience of handling complex offenders.“This will alarm many survivors of abuse that are desperately concerned about their safety, particularly when there are real challenges in delivering tougher community supervision,” she said.An early release scheme in 2024 included specific protections for victims of domestic abuse.Victims’ groups had objected to the proposal for 6,000 people to be freed early from September under the newSentencingAct. Debbie Adlam, the mother of the police officer Andrew Harper, said last month that the proposed inclusion of two of her son’s killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – was “another letdown” for their family.Prisoners serving longer sentences of four years or more would be eligible for release at the halfway point of their term, rather than at two-thirds as had previously been the case.The changes were due to be phased in, beginning with prisoners serving sentences of less than 575 days, going up to prisoners jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release in June next year.The government has said that, after listening to victims’ concerns, rapists and child sexual offenders will not be eligible for the sentencing changes.Prisoners serving time for some sexual or violent offences where the automatic release stage is set at two-thirds will become eligible for release at the halfway point, provided they have not committed serious breaches of prison rules.This applies to Bowers and Cole, two of Harper’s killers, who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter. Henry Long, the main perpetrator, will not be subject to early release.Tiff Lynch, national chair of the Police Federation, said: “Allowing those who take an officer’s life to be released earlier to save the prison system from collapsing gravely risks undermining not only public safety but public confidence, causing real distress to bereaved families and sending entirely the wrong message about the value we place on those who protect us. The government must urgently rethink this decision.”The chief constable of Thames Valley police, Jason Hogg, said: “I am beyond disappointed the government is continuing to allow PC Andrew Harper’s killers to be released early from prison despite the overwhelming recent public outcry.“It is simple: if Andrew’s killers were convicted today, they would receive life sentences due to the law that was created in his name. They would not be eligible for early release.“We will continue to lobby the government to make the right decision.”The Ministry of Justice also announced a £10m package for victim support and said the new justice secretary, Alex Norris, would look at reviewing “outdated”Imprisonment for Public Protection sentences.Other community measures will be put in place to protect victims of crime including tougher periods of supervision and restriction zones for offenders, Burnham said.“I wanted to go even further as I know there will still be concerns about other offenders having their sentence shortened. But it’s not possible without the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing, which would put public safety at much greater risk,” Burnham said.The announcement follows days of wrangling inside the Ministry of Justice and No 10 over how to calm public anger while still ensuring that the criminal justice system does not seize up.Prisons have become a major point of political contention, with Labour blaming the Conservatives for creating the overcrowding crisis by increasing sentences while failing to build enough jails.Responding to Burnham’s announcement, the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said: “Labour whipped their MPs to vote to let rapists, paedophiles and grooming gang perpetrators out of prison early. Now they admit the Conservative campaign to stop this was right – this is a victory for victims.“But their U-turn doesn’t go far enough. Some child sex offenders and killers, like those responsible for the death of PC Harper, will still be released early. And the trauma of victims being told their abusers may be released can’t be undone.“One of Andy Burnham’s first acts as prime minister will be to let thousands of criminals – including killers and paedophiles – out early.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesSentencingCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Former neo-Nazi activist selected as Tory candidate for Somerset council election | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Joshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Joshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP
Content: Joshua Bonehill-Paine has previously described himself as a ‘nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights’.Photograph: Channel 4 News/YoutubeView image in fullscreenJoshua Bonehill-Paine has previously described himself as a ‘nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights’.Photograph: Channel 4 News/YoutubeConservativesFormer neo-Nazi activist selected as Tory candidate for Somerset council electionJoshua Bonehill-Paine, creator of satirical Crewkerne Gazette, has convictions including for harassing a Jewish MPBen QuinnPolitical correspondentMon 3 Aug 2026 14.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former neo-Nazi activist with convictions including for harassing a Jewish MP has been selected as a Conservative candidate for a local election inSomerset.Joshua Bonehill-Paine, thecreator of the viral Crewkerne Gazette series of AI clips, is due to stand for election to Somerset council next year in a new Crewkerne South district. He told the Guardian he was an executive member of the Tories’ Yeovil branch, working as an events organiser.“The branch and indeed party are fully aware of my past. Our chairman has been a vocal advocate and has supported me since I became a member of the party. I am very grateful for the support,” he said.Bonehill-Paine, who previously described himself as a “nationalist, fascist, theorist and supporter of white rights”, re-emerged in recent years as the creator of the Crewkerne Gazette, a satirical online account that has gained a cult following.While notably critical of Labour and Reform UK, its skits have cast the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, in a favourable light.Rebecca Harris, the Conservative chief whip, wascriticised earlier this yearfor reposting one video in which Badenoch and the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, were depicted as characters in the gangster film Scarface. This was after Bonehill-Paine had been revealed as the person behind the account.Bonehill-Paine has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station, and was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester.Hewas jailed in 2015for more than three years after posting “vile” antisemitic material online ahead of a planned neo-Nazi rally.In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at the then Labour MP Luciana Berger, who is Jewish, which included posting messages to his blog calling Berger a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”. He was also thefounder and leader of the National British Resistance, a far-right group.He told the Guardian on Monday that his criminal convictions had been spent and that he held various Home Office counter-extremism certifications. He said he had spoken alongside MPs where he talked about his past and highlighted antisemitism faced by Britain’s Jewish community.However, the Conservative party’s opponents on the right were quick to accuse the Tory leader of hypocrisy and being weak on claims to oppose antisemitism.A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Kemi claims the Tories have changed and they will have a new generation of candidates – it’s now clear what calibre of candidates they will be. Kemi claims to support the fight against antisemitism yet selects a convicted antisemite Nazi as a candidate. The hypocrisy is breathtaking.”The selection of Bonehill-Paine comes as Badenoch is accused of freezing out centrist Tories. Last month it emerged that all prospective Tory MPs must align with her pledge to scrap the 2050 net zero target and leave the European convention on human rights.At the weekend, a young Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network. Cody Butler claimed in a public letter that he no longer believed there was a home for one nation conservatism in the party.Badenoch told the BBC last week that she led “a brand new party full of new people” after it emerged that the former cabinet minister Grant Shapps had been rejected as a Tory parliamentary candidate.The Conservative party has been approached for comment.Get in touchContact Ben Quinn about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Ben using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. When asked to choose a recipient please switch to the Journalists list and select Ben Quinn.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailben.quinn@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsConservativesLocal politicsSomersetnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rupert Lowe’s ‘olive branch’ to Farage piles more pressure on Reform leader | Restore Britain | The Guardian
description: Restore leader has countered charges he’s splitting the right while showing his party is a very real obstacle for Reform
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Restore leader has countered charges he’s splitting the right while showing his party is a very real obstacle for Reform
Content: Nigel Farage and Rupert Lowe at the House of Commons in 2024. Lowe was suspended by Reform in 2025.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/PAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage and Rupert Lowe at the House of Commons in 2024. Lowe was suspended by Reform in 2025.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/PARestore BritainAnalysisRupert Lowe’s ‘olive branch’ to Farage piles more pressure on Reform leaderBen QuinnPolitical correspondentRestore leader has countered charges he’s splitting the right while showing his party is a very real obstacle for ReformMon 3 Aug 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareEven by the standards of their rivalry, the speed at which Rupert Lowe’s olive branch toNigel Faragemorphed into fresh recriminations between the two was swift.It began with a softly lit 12-minute video posted on Sunday by theRestore Britainleader, looking straight to camera and referring to “Nigel” as he suggested his party could be willing to cast aside its differences with Reform UK and work together.Despite being suspended by Reform in March 2025, and going on to start his own party to chip away at Farage’s vote, Lowe said the two men should put “personalities and our past disagreements aside for the good of the country”.But Farage did not appear to be tempted. Speaking at a press conference on Monday, he in effect accused Lowe of bad faith, wondering aloud about the circumstances of the “offer” and accusing him of “screaming” and “threatening” colleagues when he was in the party ranks.By midday, Lowe had accused Farage of lying when he said he had been in touch withthe Restore leader. But Lowe posted a screenshot of a curt “will call later” message from Farage on social media.Whatever the truth, the exchanges are a reminder of how Restore has emerged as a very real obstacle in Farage’s road to Downing Street.Lowe’s offer to work together came after Restore finished fourth in the Greater Manchester mayoral election, ahead of the Liberal Democrats and Tories – a relatively impressive feat for an electoral startup only months old.The party also finished third in the Makerfield byelection, the strongest Westminster electoral performancesince at least 2010by a party that has not only endorsed explicitly far-right positions but welcomed far-right activists into its ranks.Many of its policy positions – a referendum on the death penalty, bans on halal and kosher slaughter and a deportation policy informed by an ethnonationalist view of British identity – make any deal with Restore almost impossible for Reform if the latter is going to broaden its base.That’s even aside from Lowe’s other demand: that the former Tory ministers in Reform’s ranks – such as Robert Jenrick – are denied a place in any Reform government.Yet the enduring popularity of Lowe among a chunk of rightwing British voters, including Reform supporters, means Farage has to at least pay lip service to his rival’s overtures.While Restore’s vote share in Manchester and Makerfield – 8.7% and 6.8% respectively – indicated the party was a long way from winning seats, such results could cost Reform swathes of constituencies in a general election where the vote on the right was split.Contrast Farage’s vitriol to the warmer words on Sunday of the Reform MP Andrew Rosindell, who told GB News: “A lot of what he [Lowe] says will resonate with Reform voters and with British people.”It was “a matter for Rupert to talk to Nigel about”, the former Tory MP added, as he made a plea for unity on the “right of centre”.At grassroots level the relationship is complicated. In a number of local authorities, including some of Reform’s flagships, Restore is home to disillusioned councillors from Farage’s party, who have sometimes teamed up with other parties to frustrate their former colleagues.Yet on doorsteps, it’s not uncommon for canvassers to encounter voters who admire both parties and leaders.Even those concerned by the rise of a hard-right party such as Restore credit Lowe with making a clever play which both addresses some of his own problems and adds to Farage’s pressures at a time when the Reform leader faces unprecedented questions about his finances.“What Lowe’s move does for his own base, and Restore-curious types, is to negate the charge that he is splitting the vote on the right,” said Joe Mulhall, the director of research at the anti-fascism organisation Hope not Hate.“He has, from one perspective, put an offer on the table, which considering how much they seem to hate each other, has the appearance of generosity.“But from Lowe’s perspective, it’s also something which he can be pretty sure Farage would never have accepted, given that his route to power ultimately requires him courting centre-right votes. Having ethnonationalists behind him would mean endless questions.”For now, negotiations to unite Britain’s hard right appear set to be consigned to X and the studios of GB News.Just a month away too is Reform’s annual conference, an event where Lowe once enjoyed cult support from a considerable minority of activists. If questions persist about the future of both parties, it will be yet another shadow over what is meant to be a pivotal rallying point on Reform’s supposed path to power.Explore more on these topicsRestore BritainReform UKRupert LoweNigel FarageanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Judge orders return of alleged victim of trafficking sent to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Ruling quashes Home Office policy to refuse asylum seekers’ right to have trafficking claims reconsidered after initial rejection
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Ruling quashes Home Office policy to refuse asylum seekers’ right to have trafficking claims reconsidered after initial rejection
Content: People detained under the UK's ‘one in, one out’ deal with France, in Dover, Kent.Photograph: Home Office/PAView image in fullscreenPeople detained under the UK's ‘one in, one out’ deal with France, in Dover, Kent.Photograph: Home Office/PAImmigration and asylumJudge orders return of alleged victim of trafficking sent to France under ‘one in one out’ schemeRuling quashes Home Office policy to refuse asylum seekers’ right to have trafficking claims reconsidered after initial rejectionDiane TaylorMon 3 Aug 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA high court judge has ordered the Home Office to bring an alleged victim of trafficking forcibly removed to France under the“one in one out” schemeback to the UK.It is the first ruling of its kind and could lead to more people affected by the “one in one out” policy being brought back to the UK.The judge, Mr Justice Sheldon, has quashed aHome Officepolicy change to refuse asylum seekers the right to have their trafficking claims reconsidered after an initial rejection. “I have quashed it so that it is as if it never happened,” he said.The “one in one out” policy forcibly removes some people who cross the Channel in small boats in exchange for bringing a similar number from northern France legally to the UK.The government hopes the scheme will deter small boat crossings. They have reduced by more than 40% compared with this time last year, but in the last week more than1,000 peoplehave arrived and on Thursdayfour people diedattempting the journey.Asylum seekers returned to France now have a right to have trafficking cases that were initially rejected reconsidered. It is unclear how this will work in practice as many of those forcibly removed to France who have previously claimed to have been trafficked have now disappeared.Some have gone underground after being threatened by smugglers in northern France. Others have fled France after being threatened with removal to their home country or to another EU country where they were previously fingerprinted on their journey seeking asylum.The man whom the judge has ordered the Home Office to bring back from France was forcibly returned there on 27 November 2025. Reasonable grounds have been identified that he is a victim of trafficking. He is an asylum seeker from Sudan, a survivor of torture, and one of five people who challenged the home secretary’s policy change.A second asylum seeker sent to France by the Home Office, who was also involved in the legal challenge, will have his trafficking case reconsidered in France, and depending on the outcome he too may be brought back to the UK.The high court has granted the Home Office and the asylum seekers permission to appeal on various points in the judgment.Emily Soothill, of Deighton Pierce Glynn, welcomed the judge’s decision. She said: “Our client is a vulnerable victim of trafficking and torture who has suffered significantly as a result of the Home Office’s unlawful decision-making. We are delighted that the court has rightly recognised that his removal to France was unlawful and that he must therefore be brought back to the UK.“This is a highly significant decision; for our client, for other victims of trafficking who may have been unlawfully removed to France and for ensuring that the rule of law is upheld.”Elizabeth Cole, a solicitor at Duncan Lewis, also welcomed the decision. Her asylum seeker client in France, who took part in the legal challenge, now has a right to reconsideration.“The court’s decision calls into question the lawfulness of previous removals under the UK-France treaty where a negative reasonable grounds decision was made or reconsideration was denied,” she said. “We hope that this will allow a broader cohort of cases who have been removed to France unlawfully under the treaty to obtain justice and potentially return to the UK.”Home Office sources say they are carefully considering the judgment, including their options for appeal.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Completely hollow’: critics denounce Blanche deal to halt Trump slush fund | US news | The Guardian
description: Democrats say agreement – which clears way for Blanche’s confirmation – makes promises president can easily reverse
Author: Sam Levine
Headline: Democrats say agreement – which clears way for Blanche’s confirmation – makes promises president can easily reverse
Content: Todd Blanche at a cabinet meeting at Camp David last week.Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersView image in fullscreenTodd Blanche at a cabinet meeting at Camp David last week.Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersUS news‘Completely hollow’: critics denounce Blanche deal to halt Trump slush fundDemocrats say agreement – which clears way for Blanche’s confirmation – makes promises president can easily reverseSam LevineandChris Steinin WashingtonMon 3 Aug 2026 19.19 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 16.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA compromise between Todd Blanche and two Republican senators that potentially cleared the way for Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general is weak, Democrats and several experts said, as it makes promises Donald Trump can easily reverse.Blanche, the acting attorney general,posted two documentson Sunday evening showing he was withdrawing an 18 May order allowing for the creation of a $1.8bn weaponization fund and clarifying that broad tax immunity the justice department granted to Trump only applied retroactively to the president, his sons, and businesses.The agreement stemmed from a deal worked out with senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, two Republicans who had threatenedto blockBlanche’s nomination. Cornyn and Tillis said on Monday they would support Blanche when his vote comes up for the Senate judiciary committee Tuesday.“We are pleased that the Department of Justice has issued a formal order terminating the anti-weaponization fund,” Cornyn and Tillis said. “Additionally, the department has acknowledged in a binding written order that the audit settlement is limited to the plaintiffs and the scope does not extend beyond the defendants in the lawsuit, the IRS and the treasury, addressing concerns that multiple of our Republican colleagues share.”But legal experts and Democrats said what Blanche announced Sunday was far from ironclad and left room for Trump to resurrect the fund.“These assurances are not worth the paper they’re written on,” Brandon DeBot, policy director at the Tax Law Center at NYU, said in a statement. “They don’t pull back on the ongoing attempts to give the president, his family, and his affiliates unauthorized immunity from tax audits. They don’t do anything new to stop the president from trying to bring back the fund, as he threatened to this weekend. It’s abundantly clear we need congressional action.”Democratic senator Richard Blumenthal, a member of the judiciary committee, said: “Cornyn and Tillis seem to have gotten nothing. The tax immunity deal is still unlimited in terms of tax control liability, and the slush fund, or the thug fund, as I call it, is still alive and well so far as Donald Trump is concerned.”The documents Blanche released only say the prior justice department order creating the weaponization fund is rescinded. It does not modify the original settlement agreement creating the fund, reached as the result of a Trump lawsuit seeking billions in damages for the unauthorized release of his tax returns.In brief comments to reporters, Tillis defended his and Cornyn’s deals, saying the weaponization fund is “rescinded to death” and that the Texas senator had assured him “it would be very difficult for anybody to construe it as some sort of get out of audit free for any kind of future matter”.“That’s enough for me,” Tillis said.Blanche acknowledged during his confirmation hearing that Trump or his sons – the plaintiffs in the case – could theoretically sue to enforce the agreement. Trump spent the weekend praising the slush fund, andeven threatened to revive it.Trump again praised the fund on Monday, saying: “These people were treated so horribly, and this fund could’ve given them some solace.” He added that he had not seen Blanche’s agreement. “I don’t know what they agreed to,” he said.Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House judiciary committee, said Blanche’s announcement does nothing to prevent the justice department and Trump from creating the weaponization fund under a different name.Raskin said: “These hollow words are an affront to the American people, Congress and the courts, and are clearly designed to lull Senators Cornyn and Tillis into a false sense that their legitimate concerns have been addressed while leaving Blanche’s corrupt scheme fully intact.”Even if the department does not move ahead with the fund,there is another pathfor January 6 defendants to receive a payout from the federal government. A once-obscure process under the Federal Tort Claims Act allows anyone to seek damages from the federal government, first by filing a claim and then through a lawsuit.The justice department has wide discretion over whether to settle those lawsuits and some January 6 defendants are already moving through the processwith claims for millions of dollars.“This supposed ‘deal’ doesn’t prevent payouts to violent insurrectionists in the future,” Adam Schiff, a California Democrat and member of the senate judiciary committee, said in apost on X. “It doesn’t prevent the admin from bringing the slush fund back from the dead next week or using DOJ’s Judgment Fund for the same illicit purpose.”Republicans and Democrats have harshly criticized the weaponization fund and the tax immunity deal ever since they were announced in mid-May.Both aroseout of a $10bn lawsuit Trump, his sons, and business filed against the government for damages over the unauthorized release of his tax returns. The justice department did not even attempt to defend the government in the lawsuit.A federal judge latersaid it was a “bad-faith”suit designed to engineer a beneficial result for Trump. The New York Timesreportedin May that the tax immunity could potentially free Trump of a $100m penalty related to past audits of his tax returns.“Can you believe the guy, or did he and Trump announce the $1.9bn Trump justice fund in a month, and now we’re back where we started?” asked Democratic senator Sheldon Whitehouse, another judiciary committee member.“Or did they open the drive-up window at the Department of Justice for free Federal Tort Claims Act giveaways to any Maga person who asks?”Referring to Cornyn and Tillis, Whitehouse said: “It doesn’t look to me like they’ve actually pinned down the result they claim to have achieved.”The fund would have been run by five commissioners, four of whom would have been appointed by the attorney general (the fifth would have been named in consultation with congressional leadership). The fund was not required to disclose how much money it paid and to whom and aside from Trump and his sons, there were no restrictions on who could apply.The agreement Blanche announced is “completely hollow”, said Virginia Canter, chief counsel and director of ethics and anti-corruption at Democracy Defenders Action. “Nothing changes the terms of the actual settlement agreement, which cannot be modified without all parties’ consent. As a result, Blanche could reverse course tomorrow if he wanted.”Lawyers for the watchdog group Democracy Forward, which sued over the fund and secured a court order stopping it,sent a letterto the justice department on Monday noting Blanche had still declined to say under oath that the fund was not moving forward.The organization also asked the justice department whether it would seek to amend the underlying settlement agreement.“The DoJ and Acting Attorney General Blanche appear to want to have their cake and eat it too,” Skye Perryman, the group’s president, said in a statement. “They ask members of the United States Senate to believe the anti-weaponization fund is dead while they seek to preserve favor with the president through refusing to make real commitments backed up in court regarding the operation and future of the fund.”Even some Trump allies appeared unpersuaded that Blanche’s announcement amounted to the death of the fund.Mike Howell, an ally of Trump and director of the Oversight Project, a conservative watchdog group,posteda picture of Blanche’s documents on X and said they “can be undone after Tuesday. The weaponization fund is great.”Asked about the possibility of Blanche going back on his promises to the Republican senators after being confirmed, Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Senate judiciary committee, said: “Knowing how Trump works … I wouldn’t be surprised.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This quarter was otherworldly’: Palantir earnings surge past expectations | US news | The Guardian
description: Shares soar as yearly revenue up 93%, even as opposition grows to company’s role in Trump immigration agenda
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Shares soar as yearly revenue up 93%, even as opposition grows to company’s role in Trump immigration agenda
Content: Alex Karp, Palantir’s chief executive.Photograph: John Lamparski/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlex Karp, Palantir’s chief executive.Photograph: John Lamparski/Getty ImagesUS news‘This quarter was otherworldly’: Palantir earnings surge past expectationsShares soar as yearly revenue up 93%, even as opposition grows to company’s role in Trump immigration agendaJohana BhuiyanMon 3 Aug 2026 19.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a sea of companies reporting mixed financial results this quarter,Palantirstands out. Although Palantir was not immune to the AI jitters that caused industry-wide drops in share prices earlier this year, the AI and analytics company reported that its overall revenue grew 93% year over year to $1.94bn. That’s well over the $1.8bn Wall Street expected Palantir to bring in for the second quarter.The glowing financials sparked a 10% surge in share prices in the immediate aftermath. Despite growingoppositionto Palantir’sworkwith various governments including the crucial role the company plays in the Trump administration’simmigrationagenda, Palantir’s revenue from US government contracts grew 90% year over year to $809m.“This quarter was otherworldly: our US commercial revenue grew 149% year-over-year, our overall revenue grew 93% year-over-year,” Palantir’s CEO Alex Karp said.The company expects that growth to continue over the next two quarters and said they expect to bring in $2.160bn to $2.164bn in the third quarter and raised their expectations for full year revenue to between $8.150bn and $8.158bn. The company previously said it expected to bring in between $7.65bn and $7.66bn in 2026.But analysts remain unsure of whether Palantir can maintain that level of growth, or whether AI could replace some functionalities of its various software offerings.Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne said there was strong evidence existing customers are committed to Palantir and that the company has “been the clearest counter-example to the claim that enterprise AI doesn’t scale past pilots, and accelerating growth makes that harder to argue with”.“What it doesn’t settle is whether AI eventually collapses the software layer Palantir occupies, which has weighed on its stock price this year,” Bourne said in a statement.In his letter to shareholders and in interviews ahead of the earnings call, Karp took aim at the creators of large language models like OpenAI and Anthropic that use a token system to provide access to its AI.He wrote that Palantir’s partners and customers want to maintain “control over data” and not hand the keys to all their proprietary information over to the large language labs which meed to ingest as much data as possible to train their models. Karp suggested that was part of why customers are choosing Palantir over other companies.“The models have grown and thrived by essentially ingesting the entire written work product of our civilization,” Karp wrote in his letter.“We have always declined, and will continue to decline, entering into a parasitic relationship with our partners,” Karp said.Explore more on these topicsUS newsPalantirnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yen hits three-month high after Trump helps prop up currency | Yen | The Guardian
description: US and Japanese governments confirm they carried out a rare joint intervention late last week
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: US and Japanese governments confirm they carried out a rare joint intervention late last week
Content: Japan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi met Donald Trump in March.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenJapan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi met Donald Trump in March.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersYenYen hits three-month high after Trump helps prop up currencyUS and Japanese governments confirm they carried out a rare joint intervention late last weekWhy has Trump stepped in to prop up Japan’s currency?Business live – latest updatesGraeme WeardenMon 3 Aug 2026 04.34 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe yen has hit its highest level in three months afterJapan and the USlaunched a combined operation to support the Japanese currency.The yen strengthened to ¥155 to the US dollar on Monday, its highest level since early May, after Tokyo and Washington confirmed they had carried out a rare joint currency intervention late last week.Tokyo’s finance ministry said on Monday the two governments had conducted coordinated yen-buying intervention and would not hesitate to take further action.Why has Trump stepped in to prop up Japan’s currency?Read moreThe intervention came after the yen had weakened to a 40-year low of almost ¥164 to the dollar last week.Donald Trump told reporters on Sunday: “They have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we’re always there forJapan.”The yen had weakened in recent months as Japanese borrowing costs remained lower than in other advanced economies. This disparity fuelled a so-called “carry trade”, in which investors borrowed cheaply in yen to buy higher-yielding dollar assets.The yen has also suffered from investors’ concern about Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to usetax and spending measures to stimulate the Japanese economy, and her criticism of the Bank of Japan setting higher interest rates, which have also pushed up the country’s borrowing costs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBessent ‘to-do’ list shows proposal for US to buy $5bn-$10bn of Japanese yenRead moreThe US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Washington “will not hesitate to ⁠participate in further joint intervention”, while repeating calls for further interest rate rises from Japan’s central ​bank. On Saturday,a photograph of Bessent’s notebook taken during a cabinet meeting showedthat his “to do” list included buying $5bn-$10bn ⁠worth of Japanese yen.However, the Financial Times reported that Washington had sold euros to buy yen, rather than using dollars – perhaps to avoid suggesting it wanted a weaker US currency.Bank of Japan data suggested Tokyo spent as much as $36.58bn last Friday to buy yen and strengthen the local currency, Reuters reported.This is the first collaboration involving Japan and the US since March 2011 when a joint intervention was made to weaken the yen after the March Tohoku earthquake and tsunami.Lee Hardman, a currency analyst at MUFG bank, said: “The threat of further joint intervention and a faster pace of BoJ hikes should provide more support for the yen, and discourage speculators from running elevated short yen positions.”The consultancy OxfordEconomicssaid the US-Japan coordinated intervention would not be enough to reverse the trend of yen weakness.“Despite rising market speculation about faster rate hikes by the Bank of Japan, we continue to assume the central bank waits until December because the intervention reduces the risk of a sharp yen depreciation and gives the BoJ more time to assess the impact of the Middle East conflict and past rate hikes on the economy,” it said.Explore more on these topicsYenEconomicsCurrenciesJapanAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil prices plunge and Europe’s markets rally after Trump calls off Iran strikes | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude drops by 5% after US president claimed talks on Middle East peace deal would resume
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Brent crude drops by 5% after US president claimed talks on Middle East peace deal would resume
Content: Oil supertankers and merchant marine ships in the Fujairah anchorage, just off the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Barry Iverson/AlamyView image in fullscreenOil supertankers and merchant marine ships in the Fujairah anchorage, just off the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: Barry Iverson/AlamyOilOil prices plunge and Europe’s markets rally after Trump calls off Iran strikesBrent crude drops by 5% after US president claimed talks on Middle East peace deal would resumeJulia KolleweMon 3 Aug 2026 08.10 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCrude oil prices fell sharply while stocks and government bonds rallied on Monday afterDonald Trumpcancelled planned strikes on Iran and claimed peace talks were about to resume.Brent crude was trading 5% lower at $83.47 a barrel by lunchtime, after falling as much as 7.3% to $81.55 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate dropped more than 5% to $79.47 a barrel.Both global oil benchmarks jumped more than 20% in July after fighting between the US and Iran resumed, and as attacks on several tankers in the strait of Hormuz revived fears for the safety of vessels transiting the important shipping passage.UK economy faces recession if strait of Hormuz remains closed, EY warns - business liveRead moreTrump said late on Saturday on his Truth Social platform that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”.On Sunday, he said talks would start on Monday, a claim denied by Tehran.Fuel prices for UK motorists continued to rise over the weekend at a time when families are heading off on their summer breaks. Petrol hit an Iran-war high of 160.85p a litre on Monday,surpassing its previous high on Friday, and diesel rose above 180p for the first time since 9 June, according to the RAC.The motoring group’s head of policy, Simon Williams, said: “Unleaded has now risen more than 10p a litre – 7% – since bottoming out at 150.59p on 6 July while diesel is up 16p (15.8p) a litre, or 10%, almost fully reversing June’s 16.6p reduction which was the biggest monthly drop on record.”He said prices at the pump should begin to stabilise this week, though diesel could reach 185p over the next week.Kathleen Brooks, the research directorof the broker XTB, said the drop in oil prices should help support markets. “This will ease inflation fears and could also act as a dampener on bond yields, which rose sharply last week, especially at the long end, where30-year US Treasury yields jumped to their highest level for 19 years,” she added.In a positive start to August, European shares rose and US stock futures pointed to a higher open on Wall Street later.The pan-European Stoxx 600 index rose 0.5%. Energy stocks slid 2%, while travel and leisure shares gained 2.1%. The UK’s FTSE 100 index gained 30 points by midday, despite being dragged back by negative reaction toAstraZeneca’s talks about a tie-up with its US rival Bristol Myers Squibb.In bond markets, US Treasuries increased, pushing the yield on the benchmark 10-year bond down five basis points to 4.68%, a retreat from the highest level since January.Tony Sycamore, a market analyst at the investment platform IG, said: “The bigger focus is whether this week turns into a rinse and repeat of last week – with hopes of a deal collapsing as Iran digs in its heels and continues to leverage its control over the strait, potentially through an attack on a US base or a tanker transiting the waterway.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTwo tankers laden with Saudi oil crossed the Bab el-Mandeb strait out of the Red Sea over the weekend, while traffic in the strait of Hormuz slowed after reports of vessel attacks, according to shipping data.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre has reported three more tanker attacks since Saturday.On Sunday, the oil cartel Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as Opec+, agreed to increase oil production by about 188,000 barrels a day from September, unwinding output cuts.However, because of the export disruptions from the Gulf, Russia and Kazakhstan caused by the Iran and Ukraine wars, production increases by Opec+ have had little impact on prices.Elsewhere in the markets,the Japanese yen hit a three-month highafter Tokyo and Washington launched a joint operation to support the currency.Explore more on these topicsOilEnergy industryStock marketsCommoditiesGlobal economyEconomicsDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A reminder of why we have unions’: Matewan writer and director on the film’s lessons for the labor movement | US unions | The Guardian
description: John Sayles’s 1987 film, which dramatizes a 1920 labor conflict, shows how class solidarity can overcome prejudice
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: John Sayles’s 1987 film, which dramatizes a 1920 labor conflict, shows how class solidarity can overcome prejudice
Content: John Sayles: ‘I just felt like people needed a reminder of why we have unions. Without them, you don’t have anywhere to stand.’Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APView image in fullscreenJohn Sayles: ‘I just felt like people needed a reminder of why we have unions. Without them, you don’t have anywhere to stand.’Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APUS unions‘A reminder of why we have unions’: Matewan writer and director on the film’s lessons for the labor movementJohn Sayles’s 1987 film, which dramatizes a 1920 labor conflict, shows how class solidarity can overcome prejudiceMichael SainatoMon 3 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen John Sayles, a student at Williams College taking time off from his summer factory job, washitchhikingduring the summer of 1970 in West Virginia, it was often coalminers who picked him off the main interstate highways.At the time, miners were amid the wake of a contentious union election within the United Mine Workers of America. Fierce tensions had led to the murder of the union reform candidateJoseph Yablonskiand his wife in December 1969.Miners told Sayles the conflict was comparable to theMatewan Massacre, an event in 1920 he had never heard about before and, like much labor history, had largely been shelved away from the forefront of the American consciousness.US justice department dismisses charges against California union leaderRead moreLearning that bit of American history would eventually inspire Sayles to write a screenplay and direct the 1987 film Matewan.The film, starring Chris Cooper,James Earl Jonesand Mary McDonnell, depicts union organizing among coalminers and the efforts of Baldwin-Felts detective agents, hired by the Stone Mountain coal company, to stop them.In an interview with the Guardian, Sayles noted workers at the coalmine were segregated into groups based on race and ethnicity, a labor tactic referred to as ajudicious mixturemeant to prevent unionization from occurring.Yet local West Virginian, Black and Italian-immigrant miners still banded together to strike against the coal company.“When they went on strike, all three of those groups got together and went out together, and that was really interesting to me, the way that a common enemy can overcome these other prejudices that the miners had,” Sayles said.The Baldwin-Felts agents, in turn, assaulted, threatened, intimidated and even killed a miner in an attempt to shut down the union effort. A shootout between the two groups on 19 May 1920 would leave seven agents, the Matewan mayor and two miners dead.The story “was structured like a western. It ends literally with the good guys and the bad guys facing each other on Main Street at high noon,” he said, adding that it had “that kind of strong ending that was kind of perfect to make a film”.Sayles and several cast and crew of the film, including producer Maggie Renzi and actors David Strathairn, Chris Cooper, Gordon Clapp and Joe Grifasi, appeared at a July reunion screening of the film in Williamstown, Massachusetts.At the screening, Sayles and Renzi noted the film was made to resurrect a piece of labor history that was at risk of being forgotten.“I just felt like people needed a reminder of why we have unions,” Sayles told the Guardian about why he made the film. “Without them, you don’t have anywhere to stand.”Sayles notes that even after the massacre, union organizing at Matewan failed and organizing workers faced significant violent resistance, until the landmark National Labor Relations Act waspassedunder Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1935 that enshrined collective bargaining rights in the US.But workers continue to face challenges. Unionizing some industries has become even more difficult because employers can now move workplaces abroad, drastically limiting the power a union has if the work can be done anywhere else, Sayles said, citing ongoing cases of employers who shut down locations where workers were on a path to unionization, such asWalmartandStarbucks.He also emphasized workers in the US were still hampered by federal laws that restricts organizing, like theTaft Hartley Act of 1947, which prohibits national and sympathy strikes. For example, while strikes in the film industry occur, each craft is separated by its own labor union and must strike independently from one another.But collective action can bring together large coalitions that inflict change.“We’re so balkanized in this country that you almost have to have people who are totally outside of your group to join you to get enough of a mass to say, ‘No, this isn’t going to happen,’” Sayles said. “But I think that that anger and that feeling of being betrayed, when it busts out in a larger community of people who aren’t necessarily on the frontline, the way thatit did in Minnesota, and you get those numbers, then the other side actually does have to pay attention.”Explore more on these topicsUS unionsWorkers' rightsJames Earl JonesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: AstraZeneca shares fall 8.9% over merger talks with US cancer drug firm | AstraZeneca | The Guardian
description: Proposed $400bn tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb would create world’s fourth-largest drugmaker but analysts question rationale
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Proposed $400bn tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb would create world’s fourth-largest drugmaker but analysts question rationale
Content: AstraZeneca is the second-biggest listed company in the UK, with a market value of nearly £196bn.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAstraZeneca is the second-biggest listed company in the UK, with a market value of nearly £196bn.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianAstraZenecaAstraZeneca shares fall 8.9% over merger talks with US cancer drug firmProposed $400bn tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb would create world’s fourth-largest drugmaker but analysts question rationaleJulia KolleweMon 3 Aug 2026 12.32 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 03.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than £17bn was wiped off the value of Britain’s biggest drugmaker,AstraZeneca, on Monday after a report that it was in discussions to take over its US rival Bristol Myers Squibb in a deal that would create a near $400bn (£300bn) pharmaceutical group.AstraZeneca, run by Pascal Soriot, its longtime chief executive, had been worth nearly £196bn before the news broke. BMS, headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and known for its cancer treatments, was worth $133bn (£98bn).A tie-up would be one of the biggest ever pharmaceutical deals and would create the world’s fourth largest drugmaker by market value.AstraZeneca boss urges western drugmakers to move at ‘Chinese speed’Read moreAstraZeneca’s FTSE 100-listed shares plunged by 8.9% to close at a low of £115 in London as investors reacted to news of the talks, which werefirst reported by the Financial Times.That pushed AstraZeneca’s value down to about £178bn, as it lost the title of the second-biggest listed company in the UK to Shell.BMS’s shares rose 1.7% after Wall Street opened, before reversing and losing those gains by midday in New York.While talks have been held in recent months, there is no certainty that a deal will be concluded, according to sources.A deal would expand AstraZeneca’s presence in the US, where it is alreadyinvesting $50bn in research and manufacturing by 2030. It completed a direct listing of its shares on the New York stock exchange in June, and a deal with BMS could revive fears of a shift away from the UK.The news surprised analysts, who questioned the rationale behind a tie-up and noted that any deal would be closely scrutinised by regulators, given the overlap of the companies’ oncology portfolios.Analysts at Jefferies, led by Michael Leuchten, said: “‘Why’ is perhaps not yet clear to us: we suspect that most people will focus on the potential to establish an even bigger oncology powerhouse, with the resultant portfolio likely the broadest in the industry. However, beyond the regulatory hurdles we would argue that pipeline assets could be sourced elsewhere, as AstraZeneca has been doing, particularly in China.”Chris Beauchamp, a chief market analyst at the investment platform IG, said: “Though a rare example of a big UK firm buying a smaller US firm is something to warm the cockles of the British heart, it risks the departure of yet another national champion, and in any case the pair’s large cancer divisions are a major hurdle to a successful deal. BMS has struggled since 2023, and some Astra shareholders will wonder at the need to do expensive M&A when their shares are doing so well.”Some shareholders were also sceptical. “The only advantage for AstraZeneca in this rumoured combination with BMS seems to be to accelerate its US footprint and sales,” said Lucy Coutts, an investment director at JM Finn, an AstraZeneca shareholder. “On balance, BMS shareholders would be the winners of any combination with AstraZeneca and so this news will undoubtedly be received coolly by AstraZeneca shareholders,” she told Reuters.A major shareholder told the Guardian: “Bold potential move, but not yet any real detail to get our teeth into.”Lukas Leu, a portfolio manager at the AstraZeneca shareholder ATG Healthcare Investments, said a deal could boost margins through cost synergies and expand reach in neuroscience and cell therapy, but he questioned how a combined firm would position competing drugs. “I am not a big fan of mega-mergers, it kills innovation and agility,” he said.AstraZeneca, headquartered in Cambridge, England, was formed in 1999 from the merger of the Swedish company Astra AB and the UK company Zeneca Group. Zeneca had been spun off from Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI) five years earlier.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAstraZeneca’s share price has more than quadrupled during Soriot’s leadership, when it overtook its UK rival GSK in size.Under Soriot,the company fended off a hostile bid from its US rival Pfizerin 2014 that valued AstraZeneca at almost £70bn. He then successfully rebuilt the company’s drug pipeline with cancer immunotherapies – drugs that harness the body’s immune system to fight tumours – and other treatments.A week ago, AstraZeneca said it was confident of hitting its growth targets for 2030, by which time itexpects to achieve $80bn (£60bn) in annual sales, up from $59bn last year, despite the surprise failure of Wainua, one of its leading heart disease drugs in development. Soriot saidthe company must move at “Chinese speed”to ensure it did not fall behind competitors.A few days later, BMS beat Wall Street expectations with its second-quarter results and lifted its 2026 outlook. It made revenues of $12.97bn during the quarter, up 5% on a year earlier, excluding currency movements.The US company employs about 800 people in the UK. Its UK research team of 250 people isbased at Moreton on the Wirral peninsulanear Liverpool, while its commercial head office for the UK and Ireland is in Uxbridge, west London.John Murphy, a senior pharma analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said a deal made “limited strategic sense” for AstraZeneca. “Their growth outlooks are very different – double-digit earnings gains are forecast at Astra through 2030, with Bristol set for continued declines, due to multiple patent expiries – and, while both are focused on developing promising pipelines, history suggests such mega-mergers hamper pipeline progress.“Major cost savings via eradication of overlapping infrastructure is one obvious benefit but would suggest reduced confidence at Astra in its pipeline and growth outlook. A link-up in certain disease categories may be a possible area of future collaboration,” he added.AstraZeneca declined to comment. BMS was also contacted.Explore more on these topicsAstraZenecaPharmaceuticals industryMergers and acquisitionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump says | Iran | The Guardian
description: US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: US president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with Washington
Content: Donald Trump said on Monday he expected negotiations with Iran on reopening the strait of Hormuz to begin imminently.Photograph: Allison Robbert/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump said on Monday he expected negotiations with Iran on reopening the strait of Hormuz to begin imminently.Photograph: Allison Robbert/EPAIranFresh US-Iran talks are ‘last chance’ for Tehran to avoid war escalating, Trump saysUS president expects negotiations to begin in next day or two but Iran says it is not reviving talks with WashingtonPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 3 Aug 2026 15.36 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” forIranto forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday.Trump said he expected negotiations to begin in the next day or two to reopen the strait of Hormuz and create a pathway for Iran to address the US’s concerns about its nuclear programme.“The first phase is the opening of the straits. The second phase will be the denuclearisation,” he told reporters in the Oval Office. “And that will take a little while.”Trump reiterated that he was running out of patience with Iran. “This is the last chance for them to sign a good document.”Iran has been in discussions withOmanabout the creation of a temporary route through the strait that would allow commercial shipping to resume, but is not yet reviving talks with the US, Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said earlier on Monday.Esmail Baghaei denied claims by Trump that talks between the two sides covering all the major disputes between them could restart as early as Monday. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” he said.Trump claimed he had held off from launching the biggest strike on any country “since world war two” over the weekend after Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, rang him to urge diplomacy. Trump said the cancellation was conditional on Iran reaching a deal quickly.Trump says Iran talks set for Monday as Tehran and Oman discuss strait of Hormuz dealRead moreIt is thought to be the 12th time in the war between the US and Iran that Trump has called off threatened strikes.On Monday, the US president called the Iranian leadership “unbelievably duplicitous” in a post on social media.“They ask for a meeting, some would say ‘beg’, talks begin, with more scheduled in the immediate future, and they say, openly and proudly, that they’re not having any discussions, that nothing is being talked about, and they’re only dealing with ‘Oman’. They then go on to give their usual blather in saying, theStrait of Hormuzwill be operated powerfully by them, when it is already completely controlled by the United States Navy and our ‘Blockade’.”A middle route through the strait would represent progress. Iran is claiming full sovereignty over the strait and has been making demands over its routes and future management, including the possibility of charging fees in return for providing ships with maritime services.One proposal is to create a joint Omani-Iranian company that would provide all the services that insurance companies used to provide at high costs, but at lower prices, and with preferential tariffs for some countries.View image in fullscreenIran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said it was discussing with Oman the possibility of an intermediate route through the strait of Hormuz to be used temporarily.Photograph: ReutersUnlocking a mutually acceptable route through the strait is the precondition to unlocking all the other agreements laid out in the memorandum of understanding, the ceasefire document both sides signed on 18 June. Disagreements about the memorandum’s obligations has led to a resumption of the war, which has spread to the Red Sea and to Iraq.Last week, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said Tehran was demanding that ships entering the strait take a route to the north close to Iran, but that some ships could take a southern route. Iran rejected the traffic being divided evenly between the two routes, and also that a third country could start de-mining the routes.Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran: “We are now talking about a corridor that will have a round trip route, not two or three separate routes. This intermediate route is to be used temporarily until a decision is made on a fixed route.”He framed the route as an alternative to the transport separation scheme, the longstanding prewar route overseen by the UN’s International Maritime Office. He said maps had been exchanged by the two sides.Baghaedi said an agreement on a route would not solve all the problems, pointing to the continuing US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, and that unless the US approach changed, there would be no significant improvement in the situation in the strait.Recently there had been gloom in Omani circles about reaching an agreement with Iran on routes, leading to a revival of preparations for Oman’s European allies to start to clear the southern route of mines, a step that might have provoked direct conflict between Iran and European powers.In a sign of the pressure Tehran diplomats face, a statement from the Assembly of Experts, the body of clerics that elects the supreme leader, warned against investing any trust in the US, saying: “Hope for understanding and agreement with this bullying regime will lead nowhere.”However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he believed the “memorandum of understanding would prove to be the centre of gravity of our foreign relations in the future”.The Saudis’ intervention came in a week in which Riyadh attacked Iranian-backed forces inside Iraq and raised the temperature in its dispute with the Iranian-backed Houthis in northern Yemen, underlining the extent to which Saudi Arabia fears the consequence of an all-out US war against Iran spiralling out of control across the Middle East.Additional reporting by Associated PressExplore more on these topicsIranStrait of HormuzUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaOmannewsShareReuse this content

title: Mauricio Pochettino’s US return is risky, expensive and probably unnecessary | USA | The Guardian
description: In giving the head coach another World Cup cycle, US Soccer is tempting fate for negligible benefit
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: In giving the head coach another World Cup cycle, US Soccer is tempting fate for negligible benefit
Content: Mauricio Pochettino led the US to the last 16 at the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino led the US to the last 16 at the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APUSAMauricio Pochettino’s US return is risky, expensive and probably unnecessaryLeander SchaerlaeckensIn giving the head coach another World Cup cycle, US Soccer is tempting fate for negligible benefitMon 3 Aug 2026 12.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTShareMauricio Pochettino and US Soccer enjoyed their time together.Or, rather, theyenshoyedit, as Pochettino would pronounce it in his thick Argentinian accent, which charmingly carries over when he speaks English.Nevertheless, the two sides should have moved on from each other.From his 10 September 2024 appointment through the US men’s national team’s 4-1 last-16 World Cup elimination at the hands of Belgium on 6 July, Pochettino had broadly accomplished what he was brought in to do.Mauricio Pochettino agrees deal to stay as US coach through World Cup 2030Read moreHe energized a team who had grown stale. He found a playing system and style that suited a generation of USMNT players who were unprecedented in their pedigree and talent but lacked difference-makers on the World Cup stage. He coaxed from themtwo excellent performances– including a 4-1 hammering of Paraguay that was surely the best the Americans have ever looked at a World Cup – and two very good ones. Then it all caved in against Belgium after the good vibes had been ruined by a meddlesome president in all that Folarin Balogun suspension/unsuspension business.Pochettino’s spell in charge was a success.Now,he will be back, having accepted a contract offer extended to him by the US Soccer Federation before the World Cup and kept on the table after the team was eliminated a round sooner than many had hoped they would reach. Pochettino’s new deal runs through the 2030 World Cup, giving him a full cycle to try again.This is something of a gamble. The inclination to see what Pochettino will construct atop the sturdy foundations he laid is understandable, but it assumes that he even stays through the length of his new deal.It feels like the Argentinian and his staff are still here on account of the absence of opportunity elsewhere, to coach the sort of club he has worked for over the course of a decade – the likes of Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea. Perhaps he settled for a prolonged stay with the US men by default; perhaps not. Before the World Cup, Pochettino was reportedly in talks with Milan, who ultimately hired Ruben Amorim as manager instead.It seems unlikely Pochettino will actually stick around four more years as one top coaching job after another opens up and he invariably winds up on the lists of rumored candidates. Should he leave early, the team will once again be starting over mid-cycle.Besides, the job he returns to is very different from the one he has done.For the USMNT, World Cup qualifiers for 2030won’t even startuntil November of 2027, although there will be editions of the Concacaf Nations League and Gold Cup to slog through before then – to say nothing of a great many friendlies against teams you are largely supposed to beat every time. The final round of World Cup qualifying will be played in June of 2028 and the fall of 2029, after still more Nations League and Gold Cup duties. Mind you, Concacaf will have six places at the next World Cup, with a possible seventh through a playoff – as opposed to three automatic berths for the 2022 World Cup, the last edition before the tournament expanded and was hosted in this region. The stakes and peril will simply not be the same as before. The adrenaline rush of high-stakes games is an awfully long way off.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsène Wenger: US soccer development will depend on ‘consistency’ and ‘education’Read moreThen there’s the history of USMNT managers staying on for a second World Cup cycle. It’s abysmal. Bruce Arena hung on for a second World Cup and watched helplessly as the side who stunned on their way to the brink of the semi-finals in 2002 got grouped in 2006. Bob Bradley made it just a year after 2010, getting sacked after a 4-2 Gold Cup final loss to Mexico the following summer. Jürgen Klinsmann’s second cycle was a debacle and sowed the seeds for the failure to reach the 2018 World Cup. Gregg Berhalter’s return to the job after 2022 was marred by a scandal and never really got going, ending in humiliation at the Copa América on home soil and his subsequent replacement by Pochettino.Granted, all of them got more of that first cycle than Pochettino did, who parachuted into the job less than two years before the World Cup. But what each second-term failure had in common was that all the coaches struggled to keep the program fresh when the process reset.While this remains a fairly young team, they could do with an injection of fresh faces, legs and ideas. Out of the team’s longstanding core of Christian Pulisic, Tyler Adams, Weston McKennie, Antonee Robinson, Sergiño Dest and Chris Richards, only McKennie has been spared major and repeated injuries. The scare over a late knock to Richards before the tournament emphasized that while the standard and quality on the field has inarguably improved, it nevertheless feels tentative. The US were never more than an injury or two away from calamity. This was especially apparent when Pulisic was pulled at half-time against Paraguay and did not play a full 90 minutes all tournament, lasting longer than an hour only once.There is also something of an opportunity cost to keeping Pochettino on.Tax filings showthat he made more than $5m over his first seven months in the job, a sum that was reportedly padded with further payment from billionaire US Soccer supporter Ken Griffin and other sources. Griffin is once again a primary funder of Pochettino’s new deal, which keeps him among the most highly paid managers in international soccer. And while the federation got a return on that investment over the past summer, it’s worth wondering whether it makes sense to pay out that kind of money to go and play early qualifiers against Nicaragua, or to face Jamaica and Panama again and again.You wouldn’t buy a supercar just to drive it to the grocery store and back. In the next few years, the USMNT will mostly be making school runs and commuting back and forth to an office park without ever hitting the highway.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now.
