title: Sigrid Haugset stuns Tour de France Femmes favourites by storming to stage win | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Sigrid Haugset, the Norwegian national champion, shocked the established order in the Tour de France Femmes by breaking away to take the overall lead
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Sigrid Haugset, the Norwegian national champion, shocked the established order in the Tour de France Femmes by breaking away to take the overall lead
Content: Sigrid Haugset enjoys the biggest success of her career after her dominant stage win.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenSigrid Haugset enjoys the biggest success of her career after her dominant stage win.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersTour de France FemmesSigrid Haugset stuns Tour de France Femmes favourites by storming to stage winNorwegian breaks clear in stage three to take overall leadHaugset: ‘I never thought it was possible, it’s unreal’Jeremy Whittlein PolignyMon 3 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSigrid Haugset, the Norwegian national champion, shocked the established order in theTour de France Femmes, breaking away alone for 90km, to take the overall lead after winning stage three to Poligny.“I never thought it was possible,” she said, after realising she had taken the biggest success of her career and the overall lead in the sport’s biggest race. “It’s unreal. I was so dizzy at the end. I know my boyfriend would be so angry at me for not celebrating, but I couldn’t. I could not lift my arms off the bike. It was impossible.”Tadej Pogacar will ride Vuelta a España in bid to complete Grand Tour trebleRead moreHaugset’s spectacular solo effort surprised the peloton’s leading teams and on the eve of the 21km individual time trial, from Gevrey‑Chambertin to Dijon, she leads by 2min 2sec from Kim Le Court.“I was thinking about all my teammates and everyone cheering from home, so I had to give it my all,” she said. “All done in the Norwegian champion’s jersey, too – it’s fantastic.We had looked at this stage and it was the goal for this Tour. I told my father I’d get some flowers today. Tomorrow is the time trial, but I haven’t worked on it this year so I will just enjoy it.”Haugset is the first Norwegian rider to wear the yellow jersey in the Tour Femmes. The 27-year-old’s lone effort began at the foot of the second‑category Col de la Savine and was marked by an intense pursuit from the former world road race champion Lotte Kopecky, winner of the points classification in all three Grand Tours.“I thought Kopecky would catch me,” Haugset said. “I can’t believe that she didn’t, but I kept on. The team car was amazing, pushing me.”Although, in what became an epic duel, Kopecky got as close as 10sec to Haugset, she was not able to find the power to finally close the gap and the Norwegian moved clear again to win the stage by almost a minute and a half.Temperatures in the high 30s made it yet another suffocating and stifling day on the route, with the ever-present iced drinks and ice socks passed up to the riders throughout the 156km stage.As the sweat-streaked Haugset held on to win, the first sparring match between the race favourites came on the Côte de Chaux‑Champagny, 25km from Poligny, where Le Court accelerated and temporarily left her rivals in disarray. But as the narrow climb went on, with brief tentative accelerations from Kasia Niewiadoma and Demi Vollering, the main contenders regrouped and with Tuesday’s potentially pivotal time trial looming large, a truce was called.There is some uncertainty over how well the defending champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, will fare in the winding test through the Routes des Grand Crus, which includes the sharp climb of the Lacets de Marsannay.View image in fullscreenSigrid Haugset is the first Norwegian to wear the Tour de France Femmes yellow jersey.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters“It’s a real challenge for me,” she said, acknowledging her lack of time‑trialling experience, certainly compared with Vollering and Le Court. The double Olympic gold medallist said she has spent several months working to improve her time trialling, but accepts that she will have to “limit the damage” against the clock.“We made sure to put me in a more correct position on the time‑trial bike. We also set out to do quite a few aerodynamic tests on the track, and to try to find the fastest outfit.”Even so, she appears to accept she will be on the back foot as the peloton heads into the Rhone valley on Wednesday. “It’s a possibility,” she said. “I don’t know how much time I will lose, but I will give my best to lose the least possible.”Ferrand-Prévot is not the only rider worrying about time losses, after the pre-race favourite Vollering crashed early in stage three, on the climb of the Col de la Faucille. The 2023 winner remounted and was active later in the stage, but her team carried out medical checks on an injured knee on Monday evening.Much of the south-east of France, which will host the summit finish to Mont Ventoux on Friday and the Côte d’Azur stages on Friday and Saturday, remains under elevated risk of wildfires.While the climb of the Ventoux scheduled for stage seven is expected to remain intact, the current routing of the stage through the Ventoux’s foothills could be affected.In a statement, the Vaucluse prefecture asked the Tour de France Femmes organisers to consider an alternative route. The prefecture is planning a risk assessment on Tuesday and has said that an “alternative route will be implemented should the wildfire risk be considered extreme”.Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tadej Pogacar will ride Vuelta a España in bid to complete Grand Tour treble | Tadej Pogacar | The Guardian
description: Tadej Pogacar will return to the Vuelta a España for the first time since 2019
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Tadej Pogacar will return to the Vuelta a España for the first time since 2019
Content: Tadej Pogacar won his fifth Tour de France last month.Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Pool Getty/APView image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar won his fifth Tour de France last month.Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Pool Getty/APTadej PogacarTadej Pogacar will ride Vuelta a España in bid to complete Grand Tour trebleSlovene great last rode in Vuelta in 2019‘Time is right to go back,’ says five-time Tour winnerJeremy WhittleMon 3 Aug 2026 04.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheTour de France champion, Tadej Pogacar, has confirmed that he will race in the Vuelta a España, which starts in Monaco on 22 August. The five-time Tour winner will be ­seeking to match the rare achievement of long-term rival, Jonas Vingegaard, who completed a grand slam of all three Grand Tours, bywinning the Giro d’Italiain May.“I’m excited to say I’m going back to La Vuelta,” Pogacar said. “It was my first-ever Grand Tour back in 2019 and an amazing experience. Spain is a country I love to visit and race in and I think the time is right to go back.Tadej Pogacar’s ability to win unopposed stands champion out among Tour legends | William FotheringhamRead more“The motivation is high to finish off the year in a good way and the Vuelta will be a big target. The team is strong and we hope to do good things.”The Slovene made his Grand Tour debut in the 2019 Vuelta and was an overnight sensation, finishing third behind the winner, and compatriot, Primoz Roglic, while winning three stages and the best young rider classification.This year’s Vuelta includes eight mountain stages and more than 40km of individual time trials. From the opening weekend’s time trial in Monaco, the race heads to Andorra and follows the Mediterranean coast before a flurry of stages, centred on Córdoba, Málaga and Seville, lead to a closing stage in Granada on 13 September.Pogacar hinted midway through his successful Tour de France defence that he was likely to start the Spanish race, after Prince Albert of Monaco said he expected Pogacar to compete.“If the Prince says that, then the chance is high,” Pogacar said.But his post-Tour fatigue suggested the decision had still to be made. “Right now, I don’t feel fresh enough to ride the Vuelta if it started tomorrow,” he said after sealing overall victory in Paris, “but in two weeks I can still decide.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Although burnout has recently been a subject of debate in the peloton, with Vingegaard now expected to take the rest of the year offafter breaking his collarboneduring the Tour, Pogacar has a packed schedule for the rest of the year, including the World Road Race Championships in Montreal on 27 September, two weeks after the Vuelta finishes.Explore more on these topicsTadej PogacarVuelta a EspañaCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: More European countries’ FAs withdraw support for Infantino as pressure intensifies | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: The English FA and Serbia’s have followed Wales’s and Finland’s in dropping support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid as Fifa president
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: The English FA and Serbia’s have followed Wales’s and Finland’s in dropping support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid as Fifa president
Content: Gianni Infantino’s decade-long reign at the head of Fifa remains under intense scrutiny.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s decade-long reign at the head of Fifa remains under intense scrutiny.Photograph: Martin Meissner/APGianni InfantinoMore European countries’ FAs withdraw support for Infantino as pressure intensifiesFA no longer endorses Fifa president for re-electionWales and Serbia join Finland in withdrawing backingNick AmesandMatt HughesMon 3 Aug 2026 15.24 EDTFirst published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 03.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean countries began turning their backs onGianni Infantinoas moves intensified across the globe to end his crisis-hit tenure as Fifa president.The Football Association was the highest-profile of severalUefamember associations to drop its support for Infantino’s proposed re-election next year. It will write to Fifa confirming it no longer endorses Infantino for a fourth term in charge after the intense controversy surrounding his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors.Wales and Serbia publicly confirmed that they had withdrawn their backing, following a lead taken by Finland last week. Along with the FA, those federations had all previously written letters in favour of Infantino prolonging his tenure but patience has run out across the continent. The Swedish Football Association, which was one of five European FAs not to write letters of support, issued a statement confirming it would oppose his candidature in the election in March.Football Daily | Scrapped proposals, statement wars and the ongoing Infantino furoreRead moreThe FA had previously fallen into line behind Infantino, who will helm an extraordinary Fifa congress confirming the United Kingdom’s hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup in November if he is still in position. But it has been consistent in condemning his doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme, publicly and in private representations. On Saturday it called for a “full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance”, and its latest move is a further escalation.It is joined by the Football Association of Wales, which said in a statement: “The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino for re-election asFifapresident for the 2027-2031 term.“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”View image in fullscreenSeveral Uefa nations are mobilising against the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Pierre Albouy/ReutersStriking a similar tone, the Football Association of Serbia explained recent events had “seriously damaged the reputation and credibility of bothFifaand its president”, saying a withdrawal was “the only logical and rational step”.In a sign that consensus may not be easy to achieve, the Swiss Football Association stopped short of abandoning its countryman. Instead it asked for “another personal exchange of views with the Fifa president” and said it would “continue to review the developments surrounding Fifa” before the leadership election.More countries are, however, expected to withdraw their support for Infantino in what amounts to a vote of no confidence. The intended effect is for the embattled president to resign although some insiders are braced for a drawn-out process. While the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and Concacaf, which runs the sport in North and Central America, have both strongly criticised Infantino there has been no move by any of their individual federations to call back letters in favour of his re-election.Ensuring they do so may be critical to the ongoing efforts to remove Infantino quickly. There is acknowledgement in some parts of Europe that other continents should be seen taking the lead if enough of a groundswell for his departure is to be reached. Only 15 countries have publicly supported Infantino since he shelved the FFE project on Saturday but there is an appetite to form a broad coalition against his re-election quickly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, is a contender to take over if Infantino is deposed. Montagliani is understood to be in consensus with the Uefa and AFC hierarchies that new leadership is needed at Fifa.View image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani consoles Lionel Messi after the World Cup final.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAIn another blow to Infantino, lawyers acting for Uefa have ordered him and other staff to identify, locate and preserve all documents related to the FFE scheme. Their letter includes Arsène Wenger, the Fifa chief of global football development, among those obliged to comply with its order. It says Uefa is “actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints ... arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan”.Thrive Eternal, the investment firm that had been expected to lead a group taking a 20% stake in FFE, is believed to have been sent a similar letter. JP Morgan, which was enlisted for an advisory role in the scheme, is also understood to have received an order related to FFE.On Monday afternoon the US State Department denied reports that Infantino had been scheduled to meet Marco Rubio, the United States secretary of state, in a bid to stoke up support for his continued reign as president.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoThe FAFifaFootball politicsUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: Charlton up for sale again as US owners look to cash in after three years | Charlton Athletic | The Guardian
description: This would be a fifth owner in six years for the club whose current owners, a group led by Gabriel Brener, paid £15m for it in 2023
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: This would be a fifth owner in six years for the club whose current owners, a group led by Gabriel Brener, paid £15m for it in 2023
Content: Charlton’s men are in the Championship and their women have been promoted to the Women’s Super League.Photograph: Steven Paston/PAView image in fullscreenCharlton’s men are in the Championship and their women have been promoted to the Women’s Super League.Photograph: Steven Paston/PACharlton AthleticCharlton up for sale again as US owners look to cash in after three yearsOwners led by Gabriel Brener paid £15m in 2023Buyer would be the club’s fifth owner in six yearsExclusive byMatt HughesMon 3 Aug 2026 15.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharlton’s US owners have put the club up for sale just three years after taking over at the Valley. The ownership group is understood to have engaged Oakwell Sports Advisory to find what would be the club’s fifth owner in the past six years.In a sales deck sent to potential investors, which has been seen by the Guardian, Oakwell describes Charlton as “the last remaining football club upside opportunity in London”. Oakwell also claims that Charlton would provide new owners with an opportunity for five to 10 times equity growth through promotion to the Premier League, commercial expansion and investment in women’s football.Nathan Jones: ‘It’s not a forgiving world – people want their pound of flesh’Read moreOakwell did the deal that led to the Bournemouth owner,Bill Foley, buying the Prem rugby club Exeter Chiefsthis summer, and is helping the Rugby Football Leagueto secure external investment.Charlton’s location in south-east London is a plus, while the Valley is a modern stadium with a capacity of 27,000, but the club do not own the ground, which belongs tothe hated former owner Roland Duchâtelet. Having considered looking at alternative sites, last year Charlton extended the lease on the Valley until 2040.Charlton have repeatedly changed hands sincethe fans forced out Duchâteletin 2020, when the club had three owners in quick succession. Duchâtelet sold Charltonto East Street Investmentsfor just £1 in January 2020, but the consortium led initially by the former football agent Matt Southall collapsed amid in‑fighting and an acrimonious court case, with the club eventuallybought by the Danish-American business Thomas Sandgaardlater that year. In 2023, Sandgaard sold Charlton to a group of five US investors called Global Football Partners (GFP) led by Gabriel Brener via their UK subsidiary, SE7 Partners.Under GFP, Charlton returned to the Championship for the first time in five years in 2025 bywinning the League One playoff finalat Wembley, while the women’s teamwere promoted to WSL1 last season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGFP paid around £15m for Charlton three years ago but, having invested in the stadium and training ground and seen Nathan Jones’s side consolidate the club in theChampionship, will be looking for several times that figure. Charlton declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsCharlton AthleticChampionshipBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Benjamin Nygren edges Celtic past Dundee for winning start to title defence | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Benjamin Nygren’s second-half header edged champions Celtic to a 1-0 home victory against Dundee in their Scottish Premiership opener
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Benjamin Nygren’s second-half header edged champions Celtic to a 1-0 home victory against Dundee in their Scottish Premiership opener
Content: Benjamin Nygren heads in what proved to be Celtic’s winning goal against Dundee.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenBenjamin Nygren heads in what proved to be Celtic’s winning goal against Dundee.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAScottish PremiershipBenjamin Nygren edges Celtic past Dundee for winning start to title defencePA MediaMon 3 Aug 2026 16.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 20.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Nygren was quickly back on the goal trail as Celtic began the defence of their Premiership title with a 1-0 home win overDundee. Before the game, Celtic fans cheered as the captain, Callum McGregor, unfurled the flag which confirmed again a 14th title win in 15 seasons.It was all a bit flat in a first half with Martin O’Neill’s side struggling to get into their stride as the visitors posed problems. However, the Sweden midfielder Nygren, so prolific last season with 21 goals, struck with a close-range header in the 52nd minute and the goal proved enough to keep the three points in Glasgow as a new season got up and runningfor the champions.Scottish Premiership: Aberdeen’s late double stuns Hearts, St Johnstone edge thrillerRead moreCeltic supporters continue to call for new recruits to the squad but Camilo Durán, the Colombian striker signed from Qarabag reportedly for £5.5m, and Kasper Høgh, the Denmark forward who cost a club-record £11m plus add-ons from Bodø/Glimt, made their debuts.Alistair Johnston and Arne Engels, both attracting transfer interest, also started for the champions while the Dundee goalkeeper Owen Goodman came in for his debut.Høgh fired wide in the ninth minute after being set up by Nygren, then the Dane redirected an effort from Nygren past a post. Moments later at the other end, as the ball bounced around Celtic’s penalty area, Dundee’s Charlie Reilly hit the side netting with a shot from 12 yards.View image in fullscreenCeltic's Kasper Høgh (left) reacts after a missed chance against Dundee.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PASteven Pressley’s well-drilled outfit were finding joy with the high ball, either crosses or throw-ins and in the 33rd minute defender Owen Bevan got his head to the ball in the box but the Celtic goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo gathered comfortably.Five minutes later, Engels missed the best chance of the match to that point, unmarked in the visitors’ box, he headed a cross from Kieran Tierney past a post, before the Celtic left-back drew a fine save from Goodman with a close-range drive.The home side faltered at the start of the second half but when Tierney curled in a cross from the left, Nygren headed past Goodman from inside the box and the growing anxiety subsided.Quick GuideCeltic to play LASK in Champions League playoffShowCeltic will face LASK in the Champions League playoffs.Martin O’Neill’s side were drawn out first against the Austrian champions. The Linz-based club won the Austrian Bundesliga for the second time last season, finishing two points ahead of the defending champions Sturm Graz.The Hoops avoided a potential rematch with Kairat Almaty, who knocked Celtic out on penalties at the same stage last season following a goalless 210 minutes of action.The first leg will take place on 18/19 August, with the second leg the following week.PA MediaWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.O’Neill’s side probed with more purpose, the fans got more excited and the noise levels increased while Dundee’s attacks were more sporadic and less convincing, although the pace of Joe Bevan was cause for concern for the Parkhead defence. In the 67th minute Goodman threw himself down to his right to save a long-distance drive from forward Yang Hyun-jun.Celtic remained in control but as the second goal refused to arrive and the clock ticked on, some nerves returned. In the 82nd minute, Sinisalo pulled off a terrific save from the Dundee substitute Ashley Hay’s glancing header.Høgh missed another chance when he slid a shot past a post from six yards before McGregor cracked the upright with an effort from inside Dundee’s penalty area; James Forrest bent the rebound wide of the target.Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipCelticDundeematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Newcastle reject first bid from Arsenal for captain Bruno Guimarães | Newcastle United | The Guardian
description: The Premier League champions’ £70m offer for the Brazil midfielder, who has joined Newcastle for pre-season, has been turned down
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: The Premier League champions’ £70m offer for the Brazil midfielder, who has joined Newcastle for pre-season, has been turned down
Content: Bruno Guimarães has two years left on his Newcastle contract.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães has two years left on his Newcastle contract.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PANewcastle UnitedNewcastle reject first bid from Arsenal for captain Bruno GuimarãesPremier League champions have £70m offer turned downBrazil midfielder has arrived at Newcastle training campLouise TaylorMon 3 Aug 2026 11.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal have stepped up their attempt to sign Bruno Guimarãesby finally beginning formal transfer negotiations and making an opening offer, which Newcastle have rejected.Guimarães met Newcastle’s incoming manager, Matthias Jaissle, for the first time on Monday at the team’s pre-season training camp at La Manga after a post-World Cup holiday in Brazil.Jaissle heads for Newcastle after success in Saudi Arabia that has eluded so manyRead moreThere had been suggestions that the 28-year-old midfielder would fly to London for a medical at Arsenal, but instead he boarded a commercial flight to Spain.Once at La Manga, he was expected to tell Jaissle of his determination to swap Tyneside for north London, but everything hinges on whether Arsenal are prepared to meet Newcastle’s valuation for a player with two years remaining on his contract.While executives at Arsenal believe Guimarães is worth a maximum of £70m – and a bid in that ballpark was rejected on Monday – Newcastle value their captain at around £80m.If some sort of compromise seems likely given Arsenal – negotiating, initially, through intermediaries – have spent much of this summer in pursuit of a midfielder at the top of Mikel Arteta’s shopping list, Newcastle are under no pressure to sell.View image in fullscreenGuimarães has had several battles with Arsenal over the past few seasons.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersIndeed,having sold Anthony Gordonand Sandro Tonali to Barcelonaand Tottenham respectivelythis summer, they would prefer to offer Jaissle the benefit of Guimarães’s talent and experience as he rebuilds the squad.The 38-year-old was believed to be keen to assess the Brazilian’s mindset as he begins preparations for the opening Premier League match at home against Liverpool two weeks on Sunday. Although the former Al‑Ahli and RB Salzburg manager is still to be officially confirmedas Howe’s successor, Jaissle has been with his new squad since arriving in southern Spain on Saturday. Newcastle are waiting for the completion of some final paperwork before formalising his appointment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne signing completed by Newcastle on Monday involved Lukas Hornicek’s £26m move from Braga. The 24-year-old Czechia goalkeeper is expected to replace Nick Pope as the team’s first choice, with Pope now likely to leave St James’ Park.Hornicek caught Newcastle’s eye after seven clean sheetsduring Braga’s runto the Europa League semi-finals last season. At 6ft 6in, he cuts an imposing figure in goal and has been highly praised for the sort of high-calibre footwork that should improve Newcastle’s ability to play out from the back.Hull had hoped to recruit Hornicek, but he turned down a move to the promoted club last month.Explore more on these topicsNewcastle UnitedTransfer windowArsenalnewsShareReuse this content

title: On the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all time | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts at the Czech’s chip
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts at the Czech’s chip
Content: Antonin Panenka left Sepp Maier flailing in the 1976 Euros final, but not every attempt to emulate him has gone as well.Photograph: Colorsport/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAntonin Panenka left Sepp Maier flailing in the 1976 Euros final, but not every attempt to emulate him has gone as well.Photograph: Colorsport/ShutterstockSoccerOn the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all timeThe 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts at the Czech’s chipGuardian sportMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.30 EDTShareIt is 50 years since Antonin Panenka won the European Championship for Czechoslovakia with the most audacious penalty ever taken. His signature chip wasn’t instantly eponymous. A search of the British newspaper archives shows that it was barely mentioned until Francesco Tottidusted it offfor the internet generation at Euro 2000.It was at least another decade before Panenka was commonly used as a noun, and it did not have its own Wikipedia page until 2014, but in 2026 every football fan has an idea of what it means.The 50th anniversaryis the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts.A Panenka is in the eye of the beholder.Ben Lyttleton, doyen of penalties and author of the superb Twelve Yards,asked the man himselfwhat constituted a true Panenka. Their criteria is strict, based on the line of the ball, its trajectory and where it hits the net. But that disqualifies, among others, Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 World Cup final (“This penalty is the obvious misuse of the Panenka classification!”), so we’ve used a looser definition. If the ball was kissed rather than kicked, the penalty is eligible.Rob SmythView image in fullscreenThe man himself, pictured earlier this year.Photograph: Björn Steinz/The GuardianAntonin Panenka, 1976Czechoslovakia 2-2 West Germany (5-3 pens)This oneneeds no introduction.RSAntonin Panenka, 1979Czechoslovakia 2-0 FranceThe next high-profile Panenka came almost three years after Belgrade, when he fooled the France keeper Dominique Dropsywith a sensual chipin a vital European Championship qualifier. Czechoslovakia ultimately pipped an emerging France – Michel Platini et al – and finished third at Euro 80.RSDiego Maradona, 1984Napoli trainingMost of Diego Maradona’s penalties were high-wire acts, Panenkas in spirit, with the ball pointedly passed nowhere near the corner toensure maximum vaccination. We can’t find any examples of him taking an actual Panenka in a professional game, so we’re including one he took in training at Napoli. Two reasons: one, it’s Maradona; and two, the arc of his penalty shouldn’t be possible. But then we’d alreadyseen him do it in open play.RSEric Cantona, 1989Bordeaux 1-1 Beauvais (3-4 pens)In February 1989, Eric Cantona was famed more for attitude than ability, having served bans for a tackleof comic-book violence, insulting the France coach, and greeting a friendly substitution by blootering the ball into crowdand tossing his shirt. So Marseille loaned him to Bordeaux and, when a cup game against lower-division Beauvais went to penalties, he went last. Juggling his way to the spot,he tried a Panenka, but the effort held up in the wind before landing in a puddle, allowing the keeper, who’d gone the wrong way, to wander over and pick it up, confirming the upset.Daniel HarrisGianluca Vialli, 1990Monaco 2-2 SampdoriaIn the 20th century, certainly in England, a Panenka was generally referred to as a “cheeky chip”. It was also a favourite of a cheeky chap. Gianluca Vialli scored several for Sampdoria, often under extreme pressure:against Genoain the Scudetto-winning season of 1990-91, and twice during Samp’s Cup Winners’ Cup triumph of 1989-90.The firstwas against Borussia Dortmund in the last 16,the secondin the first leg of the semi-final against Arsène Wenger’s Monaco. Vialli scored two goals in four minutes that night, then two in three when Sampdoria beat Anderlecht 2-0in the final.RSMichal Bilek, 1990Czechoslovakia 5-1 USAIt’s neat that another Czech player was the first to try a Panenka at a World Cup, even if the circumstances were completely different. Czechoslovakia were 4-1 up in a group game against the USA when Michal Bilek, who had already scored one orthodox penalty, tried to pay tribute to 1976.He fluffed it. After making a simple save, the USA keeper Tony Meola barked: “Get that shit outta here!”RSGary Lineker, 1992Nottingham Forest 1-1 TottenhamNobody ever talks about the Panenkas that Gary Lineker scored. There were at least three for Tottenham, and we’re pretty sure he’s the first serial Panenka-er in English football. The first completed a hat-trick on live TV – a big deal back in 1990 – and led toa brief post-match discussionin which only one of Elton Welsby and Glenn Hoddle knew about the Euro 76 final. Lineker also scored “a nifty little Panenka”, as he put it, in a Rumbelows Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest.This one was particularly sweet– the keeper was Mark Crossley, a penalty-saving expert who had denied Lineker from the spot in the previous season’s FA Cup final.RSGary Lineker, 1992England 1-1 BrazilA kick remembered for comedic reasons, largely through Micah Richards and Alan Shearerchuckling about it every few months on their podcast. But at the time this was a moment of pathos and heartbreak,as Lineker passed up his best, if not his last, chance to equal Bobby Charlton’s all-time England goal record.Jonathan LiewView image in fullscreenWith a share of England’s goalscoring record for the taking, Gary Lineker dinks tamely into the arms of the Brazil goalkeeper Carlos.Illustration: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty ImagesEric Cantona, 1994Manchester United 1-1 Newcastle United (5-6 pens)In May 1994, Eric Cantona was untouchable, having inspired Manchester United to a league title then a double. In the FA Cup final,he’d gently rolled two penaltiesinto the same corner of the net, Chelsea’s Dmitri Kharine diving the wrong way as if compelled by the shamanic power of Gallic flair. But in a shootout against Newcastle at that summer’s illustrious Ibrox International Challenge Trophy, the success of his previous Panenka in 1989 persuaded him to try another. Pavel Srnicek obligingly dived out of the wayonly for the kick to sail over the baras United lost 6-5.DHDjalminha, 1995Guarani 2-1 InternacionalBrazil’s Djalminha, the maverick’s maverick, is best remembered for hissignature rainbow flick, so it’s no surprise he was partial to a rainbow kick from the penalty spot.The first of manywas scored against Sergio Goycoechea,whose elastic penalty saveshad taken Argentina to the final of Italia 90. “I noticed that he always jumped early and committed to a corner,” said Djalminha, “so I thought that was the moment to try the chip.” It quickly became tried and trusted.RSDwight Yorke, 1996Sheffield United 0-1 Aston VillaDwight Yorke was so sick of Mark Bosnich saving his penalties in training, he tried something completely different. It worked, so he promised to do it for real the next time Aston Villa were given a spot-kick. That was met with ridicule,but Yorke was true to his wordand settled an FA Cup tie at Bramall Lane with a goal that changed his life. “Suddenly,” said Yorke in Born to Score, “the football world was very aware of this cheeky young buck who had dared to execute such an outrageous spot-kick. I definitely detected an increased interest in me after that match.”RSGianluca Vialli, 1996Chelsea 2-4 WimbledonThere’s no Internet Panenka Database (IPDb), which makes it impossible to say categorically who did what when. ButVialli’s consolation Panenka, at the end of a game in which Chelsea were thrashed by a rampant Wimbledon, may be the first of the Premier League era. Neil Sullivan, who had been beaten from the halfway line bya very different kind of chipearlier in the season, came tantalisingly close to saving it.RSDwight Yorke, 1998Aston Villa 1-0 Arsenal“If the penalty taker has the bottle to do that, good luck to him,” said David Seaman,who was Panenka-edon the last day of the 1997-98 season. “There isn’t much a goalie can do except look pretty stupid when it goes in.” Or hold their position, which Seaman did when Yorke took another penalty against him nine months later in an epic league match between Manchester United and Arsenal. His bluff called,Yorke sidefooted wide.RSJohn Eyre, 1999Torquay 0-1 Hull CityIf only there was a transcript of the great Neville Southall’s internal monologue asthis piece of effronteryfloated gently past him.RSFrancesco Totti, 2000Netherlands 0-0 Italy (1-3 pens)In their Euro 2000 semi-final with the co-hosts, Italy put on a defensive masterclass while down to 10 men. In the inevitable shootout, Frank de Boer was denied by Francesco Toldo and Jaap Stam blasted his kick into orbit. Stam was immediately followed by Francesco Totti,whose falling leaf penaltyfoxed Edwin van der Sar and had the Dutch lurching towards despair. It also introduced the Panenka to a new generation.John BrewinView image in fullscreenFrancesco Totti brings the Panenka into the 21st century.Illustration: Henri Szwarc/Bongarts/Getty ImagesMixu Paatelainen, 2001Hibernian 0-0 HeartsA last-minute penalty to win an Edinburgh derby is the stuff of dreams – and nightmares.Mixu Paatelainen only took itbecause Hibs’ usual taker, Russell Latapy, had gone awol two days earlier. After scoring a hat-trick against Hearts earlier in the season, Paatelainen probably thought he could do anything. As his chipped effort sailed over the bar, he was disabused of the notion.RSThierry Henry, 2003Arsenal 3-2 NewcastleFive days after the Battle of Old Trafford, Arsenal kickstarted their Invincible season with a ding-dong win over Bobby Robson’s Newcastle. The winner wasteased softly down the middleby Henry. Maybe it was an unspoken message of defiance that Arsenal would continue to do things their own way. Maybe it meant nothing. Or maybe he was justtrolling Ruud van Nistelrooy.RSView image in fullscreenThierry Henry went full va-va-voom for his winning penalty against Newcastle.Illustration: Jamie McDonald/Getty ImagesMickaël Landreau, 2004Nantes 1-1 Sochaux (4-5 pens)For all the spot-kicks these keepers face, surely they’d understand the right and wrong way to disguise a Panenka.Not poor Mickaël Landreau. He had the chance to secure the 2004 Coupe de la Ligue final for Nantes, but his headlong dash failed to give his lob the requisite power. Sochaux ultimately flipped the result and won the cup.Jeff RueterLiam Lawrence, 2004Huddersfield 0-0 Mansfield (4-1 pens)Liam Lawrence scored 12 penalties, one short of Francis Lee’s English league record, to help Mansfield to the Third Division playoff final in 2003-04. When that game wheezed to a penalty competition, Lawrence was standing on the halfway line with his teammate Bobby Hassell (“a proper angry little fella”). Onthe Under the Cosh podcast, Lawrence remembered their exchange.double quotation markLLI’m gonna dink it.BHNo you’re not.LLI am, honestly. I’m gonna dink it down t’middle. He’s gonna dive; there’s no way he’s gonna stand there in a playoff final.BHLiam, don’t you fuckin’ dink that ball.He dinked that ball against the bar– “I got too much juice in my run-up” – to leave Mansfield 2-0 down after two penalties. “By the way,” Lawrence added, “the keeper did dive.”RSHelder Postiga, 2004Portugal 2-2 England (6-5 pens)Helder Postiga was a typical Tottenham signing of the era: a talent unfulfilled, sold at a loss after a single Premier League goal. His revenge on English football was to equalise in normal time of the Euro 2004 quarter-final and then send David James stumbling with Portugal’s sixth penalty,a kick so under-ampedit barely scraped over the line. Then Darius Vassell missed, the Portugal keeper Ricardo scored, and a tournament that England’s golden generation could have won had slipped from their grasp.JBPeter Crouch, 2006England 6-0 JamaicaThe then-Liverpool strikerscored an England hat-trickas part of World Cup preparations, yet many only remember him lifting the ballwell over the barfrom 12 yards. Arrogance certainly played its part, wanting to secure his treble in style, but he had to wait, earning the ire of the usually calm Sven-Göran Eriksson. “It was a golden opportunity to practise for a penalty shootout, but he made a joke out of it,” the head coach spewed. “He’s apologised.”Will UnwinView image in fullscreenJudging by his expression, Peter Crouch knew he’d got his penalty wrong as soon as he hit it.Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesArtem Milevskiy, 2006Ukraine 0-0 Switzerland (3-0 pens)You’re excused if you don’t remember this one: it cameafter 120 minutesof the most soporific footballever played.RSZinedine Zidane, 2006Italy 1-1 France (5-3 pens)The nerve to do it in a World Cupfinal.The scene was nothing new for Zidane. He’d already bagged that brace eight years earlier against Brazil; it had to be him, in his last game, dinking it off the crossbar,past Gianluigi Buffon. It was going to be the dream sendoff – untilMarco Materazzi and the anger took over.Taha HashimView image in fullscreenZinedine Zidane steps up…Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreen… and beats Gianluigi Buffon all ends up.Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Archive/PA ImagesYann Kermogant, 2010Cardiff 2-3 Leicester (agg: 3-3; 4-3 pens)To miss a Panenka is to embrace infamy. To do so in a Championship playoff is to be consumed by notoriety. In a shootout, with the decisive kick? Insanity. Kermogant, a useful French striker who found his home in England’s second tier,dollied his kickinto the body of the grateful Cardiff keeper, David Marshall. Kermogant is remembered for this moment above all others, possibly for eternity. He even hashis own Bonnie Tyler adaptation.JBSebastián Abreu, 2010Uruguay 1-1 Ghana (4-2 pens)If we were picking a Panenka XI, Sebastián Abreu would be one ofthe first names on the team sheet, so it’s apt that he administered one at a World Cup.A tumultuous quarter-final, best remembered for Luis Suárez’s handball and Asamoah Gyan missing a penalty in the last minute of extra-time, ended with the softest of executions.RSAndrea Pirlo, 2012England 0-0 Italy (2-4 pens)When England somehow prolonged their Euro 2012 quarter-final against Italy to penalties, and with his team leading 2-1 after two goes each, Joe Hart bounced and laughed, seeking to put Andrea Pirlo off … then plunged towards the corner as the ballwafted gently above him and in. “He felt I was too charged not to dive,” Hart reflected on a mood-switching moment. England missed their next two kicks, with two Italian successesfinishing them off. “I saw [Hart] making strange movements, so I hit it like that,” Pirlo confirmed afterwards.DHView image in fullscreenAndrea Pirlo icily dinks his penalty over a fired-up Joe Hart.Illustration: Matthias Schräder/APSergio Ramos, 2012Spain 0-0 Portugal (4-2 pens)For such a tactile defender, Sergio Ramos was surprisingly partial to a tender Panenka. His most important came in the Euro 2012 semi-finalagainst Portugal. Bruno Alvesmissed Portugal’s next kickand Spain went on to demolish Italy in the final.RSMaicosuel, 2012Udinese 1-1 Braga (agg: 2-2; 4-5 pens)The one that cost €20m. Maicosuel had just joined Udinese from Botafogo when his Panenkawas savedin a Champions League playoff against Braga. It was the only miss of the shootout. Udinese, coached by Francesco Guidolin, dropped into the Europa League and the big payday went to Braga. “I still can’t get it out of my head,” said Guidolin six years later. “It stalks me.”RSGraziano Pellè, 2012SC Heerenveen 2-2 Feyenoord (6-7 pens)Sudden death, the last 16 of the cup. You’re the seventh-choice penalty-taker, you have to score or it’s over, and you have the chutzpahto try aPellènka?RSRogério Ceni, 2013São Paulo 0-0 Corinthians (3-4 pens)No surprise that one ofthe great goalscoring keepersshould beat his opposite number with a Panenka. His reaction after scoring in this Campeonato Paulista semi-final shootout carried a simple message: it’s not personal, it’s strictly business. His São Paulo team lost anyway; Ceni thought he had kept them alive with a save from Alexandre Pato, but he wasfractionally off his line. Pato scored the retake emphatically.RSAlexandre Pato, 2013Gremio 0-0 Corinthians (3-2 pens)Five months later, Pato had to score to keep Corinthians in their Copa do Brasil quarter-final against Grêmio. It was an inopportune time to takeone of the worst Panenkas ever seen.RSAlexis Sánchez, 2015Chile 0-0 Argentina (4-1 pens)It’s impossible to top the historic significance of the definitive Panenka, but Alexis Sánchez came closer than anyone.His swaggering penalty, which barely left the ground, won Chile their first Copa América – andunlike Czechoslovakia in 1976,they were the hosts. The playful nature of Sánchez’s winning moment only added to the nationwide euphoria.RSAaron Ramsey, 2017Serbia 1-1 WalesThe Wales team of Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey and co regularly made history. In a World Cup qualifier in 2017, Ramseyunwittingly did soby scoring a Panenkaat the same endof the same ground in Belgrade where it all began. “I didn’t know,” he said, “but that is quite a nice touch.” In more ways than one.RSView image in fullscreenAaron Ramsey does a Panenka more completely than most.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/ReutersGeorge Calintaru, 2017Juventus Bucuresti 1-2 Steaua BucurestiA Panenka can seriously damage your health. When George Calintaru fluffed the chance to equalise for newly-promoted Juventus Bucuresti against Steaua with the last kick of the game, his teammates set upon him in frustration. He then punched a table in the dressing room and broke a finger.RSFedor Smolov, 2018Russia 2-2 Croatia (3-4 pens)Russia’s shock run to the 2018 World Cup quarter-final was soundtracked by raucous support. The crowd in Sochi met the occasion as a shootout with Croatia was all that stood between them and a semi-final. Pedants may contend thatFedor Smolov’s opening attemptlacked enough lob to qualify as a Panenka, but his tame prod up the middle made Danijel Subasic’s job easy to open the sequence in Croatia’s favour.JRLionel Messi, 2020Barcelona 2-2 Atlético MadridIf you’re going to bring up 700 career goals in an empty stadium,you might as well do it in style.RSView image in fullscreenLionel Messi’s penalty record is suprisingly human, but he got the one that gave him his 700th goal right.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty ImagesFara Williams, 2020Reading 3-1 Aston VillaThis unusual penaltyfrom Fara Williams might not satisfy the Panenka purists. But we’ve included it because it captures a recurring sub-genre: an all-time-great using the Panenka as an expression of undeniable superiority.RSAdemola Lookman, 2020West Ham 1-0 FulhamDuring his time at Fulham, Ademola Lookman attempted a Panenka against West Ham with the last kick of the gamebut his feeble chiplanded straight in the arms of Lukasz Fabianski. “I’m disappointed and angry,” said his manager Scott Parker in a rare momentof post-match honesty. “You can’t take penalties like that and he knows that.”Yara El-ShabourySanti Cazorla, 2021Al-Gharafa 0-2 Al SaddNot many players score orthodox penalties with their left and right feet, never mind Panenkas. Santi Cazorla is a member of the latter club – right footagainst Newcastle in 2014, left foot against Al-Gharafa in 2021.RSSergio Agüero, 2021Man City 1-2 ChelseaCity were set to secure the Premier League title but, in front of zero fans during Covid, Sergio Agüero did not feel the pressure. He decided tochip down the middle; Édouard Mendyalmost fell for itbut had enough time to get up and claim the ball. Chelsea went on to win, and Agüeroissued a public apology.WUView image in fullscreenSergio Agüero’s Panenka attempt almost, but crucially only almost, fools Édouard Mendy.Photograph: Shaun Botterill/AFP/Getty ImagesMarta, 2022France 2-1 BrazilBirthday gifts can be a pain to give, especially when the celebrant seems to have given themself the perfect present. Such was life if Marta was on your gift-giving list in 2022, with the Brazilian legend opening that day’s friendly against Francein sublime fashion.JRKarim Benzema, 2022Manchester City 4-3 Real MadridA moment of mischiefat the end of a pulsating and painfully serious match. Eight days later, Benzema scored a more orthodox penalty to put Madrid into another Champions League final.RSView image in fullscreenReal Madrid’s improbable run to winning the 2022 Champions League included Karim Benzema coming up clutch – again.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAchraf Hakimi, 2022Morocco 0-0 Spain (3-0 pens)If you’re going to put your country into their first World Cup quarter-final,you might as well do it in style.RSGaëtane Thiney, 2023Real Madrid 0-1 Paris FCWe can’t say for sure thatthisis the first Panenka in the Women’s Champions League, but it’s definitely the first to knock Real Madrid out of the competition.RSAntoine Mille, 2024Les Herbiers 2-2 Châteauroux (3-4 pens)In which the Les Herbiers goalkeeper Téo Hamelin is so affronted that, after savingone of the more pitiful Panenkasever taken, he flings the ball straight back at the unfortunate Mille.RSMarta, 2025Orlando Pride 2-1 San Diego WaveIf you have already missed your penalty, but opponents’ encroachment has given you a second chance, just how bold do you have to be to attempt a Panenka from the retake? That’s what Marta did in the NWSL for Orlando Pride in 2025,chipping in off the underside of the crossbarto secure a 2-1 victory over San Diego Wave, and remind everybody of her ageless class and skill.Tom GarryAlexia Putellas, 2025Roma 0-4 BarcelonaEven the greats fluff their efforts sometimes. Alexia Putellas, one of the best women’s footballers of all time, clipped a Panenkaharmlessly over the crossbarduring a Champions League victory for Barcelona when her team were only 1-0 up. She redeemed herself from the spot later in the match – that time, tucking safely into the bottom corner.TGTiaguinho, 2025Brazil U17 0-0 Paraguay U17 (5-4 pens)A Panenka is a dishbest servedcold.RSBrahim Díaz, 2026Morocco 3-0* SenegalBrahim Díaz had the chance to become a Moroccan hero when he won and then took a stoppage-time penalty that could have ended his country’s 50-year trophy wait. Instead, after a 16-minute delay caused by Senegal’s protests, his Panenkawas easily caught by Édouard Mendy. “He had a lot of time before taking the penalty, which must have disturbed him,” said the Morocco manager Walid Regragui. No kidding.Then again…YE-SView image in fullscreenBrahim Díaz’s miss saw Morocco squander their chance to win the Afcon. Or so we thought…Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty ImagesMohamed Salah, 2026Australia 1-1 Egypt (2-4 pens)Sixty-one penalties were taken at the 2026 World Cup. The surprise is thatMo Salah’s Panenka for Egypt in their shootout against Australiawas the only one. Fifty years after it came straight outta leftfield, the Panenka is now firmly part of the mainstream.RS

title: ‘They are terrified’: Como spark row with fans over controversial new stadium policy | Como | The Guardian
description: Como will revoke season tickets from fans who fail to attend four home matches, under a series of new rules that have sparked a row among supporters
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Como will revoke season tickets from fans who fail to attend four home matches, under a series of new rules that have sparked a row among supporters
Content: Como were marooned in Serie D in 2018-19 but will be playing in the Champions League this season.Photograph: Mairo Cinquetti/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenComo were marooned in Serie D in 2018-19 but will be playing in the Champions League this season.Photograph: Mairo Cinquetti/NurPhoto/ShutterstockComo‘They are terrified’: Como spark row with fans over controversial new stadium policySupporters must not miss more than three home gamesSerie A club’s chairman defends new rulesLorenzo Tondoin PalermoMon 3 Aug 2026 08.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleComo, the surprise package of last season’s Serie A, who qualified for the Champions Leaguefor the first time, will revoke season tickets from fans who fail to attend four home matches, under a series of new rules that have sparked a row among supporters.The club,coached by the former Arsenal midfielder Cesc Fàbregas, said on Monday that supporters “who miss more than three home matches without what it considers a valid reason risk having their season tickets revoked”. Another new rule bans fans from wearing the opposing team’s shirts or scarves anywhere in the stadium except the away section.Como’s ascent to Champions League offers bright note amid Serie A chaos | Nicky BandiniRead more“Demand for tickets far exceeds supply and, for that reason, I asked the club to find ways to ensure tickets for the [Giuseppe Sinigaglia stadium] end up in the hands of genuine Como supporters – those who want to be there to back the team,” the chair, Mirwan Suwarso,said in a lengthy statement on Instagram.“There have been too many occasions when away fans have celebrated inside our home sections, whileComosupporters, who would have proudly backed the team, were unable to get a ticket.”On the ban on wearing rival teams’ shirts, scarves and other symbols outside the away end, the club said the measure was introduced for safety reasons. “Our aim is to make the Sinigaglia the true home of our fans and a fortress for our team,” said Suwarso. “We want to ensure the Sinigaglia remains a place where grandparents feel comfortable bringing their grandchildren, where families can enjoy football together, and where passion never crosses the line into disrespect.”On social media, many criticised the measures as overly harsh, arguing that work commitments, health issues or family responsibilities can prevent people from attending matches without making them any less loyal to the club.La Provincia, Como’s local newspaper, said its newsroom had received dozens of calls and emails from concerned supporters. “Some worried about health problems or being unable to attend because of bad weather, as well as people who frequently travel for work,” the newspaper wrote. “They are terrified and all asking the same question: will our season tickets be taken away?”Italy’s national newspaper, Corriere della Sera, reporting reactions from supporters on social media, quoted one fan asking: “Do we need to be accompanied by our parents when we hand in our excuse, like at school?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the 2018-19 season, Como were in Serie D, the fourth tier of Italian football, after going bankrupt twice in the previous 15 years. Last season, the small northern Italian club finished fourth after an extraordinary campaign,producing a series of outstanding performancesthat surprised the football world.Explore more on these topicsComoSerie AEuropean club footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Worn in the USA: Liverpool’s pre-season tour had highs but exposed glaring gaps in the squad | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Teenager Nyoni excelled in Andoni Iraola’s first pre-season tour with Liverpool, but the head coach desperately needs transfers
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Teenager Nyoni excelled in Andoni Iraola’s first pre-season tour with Liverpool, but the head coach desperately needs transfers
Content: Andoni Iraola (second right) applauds Liverpool fans after seeing his side concede four goals in the second half against Leeds.Photograph: Shaina Benhiyoun/SPP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndoni Iraola (second right) applauds Liverpool fans after seeing his side concede four goals in the second half against Leeds.Photograph: Shaina Benhiyoun/SPP/ShutterstockLiverpoolAnalysisWorn in the USA: Liverpool’s pre-season tour had highs but exposed glaring gaps in the squadAndy Hunterin ChicagoTeenager Nyoni excelled in Andoni Iraola’s first pre-season tour, but the head coach desperately needs transfersMon 3 Aug 2026 06.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareAndoni Iraola’s first pre-season tour as the Liverpool head coach produced wins overSunderland in NashvilleandWrexham in New Yorkbefore ending ina 4-2 defeat against Leedsin Chicago. The Guardian followed the tour throughout and here are a few things we learned.Iraola’s visionwill take timeLiverpool’s second-half display against Leeds was both concerning and valuable for the Iraola as set-piece problems and a tendency to switch off – two of last season’s recurring themes – reared their ugly head again, albeit after he had made changes. Liverpool’s opening 45 minutes, however, was their best of the tour and showed how effective his front-foot, more intense style can be with the big names back. But that process is only just under way.Iraola is yet to even meet Virgil van Dijk, Cody Gakpo, Alisson, Alexis Mac Allister andnew signing Víctor Muñozsince his appointment almost two months ago, never mind coach them. They will be finally acquainted when the squad reports back for training on Wednesday, having been given a little time off to recover from Sunday night’s flight from Chicago. Mac Allister will be still absent after his World Cup exertions. There is less than three weeks to go and only two more friendlies (although it is a double-header against Como at Anfield) before Liverpool open their Premier League season at Newcastle. “I would like to say on the first day we are going to be perfect, everyone will be in place,” Iraola said. “But probably it is not going to be like this.”Head coach needs more backingFor most of the tour, Iraola was without eight first-team players due to World-Cup holidays and six because of injury, either recovering from or, as in the unfortunate Joe Gomez’s case, sustained in the US. No prizes for stating that Liverpool’s performances and adaptation to Iraola’s methods would have been much more advanced with 14 extra first-team players available. Even so, glaring gaps remain in the team when every option is taken into account.View image in fullscreenLiverpool knew about Mohamed Salah’s departure months ago, but have yet to line up a replacement.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersMohamed Salah’s departure was announced in March. Talks to end his contract one year early commenced earlier. Five months on from the announcement, he is yet to be replaced. The seriousness of Conor Bradley’s knee injury means Liverpool remain light at right-back. There are the highest hopes forJérémy Jacquetand Giovanni Leoni – the latter has transformed himself into a strapping Adonis while recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury, by the way – while 18-year-olds Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye did well in the US. But Liverpool are lacking Premier League experience in central defence and Ndukwe will be unable to play this season due to post-Brexit work permit difficulties. Gomez’s injury record means he must be considered a bonus when fit, rather than one of four options. It was interesting to hear Iraola explain how he likes wingers to play both flanks, and the advantages of switching them during a game, but Liverpool’s right side could be a problem even if they succeedin signing Bradley Barcolafrom Paris Saint-Germain.View image in fullscreenTrey Nyoni’s confident and assured displays pressed his case for more Liverpool game time.Photograph: Kamil Krzaczyński/AFP/Getty ImagesNyoni is now firmly in Iraola’splansThere was an enforced reliance on young players during the tour and Iraola was genuinely impressed by the levels many showed in training and the friendlies. Ndukwe and Talla Ndiaye, as mentioned, Lewis Koumas, Kieran Morrison and Luke Chambers were among them. But no prospect pushed their first team claims further than Trey Nyoni, who grew in stature and confidence with every outing. The 19-year-old and Rio Ngumoha were permanent fixtures in Arne Slot’s squad last season, but while the winger made 19 appearances in the Premier League, including five starts, Nyoni had to settle for six league outings from the bench. On this evidence, there will be many more this season. The midfielder looked immediately at ease with Iraola’s instructions to find forward options as quickly as possible and did so whether under pressure or by creating space for himself with intelligent movement. His pass in the buildup to Florian Wirtz’s goal against Leeds was exquisite and in keeping with his contribution overall. Nyoni said after the Leeds game he knew he had to improve this summer. He was as good as his word.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJones did not seize chanceTo pinch a phrase from Salah, Curtis Jones looked more out than in at times as he enters the final 12 months of his Liverpool contract with increasing interest from the Italian champions, Inter. Unlike Nyoni and Dominik Szoboszlai, the 25-year-old did not adapt comfortably to Iraola’s requirements for a central midfielder and particularly struggled when introduced in the second half against Leeds. But it was his petulant reaction to not receiving the captain’s armband from Szoboszlai against Wrexham that did him fewest favours.Jones was also overlooked for the captaincy when Gomez exited the opening game against Sunderland. On both occasions the armband was passed to Kostas Tsimikas, a reserve left-back who spent last season on loan at Roma. Of course, that was going to annoy a boyhood Liverpool fan and one of the more senior players on the tour, and Jones, Szoboszlai and Tsimikas all went to great lengths to laugh off the incident in the days after the Wrexham win. The row might have been overblown on social media, but givenIraola stresses the importance of the collective, Jones’s individualistic behaviour jarred with what he is trying to build.View image in fullscreenDominik Szoboszlai led the way for Liverpool on the US tour.Photograph: Daniel Bartel/Getty ImagesSzoboszlai wins popularity contestIn the absence of Salah, Andy Robertson, Van Dijk and Alisson, and in keeping with his status as Liverpool’s player of last season, Szoboszlai was undoubtedly the big attraction for fans in the US. The Hungary captain’s every introduction and contribution was met with fanatical acclaim and his was the face the media wanted on their channels. More importantly for Iraola, Szoboszlai led the way in training and his leadership was invaluable given the relative inexperience of the squad. Fresh from signing a new five-year contract, the 25-year-old is an obvious choice to fill one of the vice-captain vacancies created by the departures of Salah and Robertson.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Marc Skinner may have been a Marmite manager but Manchester United’s budget was spread thin | Manchester United Women | The Guardian
description: He divided opinion but made the most of a small budget – his successor must work with youngsters not big signings
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: He divided opinion but made the most of a small budget – his successor must work with youngsters not big signings
Content: Marc Skinner leaves Manchester United after five years, he was the longest-serving manager in the Women’s Super League.Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenMarc Skinner leaves Manchester United after five years, he was the longest-serving manager in the Women’s Super League.Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/ReutersManchester United WomenMarc Skinner may have been a Marmite manager but Manchester United’s budget was spread thinTom GarryHe divided opinion but made the most of a small budget – his successor must work with youngsters not big signingsMon 3 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShare“If we want to compete at this later stage, we’ve seen what we’ve got to do, as a club. It’s our choice now, isn’t it? We have to look at what we seriously want to achieve … It takes, sometimes, a punch in the face to wake up.”Those were the words of the Manchester United head coach Marc Skinner after his side were knocked out of the Women’s Champions League by Bayern Munich in April. Just over four months later, the bruise from that punch has faded, but so, it would seem, have the club’s ambitions to compete in the transfer market, and Skinner has decided not to get into the ring for another round.Marc Skinner leaves Manchester United Women head coach role amid transfer frustrationRead moreThe 43-year-old wanted that run to the quarter-finals to trigger further investment in the squad. The club, though, feel that the levels of spending in the transfer market are unsustainable and therefore want to focus on developing their own talent. Once that juxtaposition was firmly established this summer, it was inevitable that Skinner and United were likely to part company, as they did on Monday, to end his five years in charge.United’s Marmite manager, Skinner certainly divided opinion in the WSL. He was the league’s longest-serving manager by a distance, but arguably also the most heavily maligned coach online. In the sport, though, there are coaches who admire the job he did on – according to the most recent set of WSL club’s financial accounts – a little more than a third of the playing budget of Chelsea and around half that of Arsenal’s.View image in fullscreenMarc Skinner instructs his players in a Champions League tie against Brann in September 2025.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersFor members of the media, Skinner’s press conferences will probably be one of the most memorable aspects of his tenure, unique because of the extensive length of the former Birmingham and Orlando head coach’s answers. For example, before the 2025 Women’s FA Cup final, one of his answers was 1,000 words long.To some, his determination to provide long, considered responses was a sign of his thoughtfulness and showed an admirable desire to be transparent. To others, his drawn-out answers demonstrated an inability to be concise and this communication problem dogged his relationship with the fans throughout much of his tenure. Often, unintentionally, his words would irritate sections of the fanbase. In 2025, one former United player privately described Skinner as a “great bloke, but he goes on a bit” and it is fair to say not every player liked his team-talk style, while others enjoyed his passion.On the pitch, the 2022-23 season, Skinner’s second, was the club’s strongest as they finished second in the table, boosted by a robust defensive record, conceding 12 times in 22 games, and they came within a whisker of winning the title. Then there was the comparatively low moment of languishing in fifth in the 2023-24 campaign, counteracted bywinning the Women’s FA Cup, United’s first major women’s trophy.Yet, whether you loved him or loathed him at Leigh Sports Village, Skinner overachieved at United on a purely pound-for-pound basis, reaching four domestic cup finals – including three consecutive Women’s FA Cup finals – despite typically operating on a mid‑table budget for much of his incumbency.He was certainly not every player’s cup of tea, and there will be lessons he will need to learn from the highs and lows of his five years at the club, but now that both of the coaches who have managed United’s women in the modern era have wanted to leave, in part, because of funding issues, there are questions for the club’s hierarchy to answer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the 2024-25 season, of the eight WSL clubs to publish their wage bills via Companies House, United ranked fourth for expenditure, and it was a similar story in 2023-24. For next season, they will operate on a far smaller wage bill than the big-spending independent club London City Lionesses, and there are understood to be fears held among some staff at United that they are soon likely to be outbid for players on the basis of wages by Tottenham too.The club embarked on a new direction this summer, establishing a long-term aim to develop young homegrown players and play exciting football in line with what they believe are the traditions of the club and their culture. Yet that seems to be at odds with the targets outlined during the 2024-25 season when their “Project 150” included a “Mission 1” for the women to win a first WSL title by the club’s 150th anniversary in 2028.Whoever comes in as the club’s head coach – and an appointment is likely to happen quickly, with background checks having already been carried out on candidates – they will need to be prepared to work with youngsters and develop them rather than trying to sign established international stars. They will also have to accept that key first‑team players – such as Melvine Malard who was sold to Chelsea this summer – may well be poached by rivals.Explore more on these topicsManchester United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballcommentShareReuse this content
