title: Emma Raducanu to miss US Open with leg injury in latest fitness setback | Emma Raducanu | The Guardian
description: Emma Raducanu will miss the US Open because of the stress fracture in her right leg that she sustained during the grass-court season
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Emma Raducanu will miss the US Open because of the stress fracture in her right leg that she sustained during the grass-court season
Content: Emma Raducanu has not played since her defeat in the final at Queen’s Club in June.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenEmma Raducanu has not played since her defeat in the final at Queen’s Club in June.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAEmma RaducanuEmma Raducanu to miss US Open with leg injury in latest fitness setback2021 US Open champion out with stress fracture in legRaducanu also missed Wimbledon through injuryPA MediaMon 3 Aug 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmma Raducanu will miss the US Open because of the stress fracture in her right leg that she sustained during the grass-court season and forced her to pull out of Wimbledon.It is understood that following consultation with her medical team, Raducanu has concluded she will be unable to play in New York this month.Pat Rafter: ‘Why aren’t we producing players like Spain? I don’t know’Read moreWhile the news comes as no surprise given the nature of the injury and the fact Raducanu has only recently taken her first tentative steps back on court wearing a protective boot, it is another blow to the 23‑year‑old.Having made positive progress last summer, including winning her first matches at Flushing Meadows since lifting the trophyfive years ago, it has been a frustrating 12 months for Raducanu with more persistent physical issues.After a foot injury severely hampered her pre-season training, Raducanu spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness after initially falling unwell in early February. She finally returned for the end of the clay-court season having rehired Andrew Richardson, the coach who guided her to the US Open title, but the pair’s time on court together has been limited.Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career by reaching her biggest final since New York at Queen’s Club in Junebut it was that effortthat triggered her latest setback.She was not among the players named in Great Britain’s team for the Billie Jean King Cup finals in September and there must be question marks over whether Raducanu, who will slide from her current ranking of 49, will compete again in 2026.Raducanu did post an upbeat message on Instagram on Sunday from a break in Switzerland, calling it the “best reset ever”.Explore more on these topicsEmma RaducanuUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Transfer roundup: Chelsea sell Trevoh Chalobah and sign Jordan Henderson | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: The Chelsea academy product Trevoh Chalobah will now play under Cesc Fàbregas after Como spent £27.5m on him, while Henderson adds experience to Xabi Alonso’s squad
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The Chelsea academy product Trevoh Chalobah will now play under Cesc Fàbregas after Como spent £27.5m on him, while Henderson adds experience to Xabi Alonso’s squad
Content: Trevoh Chalobah leaves Chelsea after 19 years at the club, eight of them as a professional.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenTrevoh Chalobah leaves Chelsea after 19 years at the club, eight of them as a professional.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAChelseaTransfer roundup: Chelsea sell Trevoh Chalobah and sign Jordan HendersonChalobah to join Cesc Fàbregas at Como for £27.5mFulham sign Real Madrid’s Gonzalo García for £34mGuardian sportand agenciesMon 3 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrevoh Chalobah’s long association with Chelsea is to end after Como agreed a deal worth an initial £25.7m.The England defender’s departure was agreed on the same day the club completed the signing of Jordan Henderson.Chalobah made 105 Premier League appearances for Chelsea and established himself as a first-team option during a number of turbulent periods for the club. The move will be seen as a coupfor Como’s head coach, Cesc Fàbregas, with the former Chelsea midfielder pushing to bring the centre-back to Italy.Chelsea sign Argentina international Valentín Barco from StrasbourgRead moreThe clubs have settled on a package that includes £5.1m in performance-related add-ons and a sell-on clause. For Chelsea, the departure of another homegrown academy product – Chalobah, now 27, has been at the club since he was eight – will generate pure profit, a key factor as they continueto balance the books.On another busy day in west Londonthe new manager, Xabi Alonso, welcomed Henderson to the club after his departure from Brentford. The 36-year-old joined on a free transfer after playing 34 times for the Bees last season, a campaign that also earned him a place in England’s World Cup squad.“Given the size of the club, the manager, who I have great admiration for, and the quality of the players, this was a huge opportunity I couldn’t turn down,” Henderson said. “I was so impressed with how much the ownership ‌wantChelseato be successful and move in the right direction.”View image in fullscreenWith Jordan Henderson following Danny Welbeck to Chelsea, the club have shown a clear intent to sign more experienced players.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskHenderson came through Sunderland’s academy before joining Liverpool in 2011. He spent 12 seasons at Anfield, playing 492 games in all competitions, and captained the team toChampions League victory in 2019and the ‌Premier League title in 2020.He left Liverpoolfor Al-Ettifaqin the Saudi Pro League in 2023, but ​six months laterjoined Ajax. He moved on again last summerto join Brentford.Henderson played six minutes at the World Cupbefore breaking an armin a post-match accident after England’s last-16 victory against Mexico. He is Chelsea’s fourth English signing of the transfer window, afterthe record acquisition of Morgan Rogers​from Aston Villa,Danny Welbeck from Brightonand the teenager Harrison Bettoni from Wigan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGonzalo García has joined Fulham from Real Madrid for £34m on a five-year contract. The deal, which includes an option for the club to extend by a further 12 months, sees the 22-year-old Spanish striker reunite with former Real head coach, Alvaro Arbeloa. Garcia said: “I’m very grateful, very happy to be here. I have to thank the board and Arbeloa for the trust they’ve put in me, and I’m very, very excited to start.”Garcia had been with Real since joining in 2014 aged 10 and made 39 appearances forLos Blancoslast season, registering eight goals and three assists.César Palacios has also made the switch from the Bernabéu to Craven Cottage for an undisclosed fee. The 21-year-old attacking midfielder will wear the No 8 shirt.Explore more on these topicsChelseaComoTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Jockey Club rocks British horse racing by quitting Racecourse Association | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: The Jockey Club has announced it will quit the Racecourse Association in a move that could split British racing in two
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: The Jockey Club has announced it will quit the Racecourse Association in a move that could split British racing in two
Content: Cheltenham is among the racecourses owned by the Jockey Club.Photograph: Nigel French/PAView image in fullscreenCheltenham is among the racecourses owned by the Jockey Club.Photograph: Nigel French/PAHorse racingJockey Club rocks British horse racing by quitting Racecourse AssociationDecision triggers constitutional crisis for the BHAGrowing RCA fissure could split organisation in twoGreg WoodMon 3 Aug 2026 09.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jockey Club, which owns 15 ­British racecourses including Aintree, Cheltenham, Epsom and ­Newmarket, said on Monday it will joinAscotin resigning from the Racecourse ­Association (RCA), the trade body that ­represents all but one of the ­country’s 59 tracks, at the end of the year.The Jockey Club’s ­announcement comes two days after the RCA revealed the results of a review of its governance structure, which was launched in an attempt to prevent further resignations afterAscot announced its decisionto quit the organisation in May.Jockey Club staff cull leaves Derby feeling flat with Ascot and Goodwood riding highRead moreJim Mullen, chief executive at the Jockey Club, said the review’s ­proposal to replace a one-track, one-vote structure with four groups of racecourses holding a vote apiece “fails to address our fundamental concern that the RCA can continue to act to stifle the necessary changes needed in the industry”.Mullen said: “Nothing proposed would displace the RCA as the political representative of British racecourses and in our view, confirmed by recent discussions, the RCA would continue to vote against necessary changes such as the introduction of an independent [British ­Horseracing Authority] board and substantive changes to the fixture list.“It is our intention to work with Ascot Racecourse and other like-minded industry partners to pursue a vision based on the long-term sustainability of the sport and we are in the early stages of establishing a new organisation to do this.”The effective counterparty to the breakaway group of major racecourses is Arena Racing Company, which operates 16 courses with a business model based largely on quantity rather than quality to service the off-course betting market.The growing fissure in the RCA will split the organisation in two if some or all of York, Goodwood, Newbury and Chester, the remaining “large independent” tracks inside the organisation, decide to join the exodus.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Tuesday tipsShowCatterick:2.15 Waakabb 2.45 Iconic Times 3.15 Slack Alice 3.45 Miss Rainbow 4.15 Muhib 4.45 Havin A Flyer.Ffos Las:2.30 Safari Dream 3.00 Artemis Star 3.30 Cypriot Diaspora 4.00 Rosemary’s Rose (nap) 4.30 Arbaawy 5.00 Mythological Star 5.30 Ada Rose.Lingfield:5.18 Sub Thirteen 5.48 Langdale Lass 6.18 Minnal 6.48 Style King 7.18 Tabasko (nb) 7.48 Koko Blue 8.18 D Day Major Winter.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Jockey Club’s move also triggers a constitutional crisis for the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) and its recently appointed chair, Simon Cox.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe RCA nominates two BHA board members, dependent on the organisation being “the person most representative in Great Britain of the interests of owners of racecourses”. Without Ascot, Cheltenham, Aintree, Newmarket, Epsom and Sandown – and, quite possibly, other major tracks too – the RCA cannot realistically claim that status.A spokesperson for the BHA said on Monday the sport’s ruling body “will continue to liaise with the racecourses and other constituent bodies regarding the sport’s governance structure, and consider all proposals made.“This engagement will include the incoming BHA Chair, who formally takes up the role from 1 October. Our priority will always be to ensure that British racing is in the best position to support ongoing efforts to strengthen and grow our industry.”Explore more on these topicsHorse racingAscotHorse racing tipsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maguire survives missed cuts and controversy to headline Solheim Cup wildcard picks | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: Leona Maguire has retained her place in Europe’s Solheim Cup team despite a disappointing 2026, with the Irish golfer one of four wildcard picks
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Leona Maguire has retained her place in Europe’s Solheim Cup team despite a disappointing 2026, with the Irish golfer one of four wildcard picks
Content: Leona Maguire’s strong record for Europe at the Solheim Cup counted in her favour.Photograph: David Dermer/APView image in fullscreenLeona Maguire’s strong record for Europe at the Solheim Cup counted in her favour.Photograph: David Dermer/APSolheim CupMaguire survives missed cuts and controversy to headline Solheim Cup wildcard picksIrish golfer one of four wildcard picks for EuropeRookies Ramirez, Nadaud and Rhodes also selectedEwan MurrayMon 3 Aug 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeona Maguire has retained her place in Europe’sSolheim Cupteam despite a disappointing 2026, with the Irish golfer one of four wildcard picks named on Monday by Anna Nordqvist.Maguire joins three rookies – Julia López Ramirez, Nastasia Nadaud and Mimi Rhodes – in completing the Europe side who will attempt to reclaim the trophy in the Netherlands next month.A missed cut for Maguire in the Women’s British Open last week meant the 31-year-old had failed to play in the closing 36 holes of four from a possible five majors in 2026. In the one where she made the cut, the Women’s PGA Championship, Maguire tied 53rd. She started this week ranked 83rd in the world.Kuwaki wins Women’s Open after Henseleit’s unlucky break off marshal’s leg in playoffRead moreThese numbers are striking for a player who was tipped for greatness at a young age. There is also the matter of the controversy that surrounded Maguire at the 2024 Solheim Cup when she admitted her limited play under the captain Suzann Pettersenproved a “bitter pill to swallow”. Maguire has enjoyed positive experiences in this arena in the past, however, having starred for Europe in the Solheim Cups of 2021 and 2023. The Irish golfer has also claimed eight and a half points from a dozen Solheim Cup matches.“I would rather play alongside her than against her,” Nordqvist said of Maguire. “She is such a fierce competitor and will do anything for you on the team. I had the honour of playing with her in Spain [at the 2021 Solheim Cup]. Her matchplay record, as an amateur too, definitely helps. I’m excited to see what she can do.”Maguire’s experience was clearly key to Nordqvist’s decision. Another blunt reality is that European options were not especially strong. “I love the Solheim Cup,” Maguire said. “It brings the best out of my game and I love being part of the team.”Ramirez said she is “living the dream” after her maiden call-up. The 23-year-old from Málaga is yet to win a professional event. Nadaud did taste victory, at the Ladies European Tour event in Andalusia late last year. England’s Rhodes was the LET’s rookie of the year in 2025, when she won three times. Nordqvist hailed Rhodes as a “fierce competitor”.View image in fullscreenEsther Henseleit will bring form into the event after losing in a playoff at the Women’s Open.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PACharley Hull, Esther Henseleit, Lottie Wood, Maja Stark, Linn Grant, Céline Boutier, Carlota Ciganda and Nanna Koerstz Madsen sealed Europe’s automatic berths. Albeit more than a month has to pass until the Solheim Cup gets under way at Bernardus Golf, Nordqvist will have high hopes for Henseleit. The German was beaten to the Women’s Open titlein a playoff on Sundayby Shiho Kuwaki. In the second and defining extra hole at Royal Lytham and St Annes, Henseleit’s drive rebounded from the leg of a marshal and to the bottom of a gorse bush. Henseleit had no idea what had transpired when watching from the tee.“I thought it was further left to be honest,” Henseleit said. “It must have gotten some kind of bad bounce. At least I still had a shot and could kind of get a good angle going into the green. I didn’t have to take an unplayable or something. But, probably a bit unlucky there. That’s just links golf.”Angel Yin and Jennifer Kupcho secured spots in the US Solheim Cup team at the Women’s Open conclusion. Nelly Korda had already done likewise. Angela Stanford, the US captain, will name three captain’s picks after their qualification period ends in late August.Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupWomen's OpenGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mauricio Pochettino agrees deal to stay as US coach through World Cup 2030 | USA | The Guardian
description: Pochettino has signed a new deal that will keep him in the US for a full World Cup cycle, after leading the team to the last-16 in 2026
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: Pochettino has signed a new deal that will keep him in the US for a full World Cup cycle, after leading the team to the last-16 in 2026
Content: Mauricio Pochettino led the US to a last-16 finish at the 2026 World Cup, finishing with a 4-1 loss to Belgium.Photograph: Dirk Waem/BELGA MAG/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino led the US to a last-16 finish at the 2026 World Cup, finishing with a 4-1 loss to Belgium.Photograph: Dirk Waem/BELGA MAG/AFP/Getty ImagesUSAMauricio Pochettino agrees deal to stay as US coach through World Cup 2030Pochettino joined US national team in 2024Coach led US to last 16 at 2026 World CupPablo Iglesias MaurerandAlexander AbnosMon 3 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS men’s national team head coachMauricio Pochettinoand the US Soccer Federation have agreed to a contract extension that will keep Pochettino attached to the program through 2030, US Soccer announced on Monday.The two sides had been actively engaged in discussions on a contract extension for several months, long before the USMNT’s disappointing, last-16 exit in this summer’s World Cup, with the federation making it clear it desired Pochettino to stay. Conversations picked up in the weeks following the World Cup, with the Guardianreportinglast week that the sides had been in the “final stages” of agreeing to a deal. Financial details of the contract extension were not released, but Pochettino is expected to get a raise on top of the $6m per year he earned under his previous deal with the federation – already the largest outlay for a US head coach.The US had the biggest opportunity in the history of American soccer. They wasted it | Alexander AbnosRead moreThe Guardian understands that billionaire hedge fund manager Ken Griffin, who bankrolled US Soccer’s initial contract with Pochettino, will once again be the primary funder for the new deal. A source familiar with the agreement characterized Pochettino’s return as being in an “expanded role.” Another source said the primary focus of Pochettino and his staff will be on the senior US team, while the federation’s announcement said that the coaching staff will “advise and support” the federation on “the broader development of the full national team pathway, youth soccer, coaching education, professional league collaboration and other technical facets across the soccer community.”“It has become clear to us that there is tremendous potential to make the men’s national team program even stronger,” Pochettino said in US Soccer’s announcement. “The passion we experienced from the fans throughout theWorld Cuponly strengthened our belief in what is possible here. We are excited by the opportunity to bring all our experience and knowledge to even more areas of U.S. Soccer while helping strengthen the pathways for players, coaches and teams across the Federation.”Under Pochettino, the US’s World Cup got off to a bright start and featured arguably the program’s best-ever performance at the tournament, a comprehensive,4-1 dismantling of Paraguayin their group-stage opener. Strong efforts against Australia and Bosnia and Herzegovina followed, setting the stage for the last-16 encounter with Belgium. The US were outclassed in every way in that match, with Pochettino – along with many players – taking the brunt of the blame for the loss.View image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino’s US team put forth strong performances before crashing out of the World Cup against Belgium.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APPochettino is widely liked by players and staff, with some crediting the coach for overhauling the group’s mentality. He clashed with some players who he felt weren’t fully committed, most notably Milan midfielder Christian Pulisic, going as far as to air his grievances publicly. His relationship with the media alsocame under scrutinyin his tenure, the result of a handful of dust-ups with reporters and journalists who cover the team regularly.After the USMNT’s crashout against Belgium, Pochettino expressed pride in the work his staff had done with players. He had been at the helm for about 20 months at that point, and Pochettino suggested that the truncated tenure had only been enough to evaluate the group properly and put standards and practices in place.“With good things and not so good things,” Pochettino told the Guardian after the Belgium loss, “it was amazing, this journey. It still hasn’t been two years working here. And we all know that a process is about a four-year cycle. Today I think we closed the chapter about assessing players, playing in that competition that is so difficult. I think now we have a complete assessment from a lot of players, and if we commit to be here in the future, we have a clear idea of our decisions for the future – before, it was very difficult.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDuring his time with the US, Pochettino has put together a respectable record of 18 wins, 12 losses and one draw. His early struggles included a fourth-place finish in the 2025 Nations League and a loss to Mexico in the final of the Gold Cup, a tournament he navigated with a heavily rotated squad. He did have his highlights – the electrifying start to this summer’s World Cup, anda 5-1 thrashing of Uruguayin a friendly that ranks as one of the program’s most surprising results.Still, Pochettino was largely hired to do one job: advance the US past the last 16 and into the quarter-finals at a home World Cup. He did not manage to do so, but the federation has now offered him another chance to hit that goal in 2030.Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsWorld Cup 2026World CupMauricio PochettinonewsShareReuse this content

title: The end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online games | Games | The Guardian
description: Online multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or later
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Online multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or later
Content: A sense of mourning spoken and unspoken … Halo 3.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosView image in fullscreenA sense of mourning spoken and unspoken … Halo 3.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosGamesThe end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online gamesOnline multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or laterNicole CarpenterMon 3 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNevan Hagarty had an idea. If he and otherHalo3 players stayed online the night of 13 January 2022, they could delay the impending server shutdown. Players knew this was coming: it had happened to Halo 2when its Xbox Live servers were turned off in 2010, and a group managed to stay logged into the multiplayer serversfor weeks.And so, players gathered online before the server shutdown to pay homage and to mourn the game they loved so dearly. And, maybe, to keep it online for a little longer. “I must have played ’til about 4am the night of the shutdown, trading stories with so many players about their love of the game and their experiences over the last 15 years,” says Hagarty, 22. “It was a really wholesome experience I won’t forget.”A sense of mourning went both spoken and unspoken. Thirty-year-old fan Jimi hadn’t played Halo 3in a while but logged on to the game on shutdown day to experience the original servers just once more, later posting a video onReddit.“My team was losing really bad,” he says, “I saw a few of the other team’s people standing in the middle, and our guy standing in the middle, and everybody’s just looking at each other. I shot up once in the air, and then everybody just starts going crazy.” Someone threw a shield down, others threw grenades in the air and launched rockets. It looked almost like fireworks. “There were no people on the voice chat. There wasn’t any mutual agreement on this. Everybody just felt it and knew.”View image in fullscreenA person dressed as a character from the game at the UK launch of Halo 3.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianWhen online multiplayer came to video games in the late 90s, it meant that players from across the globe could interact with people they’d never otherwise meet. This changed the trajectory of video games, bringing people together in ways that games hadn’t before – to play, and to mourn, when their virtual worlds are doomed to die.Games go offline all the time, and people have got used to saying goodbye to their favourites. The increasing popularity of online-only live service games means more reliance on servers to host these experiences. And those servers cost money to run and maintain; in the case of recent flopHighguard, developer Wildlight Entertainment couldn’t afford to keep the game online for more than a few months.Over twenty gameshave shut off their servers already in 2026.View image in fullscreenGoing down fighting … Highguard.Photograph: Wildlight Entertainment, Inc.“People really hold on to the idea of place,” says UX and games researcher Evan Conaway, who holds a PhD in anthropology. “That we create community online at all is really remarkable. When you find it and you have it and it’s real, you have an emotional connection to it. Wanting to hold on to it is only human.”Conaway says this happens a lot in the real world, when the corner bar shutters, or a local skatepark is torn down. His research delved into the ways people commemorate online spaces, with a focus on the massively multiplayer online role-playing gameWorld of Warcraft(WoW). People play together on separate servers – or instances – which all run contained copies of WoW, and each server has its own culture created by the community. When the game changes, the culture can change, too. WoW has persisted for decades, and the game is no longer the same as it was when it was released – it’s hardly the same game it was just a few years ago.Though people still have access to WoW, they are often “gradually mourning”, says Conaway. They know that this version of the game is ephemeral. It won’t stay the same – it can’t, by design. In exchange for new content, players must accept that the spaces they inhabit online will find new forms. “The quests are different, the way things are worded is different,” he says. “The way I felt while playing it, and wandering around by myself or exploring the world, all of that is part of this meaning-making for people – just the raw experience of it.”Part of Conaway’s research centred on a group of people who wanted to literally hold on to those memories and meanings. When Blizzard Entertainment was changing its servers in 2011, it auctioned off the old server blades withautographed placardsdisplaying which server they held. It was important for some players, he says, to have a physical representation of that moment in time. He points to one server in particular, Proudmoore, which was an unofficial queer server: “For a gay person or queer person who was playing World of Warcraft at that time on that server, it does feel a little bit like a skatepark brick, like they can take home a piece of a thing.”View image in fullscreenStrength in numbers … characters from World of Warcraft, which has an online community of five million.Photograph: Blizzard EntertainmentWhen World of Warcraftplayers in China were faced with server shutdowns in2023, they were at the mercy of both Blizzard Entertainment and its Chinese partner NetEase.Games in Chinamust be published with a local company, so when Blizzard Entertainment and NetEase had a dispute, it hit the players. Millions lost not just the server but the whole game, and there was no date set for its return. It could have been months, years. Maybe never.Naturally, players wanted to gather in their servers on the day of the shutdown, 24 January 2023, to pay their respects. To do so, people started preparing – and logging in – days in advance, according to City University of Hong Kong PhD student and games researcher HongLan Xu, who joined them to document the last days.“I encountered hundreds of players, but there are millions,” says Xu. “Everybody thought it could be at least several years. They don’t know when the server will be back. It’s profound. It’s real. The shutdown is very real for them, so they gathered in the game to say farewell to their avatars, like it’s the last time.”View image in fullscreenA Chinese gamer plays World of Warcraft at an internet cafe in Beijing in 2024.Photograph: Jade Gao/AFP/Getty ImagesChinese players’ grief was mixed with anger, too, says Xu. Many in the Chinese market felt disrespected, as if Blizzard Entertainment didn’t care about them: “From a Chinese player’s perspective, the main takeaway is sometimes the capitalism of the western gaming companies [leads to] distrust.”WoW opened back up to Chinese players in August 2024. Returning players were glad to have it back, of course, but there was an unease underneath that excitement. This could happen again; they knew what it felt like to lose it all. “Virtual life attachment and this sense of loss is deep, profound,” says Xu. “It can be completely vulnerable and very uncertain.”Losing your forever-game is a uniquely sad experience. Players make a very real investment into these spaces – time, money, friendships, stories, characters, creativity. As one playerput it, “What gets me is that people poured themselves into these games. Not just cash, but actual time, actual friendships built inside them, characters they spent months on. And then one day a studio decides the numbers don’t work any more and everything just disappears.”Explore more on these topicsGamesHaloWorld of WarcraftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ring Cycle review – AI staging dispenses with drama to create banal bric-a-brac  | Opera | The Guardian
description: For the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless mess
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: For the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless mess
Content: Unexplained, mindless scrolling … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathView image in fullscreenUnexplained, mindless scrolling … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathOperaReviewRing Cycle review – AI staging dispenses with drama to create banal bric-a-bracBayreuth festival theatre, BayreuthFor the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless messFlora WillsonMon 3 Aug 2026 09.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnveiled the same week in which tech company Anthropic admitted that itsAI model Claude had gone rogue during testing, Bayreuth festival’s new AI-generated staging of Wagner’s four-partRing of the Nibelungenis at least timely. But anyone who assumes that the cycle’s obsession with knowledge, power and possession might make it an ideal forum for reflection on AI as a major contemporary frontier will be disappointed, as will anyone hopeful about AI’s creative potential within opera.Commissioned to mark the festival’s 150th anniversary, the production is “curated” – emphatically not “directed” – by a team led by German stage directorMarcus Lobbes. He apparently spent weeks in dialogue with AI models about possible interpretations of the Ring. According to the programme book, “power structures, capitalism, mythology, gender roles, nationalism”, all came up. So far, so mainstream Wagner reception. But if these human-machine exchanges were revelatory, you wouldn’t know it from the resulting staging, which uses AI “as an extension of a cultural memory that is never complete”.In plainer English: the AI system is allowed to roam archival materials from 150 years of Ring cycle productions at Bayreuth as the starting point for constantly spooling visuals projected on to a screen that is stretched the full width and height of the proscenium arch. Lobbes also asked the system to incorporate imagery chronologically, from a political or social event every year of the festival’s history as a plausible conversation topic for that season’s audience. Each scene begins with a source from the cycle’s 1876 premiere, but what happens next is determined by the system in real time during the performance.View image in fullscreenGrotesque … Bayreuth festival’s 2026 Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathThe good news is that anyone who attends another of this production’s outings definitely won’t see the same selection of visual bric-à-brac that I did. The bad news is that the principle of rapid machinic free-association will remain.So, I assume, will the constant grotesque morph and flow of visual objects. Das Rheingold and Die Walküre involved countless hands that warped horribly, producing extra fingers and nails. (Did someone adjust the settings ahead of Siegfried and Götterdämmerung, I wonder? The visual tic disappeared mid-cycle as suddenly as it emerged.) Faces appeared, only to go instantly out of focus. Some were very famous (Adolf Hitler, Queen Elizabeth II, JFK) but I struggled to identify most. Watercolour rocks became bodies became other bodies. There were rapid swings between the entirely inscrutable and the totally obvious. Alberich’s transformation into a toad triggered various mutant amphibians, there were bears when Siegfried brought one in, a rainbow for the rainbow bridge to Valhalla.double quotation markThe singers stood behind a vast projection screen like budget Star Trek monsters rooted to the spotBut there were also endless picture-library bland photos of scrap metal, creeping greenery, water droplets, abandoned rooms. I spotted design elements from various past Bayreuth Ring productions but was mostly – inevitably – unable to keep pace with the AI system’s connection-making. One low point: the appearance of a historical photo of emaciated African youths – as unexplained as everything else, but picture the results of an image-search for “European colonialism” – which flashed past during Die Walküre. This is not engaging with the complex, problematic history of Bayreuth or the Ring. It’s just another form of mindless scrolling.You’ll be wondering where the singers fitted in. Forget Wagner’s notion of the inescapably multimediaGesamtkunstwerk: this Ring presents the sonic and the visual as separate tracks, with theatrical drama kept to a minimum. Over four nights, some of today’s leading Wagnerians stood behind – yes, behind – the vast projection screen, all wearing subtle variations on a single costume design like budget Star Trek monsters. Mostly they were rooted to the spot. Recently murdered characters simply walked off; at erotic climaxes, lovers held hands; Siegfried discovered Brünnhilde despite being alone on stage.View image in fullscreenTheatrical drama is kept to a minimum … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring Cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathMichael Vollewas a magnificent, stately Wotan and Wanderer, his power unforced.Klaus Florian Vogtwas by turn Loge, Siegmund and Siegfried, in each case supple and darkly luminous with compelling diction.Elza van den Heever’s Sieglinde got better and better, blossoming in her love duet in Die Walküre.Camilla Nylund’s Brünnhilde was often wild and sometimes ungainly, but her impassioned lyricism and most intimate moments were deeply moving regardless.Mika Kares’s Hunding was all iron and velvet, his Hagen unleashing mighty, smooth torrents of sound – evil rarely sounds better.Gerhard Siegel(Mime) and Jochen Schmeckenbecher (Alberich) were more old-school baddies, respectively wheedling and raw.Peter Rosewas a rather muddy Fafner andChrista Mayerwobbly but forceful as Erda and Waltraute. The Rhinemaidens, Valkyries and Norns were exquisitely balanced and as characterised as they could be without acting.double quotation markForget Wagner’s notion of the Gesamtkunstwerk – this Ring keeps theatrical drama to a minimumConductorChristian Thielemanndrew playing from the orchestra that was occasionally poorly tuned and even scrappy, but which at its best should have been captivating: details were finely balanced and tutti passages blistering, the brass rising like an immense wave from the pit or splatting nastily for the bad guys. Tempi were often brisk (only in Siegfried did this cause coordination problems, with Vogt left struggling to keep up) but there were also precious moments of spaciousness. Yet even the silence that Thielemann left in Wotan’s devastating monologue couldn’t stop the onscreen hyperactivity that instantly dispersed all dramatic tension.There are numerous criticisms you could levy against this production from all manner of perspectives; there is, after all, something for everyone to dislike. But the most dismal was perhaps how unmoving it was – and how difficult it became to care.The Ring Cycle continues at theBayreuth festivaluntil 16 August.Explore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicAI (artificial intelligence)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mauricio Pochettino’s US return is risky, expensive and probably unnecessary | USA | The Guardian
description: In giving the head coach another World Cup cycle, US Soccer is tempting fate for negligible benefit
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: In giving the head coach another World Cup cycle, US Soccer is tempting fate for negligible benefit
Content: Mauricio Pochettino led the US to the last 16 at the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APView image in fullscreenMauricio Pochettino led the US to the last 16 at the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APUSAMauricio Pochettino’s US return is risky, expensive and probably unnecessaryLeander SchaerlaeckensIn giving the head coach another World Cup cycle, US Soccer is tempting fate for negligible benefitMon 3 Aug 2026 12.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTShareMauricio Pochettino and US Soccer enjoyed their time together.Or, rather, theyenshoyedit, as Pochettino would pronounce it in his thick Argentinian accent, which charmingly carries over when he speaks English.Nevertheless, the two sides should have moved on from each other.From his 10 September 2024 appointment through the US men’s national team’s 4-1 last-16 World Cup elimination at the hands of Belgium on 6 July, Pochettino had broadly accomplished what he was brought in to do.Mauricio Pochettino agrees deal to stay as US coach through World Cup 2030Read moreHe energized a team who had grown stale. He found a playing system and style that suited a generation of USMNT players who were unprecedented in their pedigree and talent but lacked difference-makers on the World Cup stage. He coaxed from themtwo excellent performances– including a 4-1 hammering of Paraguay that was surely the best the Americans have ever looked at a World Cup – and two very good ones. Then it all caved in against Belgium after the good vibes had been ruined by a meddlesome president in all that Folarin Balogun suspension/unsuspension business.Pochettino’s spell in charge was a success.Now,he will be back, having accepted a contract offer extended to him by the US Soccer Federation before the World Cup and kept on the table after the team was eliminated a round sooner than many had hoped they would reach. Pochettino’s new deal runs through the 2030 World Cup, giving him a full cycle to try again.This is something of a gamble. The inclination to see what Pochettino will construct atop the sturdy foundations he laid is understandable, but it assumes that he even stays through the length of his new deal.It feels like the Argentinian and his staff are still here on account of the absence of opportunity elsewhere, to coach the sort of club he has worked for over the course of a decade – the likes of Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea. Perhaps he settled for a prolonged stay with the US men by default; perhaps not. Before the World Cup, Pochettino was reportedly in talks with Milan, who ultimately hired Ruben Amorim as manager instead.It seems unlikely Pochettino will actually stick around four more years as one top coaching job after another opens up and he invariably winds up on the lists of rumored candidates. Should he leave early, the team will once again be starting over mid-cycle.Besides, the job he returns to is very different from the one he has done.For the USMNT, World Cup qualifiers for 2030won’t even startuntil November of 2027, although there will be editions of the Concacaf Nations League and Gold Cup to slog through before then – to say nothing of a great many friendlies against teams you are largely supposed to beat every time. The final round of World Cup qualifying will be played in June of 2028 and the fall of 2029, after still more Nations League and Gold Cup duties. Mind you, Concacaf will have six places at the next World Cup, with a possible seventh through a playoff – as opposed to three automatic berths for the 2022 World Cup, the last edition before the tournament expanded and was hosted in this region. The stakes and peril will simply not be the same as before. The adrenaline rush of high-stakes games is an awfully long way off.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArsène Wenger: US soccer development will depend on ‘consistency’ and ‘education’Read moreThen there’s the history of USMNT managers staying on for a second World Cup cycle. It’s abysmal. Bruce Arena hung on for a second World Cup and watched helplessly as the side who stunned on their way to the brink of the semi-finals in 2002 got grouped in 2006. Bob Bradley made it just a year after 2010, getting sacked after a 4-2 Gold Cup final loss to Mexico the following summer. Jürgen Klinsmann’s second cycle was a debacle and sowed the seeds for the failure to reach the 2018 World Cup. Gregg Berhalter’s return to the job after 2022 was marred by a scandal and never really got going, ending in humiliation at the Copa América on home soil and his subsequent replacement by Pochettino.Granted, all of them got more of that first cycle than Pochettino did, who parachuted into the job less than two years before the World Cup. But what each second-term failure had in common was that all the coaches struggled to keep the program fresh when the process reset.While this remains a fairly young team, they could do with an injection of fresh faces, legs and ideas. Out of the team’s longstanding core of Christian Pulisic, Tyler Adams, Weston McKennie, Antonee Robinson, Sergiño Dest and Chris Richards, only McKennie has been spared major and repeated injuries. The scare over a late knock to Richards before the tournament emphasized that while the standard and quality on the field has inarguably improved, it nevertheless feels tentative. The US were never more than an injury or two away from calamity. This was especially apparent when Pulisic was pulled at half-time against Paraguay and did not play a full 90 minutes all tournament, lasting longer than an hour only once.There is also something of an opportunity cost to keeping Pochettino on.Tax filings showthat he made more than $5m over his first seven months in the job, a sum that was reportedly padded with further payment from billionaire US Soccer supporter Ken Griffin and other sources. Griffin is once again a primary funder of Pochettino’s new deal, which keeps him among the most highly paid managers in international soccer. And while the federation got a return on that investment over the past summer, it’s worth wondering whether it makes sense to pay out that kind of money to go and play early qualifiers against Nicaragua, or to face Jamaica and Panama again and again.You wouldn’t buy a supercar just to drive it to the grocery store and back. In the next few years, the USMNT will mostly be making school runs and commuting back and forth to an office park without ever hitting the highway.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsMauricio PochettinocommentShareReuse this content

title: The right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen again | Ruben Andersson | The Guardian
description: The EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerable, says Ruben Andersson, professor of social anthropology
Author: Ruben Andersson
Headline: The EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerable, says Ruben Andersson, professor of social anthropology
Content: Spanish army infantry members speak with migrants near Ceuta’s border post, 2 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSpanish army infantry members speak with migrants near Ceuta’s border post, 2 August 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionSpainThe right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen againRuben AnderssonThe EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerableMon 3 Aug 2026 09.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTShareFor the European hard right and the White House, it seemed almost too good to be true: left-liberal Spain punished with a migration crisis of its own making.The histrionics came right on cue. As thousands of mainly Moroccan citizensstreamed into the tiny Spanish enclave of Ceutaat the tip of north Africa, Spain’s far-right party Vox decried a migrant “invasion”, blaming Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’sregularisationand leftist politics. The Trump administration did the same. A senior Israeli diplomat goaded Madrid over its “colonial” territories while Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area. Denmark and Finlandbacked Italy’s moveand, by the weekend, 22 EU leaders had penned aletterpointing an implicit finger at Madrid over its presumed failure to “relentlessly combat illegal migration”.But what these self-ascribed doyens of border control don’t want to understand is that it’s their panic and politicking over migration that has brought us here.Ceuta is hardly a poster-child for Spain’s otherwise liberal migration policy. Rather, since the 1990s it has been the prototype for Europe’s relentless border security battle. Drones, heat detectors, motion sensors, digital watchtowers, Moroccan Auxiliary Forces: Ceuta’s border is so thoroughly militarised that it puts even Trump’s barrier-building – let alone that of Greece, Poland or Finland – to shame.The paradox, as civil guards told me when I last visited in 2023, was that this militarisation had involved ceding control. “Rabat knows it can destabilise Spain with migration,” one chief said, as he reflected on themass entry of Moroccans in 2021, after Madrid had angered its partner by taking in Brahim Ghali, the leader of Western Sahara’s Polisario movement, for urgent healthcare. The heavily guarded fences have become a perfect foil for staging a migration crisis.While Morocco is usually tight-lipped about its intentions, at times its ministers have bluntly said it won’t play the “gendarme” of Europe unless its partners support its economic and political aims. The quiet at the border since 2021 had little to do with the aggressive security hardware, and everything to do with Madrid’s 2022 endorsement ofRabat’s planfor occupied Western Sahara. So why the latest crisis? While the facts and motives are still being established, it’s unlikely to be a coincidence that, only recently, Sánchez announced a “new phase” in relations with Algeria – Rabat’s arch-rival and supporter of Polisario.View image in fullscreenA man attempting to escape the police, Ceuta, 2 August 2026.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersSánchez blames the mass entry on people smugglers and misinformation about a recent Spanish supreme court ruling that prevents authorities from summarily expelling migrants who attempt to swim by sea to Spain’s territories in Africa. The official line from Morocco’s government is that the surge was due to “criminal organisations” and that cooperation with Spain is still “exemplary”. Yet blaming criminal organisations makes little sense: most of those who made it across were quietly returned within the day – unthinkable, if they had lost their life savings to pay smugglers. The social media rumour mill did mobilise people to cross; but crucially – according toSpanish intelligence– Moroccan law enforcement stopped controlling the border while its intelligence services failed to notify Spain about the online campaigns. Video clips and accounts from border crossers in numerous media outlets further suggest that law enforcement actively encouraged people to cross.It’s clear to anyone who knows the Ceuta border that nothing dramatic happens there without the Moroccan authorities letting it happen. Yet Spain is unable to call outMoroccoas it desperately depends on it. Instead, both Madrid and Brussels showered Rabat with praise this past week. This is the corner the EU has painted itself into: dependent on repressive and often undemocratic regimes that use migration threats for their own purposes.This has been a favoured tacticfor yearsacross the external EU borders, fromMuammar Gaddafi’s threatstoAnkara’s antics. And it’s all the more attractive to them thanks to the European obsession about unwanted migration – the higher the stakes, the bigger the rewards.The geopolitics are looking unfavourable to the EU. Since theAbraham accordswere signed in 2020, Morocco has strengthened its hand internationally through close alliances with the Trump and Netanyahu administrations. And those two governments see Spain as their arch-foe in Europe. This January, Rabat deepened its militarycooperationwith Israel. In April, a US House of Representatives committeestatedthat Ceuta and the other Spanish enclave of Melilla were “in Moroccan territory”. Israeli and Republican figures have made increasingly frequentnoisesof this kind. Recently, Morocco named ahighwaythrough Western Sahara after Trump.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreWhat all this points to is not necessarily some grand conspiracy. Rabat may well have sought to benefitopportunisticallyand then lost control of events. But it does suggest that what occurred in Ceuta was a geopolitical game with people as its pawns, leavingmore than 70 dead.European leaders have become so obsessed with “security” that they can’t see their own best interests clearly. Notably, one of the governments waving the threat of Schengen suspension was Denmark, which should know something about geopolitical blackmail against Europe. Coercive migration pressure,evidence shows, works best when destination regions are politically divided and prone to slanging matches. This is exactly what the far right and government leaders are now indulging as they nervously blame Spain and raise the spectre of another 2015 migration crisis.Having shown their hand to “partner” states and unfriendly regimes alike, these leaders will know exactly which button to push for maximum impact. Through their reaction, EU politicians are not only undermining Europeansolidarity– they are actively encouraging more crisis-generation, while abetting the anti-European forces in the White House and further afield.We need a different kind of migration politics that de-escalates panic instead of inviting it, that prioritises frank diplomacy over one-eyed “combat”, and that weakens the hand of hardmen and smugglers. European leaders could make a start on shifting this dynamic by not turning themselves into useful idiots at the first opportunity.Ruben Andersson is professor of social anthropology at the University of Oxford and author ofAge of Security: The Rise of a Global Obsession(William Collins) out 13th AugustDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
