title: Nolan’s Odyssey shows what happens when a leader’s violations are rewarded | Jamil Smith | The Guardian
description: The Greeks learn at Troy that breaking the rules works, then carry the lesson home. Nolan’s film shows how an exception becomes a habit of power
Author: Jamil Smith
Headline: The Greeks learn at Troy that breaking the rules works, then carry the lesson home. Nolan’s film shows how an exception becomes a habit of power
Content: ‘Nolan makes an argument that the methods developed for an enemy abroad do not stay abroad.’Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Nolan makes an argument that the methods developed for an enemy abroad do not stay abroad.’Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyOpinionThe OdysseyNolan’s Odyssey shows what happens when a leader’s violations are rewardedJamil SmithThe Greeks learn at Troy that breaking the rules works, then carry the lesson home. Nolan’s film shows how an exception becomes a habit of powerThis article contains spoilers for The OdysseyMon 3 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTShareIhad not read The Odyssey since I was a student. Stories change when we return to them later in life, or perhaps we are the ones who change.Christopher Nolan’s filmmade me want to find out what I had missed.More specifically, it made me want to read Emily Wilson’s translation.Her scathing essayabout the film nearly stopped me from buying her translation. I bought the book anyway.I did so because Wilson isnot simply another critic. She chairs the classical studies department at the University of Pennsylvania, is a MacArthur fellow and has translated both Homeric poems. Nolancited her version’s opening linewhen explaining what drew him to Odysseus. Her work has shaped how contemporary readers encounter Homer.Wilson’s objection is not simply that Nolan compressed a sprawling poem, or that several of Homer’s women reach the screen with less to do. Her larger objection is that “the film’s own values and vision don’t hang together”. The film condemns the Greeks for using deception to destroy Troy, then asks us to cheer when Matt Damon’s Odysseus uses deception and violence to reclaim his home.In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan worries the end of politeness will destroy civilisation. I fear he’s right | Joseph EarpRead moreWilson treats those contradictions as proof that the film has no coherent argument. But they are the argument. Nolan’s film is about what happens to victors after they discover that breaking the rules works.The Greeks did not break into Troy. The Trojans carried them inside. The horse arrived as a gift and concealed an army. The Greeks turned trust into a weapon, and victory made the violation look righteous. They sailed home having learned that deception and desecration could be justified against an enemy.Zeus’s law, as the film presents it, is less a statute than a compact: feed the stranger, honor the dead, respect another man’s household and restrain yourself when no one can stop you. These are the terms on which strangers can live together without the stronger simply taking what he wants.The key rule isxenia, the sacred obligation between guest and host. Nolan’s larger concern is what happens after violating it leads to success. Civilizations begin to fall not only when their enemies grow strong, but when the winners decide the rules were written for the losers.Athena guides Odysseus in the form of a young Trojan priestess killed during the sack his plan made possible. The choice turns memory into confrontation: he receives counsel about divine law through the face of someone his victory destroyed. Nolan has built a moral language in which victory and guilt cannot be separated.In this film, savagery begins with the collapse of obligation. Repeatedly, the Greeks treat another’s home as a supply depot. Odysseus blinds the cyclops Polyphemus after entering his cave for supplies. Later, from a safe distance, he shoots him out of spite. His men believe the act has angered Poseidon. In another episode, despite Tiresias’s warning in Hades, the crew invites its own destruction by eating the sun god’s cattle.These encounters are not merely obstacles between Odysseus and home. They record a law losing its authority one exemption at a time. Compression costs them some complexity, but Nolan has organized what remains around the repeated failure of people to honor obligations they cannot be forced to obey.Ithaca has not been spared. The suitors do not enter as invaders, but they behave like occupiers. They eat another man’s stores, treat his absence as the cancellation of his rights and assume that Penelope, Telemachus and Ithaca itself belong to whoever can establish dominance. The conduct of conquest has reached the dining table.That is where the contradiction Wilson identifies becomes the film’s point. Odysseus must use deception and violence to defend a law that Greek deception and violence helped hollow out. Nolan’s hero is less complicated than Homer’s, but the film relocates rather than removes the complication. He must restore civic order even though he helped teach the world that order was optional.Nolan stages the slaughter of the suitors largely as catharsis, encouraging the audience to enjoy the righteous violence the film has taught us to question. That gives Wilson part of her case. But he does not restore Odysseus to the throne. Odysseus cedes it to Telemachus and sets sail with Penelope to honor the men who died under his command.Wilson faults Nolan for removing Penelope’s test of the marriage bed. I found the change progressive rather than diminishing. Penelope recognizes Odysseus by his heart and skill, not his knowledge of their bed. She is judging not merely whether he is the man who left, but whether the man who returned is still worthy of being her husband.Why has Christopher Nolan got rid of all the sex in The Odyssey? | Zoe WilliamsRead moreWilson’s criticism of how the film treats women still lands. Nolan’s most devastating image of war’s cost is a murdered woman who never speaks, and Anne Hathaway, Samantha Morton, Lupita Nyong’o and Charlize Theron must supply interior lives the screenplay or the edit seldom grants them.What Nolan removes matters. So does what he builds in its place: an argument that the methods developed for an enemy abroad do not stay abroad.Last week,the Guardian reportedthat an ICE health service corps record confirms the Trump administration subjected an immigrant hunger striker to forced medical treatment, though it does not identify whether that meant force-feeding, forced hydration, catheterization or an involuntary blood draw. Force-feedingbecame notorious at Guantánamo Bay. The ICE record places such coercion within civil immigration detention. The exception becomes a practice, then a habit of government.That process is not uniquely American. Every power that suspends its rules to defeat an enemy risks teaching its institutions that the law is optional whenever officials can find the right label for the person beneath their control. Nolan asks his victor to give up what victory won him. That is the part of the story no government has adapted.Odysseus reaches Ithaca. Nolan does not end with a king restored. He ends with a victor learning that coming home is not the same as being fit to rule.Jamil Smith is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsThe OdysseyOpinionTrump administrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Christopher NolanUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Are Trump’s most blatant authoritarian moves backfiring? | Jan-Werner Müller | The Guardian
description: The president’s methods, from ‘flooding the zone’ with scandals to prioritizing loyalty over competence, could ultimately weaken rather than strengthen him
Author: Jan-Werner Müller
Headline: The president’s methods, from ‘flooding the zone’ with scandals to prioritizing loyalty over competence, could ultimately weaken rather than strengthen him
Content: ‘Total devotion to the leader can consolidate power. But it also creates a distinct vulnerability,’Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Total devotion to the leader can consolidate power. But it also creates a distinct vulnerability,’Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersOpinionDonald TrumpAre Trump’s most blatant authoritarian moves backfiring?Jan-Werner MüllerThe president’s methods, from ‘flooding the zone’ with scandals to prioritizing loyalty over competence, could ultimately weaken rather than strengthen himMon 3 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.21 EDTShareThe pattern is by now all too familiar: with every power grab Trump tries – from a fraudulent speech about voter fraud toappeals to his supreme courtto let him rig the midterms – a debate kicks off about whether these moves are signs of strength or of desperation. Maybe we keep getting caught in this debate because the question is badly posed. So much of what is distinctive about Trump’s governance during his second term can serve the consolidation of an autocratic regime andat the same timecreate particular vulnerabilities for the regime. We have to become better at identifying these weaknesses, as opposed to being shellshocked by Trump’s brazenness every single time.Aspiring autocrats operate differently in the 21st century; in previous eras, they had little hesitation about unleashing violence and committing massive human rights violations. Today, they try to fool both domestic and international audiences into thinking that democracy and the rule of law still exist. The recently deposed Hungarian prime minister, Viktor Orbán, was a master of this technique; he spent many years performing what he called “the peacock dance” to convince the European Commission (and Chancellor Angela Merkel) that he wasn’t creating a kleptocratic autocracy.This contrast between what the social scientists Serguei Guriev and Daniel Treisman have called “fear dictatorships” on the one hand and “spin dictatorships” on the other is empirically proven: there really is less violence, according to Guriev and Treisman, than in the 20th century. But elaborate efforts to fake democracy do not change the fact that violence is always kept in reserve: Putin dropped the mask entirely in 2022 and now has no hesitation to be seen as the violence-prone dictator who in one sense he always was.It is crucial to understand how Trump differs from these patterns: unlike Orbán, for instance, he was never constrained by international institutions and other powerful capitals (let alone “international public opinion” – even mentioning the term in as self-centered a country as the US seems faintly ridiculous). What’s more, his own modus operandi, from his early days as a New York real estate investor onwards, has always been to simply do things that everyone can see are illegal – the point is to create facts on the ground (think of the demolition of the East Wing) and hope that the other side will settle out of court or just live with a fait accompli.This method (strategy might be too big of a word) of illegality – and hope for impunity – now characterizes almost the entire administration. More particularly, the Trumpists have figured out that a scandal per year can spell political death, while 10 scandals a day elicit hardly a shrug, because no one, it seems, can keep up. This “flooding the zone” with scandals is in itself a means of generating power – but it also creates vulnerabilities. One never knows whether one scandal – even a relatively harmless one likethe reflecting pool disaster, combining grift and incompetence – might not focus the public’s attention after all and become a symbol for the corruption of the regime as a whole, the way that onechild abuse scandal– an Orbán ally pardoned a man convicted of covering up abuse – became the symbol of everything wrong with Orbán’s rule.Every aspiring autocrat faces a trade-off between loyalty and competence. It is no secret where Trumpists have tended to be placed on the spectrum. That total devotion to the leader – including the willingness to lie shamelessly, or at leastengage in election denial, as a de facto loyalty oath to Trump sworn in public – can consolidate power. But it also creates a distinct vulnerability, as, sooner or later, the egregiously incompetent will produce terrible outcomes, plain for all to see (at least if an effective opposition party manages to make them plain to see).McCarthyism has returned to the United States – and this time it’s even more dangerous | Judith LevineRead moreContrary to the tendency of today’s dictators shying away from violence – so as not needlessly to invoke memories of 20th-century authoritarianism and provoke resistance – Trumpists have made a spectacle of cruelty. Again, this can contribute to consolidating power – after all, the glaring impunityapparently enjoyedby the men who killed Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero sends a signal that loyalists can count themselves above the law. The spectacle might also please a Maga audience. But the fact is that, in the end, the ostentatious displays of cruelty havenot been popularwith the public at large. For now, the administration increases its power by effectively telling people “We can do whatever we want, and you can’t do anything!” But making cruelty a priority also creates images that can be turned against it.And the shameless corruption? Again, the shamelessness might easily generate a sense of hopelessness on the part of Americans watching unprecedented acts of malfeasance. But, unlike with other aspiring autocrats, the Trumpists are not really creating a coherent system of self-enrichment (the way Orbán did with what came to be called hismafia state– where tricks with public procurement were disguised well enough for many years). Under Trump, everyone just grabs whatever they can as quickly as they can. That inability to build a system is ultimately a sign of weakness; the Trumpists themselves do not really seem to believe that their rule will last, and what Mike Johnson, in a revealing moment, called the Republicans’ “protection program” – the majority in Congress – might be gone this year. Self-confident creators of autocratic kleptocracy would have stayed silent on the point – and been smarter in their approach altogether. To be sure, that is no consolation for victims of cruelty.Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton UniversityExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsViktor OrbáncommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s hypocritical new tariffs are a chance for the world to fight back | Joseph Stiglitz | The Guardian
description: The president’s pretext of stopping forced labour is only a ruse – he is trying to grab a share of global trade for the US
Author: Joseph Stiglitz
Headline: The president’s pretext of stopping forced labour is only a ruse – he is trying to grab a share of global trade for the US
Content: Most businesses and rival governments have concluded that it is better to go along and get along than to stand up to Donald Trump.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenMost businesses and rival governments have concluded that it is better to go along and get along than to stand up to Donald Trump.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersProject Syndicate economistsTrump tariffsTrump’s hypocritical new tariffs are a chance for the world to fight backJoseph StiglitzThe president’s pretext of stopping forced labour is only a ruse – he is trying to grab a share of global trade for the USMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.02 EDTShareHere he goes again. The US President,Donald Trump, is increasing and decreasing tariffs willy-nilly, violating international agreements that he himself signed and almost surely violating federal law. The only difference this time is that he has a new pretext for abusing tariffs: stopping forced labour.Of course, the administration is right that too little is being done about forced labour. But its stated concern is a ruse. With the new tariffs closely tracking the ones that Trump imposed on the basis of trade balances, are we supposed to believe that bilateral trade deficits just so happen to be highly correlated with the use of forced labour?After the supreme courtstruck downTrump’s previous tariffs, the administration imposed 150-day temporary tariffs – already deemed illegal by the courts but still under appeal even as they expired in late July – and now these new ones following an “investigation” into other countries’ supposed failure to police labour abuses. Not surprisingly, China, long a suspected source of goods produced with forced labour, has largely been given a pass. With its control of rare earths and critical minerals, China can slap Trump down whenever it wants. When another country has the means and the willingness to fight back, Trump always chickens out (TACO). This time, he didn’t even bother picking a fight with the Chinese.double quotation markNot surprisingly, China, long a suspected source of goods produced with forced labour, has largely been given a passMoreover, if Trump was really concerned about forced labour, he would address the problem at home. After all, the US has long been a centre of forced labour, owing to the loophole in the 13th amendment to the US constitution: “Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction.”This language was infamously used in the Jim Crow South to defend the use of chain gangs, and it continues to be abused throughout much of the US, with less than a quarter of US states forbidding forced labour. The US has just 5% of the world’s population but accounts fora quarter of the world’s prisoners. According to one of the most thorough studies offorced labour in the US(byMichael Poyker), nearly1.4 millionUS prisoners were employed in 2005, with roughly 600,000 working specifically in manufacturing – 4.2% of the total manufacturing workforce at the time. (Those seeking a better understanding of the US system of captive labour should also watch Ava DuVernay’s 2016 documentary,13th.)When Trump wantonly slapped tariffs on the rest of the world last year, he described the move as “reciprocal”. But in this new context, reciprocity would call for high tariffs on products made in US states that still exploit prison labour.The new tariffs against the EU are especially hard to justify, because a 2024 EU law (theCorporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive) already banned the importation of goods produced with forced labour, including those produced by subcontractors. In yet another pearl of hypocrisy, the US secretary of commerce, Howard Lutnick, previouslyclaimedthat the EU law posed “unnecessary negative burdens” on American companies, and that the US was therefore prepared to consider “all conceivable trade tools”.The EU should call out this hypocrisy and not capitulate. It should impose reciprocal tariffs on goods produced in the US states that use prison labour most extensively. Thelistof goods and companies reportedly using prison labour somewhere in their supply chain is extensive and includes leading US firms such as Burger King, Cargill, and Walmart. If Trump’s actions motivate the EU to investigate forced labour in the US, it will be doing US workers a service. (Sadly, hardly anyone in the EU has made a peep about the issue; all we have heard is a sigh of relief that Europe wasn’t hit harder.)Nor does the hypocrisy end there. To justify new tariffs againstCanada, Trump invoked a provision of the infamous Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 allowing the US to respond to discriminatory tariffs. But recall that the entire World Trade Organization system is based on nondiscrimination, a principle that Trump’s tariff policies have flagrantly defied. In this case, Canada imposed tariffs on US goods in retaliation for Trump’s discriminatory tariffs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markLest anyone forget, tariffs are just a distortionary tax that comes at the expense of American consumers and US competitivenessOnce again, Trump is subverting international law in an effort to seize a larger share of the value embedded in global supply chains, and harming theUS economyin the process. Lest anyone forget, tariffs are just a distortionary tax that comes at the expense of American consumers and US competitiveness.Trump’s tariff wars have not led to any reshoring of manufacturing. In fact, US manufacturing jobs havedeclinedby 75,000 since his second inauguration, after rising under PresidentJoe Biden. In nominal terms, the US trade deficit in goods has actually increased during Trump’s second term, reaching a record high of$1.24tn. That is no surprise to any economist. Multilateral trade deficits depend less on tariffs than on key macroeconomic variables such as domestic national savings, a metric that Trump’s record-breaking fiscal deficits have undermined.Trump gets away with his bullying because too many people, at home and abroad, have capitulated to him. Most businesses and rival governments have concluded that it is better to go along and get along than to stand up for themselves. But Trump is just like any other authoritarian leader: he needs to be feared. The longer the world gives him what he needs, the greater the disaster that awaits us all.Joseph E Stiglitzis a Nobel laureate in economics, a university professor at Columbia University and a former chief economist of the World BankExplore more on these topicsTrump tariffsProject Syndicate economistsUS economyEuropean UnionCanadaDonald TrumpEuropeTariffscommentShareReuse this content

title: Lonely planet: why are we addicted to the social media scroll when it is so clearly harming us? | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: I am hanging on to a product that makes people I loathe more super-rich while they trash the world
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: I am hanging on to a product that makes people I loathe more super-rich while they trash the world
Content: ‘I have had an at best ambivalent – and at worst deleterious – relationship with two social media platforms that I’ve had to quit cold turkey,’ writes Paul Daley.Photograph: Anatolii Frolov/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘I have had an at best ambivalent – and at worst deleterious – relationship with two social media platforms that I’ve had to quit cold turkey,’ writes Paul Daley.Photograph: Anatolii Frolov/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionLonelinessLonely planet: why are we addicted to the social media scroll when it is so clearly harming us?Paul DaleyI am hanging on to a product that makes people I loathe more super-rich while they trash the worldMon 3 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 18.36 EDTShareThere is so much talk of all the lonely people in the world right now that the pervasive state of loneliness is being called an epidemic.I don’t think that is an overstatement. I see loneliness around me all of the time. Everywhere. Not just in the faces of rough sleepers who look up at passers-by in the hope of finding eye contact and a little empathy – but also in the faces of those who rush past avoiding them, their heads wired or aired to their phones.I see it on the faces in the bus glued to screens or zoned out in the bubbles of their cars on the freeway.Academic research all over the world, including here in Australia, indicates young people areespecially proneto loneliness and its perilous repercussions for mental and physical health. Many will find this counterintuitive. Surely those of older cohorts – facing the deaths of partners, friends and siblings, the prospect of living alone or shifting into care or already there – would be experiencing more isolation?Bed rot, doomscrolling and a single goldfish: the Melbourne art show blowing loneliness openRead moreBut much about the young and loneliness makes perfect sense to me. “The young” – people up to say 25 (who I could also call super-young given the demographic precipice where I hover) are the generation of hyper-connectivity. Most of us are unhealthily yet necessarily reliant on our phones (as recentnetwork outagesillustrate too well). But it’s no stretch to say that those up to 25 (I base this partly on the unreliable science of familial observation) are, if not quite born hyper-connected then develop reliance, soon too become an addiction, to hyper-connectivity prodigiously early.Notwithstanding the questionable efficacy of Australia’s purportedunder-16 social media ban, myriad are the e-ways – through gaming and countless apps – that the young have grown up communicating through and that the rest of us use routinely. But hyper-connection (like mistaking for the real deal virtualfriendsyou’ll never meet over a cup of tea or a beer; we’ve all done it) has actually led to a global state of emotionally tactile, under-connection.Forget the young for a minute while I consider others who might bethe old. I mean people like me. For large periods of the past almost 20 years I’ve been alone (dogs aside) in a room with my thoughts and my research and keyboard for eight or 10 hours a day. But the only times I’ve tended to feel lonely has been when I’ve been tuned into social media.The scroll leaves me dead inside. Empty. Often angry.Yes, I have made some friends and contacts on social media. I have marketed my writing and done events about it online. But I have had an at best ambivalent – and at worstdeleterious – relationship with two social media platformsthat I’ve had to quit cold turkey. They only served to isolate me psychologically, emotionally and professionally.I now find that I’m close to ditching another because my user experience has become the same. My good, by many rationales successful and privileged life (no matter how rationally, how positively, myprefrontal cortexprocesses it as such) always pales compared with so many of the heavily curatedbestandhappiestandout of the parkprofessionally winninglives in my feed. If I get jammed in that scroll, the isolation begins to creep. The loneliness takes its grip.And I am not a heavy user. So, this is where I say (again), “Damn it, I’ll get off.” If it can make me feel this type of lonely, what’s it doing to the more vulnerable? Especially children I know who are transported to unknown, potentially dangerous places when online, and bored when they are not.Loneliness influencers: why are people suddenly boasting about having no friends?Read moreWell, we already know: the more extreme forms of harm include algorithmicencouragement to suicideand diet dangerously, and for others to commit violent acts of extremism as a way of“belonging”. And yet something (FOMO, a way to chat with the small communities of the genuinely like-minded I’ve met online) keeps me hanging on to a product that makes people I loathe more super-rich while they trash the world.Of course, the other side of my brain challenges me: what other highly addictive malevolent product – one that allows the wilful encouragement of suicide and violence, especially in the young, that feeds on isolation and loneliness, yet only makes it worse – would I keep subscribing to?For the truth is that the nearer I am to an unattainable analogue life, the further I feel away from loneliness.Alone, with a book – or better, a book and a dog – feels like a near perfect state of connectivity. So, too, the communal space: the museum, the gallery, the theatre, the silent shared knowing of the library … among strangers. In real life awe. With phones on silent. Momentarily e-disconnected.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistIn Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor.Explore more on these topicsLonelinessOpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: The most dynamic countries are surging ahead with high-speed rail. Others, like Britain, are stuck in the station | Christian Wolmar | The Guardian
description: Around the world, these trains have boosted economies, development and prestige. The costs of missing out are high, says transport writer and author Christian Wolmar
Author: Christian Wolmar
Headline: Around the world, these trains have boosted economies, development and prestige. The costs of missing out are high, says transport writer and author Christian Wolmar
Content: High-speed trains depart from sidings at Nanjing South railway station, China, 30 June 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHigh-speed trains depart from sidings at Nanjing South railway station, China, 30 June 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesOpinionRail transportThe most dynamic countries are surging ahead with high-speed rail. Others, like Britain, are stuck in the stationChristian WolmarAround the world, these trains have boosted economies, development and prestige. The costs of missing out are highChristian Wolmar is the author of Fast Track: The Extraordinary Story of High-Speed RailMon 3 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTShareWith all our grumbling about trains – and it is close to a national pastime – it is easy to forget the successes. There is a tale to tell, for example, about high-speed trains, that goes beyond theendless wrangling over HS2.If you look at the history around the globe, as I have, you find that high-speed trains saved the railways. An industry that was gradually sinking into oblivion, thanks to motorways and aeroplanes, has been revitalised by a technological revolution that means trains travel faster, more safely and more comfortably.Over time, beautiful but inefficient steam engines and their dirty diesel successors have been replaced by sleek modern trains that shrink distances and provide a service that their rivals on either land or in the air cannot compete with. Train travel that had been in declinehas become the preferred mode of transportfor many journeys previously dominated by aviation.But this is a revolution that almost didn’t reach Europe. In 1964, Japan became the pioneer, creatingthe Shinkansen, known worldwide as the bullet train, in effect the first motorway on rail, with dedicated tracks, a small number of stops and an at the time unprecedented top speed of 210 km/h (130mph). Nowadays trains often run at 190mph and they mayroutinely reach 250mph before the decade is out.View image in fullscreenThe world’s first maglev passenger train in Shanghai, 11 August 2002.Photograph: China Photo/ReutersBut as Japan surged ahead, 1960s Europe had fallen out of love with trains.Beeching-type cutswere the order of the day across the continent and a new invention seemed in the 1980s to be about to supersede the iron road. This was levitation technology, with trains being elevated by air or magnetism and pushed forward at great speed by rocket propulsion or magnets. Tests in France of the Aérotrain saw it reach speeds of almost 270mph, while the German government was promotingmaglev technology, funding a line running between Hamburg and Berlin.Trains were 19th century, it was said, while maglev was a technology for the 21st. But then, just as with the hyperloop,Elon Musk’s recent failed reinventionof the maglev technology, the plans for maglev fell apart, as costs soared and the practicalities of developing a whole new system running into crowded city centres proved insuperable. A 2006 disaster on the German test trackkilling 23 peopleput paid to any hopes of reviving the idea.This victory of the railways over its rivals guarantees that trains will be operating across the world in the 22nd century. The victory by rail meant high-speed rail systems emerging first in France and then across Europe in Germany, Italy and Spain. In addition, 25 countries in the rest of the world, ranging from Morocco and Turkey to Taiwan and Uzbekistan, have high-speed rail systems or are developing them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAn anti-HS2 campaigner in Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire, 19 May 2021.Photograph: Maureen McLean/Rex/ShutterstockThe rewards are great, but the subject is always controversial because the route to high-speed rail is never easy. These are megaprojects costing sums with more zeros than any other government projects except possibly defence and space travel, and to see them through needs consistent government support, a clear understanding of their purpose and a long-term budget.In all the high-speed rail schemes across the world that I examined for my book, it was a struggle to find any that were completed on time and on budget. Most achieved one of these – the UK’s HS2 and the California high-speed project being the exceptions,failing miserably on both counts– and by and large they have been successful in attracting passengers and in many cases seeing off domestic flights on their routes. Who now flies between London and Paris, or indeed Barcelona and Madrid, or Rome and Milan? Mostly only people who are interlining, that is, transferring to another flight. The sensible choice for most people will usually be a pleasant train ride with fewer security hurdles to overcome and city-centre to city-centre travel.New high-speed lines have generally been designed to relieve congestion on the busiest existing railway routes, such as Paris-Lyon or Tokyo-Osaka. But high-speed rail has also been used as a catalyst for a wider modernisation scheme, notably in Spain, which surprisingly hasEurope’s most extensive high-speed rail network,with about 2,500 miles of line, as a result of a clear government strategy to use trains to create better connections between regions and the capital, Madrid. The Spanish government, noting the success of its initial line built for the Seville Expo between Madrid and Seville, then embarked on a national programme that revived a dying rail system and changed the image of the country from a poor relative of its European counterparts to that of a self-confident, dynamic nation. High-speed rail can help do that.But for the world leader,look to Chinawhich has built 70% of the world’s mileage of high-speed lines in under 20 years. The figures are so extraordinary that they seem almost unbelievable. There are now about 31,000 miles of high-speed line with about 10,000 services carrying an average of 10 million people daily.Here, too, though, it is more than just a railway. The officials I talked to while travelling around China on its stunning network were clear about this. Many of the early lines were built between the largest cities but now the system, which they hope to increase by at least 10,000 miles by 2040, is being expanded to smaller towns and cities to create a genuinely national network. This remarkable project is seen as a way of uniting the country in the same way the railways in Germany and Italy created nations out of these fragmented countries in the 19th century.That was the original concept in the UK when HS2 was first conceived andits progenitor, Andrew Adonis, registered HS3, HS4 and HS5 as companies. We can but dream that this will ever be realised. For the story of high-speed rail I found was of go-ahead nations embracing the future, while others, including alas Britain, are being left behind.Christian Wolmar is the author of Fast Track: The Extraordinary Story of High-Speed RailExplore more on these topicsRail transportOpinionTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: The right hates The Odyssey because of its ‘wokeness’ – but it missed an even bigger threat to its worldview | Peter Swallow | The Guardian
description: The new film extols the value of a rules-based world order. That’s far more radical than any casting decision says Labour MP and classicist Peter Swallow
Author: Peter Swallow
Headline: The new film extols the value of a rules-based world order. That’s far more radical than any casting decision says Labour MP and classicist Peter Swallow
Content: In Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, civilisation is collapsing as raiders defy Zeus’s law.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesView image in fullscreenIn Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, civilisation is collapsing as raiders defy Zeus’s law.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal PicturesOpinionThe OdysseyThe right hates The Odyssey because of its ‘wokeness’ – but it missed an even bigger threat to its worldviewPeter SwallowThe new film extols the value of a rules-based world order. That’s far more radical than any casting decisionPeter Swallow is Labour MP for Bracknell, and the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on classics. Before his election, he was a classics teacher and academicMon 3 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 11.19 EDTShareFor years, a small but vocal corner of the extremely online right has looked to the ancient world to justify its polluted brand of politics. The classicist Donna Zuckerberg (sister of Facebook founder Mark) wrote a book about it way back in 2018 calledNot All Dead White Men– a deep dive into the corners of the internet where misogynists pretend ancient philosophy can justify their hatred of minorities.You would think that these self-appointed guardians of the ancient world would be excited about a blockbuster retelling one of its greatest pieces of literature, the Odyssey. Especially when Christopher Nolan’s film has been getting rave reviews, “the vast majority … written by men”, as the Guardian’sCatherine Shoard has pointed out. The Odyssey is an action-packed thriller with a fight scene every five seconds. In many ways (and I don’t mean this as a criticism of Nolan; I loved the film for all its flaws), it’s a movie designed to appeal to their tastes. And yet.Many rightwing commentators have been railing atthe film’s perceived “wokeness”for months – since well before it hit cinemas. Nolan’s biggest crime seems to have been castingLupita Nyong’o, a black woman, as Helen of Troy, the entirely mythical daughter of Zeus. In other versions of her myth, she was born out of a swan’s egg alongside her mortal sister Clytemnestra and her two brothers, who were either gods or mortals depending on which one you read. I can see why they’re worried about inaccuracy …There have been plenty of other criticisms from keyboard warriors concerned about a lack of historical accuracy in a film adaptation of an entirely fictional myth. Having a PhD in classics means I agree with them that Corinthian helmets aren’t historically accurate to the film’s bronze age setting; having a sense of proportion and an understanding of artistic licence means I don’t really care.Elon Musk has, perhaps predictably, emerged as the loudest critic, even calling Nolan an “anti-White racist” and suggesting he might use Grok to create an AI-powered Odyssey movie “that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer”. But as ridiculous as that all is, the right shouldn’t hate Nolan’s Odyssey for its inaccuracies. They should hate it because of what it has to say about the very real, very Homeric concept ofxenia.Xenia, which Nolan translates as “Zeus’s law”, was an ancient custom that governed how people were supposed to treat strangers. Zeus’s law is absolutely original toHomer. In fact, it’s a pretty fundamental part of the poem. When I taught GCSE students about the Odyssey,xeniawas one of the first concepts I’d teach them. In Homer’s Odyssey, as in Nolan’s film, it drives how different civilisations and cultures are supposed to interact with one another in society. People (and monsters such as the Cyclops) who break Zeus’s law are punished; those who uphold it (such as Odysseus’s son, Telemachus) are rewarded.But Nolan’s take onxeniais unmistakably modern. To me, it feels like an allegory for the fraying, rules-based international system. Whether it’s state sovereignty being undermined by Russia, international maritime law under threat from China or Donald Trump’s disdain for global multilateral cooperation on everything from trade to defence to the climate crisis, the rules-based order established after the second world war is under threat.At the end of the movie – spoilers – Odysseus and Penelope see their entire bronze age Greek civilisation collapsing. This is based on an actual historical event, the Mycenaean collapse. In Nolan’s retelling, it happens because the people of the sea are raiding and warring, breaking Zeus’s law.The message for a modern audience is, again, not subtle: society will collapse if we abandon our rules-based international order. If Nolan’s film really is “woke”, this is why – because it’s fundamentally a film about the value of multilateralism produced for an increasingly nationalistic world. Musk and co seem to have missed this message. But it’s the real reason why they should hate the film. It pushes back against everything the hard right are trying to achieve and instead makes clear that a commitment to international diplomacy isn’t a nice-to-have – it’s a prerequisite to civilisation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd, yes, for all those complaining, that’s not in the original poem. Nolan’s film is a reimagining. But here’s the truth about classics. Nobody gets to decide how all those wonderful ancient stories get retold, rewritten for new times or redeployed to make new arguments or share new perspectives. No one person gets to own the ancient world. Especially notElon Musk.Peter Swallow is Labour MP for Bracknell, and the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on classics. title: Finally, we have a PM for the digital age. But real change requires more than just being good on camera | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Connection with voters on screen only pays off when it’s matched with bold policies in the real world – as it has for Zohran Mamdani in New York, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Connection with voters on screen only pays off when it’s matched with bold policies in the real world – as it has for Zohran Mamdani in New York, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Andy Burnham taking a selfie during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield, 31 July 2026.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham taking a selfie during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield, 31 July 2026.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamFinally, we have a PM for the digital age. But real change requires more than just being good on cameraNesrine MalikConnection with voters on screen only pays off when it’s matched with bold policies in the real world – as it has for Zohran Mamdani in New YorkMon 3 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.03 EDTShareAndy Burnham is having a good time. I can’t remember the last time a prime minister (or indeed any high-profile British politician) actually looked as though they were enjoying what they were doing. I saw a clip the other day in whichBurnham rememberedarguing with his dad about the point of an English degree, quoted poetry and discussed the importance of mastering words. It was almost enough to make you feel sorry for Keir Starmer. In his entire time as leader of the Labour party and then the head of the government, Starmer delivered not a single unprocessed moment. No natural sentiment escaped the carapace. And here is his successor, practically oozing it.It matters. It’s good and healthy to have a leader who looks as though they want to be where they are. Whose approach isn’t that of a scold or a receiver who has taken control of the premises, or someone whose sole aim is to tenaciously clamber up to the top job and hold on for dear life.I hadn’t fully realised, until Starmer cleared off, how much his premiership gave off the sense that the public were doing a bad job. That it was somehow their fault Starmer wasn’t as popular as he thought he should have been. As though it were the public’s job to deliver stable government and stop being so restive and fickle; stop having feelings and opinions on your prime minister that show up in the polling. Poor Starmer,some said, smashed fatally against the rocks by the waves of the roiling, insentient electorate of an ungovernable country.Burnham’s approach restores the basic principle, lost for so long, that you have to woo people and establish a connection. Over the past two weeks, it looks as though it has been easier to get a replyfrom his X accountthan for business executives toestablish contactwith his team. The videos he is posting on social media are, by any measure, a remarkable departure from the old way of doing things. They collectively have a voice, an almost salesman-like pitch. They say “just hear me out”. If anything, Burnham’s posts on everything from the importance of learningpractical skillstoranking pub snacksshow how late British politics is to the game. My first sense of it all wasn’t of how revolutionary it was, but why on earth it took so long.The answer, of course, is that no one had the taste for it. The personalities of our last few prime ministers were not, to put it mildly, those of digital natives. Their styles were “cop”, “sidekick bully” and “Liz Truss”, rather than public-facing politicians keen to communicate via the platforms they actually use.Burnham’s performances may sometimes be perilously close to shtick, but he has an undeniable flair and energy for the sort of modern direct-to-camera address that could give him an edge in a media environment where the parameters have for too long been set by an overwhelmingly rightwing traditional media.Burnham knows all of this. A little too much, perhaps. The bar is in hell and so is the discourse. It takes very little to break through the grim record of the past few years and outdo stale TV and radio formats. It would be easy enough to post some good, sharp stuff on your own social media and call it a day. And if it continues that way – that is, an approach to communication which does not tackle the positions that made the atmosphere so fetid in the first place – then it will all soon become background noise, and then an irritant.Because digital political success is not just about being good on camera. Burnham’s style has been compared with that of the obvious originator of the model, Zohran Mamdani. But Mamdani shows that having aflair for direct communicationis only the first stage, the part where you get people on board. (His videos speaking in differentlanguagesduring the election campaign were gold.) You then have to keep at it and show you are new in both style and practice. That you are a strong advocate for people. And, most importantly, that you are a cheerful, unflappable threat to their enemies. “When I ran for mayor, I said I was gonna tax the rich,” Mamdani saysin a recent video. Then he comes up close, knocks the camera. “Well, today we’re taxing the rich.” His pied-à-terre tax, he told New Yorkers, will be levied on properties like the one he’s standing under, a penthouse belonging to the hedge fund CEO Ken Griffin.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham the crowd-pleaser knows how to make friends, but he’ll be defined by how he makes enemies | Andy BeckettRead moreBurnham has already done some tangible good by starting out with policies focused on people’s pockets – on bills and bus fares and VAT relief – and with an evocative drive todevolve powerfrom London. He promises “a new political model and a new economic model”. Them’s fighting words. Or should be. But his narrative lacks a clear articulation of what actually separates the needy from the predatory. Yes, at this point it is revolutionary just to name the problems, let alone do anything about them. But it will not be enough.Burnham seems satisfied with figuring out what he can get away with without that epic fight; with broadly gesturing to how bad Thatcherism and neoliberalism are, but not actually slaying them. He won’t target the under-taxed wealthy because he doesn’t want to “create new divisionsand pitch people one against another”. He is willing to keep in place the punitive immigration regime of the previous administration (whilevalorising the foreign workerswho care for his father). And while it’s early days on foreign policy, things look to be business as usual, suggesting Burnham has little appetite for resetting international relations in a period of historic flux. Even though heapologised for Labour’s stance on Gaza, he continues the previous government’spermission for the US to use some UK bases for air strikes on Iran, and is entertaining, at leastaccording to Trump, friendly discussions on “North Sea Oil, Trade, the Military Alliance, Demining of the Hormuz Strait”. There looks to be no necessary reckoning afoot with the US’s calamitous actions in the Middle East.First you change the political culture, then you can change the political model. That culture is style and presentation and some policy, yes, but to really capture lightning in a bottle, you must show that intellectual and moral barriers are being redrawn. If there is any lesson to be gleaned from our age of short-lived prime ministers, it is that all ostensible advantages – landslides, huge polling leads, mandates to deliver Brexit – dissolve under the harsh light of insincerity born from timidity. Authenticity comes from congruence. Burnham might be able to get away with a lot of the effect and some of the substance for a while, but he will only be the revolutionary prime minister he promises he is – people will onlybelievethat he is – if he breaks something other than the fourth wall.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionZohran MamdaniSocial mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Liechtenstein’s archaic abortion laws need to be modernised. But a prince is standing in the way | Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel | The Guardian
description: Substantial hurdles are faced by women who have to travel abroad to access abortion, but Hereditary Prince Alois says he will veto any changes, says writer and campaigner from Liechtenstein Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel
Author: Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel
Headline: Substantial hurdles are faced by women who have to travel abroad to access abortion, but Hereditary Prince Alois says he will veto any changes, says writer and campaigner from Liechtenstein Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel
Content: Hereditary Prince Alois speaking at Liechtenstein's National Day celebrations in Vaduz, 15 August 2024.Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHereditary Prince Alois speaking at Liechtenstein's National Day celebrations in Vaduz, 15 August 2024.Photograph: Gian Ehrenzeller/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockOpinionAbortionLiechtenstein’s archaic abortion laws need to be modernised. But a prince is standing in the wayGabriella Alvarez-HummelThe hurdles for women who have to travel abroad to access abortion are considerable, but Hereditary Prince Alois says he will veto any changesMon 3 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.16 EDTShareThe first person Maria* called when she found out she was pregnant was her doctor. The second person was a lawyer. The single mother of one was in shock, and considering terminating the pregnancy. But she first had to make sure that she wasn’t about to do something illegal, because all she knew was that abortions were forbiddenwhere she lived. “On top of the emotional mountain that was already there, I also had to deal with this,” Maria told me.She also knew she wouldn’t get any information about abortions in her own country – that’s illegal too. After making her decision, she drove to a clinic across the border. It was a stressful, if short, 45-minute drive, at the end of which another hurdle was waiting: “Oh, you’re fromLiechtenstein?” the receptionist said, according to Maria. “Then you have to pay immediately – 680 Swiss francs (£620) please.” She was taken aback and asked: “What if I can’t pay that right now?” The receptionist replied: “Then you’ll have to come back tomorrow.”Liechtenstein has one of the strictest abortion laws in Europe. This is probably not something you know about my “micro-state” – you might think of its banks, of Alpine scenery and castles fit for a Netflix romance. But in between them live real people with real lives, and every year, anestimated 40 womenwho wish to terminate their pregnancy on their own terms cannot do so in their country.But if you ask Liechtenstein’s regent, Hereditary Prince Alois, our prime minister, or random people on the street, many will tell you the same thing: there is no problem at all. Since 2015, women arelegally permittedto have an abortion outside the country, and the external border is never more than a 15-minute drive away. And anyway, it is allowed if the woman was raped or if her health is at risk, so what more could you ask for?What I, and others who are part of a new people’s initiative aresimply askingfor is what is already standard in most European countries: decriminalisation of abortion up to 12 weeks, repeal of the national ban on information about abortions, and for the procedure to be covered by health insurance. Arecent poll showsthat 62% of voters would be in favour of it if a vote were held. It should be a done deal. But no matter what the people say: the hereditary prince has already announced that he would veto any change in the law, long before a single vote has been cast.Liechtenstein is not your typical European monarchy, and theprince’s poweris anything but ceremonial. Alois can veto any bill, dismiss the government or individual ministers, appoint judges, and propose changes to the law. He usually exercises this power with restraint, and has never actually used his veto. He has only threatened to use it once, in 2011, which was the last time a popular initiativetried to legaliseabortion. With the prince’s veto looming over the vote, it was rendered effectively pointless, leading to a historically low turnout, and a52% vote against.A national debate over the monarchy’s role ensued, culminating in a vote in which more than 76% chose to preserve the prince’sveto power. This happened though after Alois and his father, Prince Hans-Adam II, had threatened to leave the country if the vote didn’t go in their favour – a move that would have plunged our nation into a severe crisis.This is why it continues to be the case that speaking out in favour of legalising abortion is regarded as speaking out against the monarchy.Alois says that the present laws are there to protect unborn life, even though he acknowledges that the abortion bandoesn’t actually preventany abortions. And our prime minister, Brigitte Haas, says she’s pragmatic anddoesn’t see a problemwith sending women across the border. I have one question: have they ever spoken to a single woman who had to cross the border for an abortion? Because if they had, they would know that the abortion ban is indeed harming those affected in several ways.Since 2022, I’ve conducted more than a dozen interviews with women from Liechtenstein who had to seek abortion care outside the country. Their stories have several things in common.Just like Maria, Liechtensteiners who seek abortion care are completely on their own. A ban on information – the last one of its kind inEurope– prevents local groups and professionals from giving advice about procedures and where to go. Pressured for time by the 12-week limit for abortions in Switzerland and Austria, they have to make phone call after phone call to find the right clinic, for which they have to pay in advance, up to 2,500 Swiss francs (£2,360). They fear legal consequences, because many don’t realise that under Liechtenstein’s law only doctors are criminally liable. And they feel stigmatised by a law telling them to deal with their problems elsewhere. As Maria puts it: “You feel so awful when you want to do it, because it’s so taboo in this country. You feel like you’re a monster.”Alois’s veto announcement may have been intended to discourage people from signing the initiative or to demotivate us campaigners. The opposite has happened: many people felt even more motivated to sign, and in a country of about 41,000 people (only around 21,000 with voting rights), we received 4,970 signatures, the second-largest tally of signatories for a popular initiative in the country’s history – equivalent to 10.5m signatures in the UK or 13.8m in Germany.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA few weeks ago I went collecting some of those signatures in the streets of Vaduz. A dad with his two kids told me he had already signed, and his young daughter asked what we were doing. I said we were collecting signatures for a cause, and if we collected enough of them, all the people in the country could vote on it. Her father added: “Well, one person has already cast his vote.”There is only one man we have to convince. We hope a very clear vote might do the trick.Gabriella Alvarez-Hummel is a campaigner and journalist from Liechtenstein, focusing on reproductive rightsDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.*Maria’s name was changed to protect her privacy.Explore more on these topicsAbortionOpinionLiechtensteinEuropeHealthWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: The inability to deliver the changes Indigenous Australians need is no longer just a moral failure but a civilisational one | Noel Pearson | The Guardian
description: After the rejection of the voice, the conversation about structural reform of the federal arrangements governing Aboriginal affairs must resume
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After the rejection of the voice, the conversation about structural reform of the federal arrangements governing Aboriginal affairs must resume
Content: Noel Pearson addresses the 26th annual Garma festival in Gulkula in the Northern Territory.Photograph: James Ross/EPAView image in fullscreenNoel Pearson addresses the 26th annual Garma festival in Gulkula in the Northern Territory.Photograph: James Ross/EPAOpinionGarma festivalThe inability to deliver the changes Indigenous Australians need is no longer just a moral failure but a civilisational oneNoel PearsonAfter the rejection of the voice, the conversation about structural reform of the federal arrangements governing Aboriginal affairs must resumeIndigenous leaders look to the future at Garma: ‘People are feeling strong again’Dance, art and Indigenous storytelling: Garma festival 2026 in picturesSun 2 Aug 2026 21.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 22.48 EDTShareTheUluru statement from the heartwas our prayer to the Australian people.There was hope in its words.The statement was written with love. It stands as probably the most beautiful unrequited letter of love in Australian political history.For those of us who urged faith, hope and love, there is an account to be given for the hopes raised, the faith urged and the love lost in the referendum.I must account for that. So, three years later, I stand here with great reluctance.What right has anyone to raise hopes when those hopes were so badly misplaced?What right has anyone to offer a vision that turns out to be a mirage?That is the source of my hesitation to speak of these things. But I cannot allow the failure of the referendum to excuse me from my responsibility to the communities who voted yes.What we sought was to secure their future. This is how the statement spoke of their predicament:double quotation markProportionately, we are the most incarcerated people on the planet. We are not an innately criminal people. Our children are aliened from their families at unprecedented rates. This cannot be because we have no love for them. And our youth languish in detention in obscene numbers. They should be our hope for the future.These dimensions of our crisis tell plainly the structural nature of our problem. This is the torment of our powerlessness.That is why these communities wanted the voice.Because from the very beginning of my public life, it was, and still is, the future of those communities – not least my own – that has been the central focus of my wakeful dreams.Our present is not good. Nor is our future assured.When I started my advocacy, grog was the main problem. It took 15 years before governments were forced by us to act.When they finally implemented the alcohol management plans we advocated, the results were fundamental. Royal Flying Doctor injury retrievals fell by more than half.A record number of First Nations people died in NSW prison custody last year. Advocates fear this year will be worseRead moreThat should have taught us something. Instead, governments repeated the same mistake. Cannabis, previously unknown to our communities, spread unhindered. Now ice is the neglected crisis.Whatever progress we made with alcohol has since been undone by governments of both persuasions, conservative and Labor.Alcoholsupply has expanded, and women and children are experiencing the worst recorded violence in more than 20 years.In 2025 alone, more than 1,100 women and children were recorded as victims of assault across Cape York’s communities. So far this year, 513 women and children have been victims of assault.Until political parties sever ties with vice industries − grog and gambling − little will change. The poor are a goldmine, said the economist Thomas Sowell. The CLP, LNP and ALP, when in power, believe it is the divine right of the vice industries to make a profit from the immiseration of our people.Child protection tells the same story.Queensland is a serial inquirer yet children entering out-of-home care has continued to rise.Under the Beattie government, Queensland spent a decade building an outsourced industry around the management of child and family crisis. They turned our children into fodder for a parasitic industry.By the time that disaster was obvious, there was another inquiry. More than a decade after the Carmody inquiry, the government this week announced its response to the third child-safety commission of inquiry in less than 30 years.In 1998, around one in five children in out-of-home care was Indigenous. Today, it is one in two.Garma festival kicks off in Arnhem landQueensland thinks it can remove its way out of this crisis. It has created a billion-dollar system that waits for harm to be done to children, instead of investing in strengthening families before harm escalates and confronting the grog that causes the dysfunction in the first place. Protecting the publicans and gambling outlets are their abiding concern.In 10 years I predict there will be more children in that system, and an even greater proportion will be Indigenous.Child protection will worsen.Youth justicewill worsen. Adult incarceration will worsen.Not because we do not know what to do but because our governments won’t let us do it.After nearly 10 years of the Palaszczuk government, Cape York made no sustained progress towards Closing the Gap – and, in critical areas, the gap widened.In the lead-up to the 2024 Queensland election, I wrote to the then premier, Steven Miles, and the leader of the opposition, David Crisafulli:double quotation markWhat we have seen is that if you pursue ‘progressive’ policies unable to deliver results, you end up having to resort to regressive policies anyway. Regressive ‘tough on crime’ law and order style approaches alone, however, also do not work. In combination, the progressive focus on more and more ineffective services and programs, and the regressive focus on tough on crime policies, can result in nothing more than entrenching disadvantage for young people, their families, and communities even further.But we have no chance under the current arrangements. Our children are caught between the Scylla of the soft bigotry of low expectations of Labor governments and the Charybdis of the hard bigotry of the Liberal Nationals.The inability of governments to deliver the reforms our people need is no longer only a moral failure but a civilisational one. The destruction of the communities of remote Australia is truly at stake.Consider what is called Indigenous expenditure. In 2010-11, governments attributed $25.4bn in direct expenditure to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians. By 2015-16, that figure had risen to $33.4bn. The figure is no longer officially updated.Australians heard these numbers and imagined that vast sums are being handed to Indigenous communities. That is not what the figures mean.In 2015-16, 82% of the expenditure attributed toIndigenous Australianswas expenditure through mainstream government services. Only a fraction is Indigenous-specific expenditure.‘A white man’s fantasy’: if we want to rebuild social cohesion, we need to acknowledge where it all started to unravelRead moreMuch of this is expended through mainstream state and territory systems. It includes Medicare, schools and hospitals. But it also includes policing, courts, out-of-home-care, youth detention and prisons.The commonwealth provides much of the funding, while the states and territories control many of the systems through which it is spent. What can you do if your state chooses to spend it on detention over education?So we have an agenda.Our plan may fall into the abyss of federalism. There simply is no precedent to change the institutional architecture required to ensure these foundational obligations: work for the parents, education for the children.These foundational obligations are owed to the future of our children.But none of this will happen under our present arrangements.The 1967 referendum gave the commonwealth parliament jurisdiction over Aboriginal affairs, which it had lacked since federation. Just 10 years later, the first crisis of federalism in Aboriginal affairs under the new power occurred in the Queensland communities of Aurukun and Mornington Island.A dispute erupted over bauxite mining in Aurukun between the then premier, Joh Bjelke-Petersen, and the community. The Uniting church supported a legal challenge in the Queensland supreme court and the privy council, leading to retribution by Bjelke-Petersen.The church was ousted. The mission became a government settlement. This was the infamous Aurukun takeover.The leaders of Aurukun implored the commonwealth through the Department of Aboriginal Affairs to assume responsibility for the community. They wanted to be free from the jurisdiction of Bjelke-Petersen’s government.The then Liberal minister for Aboriginal affairs, Ian Viner, with prime minister Malcolm Fraser’s support, legislated to enable Aurukun and Mornington Island, and other communities that so desired, to come under the jurisdiction of the commonwealth.double quotation markThere should be no need for Aboriginal affairs departments in the states and territoriesThis was the Aboriginal Councils and Associations Act of 1978, the precursor to Corporations (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders) Act 2006.The people of Aurukun were hopeful that the Fraser government would bring their community under the jurisdiction of the commonwealth.Since the 1978 betrayal by Fraser and Viner, many Indigenous organisations were formed under the association provisions of the 1978 act but the council provisions – developed specifically for Aurukun and Mornington Island – never were.The parlous history of Aurukun began then. A canteen was forced upon the community in 1985 and the destruction has continued unabated since.In the 41 years since the Aurukun takeover I have often wondered what Aurukun would have been like today had the desire to be free from the jurisdiction of the Queensland government and instead have a direct relationship with the commonwealth been honoured by Fraser.The Fraser-Viner policy from 1978 that was legislated but not acted upon must now be revisited. The communities of remote Australia must come under the jurisdiction of the commonwealth. These communities and their lands would still come under the shared jurisdiction of the relevant states and territories for most functions governed by the state’s constitutional responsibilities but the administrative relationship for Aboriginal affairs would lie with the commonwealth.There should be no need for Aboriginal affairs departments in the states and territories.This would rationalise duplicated systems and institutions. It would stop Indigenous affairs being the black hole for state and territory government budgets.A direct funding relationship between the commonwealth and the organisations representing and serving these communities would enable development agendas such as the personal responsibility and opportunity act of Cape York Peninsula to receive the budgetary support it needs to close the gap.After the rejection of the voice, the conversation about structural reform of the federal arrangements governing Indigenous affairs must resume. If not a voice, then let us ask the question Dr Martin Luther King asked two years after US civil rights laws were passed and one year before his assassination.Where do we go from here?Noel Pearson is a director of Cape York Partnership and Good to Great Schools Australia. This is an edited version of his keynote address to theGarma festivalon SaturdayExplore more on these topicsGarma festivalOpinionIndigenous AustraliansRural and regional AustraliaNoel PearsonUluru statement from the heartAustralian politicsQueenslandcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t understand what Gaz was singing. It’s about needing a hug’: how Reef made Place Your Hands | Music | The Guardian
description: ‘We were swept up in the moment and full of testosterone. The 90s wasn’t a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive’
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: ‘We were swept up in the moment and full of testosterone. The 90s wasn’t a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive’
Content: Gary Stringer and Jack Bessant of Reef play Glastonbury in 1995.Photograph: Brian Rasic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGary Stringer and Jack Bessant of Reef play Glastonbury in 1995.Photograph: Brian Rasic/Getty ImagesHow we madeMusic‘I didn’t understand what Gaz was singing. It’s about needing a hug’: how Reef made Place Your Hands‘We were swept up in the moment and full of testosterone. The 90s wasn’t a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive’Interviews byRich PelleyMon 3 Aug 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Bessant, bassWe were hanging out with the lovely producer George Drakoulias at Abbey Road. He said, “We’re going to bring in some instruments for you guys” – and replaced the fairly low-budget ones we’d been playing. I was given this beautiful 1960s Fender Jazz bass.Sometimes you pick up an instrument you’ve never touched before and immediately start playing stuff you wouldn’t normally play. It made me want to come up with something cool, James Jamerson-style, with that Motown feel. I found the riff that became the bassline to Place Your Hands, showed it to Gaz, and he came up with this chilled melody about going down by the water. When Kenwyn House, our guitarist, added that classic opening guitar riff, it changed from something mellow into something much more action-packed.It was just a lovely time to be alive. We were young and everyone in the band was talented, even though we didn’t really know what we were doing. We were rockers at heart, but we were very open-minded. We listened to everything from Motown and Bob Marley to Van Morrison’sCommon One– Summertime in England can still make me cry. I eventually bought an old Telecaster bass – you can definitely hear the reggae influence in the bass during the bridge to Place Your Hands.I’ve always thought the emotion Gaz brought to it was incredible, but I didn’t fully understand what he was singing about until quite recently. He explained that “put your hands on” was a metaphor for wanting a hug, to help him through the grief of losing his grandfather. I hadn’t realised at the time because we were young rockers, swept up in the moment and full of testosterone, with no time to think about anything. The 90s wasn’t really a time when men were encouraged to be sensitive – there were all the lads’ mags, and we were playing that game to an extent. We certainly didn’t discuss our feelings in the way we would now. Looking back, I think the lyrics are beautiful.I don’t think we’ll ever get bored of playing it because it’s so funky and full of rhythm and spirit. We’ve had quite a few lineup changes, and Place Your Hands is the song that has always pulled us together. It gets people dancing and putting their hands up – even though the lyric is actually “Put your hands on”.Gary Stringer, vocalsWe were signed to S2 in 1993, under the legendary figures Lincoln Elias and Muff Winwood. Our first album reached the Top 10, we had three Top 40 singles and played Glastonbury, so we were really happy. We were touring the west coast of the US with stoner-rock band Kyuss when Lincoln suggested we meet George Drakoulias, who had worked with Rick Rubin at Def Jam and helped discover the Beastie Boys. George turned up wearing flowing white robes, which made quite an impression, and we decided to go with him for the second album.We recorded three or four songs at Abbey Road. George hired a 1960s Fender bass. Jack was fiddling around with it and started playing what would become the bassline to Place Your Hands. Kenwyn dropped his guitar’s E string down to D and came up with the riff that sits over Jack’s bassline. At first, I sang it quite gently, but then thought: “That’s too airy-fairy.” We went to Los Angeles to finish the album with George, taking the bassline and guitar riff with us.The lyrics are about the death of my grandfather, Kenneth. I was on the tour bus when I got a call saying he had died. I went to the morgue and my auntie said: “Do you want to see Ken?” I’d seen a dead body beside the road while on a surfing trip in Morocco when I was 18, but this had a different impact. The lyrics are essentially asking for comfort – for a cuddle. That’s why it’s “Put your hands on”. I’m sure if it was “Put your hands up” the song would have been even bigger.Chris Evans was a huge supporter of the band and played the single to death on Radio 1. When you went on TFI Friday, it didn’t matter if you were Dave Grohl or Oasis – you had to do the It’s Your Letters segment and sing those words to the melody of the song you were on the show promoting. For some reason, our version of It’s Your Letters stuck. “Put your hands on” and “It’s your letters” have the same number of syllables, so they used it every week ever after.The video cost about £250,000. We were turning head over heels on wires that had to be threaded through holes cut into our trousers. Place Your Hands accounts for a lot of my income. If we had 10 songs like that, I’d be a multimillionaire.Reef perform atLakefest festivalin Eastnor, Herefordshire, on 8 AugustExplore more on these topicsMusicHow we madePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day: new characters, new flaws, new tech and brain-exploding future consequences – discuss with spoilers | Movies | The Guardian
description: Now you’ve seen the new Spidey, let’s talk about new baddies (or are they goodies?), X-Men alumni, painful relationships and a potential Spidey-pig
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Now you’ve seen the new Spidey, let’s talk about new baddies (or are they goodies?), X-Men alumni, painful relationships and a potential Spidey-pig
Content: Holding on by a thread … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Sony PicturesView image in fullscreenHolding on by a thread … Tom Holland in Spider-Man: Brand New Day.Photograph: Sony PicturesNow you've seen itMoviesSpider-Man: Brand New Day: new characters, new flaws, new tech and brain-exploding future consequences – discuss with spoilersNow you’ve seen the new Spidey, let’s talk about new baddies (or are they goodies?), X-Men alumni, painful relationships and a potential Spidey-pigThis article contains spoilers for Spider-Man: Brand New DayBen ChildMon 3 Aug 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a danger thatSpider-Man: Brand New Daymight amount to little more than a palate cleanser between the multiversal excesses of No Way Home and the all-star chaos ofAvengers: Doomsday. Why not just keep it small: a more grounded tale of New York crime-fighting, to keep the Marvel machine rolling before the inevitable return of world-ending stakes? Instead, the studio, once again in partnership with Spider-Man rights holder Sony, has produced a gamechanging comic book epic whose effects will continue being felt for years to come.The film’s biggest twist is significant enough on its own, but Brand New Day keeps widening the implications long after the initial shock has started to wear off. Characters who seemed to exist for one purpose gradually reveal another. Throwaway conversations acquire unexpected significance. New gadgets, strange abilities and apparently routine subplots all hint at much broader shifts taking place beneath the familiar web-slinging adventure. By the time the credits have rolled, the film has answered some longstanding questions, raised several more, and left audiences with a surprisingly clear idea of where theMarvelCinematic Universe (MCU) could be heading next.So if you walked out of the cinema this weekend wondering why certain revelations felt so important, what some seemingly innocuous scenes were really setting up, or whether one particular post-credit tease might have enormous implications for the years ahead, here is what the film may have been trying to tell us.Something very strange is happening toSpider-ManView image in fullscreenPeter Parker (Tom Holland) peers through a web in Spider-Man: Brand New DayPhotograph: CTMG/PAThe Peter Parker we re-encounter at the beginning of Brand New Day is in a bad place.
