Yes, he has locked up enough New York City supervillains to recreatethe Sinister Sixseveral times over, but he lives a lonely existence without his dear departed Aunt May, his girlfriend MJ or his best friend, Ned, and the last two don’t even remember who he is thanks to Doctor Strange’s spell at the tail end ofNo Way Home. As if loneliness weren’t awful enough, Spidey also finds himself struggling to control strange new powers: the organic web shooters could be useful if they can be controlled but the hypersensitive Spider-sense is a problem, while all that extra arachnid aggression only serves to increase the chances of our friendly neighbourhood hero accidentally taking down innocent bystanders. The question remains whether the hero really is falling apart or just evolving into something new.A Jean Grey for the Marvel Cinematic UniverseJust when Spidey is at his weakest, he is faced with an antagonist whose powers far outstrip those of the street-level crims he has been swatting away. At first, Sadie Sink appears to be portraying a common-or-garden body-swapping baddie who is out to hurt MJ if Parker doesn’t do what she says. But it quickly emerges, in one of the most significant moments in the series, that this is the MCU’s version of Jean Grey, a telepath with extraordinary powers whose presence means we are now firmly in the Marvel mutant era.Damage Control isnot what it wasIntroduced inSpider-Man: Homecomingas a sort of handy clean-up gang who zoom in to put everything back in its rightful place after Loki and his mates have smashed up another cityscape, the Department of Damage Control initially looks like just another one of Spider-Man’s allies in the battle against supervillain chaos. Yet it soon emerges that something more sinister is going on. All Jean wants is to rescue her sister Sara, who is being held against her will at the organisation’s secret complex – or at least she was, until scientists killed her while trying to learn how her telepathic powers worked. Led by Bill Metzger (Tramell Tillman), this new take on Damage Control seems to be transforming into the MCU’s version of the comic books’ Mutant Response Division. Then the younger Grey is trapped at the complex, effectively taking her dead sister’s place.Did Peter Parker just invent the mutant restraint collar?View image in fullscreenMJ (Zendaya) watches Spider-Man at workPhotograph: CTMG/PAHere we need to roll the plot back a little, to the chapter in which Peter approaches Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner – now happily teaching at Empire State University and sporting a decidedly less green complexion – to ask how he has managed to stop transforming into the Hulk and flattening half of Manhattan every five minutes. It turns out he has been using an inhibitor chip, whose underlying technology Peter realises could also help stabilise his own increasingly erratic mutation. Being a scientific genius in his own right, Parker builds his own version (with the help of MJ), taming those organic web-shooters, dialling back the hair-trigger aggression and regaining control of his wayward powers.Only later does the breakthrough acquire much darker significance. Peter adapts Banner’s technology into a universal inhibitor and uses a second chip to suppress Jean’s abilities during their confrontation at Damage Control. Jean ultimately overwhelms the device but its broken remains are left behind. What looked like a powerful tool against unwanted mutation could therefore become something akin to the power-dampening restraints that have long haunted the X-Men comics. Peter has probably solved his own problem – in fact, by the end of the movie, he decides he doesn’t even need the chip – but may also have invented the MCU’s first truly effective anti-mutant weapon.How manyX-Menare already out there?The question now is whether the MCU has its own (presumably youthful) versions of Charles Xavier, Wolverine and Cyclops waiting in the wings, or whether we won’t get to see them until the original 20th Century Fox-era versions have yet another swansong in the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. The New Avengers’ Yelena Belova, who spends much of Brand New Day sitting in a Russian bathhouse on Zoom, later begins decoding Damage Control’s redacted files, suggesting that the conspiracy may stretch beyond what Peter and Jean have uncovered. We no longer need ask whether mutants exist in the MCU, but rather how many the bad guys already know about, and what else Metzger has been doing to them.Ned, MJ and getting the old gang back togetherIt was inevitable Peter would reacquaint himself with the two people who matter most to him, even if neither initially has the faintest idea why the nervous young man hovering at the edge of their lives seems so familiar. The trio’s gradual reconnection risks softening the wonderfully bleak ending of No Way Home, in which Parker chose to keep his friends safe and ignorant rather than risk putting them in the sort of danger that eventually killed Aunt May. But Brand New Day does not simply reverse Doctor Strange’s spell, or restore the previous status quo at the flick of a mystical switch. Instead, it suggests Peter may have to earn his comrades’ friendship all over again. Spidey is not quite getting the old gang back together – he is being offered the much more awkward prospect of meeting them for the first time again.Exactly whichSpider-Mandid the Spider-tracker find?One of Brand New Day’s most amusing conceits is Ned’s 8-bit-style Spidey-tracker, which seems to be able to pinpoint the location of the nearest wall crawler with remarkable accuracy. It is never made particularly clear how it works, but the film’s post-credit scene suggests that the faux retro tech might have a more potent long-term use than just helping Peter’s best friend keep tabs on him. It appears to detect aSpider-Manbeyond Earth’s atmosphere, raising the obvious question of which version of Spider-Man is out in the cosmos.Given that the post-credits scene ofThunderbolts*showed the Fantastic Four’s rocket ship heading towards the MCU version of Earth, the temptation is to imagine an alternate-reality version of Spidey entering the solar system just in time to play a pivotal role in Avengers: Doomsday. The problem is that there are so many possible candidates: Tobey Maguire Spidey; Andrew Garfield Spidey; Miles Morales; Spider-Noir; Spider-Gwen; or perhaps even that weird little Spider-pig from the animated films. Then again, maybe Ned’s machine is simply on the blink after he spilled one too many caffeine drinks on it.Explore more on these topicsFilmNow you've seen itSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DayTom HollandZendayaSpider-ManMarvelSuperhero moviesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Trumpeters? We think we’re the kings of the orchestra’: Wynton Marsalis prepares to blow the Edinburgh festival away | Wynton Marsalis | The Guardian
description: It has 12 movements, 200 musicians and aims to unite America. The great US trumpeter and composer talks about his All Rise symphony, his jazz great mentors – and learning humility from his wife
Author: John Lewis
Headline: It has 12 movements, 200 musicians and aims to unite America. The great US trumpeter and composer talks about his All Rise symphony, his jazz great mentors – and learning humility from his wife
Content: ‘I was one of the youngest in the orchestra. Now I’m probably the oldest’ … Marsalis.View image in fullscreen‘I was one of the youngest in the orchestra. Now I’m probably the oldest’ … Marsalis.Wynton MarsalisInterview‘Trumpeters? We think we’re the kings of the orchestra’: Wynton Marsalis prepares to blow the Edinburgh festival awayJohn LewisIt has 12 movements, 200 musicians and aims to unite America. The great US trumpeter and composer talks about his All Rise symphony, his jazz great mentors – and learning humility from his wifeMon 3 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt Heinz Hall in Pittsburgh,Wynton Marsalisis hard to spot. When he first played this venue, in 1984, he was the prodigious 22-year-old soloist out front, blowing Haydn’s trumpet concerto under the baton of Lorin Maazel. Tonight he is embedded in the machinery: half-hidden behind ranks of strings and woodwind, a black-suited figure in the heart of his own symphony.It’s a strange way for a composer to behave – especially one whose public persona has long been associated with certainty, polemic and the upright authority of a man who can make any argument sound like a moral law. Yet Marsalis seems almost pleased by his disappearance. “It’s my piece,” he says, as we talk in his hotel room the next morning, “but it’s not my show.”double quotation markWhen you hang out with old people, you stay 19 for everThe piece is All Rise, Marsalis’s first symphony, written in 1999 – a mammoth hybrid for a 15-piece jazz band, a 50-piece orchestra and a 100-piece choir, premiered at the turn of the millennium by the New York Philharmonic with Kurt Masur. Across 12 movements, Marsalis paints a sprawling civic canvas whose building blocks are American – marches, blues, dance rhythms – and whose aspiration is almost embarrassingly large: to sound like pluralism.This year’s Edinburgh international festival has built its artistic theme around the piece: on the opening night at Usher Hall, Marsalis and hisJazzat Lincoln Center Orchestra will join the Royal Scottish National Orchestra and massed choirs. That’s more than 200 performers in total. Edinburgh has had no shortage of big opening statements over the decades, but this is a particularly pointed choice: a work first conceived as a celebration of integration, now revived in a moment when the very idea of common culture has begun to look quaint.View image in fullscreenMassed ranks … jazz band, orchestra and choirs on stage in Pittsburgh.Photograph: Gilberto Tadday/Jazz at Lincoln CenterIn the past, Marsalis could be confrontational: a man with a rulebook and a relish for battle. Today he’s mellower: quick to credit others, reject ego and talk more about collaboration than correction. He’s keen to puncture the myth that a symphonic work is the solitary utterance of genius. “All Rise was a collaborative exercise. James Oliverio, a soundtrack writer, was teaching me how to orchestrate while I was doing it. I had Milan Turković, the great Austrian bassoonist, helping me with the woodwind. But the main man was the late conductor Kurt Masur. He was always goading me to write something for him. ‘Are you afraid to write for the New York Philharmonic?’ he’d say. Kurt saw a segregated New York, and wanted a piece that brought people together.”Masur – East German, Beethovenian, exacting – was conscripted into the German army as a teen in the final months of the second world war. “I remember he told me then, ‘You think that nazism is unique to Germany? It can happen here.’ Kurt said nazism didn’t happen because people were poor: it happened because lots of Germans wanted to behave like that. And, coming from the south, I could relate to that.”For some, All Rise is exhilarating: a large-scale attempt to make American music sound like an argument worth having. For others, it feels like an impossible negotiation: two institutions – orchestra and big band – asked to behave like one. Marsalis has always been furiously outspoken about what he sees as the malign role of “fusion” in jazz, and is equally wary of the limits of fusing jazz and symphonic music. “I wanted to draw from American mythology and find intersections. Because with some music, there is no common ground.”For instance? “You’re not going to hear a jazz version of a Beethoven symphony. It’s too many chord changes.” Marsalis’s first symphony is instead built on the dance music shared by Americans. “It’s about the relationship between tango and choro; between ragtime and Anglo-Celtic fiddle music; between New Orleans marches and European band counterpoint. But you have to be aware of certain things. In classical music, the basses don’t play all the time. In our music, it plays all the time. And in classical music, the percussion is accent, but in jazz and Latin music, it’s everything.“So you have to find the common ground that you intersect with. Because if you’re not on that ground, there’s no intersection. John Coltrane said he was looking for a universal coefficient. It’s like the word mama. You say mama, it has a universal sound and feeling to it.”He talks a lot about seeking links with other musics – about what he’s learned from the Iraqi oud virtuoso Naseer Shamma, Ghanaian percussionist Yacub Addy, Irish-American violinist Mark O’Connor, and about his enduring friendships with Willie Nelson and Paul Simon. “I meet up with Paul as much as I can – we talk a lot about the relationships between African-American and Anglo-Celtic music, how that is the foundation of pretty much everything we all do.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s my piece but it’s not my show’ … Marsalis on stage in Pittsburgh.Photograph: Gilberto Tadday/Jazz at Lincoln CenterUnlike some of Marsalis’s other large-scale pieces, All Rise is not a polemic. “If you want to know how I think jazz can help democracy, listen to [2020 album] The Ever Fonky Lowdown. If you want to hear what I say about government corruption – and how our government has always been corrupt – listen to my song Super Capitalism, on [the 2007 album] From the Plantation to the Penitentiary. But All Rise is different, it’s about bringing people together.”Drawing from spirituals, gospel music and European devotional sources, All Rise is also full of God. Has his faith changed since writing it? “No. I always had a very strong spiritual faith that was not denominational, even as a kid. I came from very spiritual people. I spent a lot of time with my great uncle, who was born in 1883. He was a stonecutter for the cemetery. If you are around death that much, you become religious.“But I never believed in the dogma. I always noticed the contradictions in Christianity: the saviour was poor, the church is rich. The saviour took a vow of poverty and said, ‘Love people.’ But a lot of religious people don’t love people who aren’t into their religion. So my libretto constantly counterstates that. I draw from the Muslim call to prayer as much as the Bible.”Marsalis, now 64, is fascinated by such ecumenical statements: he remembers his father telling him to read Autobiography of a Yogi when he left high school. “That book was hard work. My dad told me to carry a notebook and write down the name of each swami. When you want to make connections, you have to really work at it.”One connection he’s worked at is his marriage. Marsalis recently married Scottish violinist Nicola Benedetti, who also happens to be director of the Edinburgh international festival. They have a daughter, Elise, born in May 2024. Their relationship is largely long-distance at the moment – lengthy FaceTime chats and phone conversations. Would he ever move to the UK? “I’m going to have to plead the fifth on that one, I’m afraid,” he says with a chuckle, but also dismisses the prospect of Benedetti joining him in New York. “She’s not going to do that,” he says with a resigned smile.View image in fullscreen‘I fell in love with Nicola when I wrote her a violin concerto’ … Marsalis’s wife Nicola Benedetti.Photograph: Andy ParadiseBenedetti, 26 years Marsalis’s junior, has been a frequent collaborator. “What really made me fall in love with Nicola was when I wrote a violin concerto for her,” says Marsalis. “After the first run-through, she sent me a list of about 40 notes. First I laughed. Then I read them. And each of them were tiny things she thought I should change. Her detail was quite incredible. ‘If you put the violas on beat one of the 58th bar, that will save us 20 minutes of rehearsal time. Maybe put the bassoon’s entry at the end of bar 112, on the four of the bar rather than the two. Maybe stress the first beat of that passage in 5/8 time.’ And so on.“I was amazed that she was able to notice all of this while playing the piece. I have so much respect for her, the time she spends practising, her dedication to the humility of study, the desire to learn, to get better. And she is completely collegiate in the way she deals with ensembles.” Has he learned humility from her? “Maybe. Trumpeters, we think we’re the kings of the orchestra, there to blow down the walls of Jericho. We think the piece only starts when we start playing. We know the strings are doing something but we can’t figure out what the hell they’re up to. Maybe I’m less like that now …”I suggest that people will already expect young Elise, with such parentage, to grow up as a virtuoso musician. “She’s a hell of a singer,” he says. “But you can’t determine what your children do. I’ve got three sons – only one is a musician. He’s mainly a visual artist, but he makes music as part of his practice. One teaches track and soccer. Another teaches literature. I never put them in any direction – I just wanted to make sure they have integrity.”How is he coping with late fatherhood? “You know, I always used to hang out with older people. All my mentors were older men – not just my father, but Clark Terry, Dizzy Gillespie, Sweets Edison, Elvin Jones, August Wilson, Romare Bearden, Ralph Ellison. And, when you’re hanging out with old people, you stay 19 for ever. But I’ve always enjoyed hanging with young people too. It’s a privilege when people come up after gigs, teenage kids with their parents, asking for advice. It takes a village to raise a child. We’re all raising the same kid.”‘I saw Herbie Hancock play with D’Angelo, and got my head blown off!’: the festival keeping alive jazz’s golden ageRead moreWhen Marsalis began running the jazz orchestra and jazz programme at Lincoln Center – New York’s pre-eminent arts complex – he was just 26. “I was one of the youngest in the orchestra, alongside legends who had worked with Ellington and Basie. Now I’m probably the oldest.” He recently announced that he will be stepping back from his executive leadership role after nearly four decades, while remaining involved artistically for a transition period.It’s easy to imagine Marsalis as an Alex Ferguson-type spectral presence, presiding warily over anyone who takes up the reins. “No, I’m not going to be like that. There are so many talented people in the band now who could carry on what I’m doing. The bassist Carlos Henriquez, the alto saxophonist Sherman Irby, tenor saxophonist and clarinetist Dan Block – all amazing professionals. But it’s not my choice: there’s a whole executive board at the Lincoln Center who will be making that decision.”Maybe stepping away from the Lincoln Center has altered his angle of vision. For decades it was his pulpit for declarations; now he sounds more interested in how musicians learn one another’s language – happy to defer, amused by his own ego. “I think about Copernicus and Galileo, about how they both observed that the Earth was not the centre of the solar system. They realised that, every time you discovered a new body, the equation became more complicated, until you stopped clinging to the old ways of looking at the universe. Maybe we all need to do that.”All Rise opens theEdinburgh international festival on 8 August. The UK premiere of Marsalis’s Concerto for Orchestra is at theBBC Proms on 13 AugustExplore more on these topicsWynton MarsalisClassical musicJazzEdinburgh festivalEdinburgh festival 2026FestivalsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ring Cycle review – AI staging dispenses with drama to create banal bric-a-brac  | Opera | The Guardian
description: For the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless mess
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: For the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless mess
Content: Unexplained, mindless scrolling … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathView image in fullscreenUnexplained, mindless scrolling … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathOperaReviewRing Cycle review – AI staging dispenses with drama to create banal bric-a-bracBayreuth festival theatre, BayreuthFor the festival’s 150th anniversary, the creative team have turned to AI to generate visuals reflecting Wagner’s tetralogy’s past, present – and future. The hyperactive result is a dismal, mindless messFlora WillsonMon 3 Aug 2026 09.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnveiled the same week in which tech company Anthropic admitted that itsAI model Claude had gone rogue during testing, Bayreuth festival’s new AI-generated staging of Wagner’s four-partRing of the Nibelungenis at least timely. But anyone who assumes that the cycle’s obsession with knowledge, power and possession might make it an ideal forum for reflection on AI as a major contemporary frontier will be disappointed, as will anyone hopeful about AI’s creative potential within opera.Commissioned to mark the festival’s 150th anniversary, the production is “curated” – emphatically not “directed” – by a team led by German stage directorMarcus Lobbes. He apparently spent weeks in dialogue with AI models about possible interpretations of the Ring. According to the programme book, “power structures, capitalism, mythology, gender roles, nationalism”, all came up. So far, so mainstream Wagner reception. But if these human-machine exchanges were revelatory, you wouldn’t know it from the resulting staging, which uses AI “as an extension of a cultural memory that is never complete”.In plainer English: the AI system is allowed to roam archival materials from 150 years of Ring cycle productions at Bayreuth as the starting point for constantly spooling visuals projected on to a screen that is stretched the full width and height of the proscenium arch. Lobbes also asked the system to incorporate imagery chronologically, from a political or social event every year of the festival’s history as a plausible conversation topic for that season’s audience. Each scene begins with a source from the cycle’s 1876 premiere, but what happens next is determined by the system in real time during the performance.View image in fullscreenGrotesque … Bayreuth festival’s 2026 Ring cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathThe good news is that anyone who attends another of this production’s outings definitely won’t see the same selection of visual bric-à-brac that I did. The bad news is that the principle of rapid machinic free-association will remain.So, I assume, will the constant grotesque morph and flow of visual objects. Das Rheingold and Die Walküre involved countless hands that warped horribly, producing extra fingers and nails. (Did someone adjust the settings ahead of Siegfried and Götterdämmerung, I wonder? The visual tic disappeared mid-cycle as suddenly as it emerged.) Faces appeared, only to go instantly out of focus. Some were very famous (Adolf Hitler, Queen Elizabeth II, JFK) but I struggled to identify most. Watercolour rocks became bodies became other bodies. There were rapid swings between the entirely inscrutable and the totally obvious. Alberich’s transformation into a toad triggered various mutant amphibians, there were bears when Siegfried brought one in, a rainbow for the rainbow bridge to Valhalla.double quotation markThe singers stood behind a vast projection screen like budget Star Trek monsters rooted to the spotBut there were also endless picture-library bland photos of scrap metal, creeping greenery, water droplets, abandoned rooms. I spotted design elements from various past Bayreuth Ring productions but was mostly – inevitably – unable to keep pace with the AI system’s connection-making. One low point: the appearance of a historical photo of emaciated African youths – as unexplained as everything else, but picture the results of an image-search for “European colonialism” – which flashed past during Die Walküre. This is not engaging with the complex, problematic history of Bayreuth or the Ring. It’s just another form of mindless scrolling.You’ll be wondering where the singers fitted in. Forget Wagner’s notion of the inescapably multimediaGesamtkunstwerk: this Ring presents the sonic and the visual as separate tracks, with theatrical drama kept to a minimum. Over four nights, some of today’s leading Wagnerians stood behind – yes, behind – the vast projection screen, all wearing subtle variations on a single costume design like budget Star Trek monsters. Mostly they were rooted to the spot. Recently murdered characters simply walked off; at erotic climaxes, lovers held hands; Siegfried discovered Brünnhilde despite being alone on stage.View image in fullscreenTheatrical drama is kept to a minimum … Bayreuth festival’s AI Ring Cycle.Photograph: Enrico NawrathMichael Vollewas a magnificent, stately Wotan and Wanderer, his power unforced.Klaus Florian Vogtwas by turn Loge, Siegmund and Siegfried, in each case supple and darkly luminous with compelling diction.Elza van den Heever’s Sieglinde got better and better, blossoming in her love duet in Die Walküre.Camilla Nylund’s Brünnhilde was often wild and sometimes ungainly, but her impassioned lyricism and most intimate moments were deeply moving regardless.Mika Kares’s Hunding was all iron and velvet, his Hagen unleashing mighty, smooth torrents of sound – evil rarely sounds better.Gerhard Siegel(Mime) and Jochen Schmeckenbecher (Alberich) were more old-school baddies, respectively wheedling and raw.Peter Rosewas a rather muddy Fafner andChrista Mayerwobbly but forceful as Erda and Waltraute. The Rhinemaidens, Valkyries and Norns were exquisitely balanced and as characterised as they could be without acting.double quotation markForget Wagner’s notion of the Gesamtkunstwerk – this Ring keeps theatrical drama to a minimumConductorChristian Thielemanndrew playing from the orchestra that was occasionally poorly tuned and even scrappy, but which at its best should have been captivating: details were finely balanced and tutti passages blistering, the brass rising like an immense wave from the pit or splatting nastily for the bad guys. Tempi were often brisk (only in Siegfried did this cause coordination problems, with Vogt left struggling to keep up) but there were also precious moments of spaciousness. Yet even the silence that Thielemann left in Wotan’s devastating monologue couldn’t stop the onscreen hyperactivity that instantly dispersed all dramatic tension.There are numerous criticisms you could levy against this production from all manner of perspectives; there is, after all, something for everyone to dislike. But the most dismal was perhaps how unmoving it was – and how difficult it became to care.The Ring Cycle continues at theBayreuth festivaluntil 16 August.Explore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicAI (artificial intelligence)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Never felt so scared’: the Cats obsessive who’s created a feral dance version of the purr-fect musical | Stage | The Guardian
description: Drew McOnie skipped school to audition for the original. It launched his astonishing career. Now he’s getting his claws into a no-pussyfooting version of the classic hit
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Drew McOnie skipped school to audition for the original. It launched his astonishing career. Now he’s getting his claws into a no-pussyfooting version of the classic hit
Content: Tails at the ready … the cast rehearse for the show at Regents Park Open Air theatre.Photograph: Mark SeniorView image in fullscreenTails at the ready … the cast rehearse for the show at Regents Park Open Air theatre.Photograph: Mark SeniorStageInterview‘Never felt so scared’: the Cats obsessive who’s created a feral dance version of the purr-fect musicalLyndsey WinshipDrew McOnie skipped school to audition for the original. It launched his astonishing career. Now he’s getting his claws into a no-pussyfooting version of the classic hitMon 3 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the age of 17, Drew McOnie was so determined to be in the musicalCatsthat he snuck out of school to audition. Four days later, he was on a flight to Germany to join the international production. (Luckily, he was at a performing arts school and they forgave him.) It was a life-changing moment: at that point, McOnie’s stellar career as a dancer, Olivier award-winning choreographer and director began – and, 23 years later, it’s all about to come full circle. McOnie has created his own version of the musical he’s been obsessed with since childhood.For any dancer growing up in the 1980s and 90s, Cats wasthemusical: dance wasn’t just an accompaniment, but instrumental to the show. Gillian Lynne’s original choreography is iconic – much copied by local dance schools and student shows of the era. Lynne was a force of nature, still doing the splits at 88, four years before she died in 2018. For McOnie, artistic director at Regent’s Park Open Air theatre and famed for his blazing choreography in Jesus Christ Superstar, it takes some nerve to remake it.double quotation markThere are a lot of kittens in the cast. My task is to make each one light up“I don’t think I’ve ever felt so scared,” he says. Not because he doesn’t think he can do it, but “because I was in the original and I adore Gillian Lynne. The challenge is to honour her with the amount of rigour she put in – to match that ferocity of spirit, that ambition.”View image in fullscreenThe energy is buzzing … McOnie and cast in rehearsals.Photograph: Mark SeniorWe might now think of Cats as a “glorious celebration of the 80s”, says McOnie, but we shouldn’t forget how original and contemporary it was when it first came out. He wants his version to feel the same to audiences today. That means movement that brings in current influences from street and commercial dance, as well as jazz and classical, “while also staying within that world of being a cat”.As I enter Studio 1 at Regent’s Park, the energy’s buzzing, the moves are sensual, low slung and slinky, earthier than the original, but with bursts of wild, joyful energy. Then the dancers suddenly go full pelt. It’s more feral than you might expect. “I don’t think many of our cats are house cats,” says McOnie.Because his youthful experience on Cats was so formative, McOnie deliberately went in search of standout student dancers to add to the mix. “There are a lot of kittens in the cast,” he says. The young dancers are so effortlessly cool, he tells me, not like Tiggerish McOnie was at their age, bouncing off the walls. But in rehearsals, he started digging beneath their inscrutable exteriors, letting them loose in solos. “One lad just completely lit up and I was like, ‘OK, there’s the teenager.’ I said, ‘I like the version of you bounding about with your eyes on fire.’ My task is to make each one of them light up.”Cats isn’t known as a particularly “cool” show, but McOnie thinks we forget how impressively out-there Andrew Lloyd Webber’s musicals can be. “They’re extraordinarily off the wall, completely form-busting and brave,” he says. He has nothing but praise for Lloyd Webber. “Honestly, my time with Andrew over the last year, with the combination of Jesus Christ Superstar and Cats, has been utterly thrilling. He’s incredibly funny. He’s very witty, he’s very sharp, and he’s really, really rigorous.” McOnie is awed by Lloyd Webber’s ability to see the big picture. “He’s like a musical architect,” says McOnie, able to glean how every detail fits into the larger show. “There’s definitely a magic about what he can hear.”View image in fullscreenWonder and joy … Gary Wilmot as Gus the Theatre Cat.Photograph: Mark SeniorMcOnie does admit Cats is a bit weird, though. Based on the TS Eliot poems in Old Possum’s Book of Practical Cats, with portraits of Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer, Macavity and Skimbleshanks, it doesn’t exactly have a strong narrative. “It sort of levitates somewhere between a choreo-poem, a ballet, a song cycle, a piece of vaudeville and a kind of pagan ritual,” he says.What it isn’t is a bunch of cute talking animals. In this production, the costumes won’t be fully formed cats, and they’re not masked. McOnie sees it as “a ritual that endows the performer with an animal form through which they can express deeply human emotion”. There’ll still be some “great glittery numbers” though, don’t worry. “Its core themes are wonder and joy.”‘I wasn’t ambitious until I was 60!’ Gary Wilmot on comedy, panto, musicals – and his Beckett-style new playRead moreI have to ask McOnie briefly about themuch-maligned Cats film. It turns out he loved a lot of things about it but thinks it was doomed from the start. “It just isn’t a filmic idea,” he says. “Cats is one of the most extraordinary expressions of theatricality of all time,” he says. “Capital-T theatre – because so much of it hangs in the imagination. You have this mass of bodies giving all of their soul to that music, with that exchange of energy live in the room.”It all comes back to Gillian Lynne’s legacy. She trusted dancers and the power of what they could do. McOnie has exactly the same animal instinct.Cats is atRegents Park Open Air theatre, London, until 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageMusicalsAndrew Lloyd WebberCatsAnimalsTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nolan’s film could make The Odyssey the most sought-after book in the US | Books | The Guardian
description: The nearly 2,700-year-old epic poem is flying off shelves at bookstores and libraries after the blockbuster film came out
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: The nearly 2,700-year-old epic poem is flying off shelves at bookstores and libraries after the blockbuster film came out
Content: Homer's The Odyssey sits on the shelves in the classic section at Borders bookstore in New York.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHomer's The Odyssey sits on the shelves in the classic section at Borders bookstore in New York.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBooksNolan’s film could make The Odyssey the most sought-after book in the USThe nearly 2,700-year-old epic poem is flying off shelves at bookstores and libraries after the blockbuster film came outMarina Dunbarin New YorkMon 3 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristopher Nolan’s new movieThe Odysseyhas already broken several records, but its most significant accomplishment might be turning a nearly 2,700-year-old epic poem into the most sought-after book in America. Libraries and bookstores alike are experiencing a rush.At the popular independent bookstore Books Are Magic in Brooklyn, New York, last week, evidence sat just inside the front entrance. A display stacked with more than a dozen editions of The Odyssey – fromEmily Wilson’s acclaimed translation to graphic novels and children’s story versions – was drawing a steady stream of browsers, many of them Gen Z readers who became interested after seeing Nolan’s latest blockbuster.Just a month ago, the store sold only a handful of copies of Homer’s classic. In July, sales multiplied by several thousand per cent.“We sold 80 copies of just the Wilson book this month,” said Nicole Vasquez, a Books Are Magic employee who helps oversee the store’s marketing. “Before, it was single digits in sales.”The whimsical bookshop, founded in 2017 by novelist Emma Straub and her husband Michael Fusco-Straub, has built a reputation as one of New York’s most influential independent booksellers, with more than 280,000Instagramfollowers and a loyal young customer base. Employees said demand had already begun climbing before they installed a dedicated Odyssey display just days ago.“As soon as the movie came out and people went to go see it, they came to read the book,” Vasquez said. And this phenomenon extends well beyond the Brooklyn arty scene.According to Circana BookScan data reported byPublishers Weekly, year-to-date US print sales across all editions of The Odyssey are up 76%. Emily Wilson’s translation, published by WW Norton, is the bestselling edition, followed by Penguin Classics’ Robert Fagles translation and Gareth Hinds’ graphic novel adaptation. Sales had already been trending upward after Nolan announced the project in December 2024, with 2025 sales rising 42% over the previous year.Wilson’s translation has also remained among Amazon’stop 10bestselling books since the film’s release, alongside Andy Weir’s Project Hail Mary, another novel enjoying renewed attention thanks to a recent successfulfilm adaptation.WW Norton said momentum had been building ever since Nolan announced the project. Louise Brockett, head of communications, told thePhiladelphia Inquirerthat domestic sales across all formats of classics scholar Wilson’s 2017 book had surpassed one million copies by early July.Booksellers say the appeal stretches beyond longtime fans of Greek mythology, with children’s adaptations becoming unexpectedly popular.“These are newer to the store,” Vasquez said, gesturing towards the children’s section that contains its own separate Odyssey display. “They’ve been selling pretty well,” she added. “People were reading about Greek mythology who really never cared about it before.”The renewed fascination has grown beyond Homer himself. Books inspired by Greek mythology – including Madeline Miller’sCirce, whose title character appears in The Odyssey – are also seeing increased interest.“There’s also retellings that are selling more,” Vasquez said. “Circe has been really popular because of the character in the movie [played to critical acclaim by Samantha Morton], so people want to read more about her.”Blockbuster adaptations often create a jump in the market for the novels they are based on. “WhenHamnetcame out, our sales forHamnetwere crazy,” Vasquez said. “When thatFrankensteinmovie came out, we sold so many copies of Frankenstein.” She expects the current surge of Homer’s epic to last another two or three months before settling back toward normal levels.Books Are Magic colleague Yeshim Kayim-Yanko said Nolan’s film has succeeded in introducing a classic that many readers previously associated only with high school English classes.“It’s nice to see people who wouldn’t have necessarily picked upThe Odysseynormally,” Kayim-Yanko said. “It’s bringing light to this classic story. People don’t usually gravitate towards it to just read on their leisure. That is what’s happening for this film.”She also believes public discussion surrounding Wilson’s translation – includingrecent criticismWilson made of the film adaptation – has only fueled curiosity.“Everybody’s just like, ‘I want to get the tea, I want to hear the gossip, and I want to read her translation,’” Kayim-Yanko said. The controversy surrounding the film started well before Wilson’s comments, withchronically onlinerightwingersrallying againstNolan’s casting decisions, insisting the film would be a flop.“That boycott wasn’t really successful, to say the least,” Vasquez said with a laugh.Libraries are also experiencing a big surge in demand, placing the poem on waiting lists across the country. The New York Public Library told the Guardian it saw a 338% increase in demand across print, audiobook and ebook editions of The Odyssey between 2 July and 30 July.“We’ve seen a huge jump in demand for The Odyssey over the past month, and are delighted that so many of our patrons are reading and even rereading this epic novel,” Brian Bannon, the library’s chief librarian and director of branch libraries and education said.The trend has also caught the attention of the nation’s largest bricks-and-mortar bookseller. Barnes & Noble’s CEO, James Daunt, toldBloomberglast Wednesday of the ancient Greek that “right now, our best-selling book is by an author called Homer.”While some rightwingers attacked the film for being too diverse some classicists leveled nearly the opposite critique, arguing that the adaptation loses much of the emotional richness and complexity that has made the story endure for nearly three millennia.Wilson, who influenced Nolan,wrote thatthe film “lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth” and had “nothing convincing to say” about the poem’s deeper themes of memory, war, family and homecoming.Classicist Mary Beard said on the Guardian’sStateside podcast, that Nolan’s adaptation underplays many of the poem’s strongest womenandlacks the poem’s “elusive sexiness”.Yet both scholars correctly predicted what they saw as becoming the film’s greatest achievement: inspiring audiences to return to Homer.Beard concluded that Nolan “is doing his best to get the general public reading again”.Explore more on these topicsBooksThe OdysseyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A gentle poetry in the everyday’: why The Straight Story is my feelgood movie | David Lynch | The Guardian
description: The latest in our ongoing series of writers picking their most beloved comfort films is a tribute to David Lynch’s gentlest movie
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The latest in our ongoing series of writers picking their most beloved comfort films is a tribute to David Lynch’s gentlest movie
Content: Richard Farnsworth in The Straight Story.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreenRichard Farnsworth in The Straight Story.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMy feelgood movieDavid Lynch‘A gentle poetry in the everyday’: why The Straight Story is my feelgood movieThe latest in our ongoing series of writers picking their most beloved comfort films is a tribute to David Lynch’s gentlest moviePatrick SmithMon 3 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat was your gateway into the Lynchian empire? Maybe it was the elliptical horror of Mulholland Drive, with its labyrinth of dream and deceit. Perhaps it was the small-town banality of Twin Peaks or Blue Velvet, the gee-whiz vernacular and cherry-pie dispositions hiding a malice so pure behind those white picket fences. Or was it Wild at Heart, that nightmarish road movie where oddballs and deviants lurk at every bend, Nicolas Cage and Laura Dern tearing through America with unbridled passion and violence?‘The plane movie I’ll watch anytime’: why Up in the Air is my feelgood movieRead moreWeirdly, it was none of those for me. In fact, my introduction toDavid Lynchcontained not one drop of sexual depravity or grisly malevolence. The film was The Straight Story and I was 15. Released in May 1999, it tells the real-life tale of Alvin Straight, a 73-year-old second world war vet who rode a lawnmower 300 miles across the midwest to reconcile with his ailing brother. While the title obviously names the main character, it also invites you to take Lynch at his word: that this is that fabled chronicler of the demented and the macabre playing it straight(ish). Think of it as Lynch does Disney: a family-friendly hymn to Americana, sparse and only a little bit strange, finding a gentle poetry in the everyday.My love for this Homeric tale deepened around a decade ago, when I was commissioned to write about the making of the film. I spoke to Mary Sweeney – Lynch’s longtime editor, producer and then partner – who told me how she’d come across the story in the first place, reading about Straight’s odyssey in the New York Times. Charmed by the man’s plucky attitude, she optioned the rights, wrote the screenplay with a childhood friend, John Roach, and brought it to Lynch.Cast in the lead role was Richard Farnsworth, a stuntman turned Oscar-nominated actor for 1978’s Comes a Horseman. A picture of stoic defiance in his red plaid jacket and cowboy hat, he nails Straight’s contradictions: stubborn yet tender, infirm yet unstoppable. There is a flinty gravitas to his work, and a low-key dignity too, shimmering in the ice-blue pools of his rheumy eyes. That he knew this was his swan song, terminally ill as he was during the shoot, means his grizzled face becomes a canvas on to which ache and acceptance paint themselves. He was 79 and lost to Kevin Spacey at the 2000 Oscars. He died later that year.The film around Farnsworth, scored with a blend of mournful Spanish guitar and folksy fiddle by Lynch stalwart Angelo Badalamenti, cruises along in perfect harmony with his talents. Serving up succour for the soul, it drifts from scene to scene with a hushed profundity, alighting on the various exchanges with people Straight meets on the road: a pregnant runaway, a woman hysterical after hitting a deer, a pair of squabbling twin mechanics and a retired John Deere employee who lets Alvin camp in his back yard. Most poignant of all, though, is a tavern scene in Iowa, where Straight, sipping a glass of milk, opens up to a fellow veteran. “That is one thing I can’t shake loose,” he laments. “All my buddies’ faces are still young. And the thing is, the more years I have, the more they’ve lost.”Throughout that sequence, Freddie Francis, the film’s venerable cinematographer, holds his lens on Farnsworth’s face, the subtle twitches saying as much as the dialogue itself. It was the final film for Francis too, and equally Oscar-worthy, though not nominated: amid sweeping vistas, crops harvested in a wash of magic-hour light and roads stretching into the infinite distance, each shot is as evocative as that one creased, weather-beaten visage.Watching it now, sinceLynch’s own death in January 2025, carries an added pathos. In his final years, he too found walking difficult, then impossible, his lungs ravaged by decades of smoking, much like Straight’s. Acclaimed though the film was, it made just $6.2m at the US box office – less than its $10m budget – and remains a relatively unknown gem. Whenever I’ve watched it with someone, though, their verdict has always been the same: that it’s deeply moving.The exquisite last scene belongs to Harry Dean Stanton, an actor who knew a thing or two about laconic devastation, having spent Wim Wenders’s Paris, Texas (my favourite movie) saying almost nothing at all. “Did you ride that thing all the way out here to see me?” says Stanton’s Lyle, glancing at the lawnmower, lip quivering, years of resentment dissolving in a single frame. “I did, Lyle,” comes the reply. It’s a flawless ending. Emerging untouched is just about inconceivable.The Straight Story is available on Disney+ and the Criterion Channel in the US, to rent digitally in the UK and on Mubi in AustraliaThis article was amended on 3 August 2026 to clarify that Richard Farnsworth died after the 2000 Oscars, not before.Explore more on these topicsDavid LynchMy feelgood movieDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80 | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: His family friendly style made the comedian a household name in the 80s and he was awarded a papal knighthood in 2015 for services to charity
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: His family friendly style made the comedian a household name in the 80s and he was awarded a papal knighthood in 2015 for services to charity
Content: ‘He brought so much laughter and happiness to countless audiences’ … Jimmy Cricket.Photograph: British Sky Broadcasting Ltd/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘He brought so much laughter and happiness to countless audiences’ … Jimmy Cricket.Photograph: British Sky Broadcasting Ltd/ShutterstockTV comedyJimmy Cricket, comedian known for his ‘And there’s more!’ catchphrase, dies aged 80His family friendly style made the comedian a household name in the 80s and he was awarded a papal knighthood in 2015 for services to charityTim JonzeMon 3 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJimmy Cricket, the northern Irish comic who became a regular fixture on British television throughout the 1980s, has died aged 80.Known for his catchphrase: “And there’s more!”, Cricket fronted his own ITV series of the same name on which he rocked his signature look of tailcoat, short trousers and wellington boots marked clearly with “L” and “R” on the wrong feet. He also appeared at the 1984 Royal Variety Performance as well as in the BBC’s long-running light entertainment vehicle The Good Old Days.A statement from his family posted on the Jimmy Cricket Facebook page read: “Our beloved Jimmy passed away this morning after a short illness. He spent his last few days surrounded by his family, love, laughter and songs.”Born James Joseph Mulgrew in Cookstown, Northern Ireland, Cricket left school aged 16 and began working as a Butlin’s Redcoat a couple of years later. After moving first to Stockport and then Rochdale, Cricket worked the northern comedy circuits in England throughout the 1970s, gaining his big break when he reached the semi-finals of TV talent show Search for a Star in 1980.He spent the 1980s as a household name, with numerous appearances in The Krankies Klub and The Good Old Days. In 1987 he was the featured celebrity on an episode of This Is Your Life. By the mid 1990s he had moved towards radio, starring in four series of the acclaimed BBCRadio2 show Jimmy’s Cricket Team alongside other comedy talent.View image in fullscreenCommitted to charity work … Cricket in 2001.Photograph: Richard Crampton/ShutterstockCricket had a reputation as a family man, marrying May Tweedie in 1972. The couple had four children. The family statement said: “Jimmy brought so much laughter and happiness to countless audiences throughout his career. Whether on stage, screen or radio, or if you met him in person. But that was nothing compared with the happiness he gave to his family. A devoted husband to May for 52 years. A wonderful dad to his four children and a very silly grandad indeed to his four grandchildren. He was our greatest champion and loved us all loudly. Forever our clown, he was cracking jokes to the wonderful NHS staff and to us all right until the end.”Cricket was known for his charity work, appearing alongside Peter Kay and Matt Lucas in the 2007 Comic Relief video for I’m Gonna Be (500 Miles) and frequently put on tours to raise funds for the Francis House Children’s Hospice in Manchester.In 2015, Cricket was awarded a papal knighthood, the Roman Catholic Church’s highest honour, by Pope Francis, in recognition of his charity work. Commenting on the award at the time, Cricket said: “The parish priest arrived and took out this certificate - it was a papal knighthood and it was in Latin. I thought, ‘He’s got the wrong fella here, is he sure it’s not the neighbour?’”He added: “I do what I love. If I can raise money by entertaining people, sure it’s not hard work. To get an honour for doing something that you love is quite a blessing.”Explore more on these topicsTV comedyComedyRadio comedyTelevisionRadionewsShareReuse this content

title: Phil Collins details serious alcoholism: ‘People were coming to say goodbye’ | Phil Collins | The Guardian
description: Pop and rock legend tells Sunday Times of drinking problem and ill health after final Genesis tour in 2021
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Pop and rock legend tells Sunday Times of drinking problem and ill health after final Genesis tour in 2021
Content: Phil Collins performing in 2019.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAView image in fullscreenPhil Collins performing in 2019.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAPhil CollinsPhil Collins details serious alcoholism: ‘People were coming to say goodbye’Pop and rock legend tells Sunday Times of drinking problem and ill health after final Genesis tour in 2021Ben Beaumont-ThomasMon 3 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePhil Collins has said that he suffered life-threatening alcoholism in recent years.Speaking to the Sunday Times, the pop and rock legend, 75, said that his drinking began after he stopped taking Antabuse, a drug that causes illness if alcohol is consumed, which he had been using since an earlier period of alcoholism.Collins describes drinking wine at breakfast time, and says his extensive alcohol intake led to him being hospitalised in November 2023, for seven months, with damage to his pancreas and kidneys.“There were some decisions to be made about ‘Do we keep Phil on life support?’ kind of thing,” he said. “My kidneys were packing up, my organs were just seizing up. People were coming to say goodbye. But I don’t remember them coming, I didn’t have no idea this was going on. They were all worried that they wouldn’t see me again. It could all have gone so terribly wrong.”He added: “I was very lucky to have come out of that. Needless to say, I haven’t had a drink since.”In 2015, Collins described a period of alcohol abuse after his 2006 divorce from third wife, Orianne Cevey. “It left me with a lot of time on my hands to think about what happened,” hetold Rolling Stone. “I went through a few bits of darkness; drinking too much. I killed my hours watching TV and drinking, and it almost killed me. But I haven’t had a drink in three years.”Collins has experienced a series of other health issues in recent years, including problems with his neck and spine that required surgery, and which mean he is no longer able to play the drums: his role on theGenesisreunion tour in 2021 was restricted to vocals. In 2016 he announced he had been diagnosed with diabetes.Ahead of the Genesis concerts in 2021, Collinstold the Guardian: “Of course, my health does change things, doing the show seated changes things. But I actually found on my recent solo tours, it didn’t get in the way; the audience were still listening and responding. It’s not the way I would have written it, but it’s the way that it is.”Genesis review – rock’s most unlikely stars go out with a bangRead moreCollins is one of the most commercially successful musicians in British history. After taking over vocal duties in Genesis from Peter Gabriel, he helped to turn them from prog darlings to mainstream hit-makers, scoring five back-to-back UK No 1 albums in the 1980s and early 1990s. His solo career was just as illustrious, with another four UK No 1 albums across the same period, featuring hits such as Against All Odds, Easy Lover and In the Air Tonight.His most recent solo album is 2010’s Going Back. Collins retired for four years after its release, but returned in 2015, telling Rolling Stone: “My kids are now 10 and 14 and they want to see what their dad does. They were in nappies when I was last on the road. They love my music and I’d like to take them out so they can enjoy it.”Explore more on these topicsPhil CollinsPop and rockAlcoholAlcoholismGenesisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Massive Attack speak about ‘surreal experience’ of being banned from Singapore over Palestinian flag | Massive Attack | The Guardian
description: British band say they are ‘proud to have made this impromptu expression with our fans in Singapore’, where open display of all foreign flags is banned
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: British band say they are ‘proud to have made this impromptu expression with our fans in Singapore’, where open display of all foreign flags is banned
Content: Massive Attack’s Grant Marshall (L) performing in 2024. The band has been banned from Singapore after holding up a Palestinian flag during their show.Photograph: Helle Arensbak/EPAView image in fullscreenMassive Attack’s Grant Marshall (L) performing in 2024. The band has been banned from Singapore after holding up a Palestinian flag during their show.Photograph: Helle Arensbak/EPAMassive AttackMassive Attack speak about ‘surreal experience’ of being banned from Singapore over Palestinian flagBritish band say they are ‘proud to have made this impromptu expression with our fans in Singapore’, where open display of all foreign flags is bannedPress AssociationSun 2 Aug 2026 22.19 EDTLast modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 23.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMassive Attack have called being banned from Singapore a “surreal experience” after displaying a Palestinian flag during their show.On Wednesday, the English trip-hop collective – whose current lineup includes Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall – played a show at the Star theatre.After unfurling and displaying a Palestinian flag while performing, they became the subject of a police investigation, which led to thembeing banned from the country.Singapore, known for its tough laws on public speech and assembly, bans the open display of all foreign flags, national emblems or banners without a permit.View image in fullscreenRobert Del Naja and Grant Marshall from Massive Attack stand with a Palestinian flag at the end of their performance in Singapore on 29 July.Photograph: Simran Panaech/ReutersOn Sunday the band issued a statement on Instagram. “Following our performance at the Star Theatre, Singapore, on 29th July, we were surprised and disappointed that our entire band was detained by the police, isolated and separately questioned – with some members subjected to hotel room searches and temporary passport confiscation,” it read.“Before we set foot on the stage and again at the end of the show, large sections of the auditorium organically led chants of ‘Free Palestine’, presumably aware but undeterred that this spontaneous expression alone could violate their government’s censorship laws.“For our part, we did not imagine that merely holding up the flag of a sovereign state recognised by 157 countries would violate any law.”Massive Attack: Boots on the Ground (ft Tom Waits) review – first single in a decade is a dark hymn for our timesRead moreThe statement continued: “On reflection, we are proud to have made this impromptu expression with our fans in Singapore who clearly felt a moral imperative to show solidarity with the people of Palestine in their ongoing reality of illegal occupation, apartheid and genocide, and we salute their courage in doing so. Right across the world, the continued inaction of the ‘international community’ is moving citizens to personal risk.”The band said the “surreal experience” was a “reminder of the importance of defending universal human rights and freedom of expression, wherever those rights are threatened”.They added: “At home in the UK peaceful protestors [are being] arrested under terrorism laws for holding up handwritten signs protesting genocide, despite appeals from all sides of the political spectrum.”Concluding the statement, Massive Attack said: “We are grateful to the people of Singapore who made us feel so welcome, and hope that the Government of Singapore will choose to ratify the UN International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and allow their citizens expressions of conscience without fear of state prosecution. As we were saying … Free Palestine.”A statement released on Saturday by the Singapore police force and the Infocomm Media Development Authority said police had investigated both Del Naja and Marshall for “their actions of support for a political cause and unfurling of a foreign flag”.The authorities said that after an investigation, which included consultation with the attorney general’s chambers, police had issued “stern warnings” to both men for allegedly breaching the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act and the Public Order Act.The statement said both men would “also be banned from re-entering Singapore” while any future applications for them to perform there would not be approved.Police “take a serious view of acts which could potentially harm the racial and religious harmony in Singapore and urge the public, including foreigners, to refrain from importing foreign politics as this can undermine our social cohesion and the rule of law”.Del Naja was among 500 people arrestedin April during a demonstration in London against the ban on Palestine Action, a group that has been proscribed in the UK.The Singapore police force has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsMassive AttackSingaporeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day makes $932m at box office in second biggest opening weekend in history | Spider-Man: Brand New ⁠Day | The Guardian
description: Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige hails ‘phenomenal’ opening, which followed box office already buoyed by The Odyssey and Toy Story 5
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige hails ‘phenomenal’ opening, which followed box office already buoyed by The Odyssey and Toy Story 5
Content: From left, Florence Pugh, Tom Holland, Zendaya and Marisa Tomei at the Spider-Man: Brand New Day UK premiere. The film has made $927m ⁠in worldwide box office so far.Photograph: Tim P Whitby/Getty Images for Sony PicturesView image in fullscreenFrom left, Florence Pugh, Tom Holland, Zendaya and Marisa Tomei at the Spider-Man: Brand New Day UK premiere. The film has made $927m ⁠in worldwide box office so far.Photograph: Tim P Whitby/Getty Images for Sony PicturesSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DaySpider-Man: Brand New Day makes $932m at box office in second biggest opening weekend in historyMarvel Studios president Kevin Feige hails ‘phenomenal’ opening, which followed box office already buoyed by The Odyssey and Toy Story 5Sian Cainand agenciesMon 3 Aug 2026 11.45 EDTFirst published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 20.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠Day brought in a blockbuster $932m ⁠in worldwide ticket sales to deliver the second most lucrative opening weekend of all time. Final figures showed the film was the biggest ever at the North American box office, with a total of $360m. This puts it just ahead of 2019’s Avengers: Endgame with $357m, not adjusted for inflation.The movie, which marks actor Tom Holland’s fourth ⁠outing as the web-slinging superhero, depicts Peter Parker fighting crime in a world that has forgotten he is Spider-Man. Zendaya, who is married to Holland, co-stars as MJ, the love of Parker’s life. The film explores Parker’s struggles ⁠with loneliness and his pursuit of human connection.Spider-Man: Brand New Day review – Zendaya saves Tom Holland’s semi-Cronenberg-style superheroRead moreInitial estimates suggested that Spider-Man: Brand New ⁠Day had grossed $927m worldwide and $355m in the US and Canada, meaning that it was not thought to have dislodged Avengers: Endgame on home territory, but when final figurescame in the total was revised upwards.Internationally, Spider-Man: Brand New Day grossed $572m, with China leading international markets with $121m in ticket sales. In Australia it had the biggest opening weekend of 2026, making $21.4m.Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige called it “a truly phenomenal opening”.Marvel Studios now boasts the four largest openings of all time at the global box office (not adjusted for inflation): Avengers: Endgame ($1.22bn), Spider-Man: Brand New Day ($932m), Avengers: Infinity War ($640m) and Spider-Man: No Way Home ($600m).Tom Rothman, ‌chairman and chief executive of Sony Pictures Entertainment’s Motion Picture Group, described Spider-Man: Brand New Day as “fundamentally a movie about friendship, about the balm of connection in all ​our lives, and that is resonant to audiences of all ages ‌and all around the world.”Spider-Man is one of the most popular of Marvel’s comic book characters, with a cinematic appeal that endures even as audiences have shown ‌signs of fatigue with the superhero genre. The latest instalment has been well-received, scoring a 90% rating from critics and 98% approval from movie-goers on Rotten Tomatoes.Greg Durkin, the founder and CEO of the entertainment research firm Enact Insight, told Reuters that the movie’s central themes of loneliness and isolation, and triumphing over drama, resonated especially with gen Z audiences.“There’s a mental health crisis now with young people in our country — it’s especially acute for young men right now. There’s a friendship crisis,” Durkin said. “The pandemic created ⁠a bunch of shock wave effects that we haven’t fully documented, much less addressed. This movie touches on some ​really important themes.“The performance of Spider-Man: Brand New Day ​fuels an already-robust summer box office, which has been ​buoyed by such major releases as Toy Story 5 and The Odyssey.Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends for Rentrak, said on Sunday that the combination of Spider-Man: Brand ​New Day with The ‌Odyssey created the “all-time biggest domestic ​weekend” in movie theaters.Actors Tom Holland, Zendaya and Jon Bernthal appear in both movies.“There’s no better ​lead-in to this movie than The Odyssey,” Dergarabedian said. “Think of how many people around the world were in movie theaters being exposed to trailers marketing for Spider-Man: Brand New Day.”The overall 2026 domestic box office performance remains below pre-pandemic levels. Year-to-date receipts are up 10% from last year, but 16% below 2019, the year before the pandemic struck, according to Rentrak.Reuters contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsSpider-Man: Brand New ⁠DaySuperhero moviesMarvelnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCSO/Järvi/Kavakos review – virtuosic violinist makes fiendishly light work of Tchaikovsky | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: The intricate concerto was paired with the world premiere of Dani Howard’s likable Concerto for Brass and a lush Scriabin symphony, all admirably led by Paavo Järvi
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The intricate concerto was paired with the world premiere of Dani Howard’s likable Concerto for Brass and a lush Scriabin symphony, all admirably led by Paavo Järvi
Content: Breathtaking … Paavo Järvi and Leonidas Kavakos at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenBreathtaking … Paavo Järvi and Leonidas Kavakos at the Royal Albert Hall.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCProms 2026ReviewBBCSO/Järvi/Kavakos review – virtuosic violinist makes fiendishly light work of TchaikovskyRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe intricate concerto was paired with the world premiere of Dani Howard’s likable Concerto for Brass and a lush Scriabin symphony, all admirably led by Paavo JärviClive PagetMon 3 Aug 2026 08.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon will be seeing a lot more of Paavo Järvi when the Estonian conductortakes the reins at the London Philharmonic in 2028. Here, on the podium with the BBC Symphony Orchestra, he proved a model of calm, control and clarity as well as the most sensitive of accompanists, shepherding a breathtaking account of Tchaikovsky’s Violin Concerto by Leonidas Kavakos.The Russian composer struggled for three years to find a soloist brave enough to take on the work’s premiere, yet Kavakos was clearly undaunted. The Greek violinist’s exceptional dexterity and pinpoint intonation at the very top of the range made light of fiendish passagework that has foxed some of the finest. The first movement’s intricate variations were exquisitely decorated, while the intensity of his playing drew spontaneous applause mid-cadenza. Järvi, for his part, was alert to the soloist’s generous rubato, keeping the orchestra in soft-shoed lockstep. As the simple eloquence of the canzonetta gave way to a helter-skelter finale, Kavakos let fly, his bow skimming the strings with unerring accuracy. A Bach encore was dispatched with similar poise and precision.View image in fullscreenPacked an emotional punch … Paavo Järvi conducts the BBC Symphony Orchestra.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCThe Tchaikovsky came hot on the heels of the world premiere of Dani Howard’s Concerto for Brass. Its subtitle, Signal, is a nod to a time when brass instruments were frequently employed as a means of communication. It opened with a buzz of violins and a view hallooing of horns in perfect fifths, the concerto’s signature interval, before the rest of the section joined the hunt. Bright, celebratory and eminently likable, the music shimmered and frothed, its energetic outbursts crowned with fluttering trumpets and underpinned by sonorous bass trombone and tuba.Generally sumptuous, if occasionally turgid, Scriabin’s Second Symphony eschews the harmonic instability of his later works, preferring to plough a lush, late-Romantic furrow. Järvi let it unfold naturally, the internal architecture rendered admirably clear. And yet, where needed, his interpretation packed a brooding emotional punch: the melancholy strivings of the opening movement, for example, or the central enchanted garden episode with its percussive climaxes. The composer himself dismissed the quasi-bombastic finale as “banal”. Perhaps – though Järvi moved heaven and earth to convince us otherwise.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicBBC Symphony OrchestrareviewsShareReuse this content
