title: TV tonight: Strictly’s Amy Dowden and Carlos Gu join Celebrity Hunted | Television | The Guardian
description: The hit survival show returns with a group of famous faces. Plus: Sally Magnusson remembers Mastermind. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The hit survival show returns with a group of famous faces. Plus: Sally Magnusson remembers Mastermind. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Amy Dowden and Carlos Gu on Celebrity Hunted.Photograph: Shine TVView image in fullscreenAmy Dowden and Carlos Gu on Celebrity Hunted.Photograph: Shine TVTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Strictly’s Amy Dowden and Carlos Gu join Celebrity HuntedThe hit survival show returns with a group of famous faces. Plus: Sally Magnusson remembers Mastermind. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Phil HarrisonandPriya ElanMon 3 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCelebrity Hunted9pm, Channel 4They’ve gathered a likable bunch for the seventh series of this survival show. Strictly’s Amy Dowden and Carlos Gu bring the glam, while comedian Brian Conley and and his daughter, Lucy, have an advantage: “Only old people know who I am,” he says. The other runaways are Love Island’s Chris Taylor and Toby Aromolaran, TV presenters JJ Chalmers and Sophie Morgan, property experts Scarlette and Stuart Douglas, and comics Jen Brister and Laura Smyth.Hollie RichardsonBritain’s Strictest Schools – Panorama8pm, BBC OneDetention for looking out of a window? Last month, Devon and Cornwall’s Athena Learning Trust announced it will dissolve and transfer its schools to other organisations after parents complainedabout strict disciplinary measures. Richard Bilton investigates the multi-academy trust and speaks to former teachers and students.HREvolution9pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenChris Packham, with a replica skull of theDorudon atrox, in Evolution.Photograph: BBC Studios/Freddie ClaireHow did we become intelligent? Which was the first animal to “think”? Chris Packham finds out in another mind-blowing evolution lesson by focusing on the super smart dolphin. He rewinds billions of years to light sensitive cells that developed into the first eyes, which would lead to the first brains. Surprisingly, moths get a mention in this quest of cleverness.HRLong Lost Family: Born Without Trace9pm, ITV1The family reunion show’s spin-off series, focused on foundlings, returns. Nicky Campbell and Davina McCall help David, who was abandoned in a London block of flats in 1960, trace his origins to France and the Netherlands. For the week’s other participant, Sarah, the story starts in a Leicester telephone box in 1983.Jack SealeSally Magnusson Remembers … Mastermind9pm, BBC FourFor many, Mastermind will always be synonymous with the urbane Magnus Magnusson. This enjoyable documentary takes a trip down memory lane with his daughter Sally, who recalls the show’s origins, her youthful excitement at its success and how it felt to have strangers yell “I’ve started, so I’ll finish!” at her in the street.Phil HarrisonSecret Lives of Gypsy Wives10pm, Channel 4In the latest instalment of this documentary reality show, we learn a bit more about the marginalisation Trewley faced at school. As she heads to Liverpool to see about potentially launching a lipliner range, will her impostor syndrome get the better of her?Priya ElanExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightReality TVDocumentaryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The August Coup by Robert Service review – the drink-soaked collapse of the Soviet Union | History books | The Guardian
description: This brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully
Author: John Simpson
Headline: This brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully
Content: A soldier in Red Square, Moscow, during the attempted coup in 1991.Photograph: Peter Turnley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA soldier in Red Square, Moscow, during the attempted coup in 1991.Photograph: Peter Turnley/Getty ImagesBook of the dayHistory booksReviewThe August Coup by Robert Service review – the drink-soaked collapse of the Soviet UnionThis brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifullyJohn SimpsonMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarxist-Leninist rule inRussialasted 74 years, and in August 1991 it effectively collapsed in just three days: clear evidence of how hollowed out it had become. In the period that followed, Russia tried parliamentary democracy and unalloyed capitalism, then sank back into autocracy. Now it’s struggling under a wholly unnecessary war against its neighbour and former possession, Ukraine.Why did the system of Lenin, Stalin, Khrushchev and Brezhnev vanish so fast, without a fight? Because that’s how regimes fall in Russia: look at tsarism in 1917. (It almost happened again in June 2023, when the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin’s men marched on Moscow largely unopposed; Vladimir Putin might have gone the way of Nicholas II had he not made some pretty wholesale promises to Prigozhin, then allegedly blown him up two months later.)Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in 1985 with the intention of saving the USSR. Instead, he oversaw its death. He was a charming, decent man but no visionary, and the two medicines he brought to the patient’s bedside,perestroika(restructuring) andglasnost(openness), proved to be wholly ineffective. The brief coup of August 1991 against him, headed by Vladimir Kryuchkov, the boss of the KGB, was the kneejerk response of a bureaucracy that knew things were going wrong but had absolutely no idea what to do about it. It failed quickly, and Gorbachev was back at his desk within days, but the coup had damaged him fatally. Four months later, at the end of 1991, he was bundled out of power by the tough, brutal, boozymuzhik,Boris Yeltsin.Robert Service, author of The August Coup,is the English-speaking world’s foremost historian of 20th-century Russia and Bolshevism. His biographies of the three major Soviet leaders, Lenin, Stalin and Trotsky, are outstanding, even in that crowded field. In writing about the death of the system that these prodigies and monsters helped to create, Service has displayed a remarkable grasp of the vast sources, and a delightfully clear writing style which makes even the complexities of Soviet bureaucracy easy to understand. Compared with his earlier subjects, the story of the coup against Gorbachev and the collapse of the USSR is moderately simple; but Service guides the reader through the chaos of the collapsing system and the machinations of the coup leaders with ease and grace.double quotation markThe acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire dayAfter the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 and the loss of the various Soviet satrapies in eastern and centralEurope, the USSR was falling apart, and Gorbachev, as its president, was shedding power and influence. No one knew how many Soviet republics would break away, and Gorbachev’s plan for running the rump of the union was bitterly contested. Yeltsin was the president of the Russian Republic, the largest, richest and most effective part of the old USSR. The two men were in angry contention. The coup leaders didn’t support either of them: they wanted to go back to a system which would restore as much Soviet power as possible. The assumption at the time was that the KGB had led the coup to protect its own interests, but Service demonstrates that Kryuchkov, the KGB boss, was much more concerned about the overall collapse of the Soviet system. And anyway, many KGB officers refused to join the coup.I was lucky enough to be in Moscow during those extraordinary days. Service captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully. The coup leaders lost their faith in what they were doing almost immediately, and many of them didn’t have much to begin with. They argued, betrayed each other, or were paralysed by fear or torpor. Most of the people involved left some account of what happened, so the records available to Service were particularly rich. He provides us with a graphic description of the fatal press conference that the plotters gave at 5pm on the first day of the coup. The acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire day and his hands were visibly shaking. The press conference was broadcast live on state television, so everyone could see the condition he was in. After that, failure was certain.The basic reason it collapsed, though, was that the plotters didn’t manage to get hold of Yeltsin. It was easy enough to imprison Gorbachev at his palatial residence, Zarya, on the Crimean coast, where he was holidaying with his wife Raisa and their daughter; but Yeltsin remained free, and had use of the Russian republic’s Moscow headquarters, known as the White House. You might expect communist plotters to be good at cutting communications and taking over the media, but no one stopped Yeltsin from phoning allies and friends around Russia and across the world. Nor did they try to prevent him making his famous speech from a tank in front of the White House, condemning the coup and pledging to support democracy. It was a good speech, and the television coverage of it was seen worldwide. Again, no one pulled the plugs. Journalists like me were able to broadcast live throughout the coup. Yeltsin stayed inside the White House, mostly protected by a small crowd of unarmed demonstrators whose numbers dropped as the first night wore on and the rain came down.Yet Yeltsin suffered from the same weaknesses as many of the plotters. In the lobby of the White House I begged to be allowed to go up to his office and interview him, but was told he was too busy speaking to world leaders and organising the opposition. Later, the former Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze arrived to see him. When he came out of the building an hour afterwards, he announced that Yeltsin had told him he would defend Russia’s freedom to the last drop of blood in his body. Stirring stuff. Three years later I reminisced with Shevardnadze about it all. He laughed. “When I got into Yeltsin’s office, he was lying unconscious on the floor with a couple of empty vodka bottles beside him.” But what about him fighting to his last drop of blood? “What do you think would have happened if I’d come out and told you I couldn’t speak to Yeltsin because he was dead drunk?”Such was the chaos and absurdity surrounding the death of the Soviet Union. In the days that followed no one had any idea where authority lay. The famously brave and entrepreneurial cameraman Rory Peck and I marched into KGB headquarters, the Lubyanka, and filmed in Kryuchkov’s own office. After that we even filmed among the ultra-secret KGB files. The next day Rory offered to buy the contents of the Central Museum of the Revolution for a million dollars. Only the fact that the official in charge couldn’t find a bank prepared to accept that much cash stopped the deal going through. We tend to forget the details of this pivotal episode. Perhaps Russia’s troubled history since 1991 has wiped them from our memories. Now Service has brought his magnificent grasp of Soviet history to the task of chronicling the ludicrous way it ended: not with a bang, but with the clink of vodka bottles.John Simpson is the BBC’s world affairs editor. His programme, Unspun World, returns to BBC Two in September. The August Coup: The Destruction of the Soviet Union and the Making of New Russia 1985-1991 by Robert Service is published by Picador (£30). title: Exhibition by Alex Hyde review – an elegiac love letter to the YBA era | Fiction | The Guardian
description: London’s 90s art scene forms the backdrop to this tale of a complex relationship between two artists whose identities become entangled in their creative collaboration
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: London’s 90s art scene forms the backdrop to this tale of a complex relationship between two artists whose identities become entangled in their creative collaboration
Content: Melancholic reflection … Alex Hyde.Photograph: Matthew DyasView image in fullscreenMelancholic reflection … Alex Hyde.Photograph: Matthew DyasFictionReviewExhibition by Alex Hyde review – an elegiac love letter to the YBA eraLondon’s 90s art scene forms the backdrop to this tale of a complex relationship between two artists whose identities become entangled in their creative collaborationKeiran GoddardMon 3 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor all the wrong reasons, Damien Hirst’s Shark (The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living) has a claim to being the most prescient British artwork of the last half-century: a grim parable of neoliberalism. In 1991, it was still possible to mistake the predatory violence of that system for a kind of animal vitality. But today, open-mouthed, dead-eyed and decayed, it speaks only of a regime preserved far beyond its natural lifespan, lauded exclusively by institutions that can profit from its ugliness.Alex Hyde’s second novel, an elegantKünstlerromanwhich plays out during a lightly fictionalised version of the YBA explosion, explores the resonance of that particular cultural inflection point: a moment when the collapse of the postwar cultural settlement, municipal culture and public institutions was transfigured decisively and ubiquitously into individualised, confessional artistic capital.It tells the story of Rabble Stone, a working-class photography student who moves to London and falls into the orbit of a moneyed, cosmopolitan artistic set who are alternately impressed, baffled and alienated by the seriousness of both her manner and her work. Among them is the unnamed artist, now deceased, to whom the novel is primarily addressed through a series of elegiac reminiscences, unpicking their entanglement as friends, muses and occasional antagonists.double quotation markQuestions of self-authorship and plagiarism are handled well enough, but will feel overfamiliar to many readersCentral to this relationship are the ways in which their respective selfhoods become intertwined and distorted via their ongoing artistic collaboration. Rabble begins to photograph the artist, a series of intimate, confrontational portraits that are eventually physically incorporated into the artist’s figurative drawings and paintings. Hyde’s descriptions of the work strongly evoke Tracey Emin, as does its subsequent journey from localised art-world curio to highly valuable, globally exhibited market commodity.Thematically, there is an air of predictability in how this all plays out. Questions of self-authorship, doubling, co-option, plagiarism and the quasi-erotics of display and representation are handled well enough, but will feel overfamiliar to many readers. There are also occasions where the language is imprecise and hesitant in ways that appear to be stylistic lapses rather than stylistic choices. Hyde leans heavily on superposition; needs are “base and noble at the same time”, faces are “ugly and beautiful at the same time”, characters feel “something and nothing at the same time”. And just as frequently, the prose lapses into a hazy self-correction that reads less as an evocation of the unreliability of memory and more as syntactic hesitance.The novel also contains passages of precise and inventive writing. Hyde is especially admirable on a rhythmic level, demonstrating comfort with the staccato and fragmentary as well as the more languid and expansive descriptive work she uses sparingly but to great effect. She writes particularly well and tenderly about bodily exhaustion, both among the working-class communities of Rabble’s youth, and the struggling artists she later encounters in New York, both made brittle by virtue of their position in the economic value chain. Similarly, the character of Duncan, an effervescent aesthete who succumbs to the ravages of addiction, is handled with delicacy, a lightness of touch that captures the horror of chasing ghosts until you finally become one.Also commendable is Hyde’s willingness to grapple with the issue that plagues ekphrastic writing in practically all of its forms. To write about images is to render things that are fundamentally spatial, relational and simultaneous into sentences that are necessarily sequential, disaggregated and hierarchical. The standard way out of this dilemma for a novelist is to focus the description such that it tells us less about the artwork than about the sensibilities and feelings of the character viewing it. In Exhibition, however, Hyde repeatedly goes a step further and engages directly with the theoretical challenge at hand, allowing Rabble to talk at length about composition, the role of the lens, the function of framing; how photographs “are not taken … they are made”.And that Rabble is a photographer, rather than, say, a sculptor or a painter, hints at what appears to me to be the novel’s central philosophical concern; namely remembrance, nostalgia and preservation. It is photographs we turn to, after all, to re-narrativise our lives, to reflect on distances travelled and the alternate turns we might have taken along the way. That feeling of melancholic reflection, of abundant futures concertinaed into the inevitability of the present, suffuses Exhibition and is its primary achievement. For just as Rabble is left mourning lost friends and collaborators, we as readers are left mourning the loss of something larger and more significant, an entire structure of possibility. Exhibition is a eulogy for a world of livable rents, radical art schools, free higher education and opportunities for working-class artists, for a society in which a life like Rabble’s, spent making beautiful things out of the people and places she loved, was not seen as a risible pipe dream or as the gate-kept preserve of the select few.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Pleasingly potboilerish tale of a woman trying to make sense of a traumatic fall that left her comatose slightly loses track of its toxic mind games
Content: Frock horror … This Tempting Madness.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenFrock horror … This Tempting Madness.Photograph: Publicity imageMoviesReviewThis Tempting Madness review – watchable psychological suspense offers Mexican standoff of gaslightingPleasingly potboilerish tale of a woman trying to make sense of a traumatic fall that left her comatose slightly loses track of its toxic mind gamesPhil HoadMon 3 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is fair to say that spending your time doodling ouroboroses and picking open your surgical scar probably indicates you are not in a fantastic frame of mind. These are coping mechanisms for Mia (Simone Ashley) after she wakes up, at the start of this capable psychological thriller, from a coma resulting from falling several storeys of an airport building. A safety net is luckily there to catch her – but she remains in mental freefall. Assaulted by stray fragments of memory, she is unable to say whether husband, Jake (Austin Stowell), who is currently in jail, was the one who pushed her over the parapet.As Mia tries to piece together shattered body and mind, her family, led by solicitous brother Ajay (Suraj Sharma), try to persuade her to cut Jake loose. But she dithers, held back by guilt about how seriously she took his own unravelling, the spiralling paranoia that made him quit his job as a New York actuary and led them to start a new life in Los Angeles. When she finally visits him in jail, is Jake gaslighting her – intent on further manipulation – when he suggests that Ajay is gaslighting her for his own ends by pushing her to break up with him? Or she gaslighting herself by giving him the benefit of the doubt in the first place? This is a Mexican standoff of gaslighting.Pulling this claustrophobic knot satisfyingly tight, director Jennifer E Montgomery occasionally snags a Vertigo-like sense of concertinaed time as she explores Mia and Jake’s troubled past. There’s a kind of mnemonic rapture in the recurring snapshot of her tumbling down the atrium in her tangerine dress, and with the circle motif omnipresent in her drawings and elsewhere, in the suggestiont that this cycle of abuse must be broken.Lurching into the past, or into Mia’s fugue states, every other minute, This Tempting Madness is heavily plot-driven without exactly being scrupulously plotted. It sometimes loses its grip on Mia’s inner state, and what may be prompting a particular spinout at a given moment. Culminating in a jarringly rough ending, it doesn’t quite have an astute enough grasp of these queasy personalities for true Hitchcockian finesse (Ajay, especially, ends up underused). But Montgomery brings visual poise to a pleasingly potboilerish wallow in toxic co-dependency.This Tempting Madness is on digital platforms from 10 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Ribbon Hero review – do-gooder princess battles giant flying earwigs in update of classic yarn | Movies | The Guardian
description: Yûki Igarashi’s adaptation of Osamu Tezuka’s influential manga is a conservative (if impressively animated) reimagining that dulls the source material’s pioneering elements
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Yûki Igarashi’s adaptation of Osamu Tezuka’s influential manga is a conservative (if impressively animated) reimagining that dulls the source material’s pioneering elements
Content: ‘Haute Euro-pageantry placed against striking 2D backdrops’ … The Ribbon Hero.Photograph: ©Twin EngineView image in fullscreen‘Haute Euro-pageantry placed against striking 2D backdrops’ … The Ribbon Hero.Photograph: ©Twin EngineMoviesReviewThe Ribbon Hero review – do-gooder princess battles giant flying earwigs in update of classic yarnYûki Igarashi’s adaptation of Osamu Tezuka’s influential manga is a conservative (if impressively animated) reimagining that dulls the source material’s pioneering elementsPhil HoadMon 3 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst-time director Yûki Igarashi should hit the jackpot here: the first big-screen adaptation for decades of Princess Knight, a seminal postwar manga series from Astro Boy genius Osamu Tezuka. But this very loose reworking is an anticlimax: conservative in solely concentrating on the girlishly feminine side of its protagonist, Sapphire (voiced by Saya), where the gender-flipping original was heralded by many as pioneering; and bland in its vanilla characterisation and dull adherence to battle-anime norms.The owner of the most prominent hair bow since Minnie Mouse, Sapphire is a princess forced into exile when a Nergal – a kind of gargantuan flying earwig – lays waste to her home kingdom of Silverland. Wandering with her lady-in-waiting Zirco (Mayumi Shintani), she takes refuge in neighbouring Goldland and, in need of cash, bags a job working in the mines that supply crystals to placate the Nergal. When another one attacks, she falls into a crystal pool that activates her head ribbon and transforms her into Princess Knight, who is capable of trouncing the interdimensional critters. Local noble Velvet (Seiran Kobayashi), keen to slip free of the Nergal yoke himself, is paying close attention.It’s understandable that Igarashi might want to pay fan service to Tezuka’s more innocent era of entertainment. But surely that should have been manageable while carving out fresh terrain for Princess Knight? Instead he simply serves up a saccharine do-gooder, always bleating about helping other people (something which proves contagious among her forgettable posse). Nor are the contractually obliged sky brawls livened up by a madcap array of special powers showcased in the likes of One Piece or My Hero Academia.The animation can’t be faulted though, encompassing an impressive array of different styles that place haute Euro-pageantry against striking 2D backdrops, along withchibi-style emotional meltdowns, and dumbshow and shadow play interludes among the mayhem. It displays the creative intrepidness in short supply elsewhere; failing to capitalise on Tezuka’s more far-out impulses means this adaptation merely registers as run-of-the-mill girl-power puff.The Ribbon Hero is on Netflix from 8 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmAnimeMangaComics and graphic novelsJapanScience fiction and fantasy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Atlas of Disappearance review – forensic quest for thousands of forgotten victims of the Spanish civil war | Movies | The Guardian
description: Researchers employ technology in a bid to identify and retrieve remains in Spain’s Valley of the Fallen, in Manuel Correa’s emotional documentary
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Researchers employ technology in a bid to identify and retrieve remains in Spain’s Valley of the Fallen, in Manuel Correa’s emotional documentary
Content: Limbo … researchers at work in Atlas of Disappearance.Photograph: True StoryView image in fullscreenLimbo … researchers at work in Atlas of Disappearance.Photograph: True StoryMoviesReviewAtlas of Disappearance review – forensic quest for thousands of forgotten victims of the Spanish civil warResearchers employ technology in a bid to identify and retrieve remains in Spain’s Valley of the Fallen, in Manuel Correa’s emotional documentaryPhuong LeMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerched on the Sierra de Guadarrama mountain range overlooking Madrid is theValle de los Caídos, a colossal memorial site constructed under the Franco regime. Supposedly a symbol of atonement and reconciliation, it has been criticised as an emblem of fascist glorification; it was where Franco was burieduntil his exhumation in 2019. There are, however, tens of thousands more bodies are trapped inside; in the aftermath of the White Terror, the corpses of those executed under the dictatorship were clandestinely removed from mass graves and deposited in the monument’s crypt. Both thought-provoking and heartwrenching, Manuel Correa’s documentary follows three grieving families and their fight to rescue their loved ones from this horrifying limbo.Here, architecture emerges as a means of oppression. Through examining various construction blueprints, the film lays bare how the crypt was specifically designed for maximum inaccessibility. The bodies of the victims were meant to languish, hidden away, in perpetuity, as does the evidence of the dictatorship’s barbarity. To combat these efforts to bury history, Correa founded the Office of Documentary Research, where activists, geographers, and architects wade through the fog of secrecy with state-of-the-art technology.View image in fullscreenRows of numbered niches containing unknown remains.Photograph: True StoryIn their hands, architectural tools are a path to liberation, as activists use forensic devices to counteract governmental delays in exhumation and retrieval. Using digital maps and 3D renderings, the clinical presentation of their work makes for a staggering contrast to the emotional testimonies of the victim’s relatives; both are driven by an unalterable sense of justice. The film ends on the evocative image of water seeping through the crevices of the Valle de los Caídos, causing internal structural damage. Monuments might crumble to the ground, but the memories of the perished will live on forever.Atlas of Disappearance is on True Story from 7 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsSpainForensic scienceFrancisco FrancoArchitectureEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Memory review – a cinematic exorcism through a child’s eye view of terror in the Chechen wars | Movies | The Guardian
description: Vladlena Sandu’s extraordinary portrait of an upbringing during the 1990s Chechen wars blends surreal tableaux with flights of imagination to lament a collective loss of innocence
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Vladlena Sandu’s extraordinary portrait of an upbringing during the 1990s Chechen wars blends surreal tableaux with flights of imagination to lament a collective loss of innocence
Content: Harmful influences … a scene from Memory.View image in fullscreenHarmful influences … a scene from Memory.MoviesReviewMemory review – a cinematic exorcism through a child’s eye view of terror in the Chechen warsVladlena Sandu’s extraordinary portrait of an upbringing during the 1990s Chechen wars blends surreal tableaux with flights of imagination to lament a collective loss of innocencePhuong LeMon 3 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in Feodosia, a Ukrainian city on the Crimean coast, Vladlena Sandu moved to her mother’s home town of Grozny inChechnyawhen she was only six. Blue skies and cerulean waters dominated her childhood, but as the Chechen–Russian conflicts erupted into full-blown wars during the 1990s, she experienced terror, bloodshed, and death. Sandu pours these traumatic memories into her feature debut, a hybrid documentary portrait that doubles as cinematic exorcism, where the demons of the past are transformed into striking collages and vignettes.Across staged tableaux infused with theatrical flourishes and surreal abstraction, reality is superseded by childlike imagination. Adults are largely absent from the frame, although their harmful influences remain. A giant red cake painted with Lenin’s face conjures the ideological education Sandu received at school, while her grandfather, who would chase her with an axe when he was drunk, is represented as a pair of bloodied hands clasping a quivering baby chick. These images – both childlike and mythological – are accompanied by Sandu’s diaristic voiceover. Spoken in present tense, the events of the past acquire a stunning urgency.While the early section of the film blooms with a similar vibrancy toSergei Parajanov’s melancholic reveries, Sandu’s teenage years take on the tones ofAndrei Tarkovsky’s metaphysical contemplations. The childlike capacity of a young girl to navigate her painful circumstances with a sense of wonder has hardened into jaded acceptance. Sandu frames this loss of innocence not merely as an individual tragedy, but a collective one also. We find out that her grandfather, too, had been a child of political oppression; his father, Sandu’s great-grandfather, was sent by the Stalin regime to the gulag. The film’s final images align the gaze of her younger self with those of countless other children, a provocative juxtaposition that foregrounds the invisible casualties of war.Memory is at the ICA, London from 6 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsChechnyaChildrenRussiareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Now You See Me Live review – magic so bombastic it may be visible from space | Stage | The Guardian
description: A quartet of conjurors, calling themselves the Horsemen, perform fine feats of escapology and mentalism that are undermined by smoke, lasers and pomposity
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: A quartet of conjurors, calling themselves the Horsemen, perform fine feats of escapology and mentalism that are undermined by smoke, lasers and pomposity
Content: It could scarcely be more pompous … (left to right) Enzo Weyne, Andrew Basso, Rafferty Coope, Gabriella Lester and Matthew Pomeroy in Now You See Me Live.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenIt could scarcely be more pompous … (left to right) Enzo Weyne, Andrew Basso, Rafferty Coope, Gabriella Lester and Matthew Pomeroy in Now You See Me Live.Photograph: Johan PerssonStageReviewNow You See Me Live review – magic so bombastic it may be visible from spaceLondon ColiseumA quartet of conjurors, calling themselves the Horsemen, perform fine feats of escapology and mentalism that are undermined by smoke, lasers and pomposityBrian LoganMon 3 Aug 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs there an opposite of close-up magic? If there is, it would look a bit like the magic in Now You See Me, which must be visible (and audible) from space. This new spectacle, heading later this year to its spiritual home of Las Vegas, spins off fromthe movie franchise of the same nameand features a quartet of conjurors (identifying, rather awkwardly, as “the Horsemen”) performing feats of escapology, mentalism and even time travel amid much bombasticsonetlumièreand self-promotion.It could scarcely be more pompous – but happily, there are plenty of entertaining tricks to keep pomp-phobes like myself onside. The Italian Andrew Basso has arguably the stoppiest showstoppers, including his recreation of Houdini’s water torture stunt, and another where he extricates himself from padlocked chains while harbouring something very undesirable in his mouth. His French counterpart Enzo Weyne delivers an arresting number with a paper bag and a lightbulb, and there’s a fine audience participation set piece inviting us all to shred, shuffle then – as if by magic! – reassemble the playing cards we were given on the way in to the theatre.Does any of this benefit from the noisy theatrics and inflated self-regard? (For the latter, see MC Matthew Pomeroy’s boast that this show is reversing magic’s historic gender inequalities, despite only one of the show’s seven acts being female.) Far from it – on more than one occasion, the estimable skills on display are undermined by the smoke and lasers, while the self-aggrandising sets expectations that not all these tricks can meet.View image in fullscreenQuickfire cameo … Eden Choi.Photograph: Johan PerssonHow much more impressive would these feats be if staged sparsely? Just ask seven-year-old audience volunteer Elektra, who cited as her favourite act the ex Britain’s Got Talent semi-finalist Eden Choi, whose quickfire cameo, a silent but deadly card manipulation sequence, requires no embellishment. It’s one of several adroit set pieces in a show that proves there’s life yet in the ancient arts of wriggling out of a straitjacket and squeezing oneself into a dynamited safe – even if I found myself wishing pestilence on the four horsemen’s overblown style.AtLondon Coliseum, until 6 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageMagicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online games | Games | The Guardian
description: Online multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or later
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Online multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or later
Content: A sense of mourning spoken and unspoken … Halo 3.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosView image in fullscreenA sense of mourning spoken and unspoken … Halo 3.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosGamesThe end of the world: how players mourn the death of their favourite online gamesOnline multiplayer changed the trajectory of games, but the cost of keeping servers running means every virtual world is doomed to die – sooner or laterNicole CarpenterMon 3 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNevan Hagarty had an idea. If he and otherHalo3 players stayed online the night of 13 January 2022, they could delay the impending server shutdown. Players knew this was coming: it had happened to Halo 2when its Xbox Live servers were turned off in 2010, and a group managed to stay logged into the multiplayer serversfor weeks.And so, players gathered online before the server shutdown to pay homage and to mourn the game they loved so dearly. And, maybe, to keep it online for a little longer. “I must have played ’til about 4am the night of the shutdown, trading stories with so many players about their love of the game and their experiences over the last 15 years,” says Hagarty, 22. “It was a really wholesome experience I won’t forget.”A sense of mourning went both spoken and unspoken. Thirty-year-old fan Jimi hadn’t played Halo 3in a while but logged on to the game on shutdown day to experience the original servers just once more, later posting a video onReddit.“My team was losing really bad,” he says, “I saw a few of the other team’s people standing in the middle, and our guy standing in the middle, and everybody’s just looking at each other. I shot up once in the air, and then everybody just starts going crazy.” Someone threw a shield down, others threw grenades in the air and launched rockets. It looked almost like fireworks. “There were no people on the voice chat. There wasn’t any mutual agreement on this. Everybody just felt it and knew.”View image in fullscreenA person dressed as a character from the game at the UK launch of Halo 3.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianWhen online multiplayer came to video games in the late 90s, it meant that players from across the globe could interact with people they’d never otherwise meet. This changed the trajectory of video games, bringing people together in ways that games hadn’t before – to play, and to mourn, when their virtual worlds are doomed to die.Games go offline all the time, and people have got used to saying goodbye to their favourites. The increasing popularity of online-only live service games means more reliance on servers to host these experiences. And those servers cost money to run and maintain; in the case of recent flopHighguard, developer Wildlight Entertainment couldn’t afford to keep the game online for more than a few months.Over twenty gameshave shut off their servers already in 2026.View image in fullscreenGoing down fighting … Highguard.Photograph: Wildlight Entertainment, Inc.“People really hold on to the idea of place,” says UX and games researcher Evan Conaway, who holds a PhD in anthropology. “That we create community online at all is really remarkable. When you find it and you have it and it’s real, you have an emotional connection to it. Wanting to hold on to it is only human.”Conaway says this happens a lot in the real world, when the corner bar shutters, or a local skatepark is torn down. His research delved into the ways people commemorate online spaces, with a focus on the massively multiplayer online role-playing gameWorld of Warcraft(WoW). People play together on separate servers – or instances – which all run contained copies of WoW, and each server has its own culture created by the community. When the game changes, the culture can change, too. WoW has persisted for decades, and the game is no longer the same as it was when it was released – it’s hardly the same game it was just a few years ago.Though people still have access to WoW, they are often “gradually mourning”, says Conaway. They know that this version of the game is ephemeral. It won’t stay the same – it can’t, by design. In exchange for new content, players must accept that the spaces they inhabit online will find new forms. “The quests are different, the way things are worded is different,” he says. “The way I felt while playing it, and wandering around by myself or exploring the world, all of that is part of this meaning-making for people – just the raw experience of it.”Part of Conaway’s research centred on a group of people who wanted to literally hold on to those memories and meanings. When Blizzard Entertainment was changing its servers in 2011, it auctioned off the old server blades withautographed placardsdisplaying which server they held. It was important for some players, he says, to have a physical representation of that moment in time. He points to one server in particular, Proudmoore, which was an unofficial queer server: “For a gay person or queer person who was playing World of Warcraft at that time on that server, it does feel a little bit like a skatepark brick, like they can take home a piece of a thing.”View image in fullscreenStrength in numbers … characters from World of Warcraft, which has an online community of five million.Photograph: Blizzard EntertainmentWhen World of Warcraftplayers in China were faced with server shutdowns in2023, they were at the mercy of both Blizzard Entertainment and its Chinese partner NetEase.Games in Chinamust be published with a local company, so when Blizzard Entertainment and NetEase had a dispute, it hit the players. Millions lost not just the server but the whole game, and there was no date set for its return. It could have been months, years. Maybe never.Naturally, players wanted to gather in their servers on the day of the shutdown, 24 January 2023, to pay their respects. To do so, people started preparing – and logging in – days in advance, according to City University of Hong Kong PhD student and games researcher HongLan Xu, who joined them to document the last days.“I encountered hundreds of players, but there are millions,” says Xu. “Everybody thought it could be at least several years. They don’t know when the server will be back. It’s profound. It’s real. The shutdown is very real for them, so they gathered in the game to say farewell to their avatars, like it’s the last time.”View image in fullscreenA Chinese gamer plays World of Warcraft at an internet cafe in Beijing in 2024.Photograph: Jade Gao/AFP/Getty ImagesChinese players’ grief was mixed with anger, too, says Xu. Many in the Chinese market felt disrespected, as if Blizzard Entertainment didn’t care about them: “From a Chinese player’s perspective, the main takeaway is sometimes the capitalism of the western gaming companies [leads to] distrust.”WoW opened back up to Chinese players in August 2024. Returning players were glad to have it back, of course, but there was an unease underneath that excitement. This could happen again; they knew what it felt like to lose it all. “Virtual life attachment and this sense of loss is deep, profound,” says Xu. “It can be completely vulnerable and very uncertain.”Losing your forever-game is a uniquely sad experience. Players make a very real investment into these spaces – time, money, friendships, stories, characters, creativity. As one playerput it, “What gets me is that people poured themselves into these games. Not just cash, but actual time, actual friendships built inside them, characters they spent months on. And then one day a studio decides the numbers don’t work any more and everything just disappears.”Explore more on these topicsGamesHaloWorld of WarcraftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 10 of Britain’s best piers for dining, nightlife and good old seaside fun | Beach holidays | The Guardian
description: From Blackpool to Bournemouth, these quintessentially British institutions celebrate a lot more than fish and chips and amusement arcades
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: From Blackpool to Bournemouth, these quintessentially British institutions celebrate a lot more than fish and chips and amusement arcades
Content: Worthing pier, opened in 1862, is fun for foodies.Photograph: Paul Mansfield Photography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWorthing pier, opened in 1862, is fun for foodies.Photograph: Paul Mansfield Photography/Getty ImagesTop 10sBeach holidays10 of Britain’s best piers for dining, nightlife and good old seaside funFrom Blackpool to Bournemouth, these quintessentially British institutions  celebrate a lot more than fish and chips and amusement arcadesRachel DixonMon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerched in our glass-fronted eyrie, 300 metres out to sea, we watch a murmuration of starlings rise and fall and swoop around us. When the show is over, we turn our attention to the food. I have a bespoke vegan menu based on the best early summer ingredients: jersey royals, asparagus, strawberries. My boyfriend orders off the weekly changing à la carte: slow-cooked beef dumplings followed by butter-poached halibut.We are atEbb, a restaurant at the end of the pier in Worthing, West Sussex, which opened in May. Its art-deco design and fine-dining dishes are a far cry from the fish-and-chip shops and ice-cream parlours more commonly found on seaside piers. But traditionalists need not despair: downstairs atPerch on the Pier, fish and chips – as well as tofish (tofu) and chips – are always on the menu, with a knickerbocker glory to round things off in fine retro style.Worthing pier, which opened in 1862, is one of Britain’s surviving 19th-century pleasure piers. “The seaside piers around the coast of Britain stand as a powerful reminder of the achievements of Victorian engineers and entrepreneurs,” says theNational Piers Societywebsite. “However, of the 100 piers that once graced our coastline, only half survive, and several of these face an uncertain future.” The society campaigns to preserve the piers for everyone’s enjoyment, and has saved several that were at risk of demolition.Worthing may well be the foodiest pier in the UK, but they all have their charms. Here are 10 well worth a stroll out to sea.Best for overnight stays:Garth pier, Bangor, GwyneddView image in fullscreenThe Pier Master’s House at Garth Pier, to the right, is now a holiday let.Photograph: Maciej Olszewski/AlamyBangor’s 458-metre (1,500ft) pier stretches out halfway across the Menai Strait, backdropped by the Eryri mountain range (Snowdonia). To coincide with its 130th anniversary this year, the Pier Master’s House at the entrance has been turned into a holiday let (from£140 a night, sleeps six). The pavilion at the far end is now a cafe, and the smaller Victorian kiosks dotted along the pier house independent businesses selling gifts, artworks and local food. There is a programme of weekend events over the summer, from busking and children’s fun days to a dog parade.Best for adventure:Bournemouth pierView image in fullscreenThe world’s first pier-to-shore zip wire .Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Live NewsBournemouth pier (first opened 1856, current structure 1880) boasts the world’s first pier-to-shore zip wire, a 250-metre dual line starting from the end-of-the-pier tower. As well as thePierZip, it hasRockReef, an indoor climbing centre with 28 climbing walls, an aerial obstacle course, a vertical slide, a “leap of faith” and caving tunnels. The pier is the best place to watch Bournemouth’sFriday fireworks(10pm, until 28 August), and there is regular live music at itsKey Westrestaurant (until 28 August). The town’s other pier,Boscombe(opened 1889), is next to free bouldering obstacles and slacklines, and near the beach volleyball courts.Best for traditional seaside fun:Britannia pier, Great YarmouthView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Eye35.pix/AlamyBritannia pier won the coveted 2026Pier of the Yearaward, taking over from last year’s winnerLlandudno, and beating runners-upHerne BayandSwanage. The 250-metre pier was built in 1858, but as with many of the original Victorian piers, it has been damaged, demolished, rebuilt (in 1901), burned down and reconstructed over the years. The current owners bought it in 2022 and have spent £2.2m restoring and upgrading it. Its attractions include a theatre, fun fair, arcades, fish and chip shop, pub and nightclub. Holidaymakers can also visit the town’sWellington pier, further south along the seafront, which opened in 1853 and has a bowling alley, arcade and ice-cream parlour.Best for culture:Penarth pier, GlamorganView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Nigel Wiggins/AlamyWhile Penarth pier dates back to 1894, as a landing jetty for the steamships in the Bristol Channel, its art-deco pavilion wasn’t built until 1929. This former dancehall has recently been restored and is now a cinema and arts centre, with year-round film screenings, art exhibitions, live music, workshops and talks.Coming up this monthis a jazz brunch, a drawing workshop, and a knitting and crocheting social, alongside summer blockbustersThe OdysseyandMinions & Monsters. There is a cafe in the pavilion, and a coffee shop, ice-cream parlour and chippy elsewhere on the pier.Best for exploration:Roker pier, SunderlandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Paul D Hunter/AlamyRoker pier is distinctive for its red-and-white striped granite lighthouse, completed in 1903. After extensive restoration, and closures due to storm damage, pier and lighthouse are now open for guided tours (£14 adults/£10 children, to 27 August). Visitors walk the length of an underground tunnel to reach the lighthouse – the route the keeper used in bad weather – then climb to the top to take in the views. For post-tour refreshments, the pier’s former toilet block is now a gin bar,Tin of Sardines, with brunch and tapas menus served on the terrace in the summer.Best for beauty:Clevedon pier, north SomersetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: PhotoPlus Magazine/Future/Getty ImagesEngland’s only Grade I-listed pier opened in 1869 to receive paddle steamer passengers from Devon and Wales. It is made from discarded wrought iron railway lines shaped into eight arches, nearly 15 metres high. In 1980, during a campaign to save it from demolition, the then poet laureate John Betjeman described it as “the most beautiful pier in England”. “Clevedon without its pier would be like a diamond with a flaw,” he said. The pier was duly saved, and now its Victorian pagoda is a cafe, its toll house is a museum and gift shop, and there is a modern restaurant, the Glass Box. The sea view from the porthole room isstreamed live24/7.Best for nightlife:Royal pier, AberystwythView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Colin Burdett/AlamyThe oldest pier in Wales (1865) was designed by Eugenius Birch, a renowned seaside architect best-known for Brighton’s now-ruined West pier. Today, Royal pier is billed as “the number one destination for competitive socialising in Aberystwyth”, with three bars and a nightclub. There is a host of activities in the Billiard Bar, including shuffleboard, augmented-reality darts, footpool and interactive mini golf; the Upstairs Bar has seven pool tables; and the Inn on the Pier is a restored Victorian boozer, with stained glass and custom tiles. DJs play chill-out tunes in the pier garden over the summer, and the Pressure Nightclub is open until 4am on Fridays and Saturdays.Best for variety: BlackpoolView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesBlackpool is the proud home of three piers:Blackpool North(1863),Blackpool Central(1868) andBlackpool South(1893). The Grade II-listed north pier is the oldest surviving Birch pier, and has an art-deco theatre, a two-tier carousel, bars and an arcade. It was sold in June and is open until at least the end of the year before a promised £10m refurbishment. The central pier has Blackpool’s Big Wheel, a funfair and a show bar with live performances. The south pier has a more high-octane funfair, with a rollercoaster, a freefalling swing and a reverse bungee ride, and is next to Blackpool’s Pleasure Beach for more adrenaline-fuelled fun. Its many food and drink options include the Gin House and a loaded jacket potato stand.Best for history:Gravesend pier, KentView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ian Goodrick/AlamyGravesend’s pier opened on the Thames in 1834, and is the oldest surviving cast-iron pier in the world. It was once a hub for steam packets to London – more than 3 million passengers used it between 1835 and 1842 – and today there are still occasional summer sailings to the capital withUber Boat by Thames Clippers. Just by the entrance to the pier is the ancientThree Dawspub, which was licensed in 1565 as the Three Cornish Choughs and renamed in 1745. This old smugglers’ haunt, which has three underground tunnels, now hosts a summer beer and music festival (7-9 August) and an Oktoberfest (18 September).Best for rainy days:Sandown pier, Isle of WightView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Steve Hawkins/AlamyThe Isle of Wight once had an incredible 11 piers, and four still survive:Ryde(the second-longest in the UK, afterSouthend-on-Seain Essex), Sandown, Totland (for sale) andYarmouth. Sandown (1879) is a particular paradise for families, whatever the weather. There is the Aztec-themed Lost World indoor crazy golf, with lighting and sound effects; the Magic Island indoor adventure play area; and Superbowl 10-pin bowling. The end of the pier has rides such as dodgems and teacups (Easter to September only); there is a cafe, ice-cream kiosk and burger bar; and Scruffy Jacks bar shows live sport.Food was provided by Ebb and Perch on the Pier. title: Rukmini Iyer’s quick and easy Thai-style cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodles – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: Enjoy this big bowl of refreshing noodle soup with turmeric and coconut milk spiked with a kick of chilli
Author: Rukmini Iyer
Headline: Enjoy this big bowl of refreshing noodle soup with turmeric and coconut milk spiked with a kick of chilli
Content: Rukmini Iyer's cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodles.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenRukmini Iyer's cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodles.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.Quick and easyFoodRukmini Iyer’s quick and easy Thai-style cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodles – recipeEnjoy this big bowl of refreshing noodle soup with turmeric and coconut milk spiked with a kick of chilliRukmini IyerMon 3 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is exactly what I want to eat when I’m under the weather: a big bowl of Thai-inspired, soupy noodles with turmeric and coconut milk, all spiked with chilli. It’s a soup base that adapts perfectly for vegetarians (add cubed tofu) or leftovers (shredded roast chicken). This makes alotof broth (hydration is important!), so serve it in your best ramen or soup bowls. The choice of noodles is yours: rice noodles (flat or vermicelli) work well for a gluten-free option, but I inevitably use my favourite straight-to-wok thick udon.Cold lemongrass and coconut prawn noodlesWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appIf you’re using tofu or leftover shredded cooked chicken, add it with the pak choi, so it simmers for four minutes in total.Prep5 minCook15 minChill2 hr+Serves22tbsp neutral oil150g fresh shiitake or chestnut mushrooms1tsp sea salt400ml tin coconut milk150g packthick straight-to-wokudon noodles2 heads pak choi, finely sliced150g prawns, peeled and deveinedFor the base1 lemongrass stalk2 spring onions, trimmed2garlic cloves, peeled1 fat red chilli4cm piece fresh ginger, peeled1cm piece turmeric root, or ½ tsp ground turmericFinely grated zest and juice of 1 lime, plus wedges to serveFinely grate all the base ingredients bar the lime juice; alternatively, roughly chop the lemongrass and spring onions, then put them in a blender with the other base ingredients (again, bar the lime juice) and blitz to a rough paste. (Do not, as I have done in the past, put a whole stick of lemongrass in the blender: the blender will break and you will be sad.)Put the oil in a large saucepan on a medium to low heat, then add the chopped lemongrass-chilli-ginger paste and fry, stirring constantly, for three minutes. Add the mushrooms, fry, still stirring, for a further five minutes, then add the salt, coconut milk and 400ml of just-boiled water. Bring the broth to a boil, then take off the heat and leave to cool. Once cooled, chill for at least two hours. (Alternatively, for a hot version, once the broth is boiling, add the pak choi and simmer for two minutes. Taste the broth, adding salt as needed, then add the noodles and prawns, and simmer for two minutes, until they are cooked through.)Just before you want to eat, bring a pan of salted water to a boil, then drop in the noodles and pak choi. Boil for a minute, then add the prawns and simmer for a further minute until they turn pink and are cooked through. Drain well, then rinse under the cold tap. Arrange the noodles, pak choi and prawns in bowls, then pour the cold broth all over the top. Season with the lime juice and serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodQuick and easySummer food and drinkNoodlesVegetablesThai food and drinkShellfishSeafoodrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Pollock tacos and hake with saffron aïoli and butter beans: Andy Beynon’s summer fish recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Perfect for cooking in the heat, these light, fresh dishes that are bursting with flavour will have you falling hook, line and sinker
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Perfect for cooking in the heat, these light, fresh dishes that are bursting with flavour will have you falling hook, line and sinker
Content: Andy Beynon’s crisp polluck tacos with grilled sweetcorn jalapeno yoghurt and lime pickled cucumberPhotograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenAndy Beynon’s crisp polluck tacos with grilled sweetcorn jalapeno yoghurt and lime pickled cucumberPhotograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodPollock tacos and hake with saffron aïoli and butter beans: Andy Beynon’s summer fish recipesPerfect for cooking in the heat, these light, fresh dishes that are bursting with flavour will have you falling hook, line and sinkerAndy BeynonMon 3 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSummer is my favourite time of year to cook fish. There are so many fantastic seasonal species available and, so long as they’re properly fresh and of good quality, they need very little intervention. I often look for lightness, freshness and acidity to bring balance and lift to a summery fish dish, whether that comes from citrus, herbs or a sharp dressing, because those elements enhance the natural flavour of the fish, rather than masking it. These recipes are ideal for relaxed summer cooking: full of flavour, yet straightforward enough for a midweek meal.Crisp pollock tacos with grilled sweetcorn, jalapeño yoghurt and lime-pickled cucumberWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep15 minPickle20 min+Cook25 minServes4For the lime-pickled cucumber1 cucumber, trimmed, deseeded and thinly slicedJuice of 2 limes1 small handful fresh mint leaves1 tsp sugarSalt and black pepperFor the jalapeño yoghurt1 fresh jalapeño, deseeded (leave the pith and seeds in if you like more heat)1 small handful coriander leaves1 small garlic clove, peeled200g Greek yoghurtJuice of 1 limeFor the sweetcornTwo corn cobs, or 300g fresh kernels1 tsp olive oilFor the pollock75g plain flour1 tsp smoked paprika½ tsp garlic powder500g pollock fillets, cut into finger-width strips1 egg, beaten100g panko breadcrumbsVegetable oil, for fryingTo serve8 small corn tortillas, or flour tortillasShredded red cabbage(optional)Coriander leavesLime wedgesPut the sliced cucumber in a bowl with the lime juice, mint, sugar and ½ tsp salt, toss to combine, then leave to pickle for at least 20 minutes.Blend or finely chop the jalapeño, coriander and garlic, then mix with the yoghurt, lime juice and a pinch of salt, and chill until needed.Brush the sweetcorn with oil, grill until lightly charred, then cut the kernels off the cob and season.Mix the flour, paprika, garlic powder, salt and pepper in a shallow bowl. One by one, dredge the fish strips in the flour mixture, then dip them in the beaten egg and coat with the breadcrumbs.Put 1cm vegetable oil in a deep-sided frying pan on a medium-high heat, then, working in batches, if need be, fry the pollock strips for two to three minutes on each side, until golden, crisp and cooked through. Drain on kitchen paper and keep warm while you cook the rest of the fish.Warm the tortillas for a few seconds on each side in a dry frying pan.To serve, spread a spoonful of jalapeño yoghurt over one side of each tortilla. Top with a little shredded cabbage, if using, then lay the crisp pollock, grilled sweetcorn and drained pickled cucumber on top. Finish with coriander leaves and a squeeze of lime.Roast hake with saffron aïoli and crabby anchovy-roasted garlic butter beans with tarragonWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appView image in fullscreenPrep10 minCook1 hrServes4For the butter beans1garlic bulbOlive oil2400g tins butter beans, drained and lightly rinsed1long red chilli, finely chopped1 handfulfresh coriander leaves4 anchovy fillets, drained and finely chopped100g white crab meat1 tbsp lemon juice1 tbsp chopped fresh tarragon, plus extra to garnishSalt and black pepperFor the aïoli1 pinch saffron threads150g mayonnaise1 garlic clove, peeled and finely grated1 tsp lemon juiceFor the hake4 hake fillets– about 150-180g each1 tbsp olive oilHeat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6. Slice the top off the garlic bulb to expose the flesh inside, drizzle all over with a little oil, then wrap in tinfoil and roast for 40-45 minutes, until soft and caramelised.Meanwhile, soak the saffron in a tablespoon of warm water for five minutes. Once steeped, stir the saffron and its water into the mayonnaise, add the garlic and lemon juice, then season lightly and chill until needed.Put the drained butter beans in a roasting tray with a tablespoon of olive oil, add the finely diced chilli and picked coriander, and toss to combine. Roast alongside the garlic for the last 20 minutes, stirring once halfway, until lightly golden.Squeeze the roast garlic flesh out of the skins, then mash to a paste. Heat a tablespoon of olive oil in a frying pan, then gently fry the anchovies, stirring, for a minute or two, until they dissolve. Stir in the garlic paste, then fold the lot through the hot roast butter beans. Gently mix in the crab meat, lemon juice and tarragon, season to taste and keep warm.At least half an hour before you want to cook it, pat dry the hake and season generously – this will give the salt time to draw out any excess moisture and firm up the fish. Put an ovenproof frying pan on medium-high heat, add the olive oil, then lay in the hake skin side down, turn up the heat to high and leave to caramelise for a minute. Flip over the pieces of fish so they’re now skin side up, then transfer to the oven and roast for five minutes, until just cooked through (the cooking time will depend on the thickness of the fish).Divide the crabby anchovy butter beans between four warmed plates, top each portion with a piece of the roast hake and serve with a generous spoonful of saffron aïoli alongside. Garnish with extra tarragon, if desired.Andy Beynon is chef/owner ofBehind, London E8Explore more on these topicsFoodFishSeafoodShellfishBeans, pulses and legumesMexican food and drinkHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content
